This simile, which makes the meaning known, has been shown by the wise. The Great Nāgas (Arahants) will understand the virtues of the Nāga (the Buddha) taught by the Nāga (the Buddha), [established in their own special qualities].
260:
“Free from lust, free from hatred, free from delusion, free from taints, that Nāga (the Buddha), abandoning the body, being free from taints, will attain Parinibbāna.” — He spoke these verses.

In those verses, ‘mānussabhūtaṃ’ means born among humans, or having attained the state of a human. For the Teacher, although he is liberated from all destinations (gati) through the attainment of the knowledge of the destruction of taints (āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa), he is still called a ‘human’ by virtue of the rebirth taken in his final existence. However, by virtue of his qualities, he is the ‘Atideva’ (God above gods) and ‘Atibrahma’ (Brahma above Brahmas). ‘Sambuddhaṃ’ means one who has realized the truths that should be known by himself. ‘Attadantaṃ’ means self-tamed. The Blessed One is tamed by the noble path produced by himself, with the supreme restraint from the eye... (etc.) ...to the mind. ‘Samāhitaṃ’ means concentrated by the eightfold concentration (samādhi) and the concentration of the Path and Fruition.

‘Iriyamānaṃ brahmapathe’ means one who exists by virtue of entering into the fourfold Brahma-vihāras or the noble Fruition Attainment (phala-samāpatti). Although the Blessed One does not always dwell in the aforementioned Brahma-path, it is said ‘iriyamānaṃ’ (dwelling/moving) because of his ability to dwell there and his inclination towards it. ‘Cittassūpasame rataṃ’ means delighting in Nibbāna, the cessation of all formations (saṅkhāra), which is the cause for the tranquility of the mind.

‘Yaṃ manussā namassanti sabbadhammāna pāragūṃ’ means that wise kings and other humans pay homage to that Fully Enlightened One who has reached the far shore (pāragū) of all dhammas such as the aggregates (khandha) and sense bases (āyatana) in six ways: reaching the far shore of higher knowledge (abhiññā), full understanding (pariññā), abandoning (pahāna), development (bhāvanā), realization (sacchikiriyā), and attainment (samāpatti), thereby reaching supreme perfection. Honoring him with practice according to the Dhamma, they are inclined, leaned, and bent towards the Blessed One in body, speech, and mind. ‘Devāpi taṃ namassanti’ means not only humans, but indeed, gods in immeasurable world systems also pay homage to that Blessed One.

‘Iti me arahato sutaṃ’ shows that “thus I have heard” in the presence of the Blessed One, who is worthy of offerings (Arahat) due to reasons such as being far from defilements, and in the presence of persons such as the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta) who say, “The Teacher of gods and humans,” etc.

‘Sabbasaṃyojanātītaṃ’ means one who has transcended all ten fetters (saṃyojana) along with their latent tendencies (vāsanā) through the four paths as appropriate. ‘Vanā nibbanaṃ āgataṃ’ means one who has come from the forest of defilements to Nibbāna, which is free from that forest. ‘Kါmehi nekkhamma-rataṃ’ means one who has emerged from all sense pleasures and delights in renunciation (nekkhamma) consisting of monkhood, jhāna, vipassanā, etc. ‘Muttaṃ selāva kañcanaṃ’ means like gold that has come out of the rock, having the nature of essence extracted from the non-essential; the connection is that “gods also pay homage to that Blessed One.”
261:
That Nāga (the Buddha) is indeed exceedingly radiant; he certainly does not commit evil (āguṃ) and does not go to a new existence; he is endowed with strength like a Nāga (noble elephant). The Fully Enlightened One, who has received the name ‘Nāga’, is ‘accaruci’ (exceedingly radiant), meaning he shines and is beautiful, surpassing the world with its gods through his physical radiance and the radiance of his wisdom. How? Just as the Himalaya, the king of mountains, surpasses other mountains with its qualities such as being firm, heavy, and having great essence, so he surpasses them—this is the meaning. He surpasses all those named ‘Nāga’, such as serpent-nāgas, elephant-nāgas, and man-nāgas, or the Nāgas who are learners (sekha), non-learners (asekha), and Paccekabuddhas. ‘Saccanāmo’ means he is named Nāga in truth. He himself will explain that truth of being named Nāga with the words “He does no evil,” etc.

Now, wishing to show the Buddha-Nāga by way of his limbs, he first shows him by name, saying, “That Nāga does no evil.” Because he does not commit any evil (āguṃ) or sin at all, he is called ‘Nāga’. ‘Soracca’ means virtue (sīla). ‘Avihiṃsā’ means compassion (karuṇā). Since these two are the precursors of the entire mass of qualities, they are appropriate as the two front feet of the Buddha-Nāga; thus he said, “Those two are the feet of the Nāga.”

Wishing to speak of the back feet, he said, “Mindfulness and clear comprehension are the other (back) feet of that Nāga.” There is also a variant reading ‘tyāpare’. The word division is ‘te apare’. Because faith (saddhā) is the trunk (hand) of this Nāga in taking up blameless dhammas, he is called ‘one with the trunk of faith’. Because the very pure feeling and equanimity (upekkhā) consisting of various types of knowledge are the white tusks of this Nāga, he is called ‘one with the white tusks of equanimity’.

Wisdom (paññā) is the head; the basis of that wisdom is mindfulness; thus he said, “Mindfulness is the neck, wisdom is the head.” ‘Vīmaṃsā’ means the investigation of dhammas. Just as the investigation of an elephant-nāga consists of touching and smelling with its trunk what should or should not be eaten, so the investigation of the Buddha-Nāga is the contemplation of dhammas such as wholesome states. Because they dwell here in harmony, it is called ‘samāvāsa’ (dwelling in harmony); the belly, being the container, is the ‘samāvāsa’. Because it is the basis for higher knowledge and tranquility, the Dhamma known as tranquility (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) dwells in harmony in the belly of this Nāga; thus he is called ‘one with the Dhamma-belly-dwelling’ (dhammakucchisamāvāsa). ‘Viveka’ means the seclusion from the substrata of existence (upadhi-viveka). Because it is the final part of that Buddha-Nāga, seclusion is called the tail.

‘Jhāyī’ means one who habitually meditates by way of object-scrutinizing meditation (ārammaṇūpanijjhāna). ‘Assāsarato’ means delighting in Nibbāna, which is the supreme relief. “Well-concentrated within himself” means...
262:
To show that such composure, being well-concentrated in the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) which is the object, is well-concentrated at all times, it is said: "The elephant, while walking, is composed," and so forth. Indeed, because the Blessed One has abandoned restlessness (uddhacca) along with its latent tendencies (vāsana) and is free from distraction, he is always composed. Therefore, whatever posture he adopts, it should be understood that he adopts that posture only with composure.

"Sabbattha" (everywhere) means having a closed conduct in every sense-object and in every sense-door in every way. Therefore, it is said: "All bodily actions are preceded by knowledge and follow after knowledge," and so forth. "Esā nāgassa sampadā" (This is the elephant's accomplishment) means the accomplishment of the Buddha-elephant, which is full of virtues, as already mentioned or to be mentioned in such phrases as "He does no wrong" and "The Fully Enlightened One."

"Bhuñjati anavajjāni" (He eats blameless things) means that because he has reached the supreme perfection of Right Livelihood (sammā-ājīva), he partakes of alms-food and meals that are not to be censured. Having completely abandoned wrong livelihood along with its latent tendencies, he does not partake of blameworthy or censurable food, but partakes only of blameless food. In partaking thus, the connection is that he eats while avoiding hoarding (sannidhi).

"Saṃyojanaṃ" (Fetter) refers to the ten kinds of fetters capable of causing one to sink in the round of rebirths, because they bind the continuity of beings to the suffering of the round. "Aṇuṃ thūlaṃ" (Small and large) means small and great. "Sabbaṃ chetvāna bandhanaṃ" (Having cut all bonds) means having cut the bond of defilements (kilesa) without remainder through the Path Knowledge (magga-ñāṇa). "Yena yena" (By whichever) means by whichever direction or region.

For example, just as a white lotus born in the water grows in the water but is not smeared by the water due to its nature of being unsmeared, even so, the Buddha, though born in the world and dwelling in the world, is not smeared by the world because of the absence of the smears of craving (taṇhā), wrong view (diṭṭhi), and conceit (māna).

"Gini" means fire. "Anāhāro" means fire without fuel.

"Atthassāyaṃ viññāpanī" (This is an explanation of the meaning) refers to this simile of the elephant which makes clear and reveals the meaning of the object of comparison, which is the virtue of the Teacher. "Viññūhi" (By the wise) refers to those who discern the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths realized by the Teacher, spoken with reference to himself. The phrase "Viññissanti" (They will understand) and so forth is the statement of reason. The meaning is: "Because the Great Elephants, the taintless ones (khīṇāsava), established in their own domain of knowledge, will understand the Great Elephant, the Tathāgata, as taught by me, the Elephant; therefore, I have spoken this simile for the purpose of making it known to other worldlings (puthujjana)."
263:
"Sarīraṃ vijahaṃ nāgo, parinibbissatyanāsavo" means that the Great Elephant, the Fully Enlightened One, who became taintless through the Nibbāna with fuel remaining (saupādisesa-parinibbāna) at the foot of the Bodhi tree, will now, while relinquishing the body and the individual existence, attain parinibbāna through the Nibbāna without fuel remaining (khandha-parinibbāna).

Thus, adorning with fourteen similes, praising the virtues of the Teacher with sixteen verses and sixty-four lines (pādas), he concluded the teaching with the Nibbāna element without fuel remaining (anupādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu).

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Udāyī is finished.

## The Commentary on the Book of Sixteens is finished.
264:
## 16. Vīsatinipāta
## 1. Adhimuttattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

In the Vīsatinipāta, the verse beginning with "Yaññatthaṃ vā" is the verse of another Elder Adhimutta. What is its origin? This Elder had also made a resolution under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merits in various existences. During the time of Atthadassī Buddha, he was born into a wealthy family. Upon reaching maturity, after the Buddha had attained Parinibbāna, he served the Saṅgha and performed great acts of almsgiving. Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans. In this Buddha's era, he was born in the womb of the sister of the venerable Elder Saṅkicca and was given the name Adhimutta. When he came of age, he was ordained under his maternal uncle, the Elder, and practiced Vipassanā. While still in the stage of a novice (sāmaṇera), he attained Arahantship. Regarding this, it is stated in the Apadāna:

"When the Lord of the World, Atthadassī, the Supreme Man, had attained Parinibbāna, I served the Saṅgha of monks with a clear and devout mind.

Having invited the Saṅgha of monks, who were upright and composed, I constructed a pavilion of sugarcane and offered a meal to the supreme Saṅgha.

In whatever state I was born, whether as a deva or a human, I surpassed all beings; this is the fruit of that meritorious deed.

For eighteen hundred aeons, because of the gift I gave then, I have not known a woeful state; this is the fruit of the gift of sugarcane.

I have attained the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā)... and have fulfilled the Buddha's teaching."

Having attained Arahantship, he spent his time in the bliss of meditative attainment (samāpatti). Wishing to receive higher ordination (upasampadā), he thought, "I will ask permission from my mother," and while traveling to his mother's place, he encountered five hundred bandits on the way who were wandering in search of meat to make a sacrificial offering to a deity. The bandits captured him, thinking, "This will be the sacrifice for the deity." Although captured by the bandits, he remained without fear or trembling, standing with a very serene countenance. Seeing him, the bandit leader was filled with wonder and amazement, and wishing to praise him, spoke these verses:
265:
“In the past, we have killed beings either for the purpose of sacrifice or for the sake of wealth. Those beings, while being held by us, became helpless, trembled due to the fear of death, and lamented.

But for you, there is no state of fear; moreover, your complexion becomes even more serene. Why do you not lament in the face of such great danger?” Thus, he spoke two verses.

In those verses, “yaññatthaṃ” means for the purpose of sacrifice or for the purpose of making a sacrificial offering to deities. The word “vā” is used in the sense of an alternative (vikappanattha). “Dhanatthaṃ” means for the purpose of plundering wealth. “Ye hanāma mayaṃ pure” means those beings whom we have killed in the past. Here, the present tense “hanāma” is used in the sense of the past. “Avase” means making them helpless and not under their own control. “Taṃ” refers to those people. Some also read it as “avasesaṃ.” It means excluding that one person among those we captured, the rest; or this itself is the original reading. “Bhayaṃ hoti” means the fear of death arises. Because of that fear of death, they tremble and lament; they tremble with mental terror and lament, saying things such as, “Masters, we will give you such and such wealth, we will become your slaves.”

“Tassa te” means to you, whom we, wishing to deprive of life for the sacrificial offering to the deity, have threatened with raised swords. “Bītattaṃ” means the state of being afraid, or it means fear. “Bhiyyo vaṇṇo pasīdati” means your facial complexion is even more serene than your natural complexion. It is said that at that time, a great joy and happiness (pīti-somanassa) arose in the Elder, thinking, “If these people kill me, I shall now attain Parinibbāna without clinging; the burden of suffering will be gone.” “Evarūpe mahabbhaye” means when such a great fear of death has arrived. Alternatively, this locative case expresses the sense of cause (hetu).

Now, the Elder, wishing to teach the Dhamma by way of giving a reply to the bandit leader, said:

“O leader, there is no mental suffering for one who is without longing. All fears have indeed been transcended for one whose fetters are destroyed.

Because the craving that leads to existence is destroyed, and the Dhamma is seen as it truly is, there is no fear in death, just as in the laying down of a burden.

I have well-lived the holy life, and the path has been well-developed by me. I have no fear of death, just as in the ending of diseases.”
266:
“I have practiced the holy life well, and the path has been well-developed. I have seen the realms of existence, which are devoid of pleasure, as if I had drunk poison and vomited it out.

Without clinging through craving and views, I have reached the other shore of Nibbāna; having performed the task of the path, I am free from taints (āsavas). Like one released from the place of execution, I rejoice at the end of life.

I have reached the supreme nature of Dhamma and have no desire for the whole world. Like one escaped from a burning house, I do not sorrow at death.

Whatever collection of things exists in this world, or whatever existence is obtained, all these formations are without mastery; so the Great Sage has said.

One who knows that truth as taught by the Buddha does not grasp any existence, just as one does not grasp a red-hot iron ball.

I have no thought of ‘it was,’ nor do I have the thought ‘it will be.’ Formations will pass away; what is there to lament in that passing?

O Headman (Gāmaṇī), for one who sees the pure arising of phenomena and the pure succession of formations as they really are, there is no fear.

When one sees the world of formations as equal to grass and wood through wisdom, not finding any sense of ‘mine,’ one does not sorrow, thinking ‘I have nothing.’

I am weary of this body, and I have no desire for existence. This body will break up, and there will be no other new body.

Do whatever you wish with this body. Because of that action, there will be neither anger nor affection in me.” Thus, he spoke these verses.

“Hearing those wonderful and hair-raising words of the Elder Adhimutta, the robbers laid down their weapons and said this.” This verse was spoken by the reciters of the Council (Saṅgītikāras). The following three verses are the dialogue of questions and answers between the robbers and the Elder:
267:
“Venerable sir, by doing what action, or who is your teacher? Relying on whose teaching is this state of fearlessness at the time of death obtained?”

“My teacher is the All-Knowing, the All-Seeing, the Victor (Jina) who has conquered the five Maras. That Teacher is the Great Compassionate One, the Buddha, the Healer of the afflictions of all worldlings.

He has taught this unsurpassed Dhamma that leads to Nibbāna, the end of defilements. Relying on his teaching, this state of fearlessness is obtained.”

Hearing the well-spoken words of the sage, the robbers laid down their weapons and tools. Some of them abstained from robbery, and some requested ordination.

Having ordained in the Sugata’s Dispensation, developing the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅgas) and the five powers (balas), those wise ones with uplifted and joyful minds and restrained faculties reached the unconditioned state of Nibbāna.”

These verses were also spoken by the reciters of the Council (Saṅgītikāras).

In those verses, ‘O Headman, for one without longing, there is no mental suffering’ means that for one like me, who has no longing through craving, there is no mental suffering or distress, just as there is no pus in the nature of blood. By showing the absence of distress, he speaks of the absence of fear. Therefore, he said, ‘All fears have been transcended.’ ‘All fears have been transcended’ means that for an Arahant whose fetters are destroyed, the twenty-five great fears and all other fears are definitely transcended and gone.

‘When the Dhamma is seen as it really is’ means when the Four Noble Truths are seen as they really are through the wisdom of the path, by way of full understanding (pariññā), abandoning (pahāna), realization (sacchikiriyā), and development (bhāvanā). ‘Maraṇe’ means because of the cause of death. ‘Like laying down a burden’ means just as a man sinking under a heavy load on his head does not fear when that load is laid down or removed, so should this simile be understood. This is true; the Blessed One said: ‘The five aggregates are indeed a heavy burden, the person is the carrier of the burden. Taking up the burden of the aggregates is suffering in the world; laying down the burden is happiness.’ ‘Suciṇṇam’ means well-practiced. ‘Brahmacariyam’ refers to the holy life of the Dispensation reached through the three trainings (sikkhā)...
268:
“The five aggregates are indeed burdens,
The person is the carrier of the burden.
Taking up the burden is suffering in the world,
Laying down the burden is happiness.”
Thus it was taught (in the Saṃyutta Nikāya).

'Suciṇṇam' means conduct that is well-practiced. 'Brahmacariyam' means the noble life of the Dispensation, which encompasses the three trainings. Because of such practice, the Noble Eightfold Path, consisting of eight factors, has also been well-developed. 'Rogānamiva saṅkhaye' means just as a patient afflicted by many diseases feels joy and gladness when those diseases are exhausted, similarly, in death, which is the exhaustion of the disease of the aggregates, there is no fear for one like me.

'Nirassādā bhavā diṭṭhā' means I have seen the three realms of existence as being without gratification and devoid of delight, being oppressed by the three types of suffering and scorched by the eleven fires. 'Visaṃ pitvāva chaḍḍitaṃ' means it is as if one had mistakenly drunk poison and then vomited it out; it means I have no fear of death.

'Mutto āghātanā yathā' means just as a person led by thieves to an execution ground to be killed feels joyful and delighted when escaping by some means, similarly, having reached Nibbāna, the far shore of Saṃsāra, I am one who has reached the far shore (pāragū). Being without clinging through the four types of grasping, and having completed the sixteen tasks such as full understanding (pariññā), I am one who has done what was to be done (katakicco). Being free from taints (anāsavo) such as the taint of sensual desire, I am joyful and glad because of the exhaustion of life.

'Uttamaṃ' means the noble or supreme. 'Dhammataṃ' means the nature of phenomena. It refers to the state of being stable (tādi) towards desirable and undesirable objects due to the attainment of Arahantship. 'Sabbaloke' means even in the entire world associated with long life, abundant happiness, and so forth, there is no desire or longing. 'Ādittāva gharā mutto' means just as a person who has escaped from a house burning and blazing on all sides does not grieve over the cause of that escape, similarly, an Arahant whose taints are exhausted does not grieve over the cause of death.

'Yadatthi saṅgataṃ kiñci' means whatever association there is in this world, whether with beings or formations (saṅkhāra). According to the variant reading 'saṅkhataṃ', it means that which is produced by the combination of causes, the dependently arisen (paṭiccasamuppanna). 'Bhavo vā yattha labbhati' means the process of rebirth (upapattibhava) obtained among the groups of beings. 'Sabbaṃ anissaraṃ etaṃ' means all these phenomena are without a master; no one can exercise mastery here saying, "Let it be thus." Thus it was said:
269:
The Great Sage (Mahesi), the Buddha, said: "All phenomena are non-self." Therefore, one who knows "This is without a master" does not grieve at death—this is the connection.

"Does not grasp any existence" means that a noble disciple knows those three realms of existence through the path-wisdom accompanied by insight-wisdom, just as taught by the Blessed One: "All formations are impermanent," etc. Just as a man desiring happiness does not grasp with his hand an iron ball that has been heated all day, similarly, he does not grasp any existence, small or great; he does not produce craving for that existence.

"It does not occur to me: 'I have been'" means that the occurrence of the mind through the view of self, such as "In the past I was such a person," no longer exists for me. This is because the view has been properly uprooted and the nature of phenomena (dhamma-nature) has been well seen. "It does not occur to me: 'I shall be'" means because of seeing the nature of phenomena, the doubt "In the future, how shall I be? What shall I become?" does not occur to me either. "Formations will pass away"—this alone occurs to me: "Only formations are proceeding according to causes; there is no self or anything belonging to a self here. And they will pass away, they will perish, they will break up moment by moment." For one like me who sees thus, what lamentation could there be regarding those formations?

"Suddha" (pure) means mere, unmixed with the essence of a self. "Dhammasamuppāda" (arising of phenomena) means the arising of effects due to causes, the mere proceeding of phenomena like formations due to causes like ignorance. "Saṅkhārasantati" (continuity of formations) means the sequence of formations divided into defilements, kamma, and results (vaṭṭa). "One who sees according to reality" means one who knows according to truth through path-wisdom accompanied by insight.

"Seeing the world as equal to grass and wood" means, for example, when someone takes grass or wood that has no owner in the forest, another person does not think, "This person is taking my property." Similarly, when one sees the world of formations with wisdom as being ownerless, like grass and wood, that noble person, not finding or making any sense of "mine" in that world of formations, says, "It is not mine." He does not grieve, thinking, "Alas, that was I, but now that sense of 'mine' is no more."

"Weary of the body" means being weary of this body which is without essence, which discards happiness, which is painful, ungrateful, and by nature impure, foul-smelling, loathsome, and repulsive. This...
270:
Being weary of this body, I remain thus. "No desire for existence" means having no desire for any form of existence; it is the state of not longing for even a single existence. "This body will break up" means this body of mine will now break up, either through your efforts or the efforts of others, or in another place. "And another body will not arise" means because there is no more rebirth, another body will not arise for me in the future.

"What business do you have with this body?" means if you have any purpose or business with this body, do as you wish, if you so desire. "Because of that, for me (anger or affection does not arise)" means due to the reason of you performing whatever business you wish, regarding this body (anger or affection does not arise in me). "Therein" refers to those who act in such a way and those who do not. "Anger and love will be" means that resentment (paṭigha) and affection (anunaya) will not arise respectively. This is the meaning because all attachment and concern for one's own existence have been entirely abandoned. Even though anger and craving do not exist toward other things for other reasons, the word "therein" is spoken regarding that body by the power of the Dhamma he has attained.

"Of him" refers to the Elder Adhimutta. "That word" refers to hearing the words that demonstrate the absence of fear of death, starting with "There is no mental suffering," which are indeed wonderful and hair-raising. "Young men" (māṇavā) refers to the thieves. Thieves are often called "māṇava," as in the Pali passages such as "they go with the māṇavas (thieves) who have committed deeds and those who have not."

"Venerable sir, having done what?" means "Venerable sir, by practicing what kind of austerity, or who is your teacher, and by relying on whose instruction and advice do you attain this state of fearlessness at the time of death?" They spoke thus by way of inquiry into this meaning.

Hearing the words of those thieves, the Elder, wishing to give them an answer, spoke the words beginning with "Sabbaññū" (The Omniscient One). In those words, "Sabbaññū" means the Omniscient One, because he knows everything in all its aspects—past and so forth—without the instruction of others, having attained the Unobstructed Knowledge (anāvaraṇañāṇa) which arises according to his wish and is capable of penetrating all dhammas. Because he sees everything with that very "All-Seeing Eye" (samantacakkhu), he is called "Sabbadassāvī" (The All-Seer). In whomsoever there is Unobstructed Knowledge, that very knowledge is called Omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa). There is no contradiction with the Pali text on Uncommon Knowledge (asādhāraṇañāṇa). This is because the single knowledge is spoken of in two ways to show its unique nature, which is not shared by others, based on the way the object arises. Everything that should be said regarding this matter should be understood according to the method already explained in detail in the commentary on the Itivuttaka. Therein—
271:
It should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. He is called "Jina" (The Conqueror) because he has conquered the five Maras. He is called "Mahākāruṇika" (The Great Compassionate One) because he directs his mind toward all groups of beings, distinguished by various grades such as low and so forth, and because he is endowed with great compassion. He is called "Satthā" (The Teacher) because he instructs those to be tamed according to their needs regarding the benefits of the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal. Precisely because he is such a teacher, he is called "Sabbalokatikicchaka" (The Physician of the Whole World) because he treats the disease of defilements of the entire world. The connection should be understood as: "The Fully Enlightened Buddha is my teacher." "Khayagāmī" means the Dhamma that leads to Nibbāna.

When the Elder had thus revealed the virtues of the Teacher and the Dispensation, some thieves gained faith and went forth as monks, while others declared themselves lay followers (upāsakas). Wishing to clarify this matter, the Elders who recited the Dhamma (Dhammasaṅgāhakas) spoke the two verses beginning with "Sutvāna corā." In those verses, "Isino" refers to the Elder Adhimutta, called "Isi" (Sage) because he seeks the higher training in virtue and so forth. "Nikkhippa" means having discarded or abandoned. "Satthāni ca āvudhāni ca" refers to weapons such as swords and weapons such as bows and quivers. "Tamhā ca kammā" means abandoning that trade of thievery.

Those thieves, having attained the state of monks in the Dispensation of the Sugata (the Well-Gone One) who is endowed with the beautiful going and so forth, became uplifted in mind, being endowed with the joy characterized by elation attained through special meditation; they reached gladness, had their faculties developed, and by attaining the path of Arahantship, they reached the unconditioned Nibbāna. The Elder Adhimutta, having made the thieves free from anxiety, left them there, went to his mother, asked for her permission, and then returned. He went with them to his preceptor, had them ordained as novices, and then granted them full ordination. Then he taught them the subjects of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna), and before long, they were established in the fruit of Arahantship. Therefore, it is said: "Pabbajitvā...pe... asaṅkhataṃ."

## The Explanation of the Verses of the Elder Adhimutta is Finished.

## 2. Explanation of the Verses of the Elder Pārāpariya

The verse beginning with "Samaṇassa ahu cintā" is the verse of the Venerable Pārāpariya. What is the origin story? This Elder also, having made aspirations under previous Buddhas and accumulating wholesome deeds that are strong conditions for the ending of the cycle of rebirth in various existences, wandered only in happy realms. When this Buddha appeared, he was born as the son of a certain wealthy Brahmin (brāhmaṇamahāsāla) in the city of Sāvatthī.
272:
Having accumulated merit, which is a powerful cause for the cessation of the round of rebirths in various lives, he wandered only in the happy realms. When our Gautama Buddha appeared, he was born as the son of a wealthy Brahmin (Brāhmaṇa Mahāsāla) in the city of Sāvatthī. When he reached maturity, he became known by his clan name, Pārapariya. This Pārapariya mastered the three Vedas and achieved perfection in the Brahmin arts. One day, while the Teacher was delivering a Dhamma discourse, he went to the Jetavana monastery and sat at the edge of the assembly. The Teacher, observing his inclination, preached the Indriyabhāvanā Sutta (M. Ni. 3.453). Upon hearing that Sutta, Pārapariya gained faith and went forth into the monkhood. Having learned that Sutta, he repeatedly reflected on its meaning. The manner in which he reflected will become clear in these verses. While reflecting in this way, the Elder Pārapariya established insight (vipassanā) by way of the sense bases (āyatana) and soon attained Arahantship. Later, wishing to reveal the manner of his reflection, he spoke thus:

To the monk of the Pārapariya clan, who was sitting alone in seclusion and meditating, this thought occurred:

In what sequence, with what practice, and with what conduct should a man fulfill his duty as a monk, so that he may live without harming any living being?

The faculties of men lead both to welfare and to harm. Unguarded faculties lead to harm, while guarded faculties lead to welfare.

One should well-guard the faculties alone. While securing the faculties, one who fulfills his duty as a monk should not harm any living being.

If one does not restrain the eye-faculty as it wanders among forms at will, and does not see the danger, he will certainly not be liberated from suffering.

If one does not restrain the ear-faculty as it wanders among sounds at will, and does not see the danger, he will certainly not be liberated from suffering.

If one indulges in odors without seeing the way to escape from them, being obsessed with those odors, he will not be liberated from suffering.

One who constantly remembers sour, very sweet, and very bitter tastes, and is greedy with craving for tastes, does not understand his own heart (which seeks the end of suffering).
273:
One who constantly reflects on beautiful and pleasant tangible objects and is infatuated with lust, experiences various kinds of suffering rooted in lust.

If a person is unable to guard his mind from these things, then suffering caused by these five sense objects follows him.

This body is full of pus and blood, and it is full of many impurities. It is beautiful only on the outside, like a decorated casket made by a skilled person.

Just as one who licks a razor smeared with honey does not realize the danger, so people do not realize the suffering that is bitter but pleasant and associated with affection.

One who is intensely attached to the form of a woman, the voice of a woman, the touch of a woman, and the scent of a woman, experiences various kinds of suffering.

All the streams of feminine objects flow into the five sense doors. An energetic person is able to block and restrain those streams.

Only such a person is one who has attained his goal, who stands in the Dhamma, who is skilled, and who is discerning. Even while enjoying himself, he should perform only those tasks associated with the Dhamma and his welfare.

One should avoid sinking into useless matters. A discerning and heedful person should avoid such useless work, not regarding it as a duty.

Whatever task is associated with welfare and whatever delight is found in the Dhamma, one should undertake and practice that. For that delight is indeed the supreme delight.

Through various means, great and small, one covets the property of others. By killing, harming, or causing grief to others, one commits robbery and violence.

Just as a strong carpenter drives out an old peg with a new peg, so a skilled person removes the unwholesome faculties by means of the faculties of insight (vipassanā).
274:
"Developing faith, energy, concentration, mindfulness, and wisdom, and having slain the five (defilements) with the five (faculties), the brahmin (arahant), free from suffering, goes (to Nibbāna). He is one who has attained the goal, one who stands in the Dhamma; having followed the Buddha's instructions completely and entirely, that man attains happiness." He spoke these verses.

In those verses, "samaṇassa" means of the one who has gone forth (the monk). "Ahu" means was. "Cintā" means reflection on the Dhamma, investigation of the Dhamma. "Pārāpariyassa" means of the one belonging to the Pārāpariya lineage; they also read it as "Pārācariyassa." "Bhikkhuno" means of the one who is habituated to seeing danger in the cycle of births (saṃsāra). "Ekakassa" means of the one who is alone, without a companion; by this, he shows physical seclusion (kāyaviveka). "Pavivittassa" means of the one who has initiated seclusion by suppressing defilements through the cause of seclusion; by this, he shows mental seclusion (cittaviveka). Therefore, he said "jhāyino." "Jhāyino" means of the one who is habituated to meditation, of the one who is devoted to wise reflection (yoniso manasikāra). The Elder says all this by treating himself as if he were another.

He shows that reflection with the words beginning with "Kimānupubbaṃ." There, in the first verse, "kimānupubbaṃ" means the sequence or order. What is the order in the practices and conducts that are to be mentioned? In what order should they be practiced? This is the meaning. "Puriso kiṃ vataṃ kiṃ samācāraṃ" means: what kind of virtue and conduct, called "vata" because it is to be undertaken, should a man desiring benefit practice so that he may be a doer of his own duty and not harass or harm any being? One's own duty is the practice of a monk (samaṇadhamma), which in brief is virtue, concentration, and wisdom. For one who fulfills those qualities, there is not even a hint of harming others. If there were such harming, the very state of being a monk would no longer exist.

As the Blessed One said: "He is not one gone forth who strikes another; he is not a monk who harasses another" (Dhp. 184). Here, by the word "vata," the virtue of avoidance (vāritta-sīla) is taken. By the word "samācāra," because it is to be well-practiced, jhana, insight (vipassanā), etc., are taken along with the virtue of performance (cāritta-sīla). Therefore, the virtue of avoidance is primary. Even so, since all virtue is well-protected and well-guarded when the restraint of the faculties (indriya-saṃvara) is accomplished, he wishes to show the restraint of the faculties first, [showing] the disadvantages and advantages in not guarding and guarding the faculties.
275:
Desiring to clarify the disadvantages and advantages, he spoke the words beginning with "Indriyāni manussānaṃ." In that text, "indriyāni" is an indication of the things to be guarded; therefore, it is said that they are the six faculties, such as the eye. "Manussānaṃ" is an indication of the persons suitable for guarding. "Hitāya" means for the sake of benefit. "Ahitāya" means for the sake of non-benefit. "Honti" is the remaining word (to complete the sentence). But how do those very same [faculties] lead to both benefit and non-benefit? He said "rakkhitāni," etc.

The meaning is: for a person whose faculties, such as the eye, are not closed with the door-panel of mindfulness, they lead to non-benefit because they serve as doors for the occurrence of evil states such as greed (abhijjhā) regarding forms and so on. When they are closed, they lead to benefit because of the absence of those [evil states].

Because the restraint of the faculties, when perfected, fulfills the perfection of virtue; the perfection of virtue fulfills the perfection of concentration; the perfection of concentration fulfills the perfection of wisdom; therefore, showing that the guarding of the faculties is the very root of the practice for one's own benefit, he said "Indriyāneva sārakkhanti." One who guards well with the protection preceded by mindfulness, first guarding the faculties well through wise reflection, acts as if closing those [faculties] so that the thieves of unwholesome states cannot enter through those various doors and plunder the goods of wholesome states in the mental continuity. In the word "sārakkhanti," the sound "saṃ" is changed to "sā," as in words like "sārāgo." There is also a variant reading "saṃrakkhanti." The phrase "indriyāni ca gopayanti" is a synonym for that "sārakkhanti"; the purpose of using synonyms should be understood according to the method stated in the Netti Commentary.

"Attano kiccakarīssa"—by this text, he shows the practice for one's own benefit. "Na ca kañci viheṭhaye"—by this text, he shows the practice for the benefit of others. Or, by both, he shows only the practice for one's own benefit, because not harming others is also a practice for one's own benefit. Or else, by both phrases, he shows the practice for one's own benefit, because for a worldling (puthujjana) and a trainee (sekha), the practice for the benefit of others is also a practice for one's own benefit.

Having thus briefly shown the side of purification (vodāna) [by saying] that guarded faculties lead to benefit, he spoke the words beginning with "Cakkhundriyaṃ ce" to show the side of defilement (saṃkilesa) by analyzing how unguarded faculties lead to non-benefit. In that text, "cakkhundriyaṃ ce rūpesu gacchantantṃ anivārayaṃ anādīnavadassāvī" means: if a person does not restrain the eye faculty as it goes towards visible forms—pleasant or unpleasant, of various kinds such as blue or yellow—and as it occurs according to its liking, and if he is not one who sees the danger in such occurrence, he does not see the fault or danger in the present life and in the future. There is also a reading "gacchantantṃ anivārayaṃ anissaraṇadassāvī." There, if a monk stays in "merely seeing" through the arrangement called "it will be merely the seen," and directs that "merely seeing" towards the form by the power of mindfulness and clear comprehension, then seeing that form is called seeing the escape from the cycle of births.
276:
There is also a reading: "One who does not see the escape should restrain the (faculty) that goes (towards objects)." In that context, one who stays in just the seen, in the manner stated as "In the seen, there will be only the seen" (S. iv. 95), and who proceeds in the base of visible forms by the power of mindfulness and clear comprehension, is called "one who sees the escape" in that visible form base. By the opposite of what has been stated, one should be understood as "one who does not see the escape." "He is not released from suffering" means that such a person is indeed not released from the suffering of the round of rebirths. Here, "non-restraint of the eye-faculty" means acting in such a way that unwholesome states like covetousness and so on can flow in through that eye-door. In essence, this should be understood as the non-arising (non-exertion) of mindfulness and clear comprehension. The same method applies to the remaining faculties.

"Adhimucchito" means reaching a state of confusion through clinging craving. "Ambilaṃ" refers to the sour taste. "Madhuraggaṃ" refers to a mass of sweet taste. Likewise, "tittakaggaṃ" (a mass of bitter taste). "Anussaraṃ" means repeatedly thinking about various tastes by the power of enjoyment. "Ganthito" means being tied to various tastes by craving for tastes. They also read it as "gadhito," which means having reached the state of greed. "Does not know the application of mind" means not knowing or not noting the mind that arose at the moment of renunciation, such as "I will make an end of suffering." Because of being greedy for the pleasant craving for tastes, one does not know, does not understand, and does not practice the blameless dhammas within the heart of the Sasana.

"Subhāni" means beautiful things. "Appaṭikူlāni" means delightful and desirable objects. "Phoṭṭhabbāni" means touches (contacts) classified as clung-to (upādiṇṇa) and not-clung-to (anupādiṇṇa). "Ratto" means being lustful through passion (rāga) which has the nature of attachment. "Rāgādhikaraṇaṃ" means because of the cause of passion. "Experiences various sufferings" means obtaining various kinds of suffering in the present life by the power of the fever of passion, etc., and in the future life by the power of the burning of hell, etc.

"Manaṃ cetehi" refers to the mind-door and by these various mental objects such as visible forms, etc. "Naṃ" refers to that person. "Sabbehi" means by all five objects. This is what is meant: If a person cannot protect or guard the mind-door from the five things such as visible forms already mentioned and from the variety of mental objects, by restraining the evil kamma that tends to arise therein, then because of that lack of protection, the suffering rooted in that cause follows that person. In following, it follows by means of all things that are object-conditions, including the five objects like visible forms together with the sixth object. In this matter, because the eye-faculty and the ear-faculty have the nature of taking objects that have not yet reached them...
277:
The statement 'Restrain the one that goes' is said [referring to the eye and ear faculties which take objects not yet reached]. The other faculties are said to 'partake in scents, etc.' because they take objects that have already reached them. Even in saying so, craving for taste (rasataṇhā) and craving for tangibles (phoṭṭhabbataṇhā) are particularly strong for beings; therefore, it should be noted that it is said, 'one who is greedy for the craving for taste, one who repeatedly recollects tangibles.' Having thus shown the suffering that arises due to non-restraint in the six objects through the six doors for a person who does not guard the doors, and because this non-restraint occurs due to not penetrating the nature of the body, [the Teacher] spoke the two verses beginning with 'Pubbalohitasampuṇṇaṃ.' The meaning of those verses is: This body is filled with pus and blood; it is also filled with many other foul things such as bile and phlegm. This body is made beautiful and smooth by a skilled craftsman among men, decorated as if with lacquerwork, etc. [like a casket]. Inside, however, it is filled with impurities such as excrement and is delightful only on the surface of the skin, deluding the foolish. It is bitter because of its nature of suffering and because it causes torment through sufferings such as hell. It has a sweet enjoyment because it is perceived as delightful through baseless imagination. Because of that enjoyment, it is bound to affection. It is painful because it is difficult to endure and is unpleasant. The multitude of people who do not know that they will experience great suffering through greed for enjoyment in such a body should be seen like a man greedy for sweetness who licks the edge of a razor.

Now, the objects of the eye, etc., such as visible forms, have been mentioned; these objects are especially desirable to a man when they are connected with a woman. Therefore, wishing to show that restraint should be practiced regarding those feminine objects, [the Teacher] spoke the words beginning with 'Itthirūpe.' In that context, 'Itthirūpe' refers to the color known as the base of visible forms (rūpāyatana) produced by the four causes of a woman. Alternatively, any color connected to the body, such as the ornaments worn by a woman, or scents, cosmetics, or worn garlands, which serves as an object for a man's eye-consciousness—all this should be known simply as 'feminine form.' 'Itthisare' refers to the sounds of a woman's singing, talking, laughing, and crying. Alternatively, the sounds of clothes and ornaments worn by a woman, and the sounds of flutes, lutes, conchs, and drums produced by a woman's effort, should also be understood as being included here under the term 'feminine voice.' All such sounds pull at a man's heart. 'Itthirase' is stated in the Pali according to the base of taste (rasāyatana) produced by the four causes. Some teachers speak of 'the taste of responsiveness' (assavarasa) such as 'What shall I do?' and 'the taste of use' (paribhogarasa). The taste of betel, etc., applied to a woman's lips, and the taste of rice, etc., given by that woman—all this should also be known simply as 'feminine taste.' Regarding tangibles...
278:
Some teachers speak of the taste of use (paribhoga-rasa) and the taste of woman (itthi-rasa). In fact, the taste of saliva (from betel, etc.) smeared on a woman's lips, and the taste of gruel, rice, and so on given by that woman to a man—all this should be understood simply as 'the taste of woman' (itthi-rasa). Regarding touch (phoṭṭhabba), the touch of a woman's body and the touch of clothes, ornaments, flowers, and so on worn on a woman's body should be understood simply as 'the touch of woman' (itthi-phoṭṭhabba). Here, in the Pali text 'itthi-rūpe itthi-sare' (in the forms of women, in the sounds of women), it should be noted that the taste of woman is also included by the word 'api'.

'Itthi-gandhesu' (in the scents of women) refers to the scent-bases of a woman arising from four causes. The natural body odor of a woman is indeed a foul smell. Some women have the smell of a horse, some the smell of a sheep, some the smell of sweat, and some the smell of blood. Even though the smell is foul, those who are extremely foolish are nonetheless infatuated with those women. However, from the body of the Queen-treasure of a Cakkavatti (Universal Monarch), the scent of sandalwood wafts, and from her mouth, the scent of a lotus wafts. Since this kind of scent does not occur in all women, the external scents such as perfumes applied to a woman's body should also be understood as 'the scent of woman' (itthi-gandha).

'Sāratta' means being well-infatuated, attached, or intoxicated. This term should also be applied to 'itthi-rūpe' and the others. 'Vividhaṃ vindate dukkhaṃ' (experiences various sufferings) means that due to attachment to a woman's form and so on, one obtains various kinds of suffering, such as being killed or bound in the present life, and being subjected to the fivefold bonds and so on in the future life.

'Itthi-sotāni sabbāni' (all the streams of women) means that the five streams of craving flow without exception toward the five sense objects of a woman, such as her form. 'Pañcasu' (in the five) refers to the five sense-doors of a man. 'Tesaṃ' (of those) refers to those five streams of craving. 'Āvaraṇaṃ' (obstruction) means restraint (saṃvara). One who is able to maintain restraint by establishing mindfulness and clear comprehension (sati-sampajañña) so that non-restraint (asaṃvara) does not arise is called energetic (vīriyavā/āraddhavīriya), striving for the abandonment of unwholesome states and the attainment of wholesome states.

Having thus shown the practice of a monk regarding sense objects such as forms, the Buddha now spoke the words beginning with 'So atthavā' to show the practice of laypeople. Therein, 'So atthavā, so dhammaṭṭho, so dakkho, so vicakkhaṇo' means that such a person in this world is one who possesses wisdom, stands in the Dhamma, is clever in the Dhamma, is skillful in the Dhamma, or is one who is diligent and skillful in duties to be performed. 'Kareyya ramamānopi, kiccaṃ dhammatthasaṃhitaṃ' means that even while delighting in home life, one should perform various duties that are not devoid of Dhamma and welfare. One should bring about wealth not yet arisen, protect and use wealth already arisen. One should pursue the three goals of life (tivaggattha) without conflict with one another and without oppressing others.
279:
This is the meaning. This method is spoken in terms of persons like King Bimbisāra and others, who live according to the three goals of life (tivaggattha) without contradicting right practice. It should be understood that it is not spoken in terms of just any random person.

'Attho sīdati saññuttaṃ' means if it is a matter established by grasping the present welfare accompanied by refinement in this world (then it should be done). 'Vajje kiccaṃ niratthakaṃ' means one should abandon a useless task that is devoid of future benefit and unconnected to welfare. Thinking 'that is not a task (to be done)', 'appamatto vicakkhaṇo'—a wise person who is diligent through the non-absence of mindfulness and skillful due to the presence of investigative wisdom—should avoid that task, thinking 'I should not perform this task connected to harm'.

Having thus avoided it, 'Yañca atthena saññuttaṃ, yā ca dhammagatā rati. Taṃ samādāya vattetha' means whatever is connected to welfare and benefit, categorized as present and future, and brings about both types of benefit, and whatever delight there is in the higher wholesome Dhamma accompanied by tranquility and insight (samatha and vipassanā)—one should practice by properly taking up and grasping both of these. In accordance with the saying, 'The delight in Dhamma conquers all delights' (Dhp. 354), that delight in Dhamma is indeed called the supreme delight because it leads certainly to the ultimate goal.

As for the task connected to sensual delight (kāma-rati) which was called a useless task, the words beginning with 'Uccāvacehi' were spoken to show its nature of being connected to harm. In that text, 'Uccāvacehi' means by means of both great and small. 'Upāyehi' means by various methods. 'Paresamabhijigīsati' means one desires to take what belongs to others, or causes others to lose in every way, or conquers others by killing, striking, and causing grief, and then plunders what belongs to others by force. This is what is meant: a person who, for the sake of sensual pleasure, kills, causes to be killed, and causes grief to others, striving to take others' property by various means such as house-breaking, highway robbery, and violent theft, acts with force, plunders, and desires others' wealth, causing them loss—that task of his, based on sensual delight, is entirely base because it is connected to harm. By this, the Buddha illustrates the absolute supremacy of the delight in Dhamma as the opposite of that sensual delight.

Now, to clarify the restraint of the senses, which was mentioned as 'one who is able to restrain them', along with the means, the Buddha spoke the verse beginning with 'Tacchanto āṇiyā—'.
280:
“Just as a strong woodworker removes a peg within wood with another strong peg, even so, a skilled monk, wishing to remove the sense faculties such as the eye with the power of insight, removes them with the faculties themselves,” he said.

If it is asked, “By which factors does he remove them?” he said, “Faith,” and so forth. The meaning of that passage is: developing and increasing these five faculties that ripen liberation—namely, faith (saddhā) characterized by determination (adhimokkha), energy (vīriya) characterized by exertion (paggaha), concentration (samādhi) characterized by non-distraction (avikkhepa), mindfulness (sati) characterized by presence (upaṭṭhāna), and wisdom (paññā) characterized by vision (dassana). By means of these five faculties, he destroys the five sense faculties such as the eye by abolishing their state as doorways for the arising of defilements like lust and aversion. Having cut off the defilements that depend on those faculties through the Noble Path, the Arahant (Brahmin), being thus free from suffering and pain, reaches only the Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna).

“So atthavā” means that the aforementioned Arahant is called “one who has the benefit” (atthavā) because he is endowed with the supreme benefit. He is called “one established in Dhamma” (dhammaṭṭha) because he is established in the Dhamma that leads to the fruit of Arahantship. He abides by practicing according to the instruction, having followed the teaching which is the word of the Blessed Buddha entirely and without remainder. Because he thus abides, that supreme man increases the bliss of Nibbāna.

In this way, because the Elder revealed his practice by way of clarifying his own thoughts, this very verse should be understood as his declaration of final knowledge (aññābyākaraṇa).

## The Commentary on the Verses of Pārāpariya Thera is Finished.

## 3. Telakānittheragāthāvaṇṇanā

The verse beginning with “Cirarattaṃ vatātāpī” is that of the Venerable Telakāni Thera. What is its origin? This Elder had also performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and had accumulated wholesome roots that serve as a support for liberation from the cycle of rebirth in various existences. In this Buddha-dispensation, even before the birth of the Teacher, he was born into a certain Brahmin family in Sāvatthī and received the name Telakāni. When he reached maturity, being endowed with sufficient supporting conditions, he became disgusted with sensual pleasures, abandoned the household life, and ordained as a wandering ascetic (paribbājaka). Having an inclination toward liberation from the cycle of rebirth, he wondered, “Who in this world has reached the other shore?” and so forth...
281:
While wandering in search of liberation (vimokkha), he approached various ascetics and Brahmins and asked them questions, but they were unable to provide satisfactory answers. Because of them, he wandered about with an unsatisfied mind. Then, when our Blessed One had appeared in the world and was working for the benefit of the world by setting in motion the Noble Wheel of Dhamma, one day he approached the Teacher, heard the Dhamma, gained faith, and ordained. While applying himself to the practice of insight (vipassanā), he soon established himself in Arahantship. One day, while sitting with other monks, he reflected on the special attainment he had reached and, recollecting his practice accordingly, he spoke to the monks to inform them of it all:

“Oh, for a long time I have been searching repeatedly for liberation, contemplating the Dhamma, and questioning ascetics and Brahmins, yet I did not find the peace of mind (the Noble Dhamma).

“Who in this world has reached the other shore of Nibbāna? Who has reached the path of liberation that enters Nibbāna? Whose Dhamma, which understands the ultimate truth without distortion, shall I accept and practice?

“Like a fish that has swallowed a hook which is like bait, or like the Asura Vepacitti bound by the snare of Sakka, the king of gods, I have fallen into the inner crookedness of wrong views.

“That bond of defilements pulls me; I am not yet free from this sorrow and lamentation. Who in this world will cut my bonds and proclaim the path of liberation?

“Which ascetic or Brahmin shall I ask, who can show the perishable nature of things and the way to liberation? Whose Dhamma, which removes aging and death, shall I accept and practice?

“Bound by the knot of doubt and uncertainty, joined with the power of intense rivalry, fallen into anger and stubbornness, and torn by the craving of greed;

“Look at the fierce arrow (of wrong view) arising from the bow of craving, which has thirty forms and is born in the heart, standing there having pierced the mind.

“As long as wrong view is not removed, other views cannot be abandoned. Pierced by that arrow and burning with wrong thoughts, I tremble like a leaf shaken by the wind that has fallen from its branch.

“Arising within me, this body of mine which I cherish, having the six sense-contacts as its cause, is constantly burning with the fire of craving; in that very body, craving arises at all times.”
282: I see no one who can heal this arrow of wrong view; no one (other than the Buddha) can pull out this arrow which is to be doubted for its removal by other weapons or mantras. Who can pull out this arrow of defilements that dwells within without weapon or wound, yet oppresses my whole body? May that Noble One, who possesses the Dhamma and expels the poison of defilements, show me the hand and the dry land of relief as I fall into the deep ocean of saṃsāra. I am submerged, head and all, in the lake of saṃsāra, where the mire of lust is hard to extract, and where deceit, envy, rivalry, sloth, and torpor spread. The currents of wrong thought, rooted in lust, carry away the one of evil views, with the thunder of restlessness and the clouds of fetters. The currents of craving flow everywhere; the creeper of craving springs up and stands. Who can block those currents? Who can cut that creeper? Venerable Sir, please build a bridge to well restrain the currents of craving. Let not the current of craving born in your mind suddenly destroy me like a tree. To me, thus fearful and seeking escape from the suffering of saṃsāra, there is the Buddha, the refuge, who possesses the weapon of wisdom and is frequented by the assembly of Noble Ones. He gave a ladder—well-gone, pure, made of the essence of Dhamma, and firm—to me who was being swept away in the flood, and said, 'Do not fear!' Ascending the palace of the foundations of mindfulness, I contemplate this body which I previously regarded as a being delighting in the existing group (sakkāya). When I saw the Path, which is like boarding a boat, I then saw the supreme harbor without clinging to self. To abandon the sting of craving that arises within oneself and is produced by craving for existence, he taught the supreme Path so that those cravings may not arise again.
283: 'The Buddha, who washes away the poison-like defilements, has removed my bond which had been latent for a long time and established for a long duration.' He spoke these verses. In that verse, 'cira-rattaṃ vata' means 'it has indeed been a long time.' 'Ātāpī' means one who is energetic, possessing the effort exerted in seeking the Dhamma of liberation. 'Dhammaṃ anuvicintayaṃ' means repeatedly reflecting on and searching for the Dhamma of liberation, thinking, 'What is the nature of the Dhamma of liberation? How can it be attained?' 'Samaṃ cittassa nālatthaṃ, pucchaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇe' means that although he asked various sectarian ascetics and brahmins about the Dhamma of liberation, he did not obtain or reach the Noble Dhamma which is the cause of peace for the naturally unpeaceful mind and the escape from the suffering of the round. The passage beginning with 'Ko so pārangato' shows the manner of questioning. In that Pali, 'Ko so pārangato loke' means 'Among the ascetics and brahmins in this world who claim to be teachers, who is the one who has reached Nibbāna, the further shore of saṃsāra?' 'Ko patto amatogadhaṃ' means 'Who has attained the path of liberation that stands in Nibbāna?' 'Kassa dhammaṃ paṭicchāmi' means 'Whose teaching of an ascetic or brahmin shall I accept and practice?' 'Paramattha-vijānanaṃ' means knowing the ultimate meaning, referring to one who can teach the non-perverted arising and ceasing. 'Anto-vaṅka-gato āsi': because of the crookedness of mind, wrong view is called 'vaṅka' (crooked). Or all defilements are called 'vaṅka'. 'Anto' means inside the one with a crooked heart. Or it means the crookedness of defilements that occurred within the heart. 'Maccho va ghasamāmisaṃ' means like a fish eating bait, like a fish that has swallowed a hook. 'Baddho mahindapāsena vepacittyasuro yathā' means just as the Asura king Vepacitti, bound by the snare of Sakka (Mahinda), could not live as he wished and reached great suffering, similarly, I was previously bound by the snare of defilements, unable to live as I wished and reached suffering. 'Añchāmi' means 'I pull.' 'Naṃ' refers to the snare of defilements. 'Na munjāmi' means 'I do not let go.' 'Asmā sokaparidevā' means 'from this round called sorrow and lamentation.' The meaning is: just as a deer or a pig bound by a snare, not knowing the way to escape, struggles and pulls that snare, making the bond even tighter, so I...
284:
Formerly, being bound by the snare of defilements (kilesa), not knowing the means of liberation, and trembling through the power of bodily volition (kāyasañcetanā) and so forth, I could not escape from those defilements. On the contrary, making those defilements firm, I reached even greater defilements through sorrow and so forth. 

In the phrase "Who in this world will release my bonds and make me known to Enlightenment (sambodhi)?", the meaning is: Who in this world, while releasing me from this bond of defilements, will announce (show) to me the path of liberation (vimokkhamagga) named "Enlightenment" because one awakens by this [path]? Some also read it as "bandhamuñcaṃ"; it is construed as Enlightenment which releases from bonds or the releaser of bonds.

Ādisanta means teaching. Pabhaṅguna means the destruction of defilements, or teaching the arising of the Dhamma that destroys defilements. Whose Dhamma shall I receive (practice) that removes old age (jarā) and death (maccu)? "Paṭipajjāmi" is also a variant reading; the meaning is the same.

Vicikicchākaṅkhāganthita means bound by doubt (vicikicchā) occurring in the manner of "Was I in the past?" and so forth, and by uncertainty (kaṅkhā) occurring in the form of wavering and agitation. Sārambhabalasañyuta means associated with powerful overbearingness (sārambha), characterized by doing more than what is usually done. Kodhappattamanatthaddha means the intense piercing of craving (taṇhā) which has reached the state of hardness of mind associated with anger in all matters.

Because of reasons such as not obtaining desired gains, craving arises as if it were tearing apart the minds of beings. Because it has the power to pierce even one standing far away, craving itself arises like a bow; because it arises from that bow of craving, it is called the arrow of views (diṭṭhisalla). Since that arrow has thirty divisions—twenty types of personality belief (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) and ten types of wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi)—it is said to be "associated with twice fifteen"; the meaning is twice the fifteen-fold divisions. "Behold that [arrow of wrong view] which is in the chest, very strong, which having pierced the heart remains in that very heart"—this is said addressing oneself.

Anudiṭṭhīnaṃ appahāna means the cause of the non-abandoning of the remaining views which are secondary views (anudiṭṭhi). As long as personality belief (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) does not depart from the mental continuity, the non-abandoning of the view of eternalism (sassatadiṭṭhi) and so forth is certain. Saṅkappaparatėjita means encouraged or urged in the practice characterized by relying on others through wrong thought (micchāvitakka). Pierced by that arrow of view, just as it remains striking the heart, I tremble; I revolve here and there through the power of eternalism, annihilationism (uccheda), and so forth.
285:
It has the meaning: like a tree leaf released from its stalk, being moved by the wind (māluta).

"Arisen within me" means: just as in the world a so-called arrow arises from outside and, having pierced the inside, causes pain; it is not like that. This [arrow of craving], however, arises within my own self (attabhāva). That collection of the six sense bases (chaphassāyatana) called the "self" is quickly burned like a fire that burns a house. How? Like a fire burning a house, it burns one's own self, and in whatever body it arises, it moves (proceeds) right there.

I do not see that physician (bhisakka) who is skilled in such treatment, who can cure the arrow of wrong view. Which physician would pull out this arrow of views and arrow of defilements? Even if he pulls it out, it should be construed as: it is not possible to cure the arrow of doubt (vicikicchita) by inserting a probe like a rope with a string-like edge, cutting with a weapon, or by other applications of mantras and medicine. "Vicikicchita" is merely an illustration. The meaning should be understood through the power of all arrows of defilement.

"Without a weapon" means being devoid of a weapon. "Without a wound" means being without a wound. "Staying dependent on the interior" means staying dependent on the heart, which is called the interior. "Without harming" means without oppressing. There is also a reading "ahiṃsā", meaning by non-harming or non-oppressing. The summary meaning here is: Who indeed, without taking any weapon and without making a wound, and therefore without causing pain to all the limbs, will pull out the arrow of defilement—which has reached the interior of my heart and is truly an arrow in the ultimate sense because it causes oppression, pierces within, and obstructs within?

Thus, having shown the manner of his previous thoughts with ten verses, he spoke "Dhammappati hi so seṭṭho" and so forth to show that very manner in another way. There, "Dhammappati" means having the Dhamma as cause (arisen because of the Dhamma). "Hi" is merely a particle. "So seṭṭho" means that person is excellent. "Vicikicchitaṃ" [Note: likely referring to Visadosappavāhako in the Pali] means one who cuts off and removes the poison of my defilements such as lust (rāga). Who indeed, while comforting me who has fallen into the very deep flood (ogha) of saṃsāra by saying "Do not fear," would show the dry land of Nibbāna and the hand of the Noble Path (ariyamagga) that leads to that Nibbāna?
286:
“Rahadehamasmi ogāḷho” means: I have entered into the great lake of Saṃsāra by way of plunging in headfirst. “Ahāriyarajamatttike” means: in that lake which has the fine mud of the dust of lust (rāga) and so forth, which cannot be removed. There is also a variant reading “Ahāriyarajamantike,” which means: in the dust of lust and so forth, which is difficult to extract among the lust and so forth present nearby. Deceit (māyā), characterized by concealing existing faults; envy (usūyā), characterized by the inability to endure the success of others; presumption (sārambha), characterized by overbearing conduct; sloth (thina), characterized by mental dullness; and torpor (middha), characterized by physical dullness—these evil states spread in that lake. In the place where such deceit, envy, presumption, sloth, and torpor spread (in the word 'mapatthaṭe', the letter 'ma' is merely a euphonic conjunction), it means: in the lake spread over by these aforementioned unwholesome states.

“Uddhaccameghathanitaṃ saṃyojanavalāhakaṃ” is spoken with a reversal of terms. It refers to persons who have the thunder of restlessness (uddhacca), which is of an unsteady nature, and the clouds of the ten fetters (saṃyojana). Wrong thoughts (micchā-saṅkappa) based on lust, which are like a great flood of water, being established in the foul (asubha) and so forth, pull me, who have wrong views, towards the ocean of the lower realms (apāya).

“Savanti sabbadhi sotā” means: these five floods—the flood of craving (taṇhā), the flood of views (diṭṭhi), the flood of conceit (māna), the flood of ignorance (avijjā), and the flood of defilements (kilesa)—flow towards all sense objects such as forms (rūpa) by way of the eye-door and so forth; and because they flow from all parts as “craving for forms” and so forth, they flow everywhere. “Latā” (creeper) refers to craving (taṇhā), which is like a creeper because it entwines and binds. “Ubbhijja tiṭṭhati” means: it breaks through the six doors and remains established in sense objects such as forms. Who, as a superior man, can block these floods of craving and so forth flowing in my continuity with the bridge of the Path? Who can cut that creeper of craving with the weapon of the Path?

“Velaṃ karotha” means: build a shore or a bridge that blocks those floods of craving. “Bhaddante” is a term showing the manner of address. “Mā te manomayo soto” means: while even a fool can block a coarse water flood by making a bridge, this subtle flood made of mind is difficult to block. If that mental flood increases like a water flood, the tree standing on the bank...
287:
While a water flood can be blocked by building a bridge, this mental flood of craving is subtle and difficult to block. Just as that water flood, when it increases, destroys a tree standing on the bank by making it fall, so too this flood of craving causes you, who are on the bank of the lower realms (apāya), to suddenly fall into that ocean of the lower realms. Therefore, may that flood of craving not destroy me, and may it not lead me to ruin and destruction.

In this way, this Elder, having reflected on formations (saṅkhāra) in previous lives and having reached maturity of knowledge, now reflects on the suffering of existence. After showing how he grasped the defilements such as doubt (vicikicchā), he now shows how he became stirred (jātasaṃvego), sought the wholesome, went to the Teacher, and what special attainment he focused on, saying “Evaṃ me bhayajātassa” and so forth. In that passage, “Evaṃ me bhayajātassa” means: to one who is afraid in Saṃsāra in the manner described, seeking Nibbāna (the other shore) from this shore of the round of rebirth which is full of danger. Because he possesses the weapon of wisdom (paññāvudha) that cuts off defilements and is the refuge of the world including devas; because he is the Teacher (satthā) who admonishes beings according to their needs for benefits in this life and so forth; and because he is attended and served by the assembly of noble ones (isisaṅghanisevito) such as the chief disciples—the Buddha gave the firm ladder of insight (vipassanā), well-constructed by the knowledge of teaching, pure and free from defilements, made of the essence of Dhamma like faith and wisdom, and unshakeable by opposing states, to me who was being carried away by the great flood (ogha). While giving it, he comforted me saying, “By this ladder, you will find safety,” and said, “Do not fear.”

By that ladder of insight, ascending the palace of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), complete with the four stages of the fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala) obtained through mindfulness of the body and so forth, I realized the Four Noble Truths with the knowledge of the Path. Having thus realized the Truth, I abandoned all that I previously thought was the essence—the multitude of sectarians who delight in the existing body (sakkāya) as “I” and “mine” and the self (atta) they imagined. When I truly saw the path of insight, which is the cause for boarding the boat of the Noble Path, from then on, without keeping those sectarians and the self in mind, I truly saw the Noble Path, which is like a landing place for crossing to the shore of the deathless Nibbāna and is superior to all wholesome states.

After attaining this peerless Path, wishing to praise the Fully Enlightened Buddha who showed this Path, he spoke the words beginning with “Saññāsayaṃ sakkaṃ attasamuṭṭhānaṃ.” In that Pali, “sakkaṃ” refers to views, conceit, and so forth. “Attasamuṭṭhānaṃ” refers to that which arises in the individual existence (attabhāva) called 'self' because it is the base for the notion of 'I', arising from and depending on craving for existence (bhava-taṇhā). Indeed, that craving is the base for the perception of views and conceit...
288:
It means truly seeing the Noble Path, which is like a landing place for crossing to the other shore of the Deathless Nibbāna, and which is superior to all paths and all wholesome states.

Having thus declared his own attainment of the unsurpassed path, he now spoke the words beginning with "Sallaṃ attasamuṭṭhānaṃ" wishing to praise the Blessed One who taught that path. In that verse, "sallaṃ" refers to the dart of defilements such as wrong view and conceit. "Attasamuṭṭhānaṃ" means that which arises in the individual existence (attabhāva) called "self" because it is the base where the conceit "I" occurs. "Bhavanettippabhāvitaṃ" means that which is produced by craving for existence or depends on craving for existence. Indeed, that craving is the cause for the arising of wrong view, conceit, and so on. To prevent the recurrence and arising of those aforementioned unwholesome states, "desesi maggamuttamaṃ" means He taught the Noble Eightfold Path, which is supreme, excellent, and pure, as well as the path of insight (vipassanā-magga) which is the means to it.

"Dīgharattānusayitaṃ" refers to defilements that have long been dormant in the continuity of existence throughout the beginningless saṃsāra, gaining strength by being fit to arise when conditions are met, and thus prevailing over the continuity that has existed for a long time. "Ganthaṃ" refers to the bodily ties such as covetousness and so on. The Blessed One, who dispels the fault of the poison of defilements that act as a bond in my continuity, has caused them to be abandoned through the power of His teaching. Indeed, when the bonds are abandoned without remainder, there are no defilements left unabandoned.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Telakāni Thera is finished.

## 4. Commentary on the Verses of Raṭṭhapāla Thera

The verses beginning with "Passa cittakataṃ" are those of the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla Thera. What is the background story? This Raṭṭhapāla is said to have been born into a wealthy householder family in the city of Haṃsavatī long before the appearance of Padumuttara Buddha. Having reached maturity, after his father's death, he was established in the life of a householder. Seeing the immeasurable wealth inherited through generations shown to him by the treasurer, he thought, "My father, grandfather, and great-grandfather were unable to take this mass of wealth with them. It is proper for me to take it with me." Thus, he gave great alms to the poor, travelers, and others. While attending to an ascetic who had attained direct knowledge, he was encouraged by that ascetic to attain sovereignty in the celestial realm. He performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and, after passing away from there, became a deity. While serving as a celestial king in that realm, he lived out his lifespan and, after passing away, was born as an only son in a family capable of reconciling those who were divided in the human world. At that time...
289:
Having passed away from the celestial realm and being reborn there again, he enjoyed celestial bliss and remained there for the full lifespan. Passing away from there, he was reborn in the human world as an only son in a family capable of sustaining a broken kingdom.

At that time, Padumuttara Buddha appeared in the world and, having set in motion the excellent Wheel of Dhamma, led veneyya beings to the ground of safety known as the great city of Nibbāna. Then, that clansman, having gradually reached the age of discretion, went to the monastery one day with lay followers. Seeing the Teacher preaching the Dhamma, he sat at the edge of the assembly with a confident mind. At that time, the Teacher appointed a certain monk to the foremost position among those who had gone forth out of faith. Seeing this, the clansman, with a devoted heart, set his mind on that goal. He performed a great alms-giving for seven days with great honor to the Blessed One, who was surrounded by a hundred thousand monks, and made an aspiration. The Teacher, seeing that his aspiration would be fulfilled without obstacle, prophesied: "In the future, in the dispensation of the Sammāsambuddha named Gotama, you will be the foremost among those who go forth out of faith." He paid homage to the Teacher and the Saṅgha of monks and departed from his seat. Having performed meritorious deeds throughout his life there, he passed away and wandered through the realms of gods and humans. Ninety-two aeons ago, during the time of Phussa Buddha, when the three princes who were half-brothers of the Teacher were attending to Him, he assisted in their meritorious activities.

Thus, having accumulated many wholesome deeds in various lives and wandering only in happy destinations, he was born in the house of Raṭṭhapāla the Treasurer in the market town of Thullakoṭṭhika in the Kuru country during the time of this Buddha's appearance. Because he was born in a family capable of sustaining a broken kingdom, he was named "Raṭṭhapāla" according to his lineage. Growing up with a large retinue and gradually reaching youth, he was married to a suitable wife by his parents and established in great fame, enjoying prosperity similar to celestial bliss. Then, while the Blessed One was wandering through the Kuru country, He arrived at Thullakoṭṭhika. Hearing that news, the clansman Raṭṭhapāla approached the Teacher. Having heard the Dhamma from the Teacher, he gained faith and desired to go forth. After fasting for seven days and with great difficulty obtaining permission from his parents, he approached the Teacher and requested ordination. By the command of the Teacher, he went forth under a certain elder. Practicing with wise reflection and developing insight, he attained Arahantship. This is stated in the Apadāna:

To Padumuttara Buddha, the greatest in the world, endowed with such qualities,
I offered a noble elephant with tusks like plow-poles, rutting, endowed with the seven treasures, along with its keeper.
Having had that elephant valued, I built and offered a monastery for the Saṅgha.
