I caused fifty-four thousand palatial residences to be built.
I also offered a great alms-giving to Padumuttara Buddha.
The Teacher, the Great Hero, the Self-Awakened One, the Supreme Person, expressed His appreciation.
Making all those people joyful, He preached Nibbāna.
The Buddha named Jalajuttama, who is compassionate, sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks, spoke this verse regarding my gift.
290:
Having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One and having gained faith, I wished to ordain. I fasted for seven days, and after much difficulty, I asked my parents for permission. I approached the Blessed One and requested ordination. By the command of the Blessed One, I ordained under a certain elder. Developing insight through wise reflection, I attained the fruit of Arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

To the Blessed One Padumuttara, the Foremost in the world, the Such-like One, I offered a noble elephant, with tusks like poles, great and rutting, endowed with the seven gems, together with its trainer.

Having that elephant—adorned with a white parasol, fully equipped, and with its trainer—valued, I had a Saṅghārāma monastery built.

I had fifty-four thousand palaces built. Having made a great offering, I dedicated them to the Great Sage.

The Great Hero, the Self-become, the Supreme Person, expressed appreciation. Gladdening all the people, he taught the state of the Deathless.

The Buddha named Jalajuttama, sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks, prophesied about my gift. He spoke these verses:

'This man has built and offered fifty-four thousand palaces. I shall declare the result; listen to my words.

There will be eighteen thousand gabled houses, arisen in the highest heaven, all made of gold.

Fifty times he will be the lord of devas, exercising celestial sovereignty. And fifty-eight times he will be a Wheel-turning Monarch.

One hundred thousand aeons hence, a Teacher named Gotama by clan, born of the Okkāka family, will arise in the world.

Falling from the deva world, urged by his pure root of merit, he will then be reborn in a wealthy family of great riches.

Later, having gone forth, urged by his pure root of merit, he will be a disciple of the Teacher named Raṭṭhapāla.

With a mind directed toward striving, peaceful, and free from acquisitions, having fully understood all taints, he will attain Nibbāna, free from taints.'

Rising and renouncing (after the fast), I abandoned the perfection of wealth. I have no more love for wealth than for a lump of spit.
291:
My energy, which carries me to Nibbāna, is like a beast of burden. In the Dispensation of the Fully Enlightened One, I bear this final body.

The four analytical insights, the eight liberations, and the six supernormal powers have been realized. The Buddha's bidding has been done.

After attaining Arahantship, the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, having asked the Teacher for permission, went to Thullakoṭṭhika to see his parents. While wandering for alms in order in Thullakoṭṭhika, he received some stale gruel (kummāsa) from the previous evening at his father's house. He consumed it as if it were nectar. Invited by his father for the next day, he accepted. On the second day, after eating the almsfood at his father's house, he approached the women of the harem (his former wives) who were adorned and prepared. They tried to entice him, saying, "Master, what are those celestial nymphs like, for whose sake you lead the holy life?" and so on. Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, wishing to change their intent, preached a discourse connected with impermanence:

"Look at this beautified image, a mass of sores, erected, diseased, much-fancied, in which there is no stability or permanence.

Look at this form beautified with jewels and earrings; a skeleton wrapped in skin, it looks beautiful only with clothes.

The feet are reddened with lac, the face is smeared with powder. It is enough to delude a fool, but not one who seeks the Far Shore.

The hair is braided in eight ways, the eyes are smeared with collyrium. It is enough to delude a fool, but not one who seeks the Far Shore.

Like a new, decorated collyrium box, this foul body is adorned. It is enough to delude a fool, but not one who seeks the Far Shore.

The hunter has set the snare, but the deer did not touch the net. Having eaten the bait, we go while the hunter laments."

In those verses, 'cittakataṃ' means made beautiful with clothes, ornaments, flowers, and perfumes. 'Bimbaṃ' refers to the physical body (attabhāva) adorned with major and minor limbs in appropriate places such as height, etc. 'Arukāyaṃ' means the body which is entirely a sore because it constantly oozes from the nine openings. 'Samussitaṃ' means erected with three hundred bones. 'Āturaṃ' means always pained because it must be constantly maintained in one of the postures; always ill. 'Bahusaṅkappaṃ' means much-fancied by fools who imagine what is not as what is. 'Yassa natthi dhuvaṃ ṭhiti' means...
292:
“The snare of the deer is broken; the deer does not approach the net. Having eaten the bait, we go, while the deer-hunter remains grieving.” — He spoke these verses.

In those verses, ‘cittakataṃ’ means artfully made. It refers to being made beautiful with garments, ornaments, flowers, and so forth. ‘Bimbaṃ’ refers to the physical body (attabhāva) adorned with major and minor limbs in appropriate proportions, such as length. ‘Arukāyaṃ’ refers to the body of sores, which is entirely a mass of sores or an ailing body because of the impurities oozing from the nine openings and the pores. ‘Samussitaṃ’ means erected or propped up by three hundred bones. ‘Āturaṃ’ means having a nature of constant affliction (gilāna) because it must be perpetually maintained through the change of postures. ‘Bahusaṅkappaṃ’ means much imagined, where foolish people attribute qualities that do not exist and conceive of it in many ways. ‘Yassa natthi dhuvaṃ ṭhiti’ means that this body has no permanence or stability. In reality, it has only the nature of breaking, scattering, and dissolving. “Look at that body,” he says, referring either to a person standing nearby or to himself.

‘Rūpaṃ’ refers to the physical body. It is called ‘form’ (rūpa) in such passages as, “Depending on bones, sinews, flesh, and skin, space is enclosed, and thus it comes to be known as ‘form’.” ‘Maṇinā kuṇḍalena ca’ means artfully made with gems and earrings found in head ornaments and the like. ‘Aṭṭhiṃ tacena onaddhaṃ’ should be construed as: “Behold the bones, numbering more than three hundred, bound by moist skin.” In the phrase ‘kuṇḍalena ca’, the word ‘ca’ (and) includes the remaining ornaments and decorations. ‘Saha vatthehi sobhati’ means that this form, though artfully made with gems, is beautiful only when covered with clothes, and not when uncovered. For those who read ‘aṭṭhitacena’, it means it is beautiful because it is covered with bone and skin.

‘Alattakakatā’ refers to feet well-dyed with lac (red dye). ‘Mukhaṃ cuṇ္ṇakamakkhitaṃ’ refers to a face smeared with face powder. This is said in reference to those devoted to decoration who remove pimples with mustard paste and bad blood with fine clay before applying face powder. ‘Alaṃ’ means a nature that is sufficient or capable of deluding the minds of foolish worldlings (puthujjana) who delight in the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) and do not seek the far shore (Nibbāna). For those seeking the far shore and delighting in the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa), it is not sufficient to delude them.
293:
“Aṭṭhāpadakatā” refers to a hair arrangement called “aṭṭhapada,” made in an eight-fold pattern, where the hair is cut in the front to cover the forehead. This aṭṭhapada is also called “alaka.” “Nettā añjanamakkhitā” refers to eyes anointed with collyrium such that the shadow of the collyrium is visible both inside and at the two corners of both eyes.

“Añjanīva navā cittā, pūtikāyo alaṅkato” means that just as a new collyrium tube is variegated with floral designs, sea-monster teeth patterns, and so forth, and is smooth, bright, and beautiful on the outside but not beautiful on the inside; even so, the bodies of these people, adorned with bathing, perfumes, clothes, and ornaments, are bright on the outside but remain filled with various kinds of foul impurities on the inside.

“Odahi” means he set (the trap). “Migavo” means the deer-hunter. “Pāsaṃ” means a stick-trap or net. “Nāsadā” means did not touch or collide with. “Vāgurā” means a snare or net. “Nivāpaṃ” means fodder such as grass thrown for deer to eat. The Elder used this simile to make the meaning clear. The meaning here is: For example, just as a hunter sets a stick-trap to kill deer, scatters bait, and remains hidden, a clever deer endowed with speed and effort eats the bait as it pleases without touching the snare and leaves while the hunter cries out, “Alas, the deer has deceived me!” Another strong, clever, and swift deer goes there, eats the bait, breaks the snares here and there, and leaves while the hunter grieves, “Alas, the deer has deceived me; the snare is broken!” In the same way, we too, in the past when we were worldlings, enjoyed the riches bestowed by our parents to bind us, yet we emerged without being attached to those various objects. Now, having entirely cut off all defilements (kilesas) and being without snares, we shall eat the food given by them and go while they are grieving.

Thus, the Elder shows the parents as the hunter, gold, silver, and the harem as the net and snare, the riches enjoyed in the past and the food enjoyed now as the bait-grass, and himself as the great deer. Having spoken these verses, he flew into the air and sat on the auspicious stone slab in King Koravya’s Migāzina garden. It is said that the Elder’s father had the bolts fastened on the seven gate-towers and ordered the men...
294:
(The father of the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla) ordered the door-bolts to be fastened and commanded the men, "Do not allow him to go outside; remove the saffron-dyed robes and have him wear white clothes." Therefore, the Elder departed through the air. Then, King Koravya, hearing that the Elder was staying there, approached him, exchanged pleasant and friendly greetings, and asked, "O Raṭṭhapāla, in this world, those who go forth into the homeless life do so because they have reached ruin through disease, or ruin through loss of wealth, or ruin through loss of relatives. But you have not encountered any such ruin; why then have you gone forth?" Then the Elder spoke of his own state of seclusion based on these four summaries of the Dhamma: "The world is swept away, it is unstable; the world is without shelter, without a master; the world has nothing of its own, one must leave everything behind; the world is insufficient, insatiable, a slave to craving" (M. Ni. 2.305). Reciting the following verses in accordance with that teaching, he said:

"I see in the world wealthy men who, having acquired riches, do not give out of delusion; greedy, they hoard their wealth and crave even more sensual pleasures."

"A king, having forcibly conquered the earth and ruling the land bounded by the ocean, remains unsatisfied with this side of the sea and even desires the further shore of the ocean."

"The king and many other people reach death without being free from craving; being still deficient, they abandon the body; indeed, there is no satisfaction through sensual pleasures in the world."

"Relatives weep for him, with hair dishevelled, saying, 'Alas, would that our relative were immortal!' Wrapping him in a cloth, they carry him out, place him on a pyre, and then burn him."
295:
The deceased is burned while being prodded with stakes; he must depart, abandoning his possessions with only a single shroud. For one who is dying, relatives, friends, or even companions cannot be a refuge.

Heirs take over his wealth, but the being goes according to his own kamma. Nothing follows the dying person—neither children, nor wife, nor wealth, nor kingdom.

One cannot obtain long life through wealth, nor can one ward off old age with riches. The wise say this life is very short; it is impermanent and subject to change.

Both the rich and the poor experience the touch of death; the fool and the wise are touched by it just the same. But the fool, being struck by his folly, lies troubled, while the wise man, though touched by that contact, does not tremble.

Therefore, wisdom is indeed better than wealth, for by wisdom one reaches the end of existence (Nibbāna) even in this life. Because of not reaching Nibbāna, the fool, being deluded, performs evil deeds in various states of existence.

He wanders repeatedly in Saṃsāra, undergoing rebirth and going to the world beyond. The one of little wisdom, believing in the fool's conduct, also undergoes rebirth and goes to the world beyond.

Just as a thief caught at the scene of a break-in is punished for his own evil deed, so too, after death, a being of evil character is punished in the world beyond because of his own evil kamma.
296:
## 
Sensual pleasures are diverse, sweet, and delightful. They agitate the mind with various forms and appearances. O Great King, seeing the danger in sensual pleasures, I have renounced the world.

Just as fruits fall from a tree, so do beings, whether young or old, perish when the body breaks up. O Great King, seeing this also, I have renounced the world. The faultless state of monkhood is indeed superior.

I have renounced with faith and am fully established in the Dispensation of the Conqueror. My renunciation is not in vain; I partake of alms-food as one who is debtless.

Seeing sensual pleasures as a burning fire, gold and silver as weapons, the suffering of entering the womb, and the great danger in hells (I have renounced).

Knowing this danger at that time, I gained spiritual urgency (saṃvega). Pierced by that urgency, being tranquil, I have reached the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya).

I have served the Teacher, I have fulfilled the Buddha's Dispensation. The heavy burden has been laid down, and the cord of existence (bhavanetti) has been uprooted.

That purpose for which I renounced the home life for the homeless life—that goal, the destruction of all fetters, has been attained by me. He spoke these verses.

Among those verses, 'Passāmi loke' means: O Great King, I see in this world people who are wealthy, endowed with riches, and prosperous. However, though they have obtained wealth and are established in prosperity, they do not give anything to recluses, brahmins, and others. Why? Because of delusion and the absence of the wisdom of ownership of actions (kamma-ssakatā-paññā). Overcome by greed, those greedy ones only accumulate and store up whatever wealth they have obtained. They greatly long for sensual pleasures beyond what they have already acquired, thinking, 'May I obtain such enjoyments,' and they exert effort in accordance with that longing.
297:
Desiring to show an example of excessive craving for sensual pleasures, he spoke the words beginning with "Rājā." In that context, "pasayhappathaviṃ vijetvā" means having conquered the land of one's lineage by force. "Āvasanto" means ruling. "Oraṃ samuddassa" means that even if one obtains the entire near side of the ocean, being of an insatiable nature, one would still crave the other side of the ocean, such as other islands.

"Avīta-taṇhā" means having a nature where craving has not yet departed. "Ūnāva" means being simply incomplete in one's desires. "Kāmehi lokamhi na hatthi titti" means that for those whose minds are destroyed by craving, there is no such thing as satisfaction through objective sensual pleasures in this world.

"Kandanti naṃ" means that referring to the dead man, they perform weeping while praising his virtues. "Aho vata no amarā ti ca" means they also say, "Oh, would that our relatives were immortal (lived long)." Here, for the sake of ease in reciting the verse, "vata" is spoken with a long vowel as "vatā."

"So ḍayhati sūlehi tujjamāno" means that the dead person is pierced with stakes by those who burn the corpse so that it may burn well (as he is being cremated). "Tāṇā" means those who provide protection.

"Yena kammaṃ" means according to one's karma. "Dhanaṃ" refers to any object that is regarded as wealth. Again, the word "dhanaṃ" is used in reference to gold and silver.

Having stated the lack of remedy for sensual pleasures and old age with the words beginning with "Na dīghamāyuṃ," he spoke the words beginning with "Appaṃ hi" to show the impermanence of those sensual pleasures. "Phusanti" means they touch or encounter undesirable contact. It shows that in such encounters, being wealthy or poor is not the cause. "Phassaṃ bālo ca dhīro ca tatheva phuṭṭho" means that just as a fool encounters pleasant and unpleasant contact, in the same way, a wise person also encounters pleasant and unpleasant contact. In this regard, there is no difference between the fool and the wise.

This, however, is the difference: "Bālo hi bālyā vadhito va seti" means that when a foolish person is touched by any painful state, he sleeps (remains) as one oppressed by his own folly, grieving, wearying himself, and beating his breast while lamenting. Turning this way and that, resisting and trembling. "Phassaphuṭṭho" means that when the wise person is touched by painful contact, he does not tremble; for him, not even a slight tremor occurs.
298:
Therefore, because such is the occurrence of worldly conditions for the fool and the wise, wisdom is indeed better than wealth. "By which wisdom one reaches the end (Nibbāna) in this world" means that wisdom is more praiseworthy than wealth because, through that wisdom, one attains Nibbāna, which is the end of existence. "Abyositattā hi" means because of not having completed the as-yet-unattained Nibbāna. "Bhavābhavesu" means in existences great and small.

"Upeti gabbhañca parañca lokaṃ saṃsāramāpajja parampari" means that a person who commits evil deeds and undergoes repeated wandering in Saṃsāra enters the womb and the next world; he is not liberated from conception and birth in the next world. Believing in the behavior of that evil-doer and assuming "I have a self," another fool of little wisdom also practices like him and thus enters the womb and the next world; he cannot escape from it.

"Coro yathā" means just as a thief of evil character, while breaking into a house, is caught at the breach by guards and is beaten with rods and so on because of his own deed of house-breaking, or is oppressed and bound by the king's men. "Evaṃ pajā" means this world of beings, having committed evil deeds in this life, upon reaching the next life, is oppressed in hell and other states because of that karma, being tormented by the fivefold binding and other punishments.

Thus, having explained the four Dhamma summaries (Dhammuddesa) as appropriate through these eleven verses, he now spoke the words beginning with "Kāmā hi," desiring to manifest his own renunciation out of faith and the reaching of the summit of the monk's task, having seen the danger in sensual pleasures and Saṃsāra. In that Pali, "kāmā" refers to objective sensual pleasures (vatthukāma) such as delightful forms and so on. Subjective sensual pleasures (kilesakāma) refer to all varieties of lust. Here, however, only objective sensual pleasures should be understood. They are "citrā" (variegated) because of their many forms such as visual objects. They are "madhurā" (sweet) because they have a desirable nature that is enjoyed by the world. They are called "manoramā" (mind-delighting) because they delight the minds of foolish worldlings. "Virūparūpena" means with various appearances and various natures. Those sensual pleasures are variegated by way of forms and have various colors such as blue. Thus, by showing enjoyment through those various forms, they disturb the mind and do not allow one to delight in the monk's Dhamma. Having seen the danger in the cords of sensual pleasure, such as having little enjoyment and much suffering, I have renounced for that reason (seeing that danger).
299:
Just as the fruits of a tree fall at some place, whether in their ripe stage or unripe stage, due to external effort or naturally, in the same way, beings, whether young or old, surely fall when the body breaks up at death. "Seeing this also" means seeing such impermanence (anicca) with the eye of wisdom. The meaning is that one sees not only the danger due to the lack of gratification, etc., but also impermanence. "Apaṇṇaka" means the state of a recluse (samaṇa) which is unerring and is indeed superior and noble.

"With faith" means having believed in kamma, the results of kamma, the Buddha's perfect enlightenment, the excellence of the Dhamma, and the Sangha's good practice. "One who has reached the Teacher's Dispensation" means one who has entered upon the right practice in the Dispensation of the Teacher. Because of having attained the fruit of Arahatship, my going forth is not in vain (not void). Only because of having attained that, I enjoy my food without debt, through the power of being free from defilements, by way of master's enjoyment (sāmiparibhoga) due to the state of being a master.

"Seeing sensual pleasures as a burning fire" means seeing both the objects of sensuality (vatthukāma) and the defilements of sensuality (kilesakāma) as burning with the eleven fires. "Gold as weapons" means seeing all varieties of gold, whether worked or unworked, as sharpened weapons because they bring about harm. "Conception in the womb is suffering" refers to the suffering of the entire cycle of rebirth (saṃsāra) starting from conception. "There is great fear in the hells" means seeing the great fear found in the eight great hells along with the peripheral (ussada) hells in all places; this is how it should be connected.

"Knowing this danger" means knowing the danger and fault in saṃsāra, such as the burning of sensual pleasures. "Then I attained spiritual urgency (saṃvega)" means obtaining urgency regarding existence, etc., at the time of hearing the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher. "Being then one who was pierced" means that while being a layman, one was pierced by the spikes of lust, etc., but now, having come to the Teacher's Dispensation, one has reached the destruction of the taints (Arahatship). Alternatively, "viddho" means having pierced and realized the Four Noble Truths. The remaining words are easy to understand as they have been explained in various places.

Thus, after the Elder preached the Dhamma to King Koravya, he returned to the presence of the Teacher. The Teacher, later sitting in the midst of the assembly of Noble Ones, appointed the Elder to the foremost position (etadagga) among those who went forth through faith.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Raṭṭhapāla is Finished.

The verses beginning with "Rūpaṃ disvā sati muṭṭhā" are the verses of the Venerable Mālukyaputta. The story of this Elder has already been told below in the Chakkanipāta. The Elder, established in the fruit of Arahatship, spoke these verses as a Dhamma teaching to his relatives. While he was a worldling in this Dispensation...
300:
## 5. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Mālukyaputta

The verses beginning with "Rūpaṃ disvā sati muṭṭhā" are the verses of the long-lived Mālukyaputta. The story of this Elder has already been told below in the Chakkanipāta. The Elder, established in the fruit of Arahatship, spoke these verses by way of a Dhamma teaching to his relatives.

When he was a worldling in this Dispensation, he requested: "Venerable Sir, I pray, let the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma in brief." Being thus requested, the Blessed One asked: "Mālukyaputta, what do you think of this? Regarding those forms cognizable by the eye that you have not seen, have never seen before, do not see now, and for which you have no thought 'I would see them'—do you have any desire, lust, or affection for them?" "No, Venerable Sir," he replied. "Regarding those sounds cognizable by the ear... those things cognizable by the nose, tongue, body, and mind that you have not known, have never known before, do not know now, and for which you have no thought 'I would know them'—do you have any desire, lust, or affection for them?" "No, Blessed One," he replied.

"Mālukyaputta, in this case, regarding things to be seen, heard, sensed, and cognized: in the seen there will be only the seen; in the heard, only the heard; in the sensed, only the sensed; in the cognized, only the cognized. Mālukyaputta, when for you in the seen there is only the seen, in the heard only the heard, in the sensed only the sensed, and in the cognized only the cognized, then, Mālukyaputta, you are not 'by that.' When, Mālukyaputta, you are not 'by that,' then, Mālukyaputta, you are not 'in that.' When, Mālukyaputta, you are not 'in that,' then, Mālukyaputta, you are neither here, nor beyond, nor in between the two. This itself is the end of suffering." When the Dhamma was thus taught in brief, he showed his thorough mastery of that Dhamma by saying:

Seeing a form, for one who attends to the sign of the pleasant, mindfulness is lost.
With a mind full of lust, one experiences it, and remains clinging to that form.

For him, many feelings originating from the form increase.
Greed and distress afflict his mind.
For one who thus accumulates suffering, Nibbāna is said to be far away.

Hearing a sound, for one who attends to the sign of the pleasant, mindfulness is lost.
One with a mind full of lust experiences it, and remains clinging to that sound.
301:
For him, many feelings arise having sound as their source. Both covetousness (abhijjhā) and vexation (vihesā) oppress his mind. For one who thus accumulates [defilements], it is said that there is suffering; for him, Nibbāna is said to be in a distant place.

Having smelled an odor, for one who attends to the sign (nimitta) of the agreeable, mindfulness is lost. With a lustful mind, he experiences [that odor] and remains attached to it. For him, many feelings arise having odor as their source. Both covetousness and vexation oppress and harass his mind. For one who thus accumulates [the formations of existence through delight], it is said that there is the suffering of the round (vaṭṭadukkha); for him, Nibbāna is said to be in a distant place.

Having tasted a flavor, for one who attends to the sign of the agreeable, mindfulness is lost. With a lustful mind, he experiences that flavor with delight; he remains attached to that flavor [thinking it is pleasant]. For him, many feelings arise having flavor as their source. Both covetousness and vexation oppress and harass his mind. For one who thus accumulates, there is the suffering of the round; for him, Nibbāna is said to be in a distant place.

Having felt a touch (tangible object), for one who attends to the sign of the agreeable, mindfulness is lost. With a lustful mind, he experiences that touch with delight; he remains attached to that touch. For him, many feelings arise having tangible objects as their source. Both covetousness and vexation oppress and harass his mind. For one who thus accumulates, there is the suffering of the round; for him, Nibbāna is said to be in a distant place.

Having known a mental object, for one who attends to the sign of the agreeable, mindfulness is lost. With a lustful mind, he experiences that mental object with delight; he remains attached to that mental object. For him, many feelings arise having mental objects as their source. Both covetousness and vexation oppress and harass his mind. For one who thus accumulates, there is the suffering of the round; for him, Nibbāna is said to be in a distant place.

Having seen a form, being mindful and reflective, he is not lustful for forms. With a detached mind, he experiences [the object] and does not remain attached to that form [through craving and so on].
302:
Just as for that practitioner who sees a form and experiences the feeling arising from that form, states such as covetousness do not arise; in the same way, the round of defilements (kilesavaṭṭa) is exhausted and not accumulated. Thus, that practitioner, being endowed with mindfulness and wisdom, conducts himself. For one who thus destroys the suffering of the round through path-wisdom (magga-paññā), the suffering of the round is exhausted. For such a person, Nibbāna is said to be near.

Having heard a sound, being mindful and reflective, he does not give rise to lust for sounds. With a detached mind, he experiences it without delight or pleasure. He does not remain attached to that sound through the power of craving, conceit, and views (taṇhā, māna, diṭṭhi).

Just as for that practitioner, states such as covetousness do not arise when hearing a sound; in the same way, for one who experiences the feeling arising from that sound, the round of defilements is exhausted and not accumulated. Thus, that person, being endowed with mindfulness and wisdom, dwells with the practice of abandoning defilements. For one who is accustomed to destroying the suffering of the round through path-wisdom, the suffering of the round does not increase. For such a person, Nibbāna is said to be near.

Having smelled an odor, being mindful and reflective, he does not give rise to lust for odors. With a detached mind, he experiences it without delight or pleasure. He does not remain attached to that odor through the power of craving, conceit, and views.

Just as for that practitioner, states such as covetousness do not arise when smelling an odor; in the same way, for one who experiences the feeling arising from that odor, the round of defilements is exhausted and not accumulated. Thus, that person, being endowed with mindfulness and wisdom, dwells by the power of abandoning defilements. For one who destroys the round of phenomena (vaṭṭadhamma) through path-wisdom, Nibbāna is said to be near.

Having tasted a flavor, being mindful and reflective, he does not give rise to lust for flavors. With a detached mind, he experiences it without delight. He does not remain attached to that flavor through the power of craving, conceit, and views.

Just as for that practitioner, states such as covetousness do not arise when tasting a flavor; in the same way, for one who experiences the feeling arising from that flavor, the round of defilements is exhausted and not accumulated. Thus, that person, being endowed with mindfulness and wisdom, dwells with the practice of abandoning defilements. For one who destroys the suffering of the round through path-wisdom, the suffering of the round does not increase. For such a person, Nibbāna is said to be near.

Having felt a tangible object, being mindful and reflective, he does not give rise to lust for tangible objects. With a detached mind, he experiences it without delight or pleasure. He does not remain attached to that tangible object through the power of craving, conceit, and views.

Just as for that practitioner, states such as covetousness do not arise when touching a tangible object; in the same way, for one who experiences the feeling arising from that tangible object, the round is exhausted and not accumulated. Thus, that person, being endowed with mindfulness and wisdom, dwells by practicing the abandonment of defilements. For one who destroys the suffering of the round through path-wisdom, the suffering of the round does not increase. For such a person, Nibbāna is said to be near.

Having known a mental object, being mindful and reflective, he does not give rise to lust for mental objects. With a detached mind, he experiences it without delight or pleasure. He does not remain attached to that mental object through the power of craving, conceit, and views.
303:
"When one knows the Dhamma and experiences feeling, [the round of suffering] is exhausted and not accumulated. Thus, he wanders mindfully. For one who thus does not accumulate suffering, Nibbāna is said to be near." He spoke these verses.

In those verses, "rūpaṃ disvā" means perceiving a visual object, which is cognizable by eye-consciousness, through the eye-door. "Sati muṭṭhā, piyaṃ nimittaṃ manasi karoto" means for one who does not stop at merely seeing that visual object but attends to the beautiful sign, mindfulness is lost because of unwise attention by way of grasping the beautiful aspect. When mindfulness is thus lost, one experiences that visual object with a lustful mind; being lustful, greedy, and attached, one continuously experiences, relishes, and delights in it. For such a person, "tañca ajjhosatiṭṭhati" means being deeply attached to that visual object and remaining fixed, swallowing it and completing it while reflecting, "It is pleasant, it is pleasant."

For such a person, many feelings such as pleasure, which are rooted in the visual object, increase as causes for the arising of defilements. "Abhijjhā ca vihesā ca, cittamasūpahaññati" means the mind of that person is oppressed and afflicted by covetousness (abhijjhā) arising through lust for a pleasant visual object, and by distress (vihesā) characterized by sorrow etc., arising through anger toward an unpleasant visual object or through the change and transformation of a pleasant visual object. "Evamācinato dukkhaṃ" means for one who accumulates the formations leading to existence (bhavābhisaṅkhāra) through relishing various feelings in the manner described, the suffering of the round (vaṭṭa-dukkha) occurs. Therefore, the Blessed One taught: "With feeling as condition, craving arises... [up to] ...the origin of the mass of suffering." For such a person, Nibbāna is said to be far; it means Nibbāna is difficult for him to attain. In the verses beginning with "saddaṃ sutvā" (having heard a sound), the meaning should be understood in the same manner. In those verses, "ghatvā" means having smelled, "bhotvā" means having eaten (tasted), "phussā" means having touched, and "dhammaṃ ñatvā" means having known a mental object.

Having thus shown the round of suffering for one who is lustful toward the objects of the six doors, he now spoke the verses beginning with "na so rajjati rūpesu" to show the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa) for one who is detached from those objects. In that verse, "na so rajjati rūpesu, rūpaṃ disvā paṭissato" means that person, having seen a visual object...
304:
...having perceived the visual object that has come into range through the stream of eye-door consciousness, becomes one who is mindful because of acting with clear comprehension through the four types of clear comprehension. Such a person is not lustful toward visual objects and does not give rise to passion; rather, he experiences them with a detached mind. Knowing the visual object as it really is, through its arising and so on, he becomes weary of it. Being weary, he experiences that visual object and the feeling arisen therein with a detached mind. Such a person, because he does not cling to or remain fixed in that object, and because he has a mind well-detached from that visual object, does not settle into it through craving, conceit, and wrong view as "This is mine, this I am, this is my self."

"Yathāssa passato rūpaṃ" means for that yogi, just as covetousness and so on do not arise in that visual object, so it is for one who views the visual object as impermanent and so on. "Seveto cāpi vedanaṃ" means for one who makes use of the feeling arisen in dependence on that visual object and the mental states associated with that feeling as an object of use. "Khīyati" means the entire round of defilements reaches exhaustion and termination. "Nopacīyati" means it is not accumulated; it does not reach accumulation. Thus, he wanders and dwells mindful and clearly comprehending through the practice of removing defilements. "Evaṃ apacinato dukkhaṃ" means for one who destroys the entire suffering of the round through the path-wisdom (magga-paññā) that leads to the diminution [of existence], as described. "Santike nibbānaṃ vuccati" means it is said to be in the very presence of the Nibbāna element with residue and the Nibbāna element without residue, because of the realization of the unconditioned element. In the verses beginning with "na so rajjati saddesu," the meaning should be understood in this very same way.

Thus, the Elder, having declared through these verses that he had upheld the instruction of the Teacher, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Teacher, and departed. Before long, having developed insight, he attained Arahantship.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Mālukyaputta Thera is finished.

## 6. Commentary on the Verses of Sela Thera

"Paripuṇṇakāyo" and the following verses are those of the Venerable Sela Thera. What is the background story? It is said that this Sela Thera was born into a good family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. Upon reaching maturity, he became a leader of a group. He encouraged three hundred men, and together with them, he built a Perfumed Chamber (Gandhakuṭi) for the Teacher. When it was completed...
305:
After rising from his seat, paying homage to the Blessed One, and departing, he soon developed insight and attained the fruit of Arahantship. Thus it should be noted. The commentary on the verses of Elder Mālunkyaputta is finished.

## 6. Selattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

The verses beginning with 'Paripuṇṇakāyo' are those of the Venerable Elder Sela. The background story of these verses is as follows: In the time of the Buddha Padumuttara, this Elder Sela was born into a good family. Upon reaching maturity, he became a great teacher of a sect, and having established three hundred people [in virtue], he built and offered a Gandhakuṭi (perfumed chamber) for the Blessed One. In that Gandhakuṭi, he provided a great donation (mahādāna) to the Buddha and the community of monks, and honored the Buddha and the monks by offering three robes to each.

Due to that meritorious deed, he resided only in the deva world for the duration of one buddhantara. Passing away from there, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans. In the time of our present Buddha's arising, he was reborn into a brahmin family in the brahmin village named Āpaṇa in the Aṅguttarāpa country, and received the name 'Sela'. Upon reaching maturity, he attained mastery in the three Vedas and all the brahminical arts. He resided in the village of Āpaṇa, teaching the mantras to three hundred young students.

At that time, the Blessed One, having departed from Sāvatthī, was wandering through the Aṅguttarāpa country together with twelve hundred and fifty monks. Seeing the maturity of the knowledge of the brahmin Sela and his disciples, the Blessed One stayed in a certain forest grove. Then, an ascetic named Keṇiya, hearing of the Blessed One's arrival, went there and invited the Blessed One along with the community of monks for the next day's meal. He then prepared many kinds of food and delicacies in his own hermitage.

At that time, the brahmin Sela, while walking for exercise with his three hundred students, entered Keṇiya's hermitage. Seeing the ascetics preparing the requirements for the offering, such as splitting wood and preparing the hearths, he asked, 'Keṇiya, is a great sacrifice (yañña) being prepared?' and so on. When Keṇiya replied, 'The Buddha, the Blessed One, has been invited by me for tomorrow's meal,' Sela, upon merely hearing the word 'Buddha,' became extremely joyful, uplifted, and filled with rapture and happiness. Immediately, he approached the Blessed One with his students, exchanged greetings, and sat in a suitable place, observing the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (mahāpurisalakkhaṇa) on the Blessed One's body.

'One endowed with such marks must either become a Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti) or a Buddha who has removed the veil [of ignorance] from the world. This person is a renunciant, yet I do not know whether he is a Buddha or not. I have heard this said by aged brahmins, teachers, and teachers of teachers: "Those who are Worthy Ones (Arahats), Fully Enlightened Buddhas, reveal themselves when their own virtues are being praised." For one who is not a Fully Enlightened Buddha, if praised with the virtues of a Buddha in his presence, would become embarrassed and confused due to the lack of the knowledge of fearlessness (vesārajja) and the inability to withstand scrutiny. What if I were to praise the ascetic Gotama in his presence with suitable verses?' Having thought thus, he praised him as follows:

'You have a perfect body, you are radiant, well-born, and beautiful to behold. You are golden-hued, O Blessed One; you have very white teeth and are full of energy.'
306:
'For a well-born man, whatever marks there are, all those marks of a Great Man are on your body.'

'With clear eyes and a beautiful face, tall, straight, and majestic, you shine like the sun in the midst of the community of monks.'

'A monk of beautiful appearance, with skin like gold—what is the use of being a monk for you who are of such supreme beauty?'

'You deserve to be a King, a Wheel-turning Monarch, the best of charioteers, a conqueror of the earth bounded by the four oceans, the lord of Jambudīpa.'

'Kshatriyas and wealthy kings would be your followers. O Gotama, King of kings, Lord of men, exercise your sovereignty.' Thus he praised the Blessed One with these six verses.

In those verses, 'Paripuṇṇakāyo' means having a perfect body because of being endowed with the thirty-two very distinct marks of a Great Man and having complete major and minor limbs. 'Surucī' means having a beautiful bodily radiance. 'Sujāto' means being well-formed through the perfection of height, girth, and shape. 'Cārudassano' means having an appearance that is delightful, not repulsive, and which creates a sense of never being satisfied even when looking for a long time. Some teachers, however, say 'Cārudassano' means having beautiful eyes. 'Suvaṇṇavaṇṇo' means having a color like gold. The word 'asi' (you are) should be read in conjunction with all the terms, such as 'Paripuṇṇakāyo asi' and so on. 'Susukkadāṭho' means having very white teeth (canines). From the Blessed One's teeth, white rays emerge like moonlight. 'Vīriyavā' means being endowed with extraordinary energy due to the fulfillment of the perfection of energy (vīriya-pāramī), the undertaking of energy endowed with four factors, and the attainment of the fourfold right efforts (sammappadhāna).

'Narassa hi sujātassa' means for a Great Man who is well-born through the fulfillment of either the thirty perfections or the noble duties of a Wheel-turning Monarch. 'Sabbe te' means all those [marks] that [indicate] the state of a Great Man in the world...
307:
Because they manifest the state of the supreme person, they are called 'byañjana' (marks). The qualities of the physical form—consisting of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (Mahāpurisalakkhaṇa), such as well-planted feet, and the eighty minor marks (anubyañjana), such as copper-colored nails and high nails—exist in your body without exception; this is how the remaining words should be understood.

'Mahāpurisalakkhaṇa' (Marks of a Great Man) is said because the teacher wishes to conclude with another expression regarding the marks previously mentioned.

Now, wishing to praise the Blessed One with the marks that he himself admires, he said 'Pasannanetto' and so on. The Blessed One has clear eyes because of the perfection of the five-colored sensitivity (pasāda). He has a beautiful face (sumukho) because his face is like the full moon. He is stately (brahā) because of the perfection of his height and circumference. He is straight (uju) because his body is straight like that of Brahmā. He is powerful (patāpavā) because he is possessed of splendor.

Now, to illustrate that very state of being powerful with the simile of the sun, he said 'Majjhe samaṇasaṅghassa' and so on. In that Pali, 'You shine like the sun' means that just as the sun, when it rises, dispels all darkness and shines while creating light, even so, you shine while dispelling all the darkness of ignorance both internally and externally and creating the light of knowledge.

He is called 'Kalyāṇadassana' (beautiful to behold) because his appearance is lovely and brings about the perfection of sight for beholders, and because he is endowed with the five excellent visions (dassana). 'Uttamavaṇṇino' means 'of one who is endowed with an excellent complexion.'

'Cakkavattī' (Wheel-turner) means he turns the Wheel of Treasure (cakkaratana); he turns the world by the four wheels of success (sampatticakka); and through those wheels, he causes others to turn. Because the turning of the wheels of postures (iriyāpathacakka) for the benefit of others exists in that king, he is called 'Cakkavattī.' Alternatively, because the turning of the wheel of authority (āṇācakka), which cannot be overcome by others due to his being endowed with the four wonderful qualities and the bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu), exists in that king, he is also called 'Cakkavattī.' 'Rathesabho' means a noble bull-like man among charioteers, meaning a great charioteer. 'Cāturanto' means the lord of the earth bounded by the four oceans. 'Vijitāvီ' means one who has achieved victory. 'Jambusaṇḍassa' means 'of Jambudīpa'; he said this to show his manifest sovereignty. However, a Cakkavattီ is indeed the lord of all four great continents along with their minor islands.
308:
'Khattiya' refers to those who are of the warrior/noble class by birth. 'Bhogi' refers to those who enjoy wealth. 'Rājā' refers to any individuals who exercise kingship and rule. 'Anuyantā' refers to the retinue and attendants. 'Rājābhirājā' means a king who is worthy of being honored by kings, implying a Universal Monarch (Cakkavattī). 'Manujindo' means a leader of men, meaning a supreme lord of men.

When Sela the Brahmin had spoken thus, the Blessed One, wishing to fulfill Sela's heart's desire—thinking, 'When those who are Worthy Ones, Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas, have their virtues spoken of, they reveal themselves'—uttered this verse:

"I am a King, Sela, (Sela, said the Blessed One) the supreme King of Dhamma.
By Dhamma, I turn the wheel,
The wheel that cannot be turned back."

In that verse, this is the meaning: Sela, you say to me, 'You deserve to be a King, a Universal Monarch'; do not be concerned about that, for I am a King. Even though there is kingship, just as another king might rule over a hundred yojanas, or two, three, four, or five hundred yojanas, or a thousand yojanas, or even as a Cakkavattī ruling up to the boundaries of the four continents, I do not have such a limited domain. For I am the supreme King of Dhamma, and I rule over the world systems from the highest heaven (Bhavagga) down to Avīci [hell] and across immeasurable world systems. Among beings who are diverse, such as those without feet and so on, I am the supreme. There is no one equal to me in virtue (sīla) ... [as above] ... or in the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimuttiñāṇadassana); how could there be anyone superior? Being such a supreme King of Dhamma, I turn the wheel by means of the Dhamma known as the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma), such as the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), which is supreme—the wheel of authority (āṇācakka) by saying, 'Abandon this, attain and dwell in that,' and so on. Or, I turn the wheel of Dhamma (dhammacakka) itself by means of the scriptural Dhamma (pariyatti-dhamma), such as, 'Now this, monks, is the noble truth of suffering.' 'The wheel that cannot be turned back' means it is a wheel that cannot be stopped by a recluse ... [as above] ... or by anyone in the world.

Seeing the Blessed One thus revealing himself, Sela the Brahmin, filled with joy and happiness, for the sake of further confirmation—
309:
The brahmin Sela addressed the Blessed One with two verses: "Venerable Gotama, you claim: 'I am the peerless King of Dhamma, the Fully Enlightened One.' You say: 'I set the wheel in motion by means of the Dhamma.' Who, then, is your general? Who is the disciple who follows in the wake of the Teacher? Who continues to roll the Wheel of Dhamma set in motion by you?"

In those verses, "Who is the general?" (ko nu senāpati) is a question asking who is the general capable of further rolling the wheel set in motion by the Lord, the King of Dhamma, in accordance with the Dhamma.

At that time, the Venerable Sāriputta was sitting on the right side of the Blessed One, shining with glory like a heap of gold. Desiring to point out the Venerable Sāriputta, the Blessed One spoke this verse:
"Sela, the peerless Wheel of Dhamma set in motion by me,
Is further rolled by Sāriputta, who has followed in the wake of the Tathāgata."

In that verse, "anujāto tathāgataṃ" means one who is born following the Buddha, one who is born into the Noble Birth (ariya-jāti) because of the Tathāgata.

Thus, having answered the question asked by the brahmin Sela, "Who is your general?", and desiring to remove the doubt of the brahmin Sela regarding his statement "You claim to be the Enlightened One," the Blessed One spoke this verse to make him understand: "I do not claim to be a Buddha merely by assertion; rather, I am a Buddha for this reason:
'O Brahmin, what should be known is known by me with higher knowledge; what should be developed has been developed;
What should be abandoned has been abandoned by me. Therefore, O Brahmin, I am a Buddha.'"

In that verse, "what should be known" (abhiññeyya) refers to the Four Truths, the Four Noble Truths. The term "abhiññeyya" is used to include the Four Truths, the Four Noble Truths, in a general sense. Among those Noble Truths, the Truth of the Path (magga-sacca) which should be developed, and the Truth of the Origin (samudaya-sacca) which should be abandoned...
310:
By taking both of these (the Truth of the Path and the Truth of the Origin), the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca) and the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca), which are the results of the Path and the Origin respectively, are also included, because the result is accomplished by taking the cause. Therefore, regarding those Noble Truths, the statement "What should be realized (the Truth of Cessation) has been realized; what should be fully understood (the Truth of Suffering) has been fully understood" is also implied. Alternatively, by the statement "What should be known with higher knowledge has been known with higher knowledge," the state of being a Buddha who knows all knowable things (ñeyya) with higher knowledge is declared in brief. Then, desiring to show a part of that Buddhahood in detail, he said, "What should be developed has been developed," and so on. Or else, by the words "What should be developed has been developed; what should be abandoned has been abandoned," he begins by praising his own perfection of knowledge (ñāṇa-sampadā) and perfection of abandonment (pahāna-sampadā). Since these perfections are the foundation, he intends to imply that all the Buddha's virtues have been praised, and thus he said: "Therefore, O Brahmin, I am a Buddha." By the inclusion of "what should be known is known" (abhiññeyya abhiññāta), all forms of true knowledge (vijjā) and liberation (vimutti) are included. Thus, desiring to show the nature of the Four Truths along with their results and the perfection of their causes, he clarifies his Buddhahood through the reasoning: "Having known everything that should be known, I have become a Buddha."

Thus, having revealed himself in the primary sense, and desiring to encourage the brahmin to overcome doubt regarding him, he spoke these three verses:
"Dispel your doubt in me, O Brahmin; have confidence.
It is rare to have the sight of the Fully Enlightened Ones frequently.

Those whose appearance in the world is rare and frequent,
I am such a Buddha, O Brahmin, the peerless surgeon.

Having become sublime, incomparable, the crusher of Māra's army,
Having brought all enemies under control, I rejoice, fearing nothing from any quarter."

In those verses, "vinayassu" means dispel or cut off. "Kaṅkhaṃ" refers to the doubt of vicikicchā. "Adhimuccassu" means make a decision, or believe that he is the "Fully Enlightened One" (Sammāsambuddha). "Dullabhaṃ dassanaṃ hoti sambuddhānaṃ" is because the world can be void of Buddhas for even incalculable aeons. "Sallakatto" means one who extracts the darts such as lust (rāga). "Brahmabhūto" means reaching the most excellent state. "Atitulo" means one who has transcended comparison, the peerless one. "Mārasenappamaddano" means the crusher of Māra's army, as it is said, "Sensual pleasures are your first army." "Sabbāmitte" refers to the five kinds of Māra: Khandha-māra, Kilesa-māra, Abhisaṅkhāra-māra, Maccu-māra, and Devaputta-māra...
311:
...having brought all these enemies—known as Khandha-māra, Kilesa-māra, Abhisaṅkhāra-māra, Maccu-māra, and Devaputta-māra—under his control, he rejoices without any danger through the bliss of concentration (samādhi-sukha), the bliss of fruition (phala-sukha), and the bliss of Nibbāna.

When this was said, the brahmin Sela immediately felt devotion toward the Blessed One and, desiring the monkhood, spoke these three verses:

"Listen, sirs, to this word spoken by the Visionary One, the Great Hero, the Surgeon, who roars like a lion in the forest.

Having seen the Sublime One, the Incomparable One, the Crusher of Māra's army, who would not be inspired with confidence, even if he were of low birth?

Whoever wishes to follow me, let him follow; whoever does not wish to follow, let him go. As for me, I shall go forth in the presence of the One of Excellent Wisdom."

This was spoken because he was urged by his mature supporting condition (upanissaya-sampatti). In those verses, "kaṇhābhijātiko" means one of low birth, one who is established in a state where darkness is the destination.

Then those young men, being also endowed with past supporting conditions, desired the monkhood right there and spoke this verse:
"If this teaching of the Fully Enlightened One is pleasing to the venerable Sela, we too shall go forth together in the presence of the One of Excellent Wisdom."

They spoke thus because they were sons of good family who had made special aspirations together with the brahmin Sela. Then the brahmin Sela, with a heart pleased with those young men, desiring to request the monkhood while pointing them out, spoke this verse:
"O Blessed One, these three hundred brahmins request with joined palms: 'We shall lead the holy life in your presence, O Blessed One.'"
312:
Then the Blessed One, because Sela had been the leader of those three hundred men and had planted the roots of merit during the time of Padumuttara Buddha as mentioned below, and because in this final life he was born as their teacher, and because his wisdom and their wisdom had matured, and because they possessed the strong supporting condition (upanissaya) for the 'Ehi Bhikkhu' ordination—wishing to ordain all of them through the 'Ehi Bhikkhu' method—uttered this verse:

"Sela, the holy life is well-expounded (by me, the Buddha);
It is visible here and now, and immediate in its results.
In this Dispensation, for one who is diligent and trains in the three trainings,
Ordination is not in vain."

In that verse, 'sandiṭṭhika' means visible here and now. 'Akālika' means the fruit is attained without delay in time because the fruit arises immediately after the path. 'Yattha' refers to that which has a cause (the ordination caused by the holy life of the path is not without benefit). Alternatively, 'yattha' means in this Dispensation, referring to one who is diligent, not devoid of mindfulness, and trains in the three trainings.

Having spoken thus, the Blessed One said, "Come, monks (Etha, bhikkhavo)." At that very moment, they all appeared with psychic-made bowls and robes, like elders of sixty years' standing, and having respectfully prostrated to the Blessed One, they surrounded Him. Having ordained in this way and striving in the work of insight (vipassanā), Elder Sela, along with his followers, attained Arahantship on the seventh day. Concerning this, it is stated in the Apadāna:

"In the city of Haṃsavatī, I was a street master (vīthisāmī).
I gathered my relatives and spoke these words:
'The Buddha has arisen in the world, the unsurpassed field of merit;
He is the recipient of offerings for the entire world.'

Khattiyas, merchants, and Brahmins of great wealth,
With confident and joyful minds, performed communal merit.
Elephant riders, cavalry, charioteers, and infantry,
With confident and joyful minds, performed communal merit."
313:
"Famous princes, traders, and Brahmins,
With confident and joyful minds, performed communal merit.

Cooks, barbers, bath-attendants, and florists,
With confident and joyful minds, performed communal merit.

Laundrymen, weavers, leatherworkers, and barbers,
With confident and joyful minds, performed communal merit.

Arrow-makers, turners, leatherworkers, and carpenters,
With confident and joyful minds, performed communal merit.

Blacksmiths, goldsmiths, and likewise tin-smiths and copper-smiths,
With confident and joyful minds, performed communal merit.

Hired laborers, servants, and many slaves and workers,
According to their own strength, performed communal merit.

Water-carriers, wood-cutters, farmers, and grass-cutters,
According to their own strength, performed communal merit.

Flower-sellers, garland-makers, vegetable-sellers, and fruit-sellers,
According to their own strength, performed communal merit.

Courtesans, pot-carrying maids, cake-makers, and fish-sellers,
According to their own strength, performed communal merit.

'Come, friends, let us all assemble and form a group together;
We shall make offerings to the Buddha, the unsurpassed field of merit.'

Hearing my words, they formed a group at that very moment;
They had a well-constructed assembly hall (upaṭṭhāna-sālā) built for the Saṅgha of monks.

Having completed that hall, with an uplifted and joyful mind,
Surrounded by all of them, I approached the Fully Enlightened One.

Approaching the Fully Enlightened One, the Protector of the World, the Bull among Men,
And having prostrated at the Teacher's feet, I spoke these words:"
314:
"'O Heroic Buddha, these three hundred men as one group,
Hand over this well-constructed assembly hall to You, O Sage.'

'O Visionary One, please accept it in front of the Saṅgha of monks.'
In front of those three hundred men, (the Buddha) spoke these verses:

'The three hundred and their leader (Sela) have come together as one.
Having performed this merit (sampatti), you shall all enjoy its benefits.'

'When the final birth is reached, you shall experience the unsurpassed state of coolness,
The unaging, the deathless, the peaceful Nibbāna.'

Thus did the Buddha, the All-Knowing, the Supreme Ascetic, prophesy.
Hearing the Buddha's words, I felt great joy.

For thirty thousand aeons, I delighted in the celestial realm.
Five hundred times I was the lord of gods and ruled as king of gods.

A thousand times I was a Cakkavatti king.
While I was king of gods, the great gods paid homage to me.

When I ruled as king in this human realm, my followers were my kinsmen.
When the final birth was reached, there was a Brahmin named Vāseṭṭha.

He had a hoard of eighty crores of wealth; I was the son of that Brahmin.
My name was Sela, and I reached the far shore of the six limbs of the Vedas (chaḷaṅga).

While wandering on foot, surrounded by my pupils,
I saw the ascetic named Keṇiya, who bore a mass of matted hair.

Seeing the prepared offerings (sacrifice), I spoke these words:
'Is there a marriage giving a son (āvāha) or taking a daughter (vivāha), or has a king invited you?'

'I wish to perform a sacrifice and have invited Brahmins who are like gods.
I have not invited a king; I have no other sacrifice to perform.'

'I have no marriage giving a son nor taking a daughter.
(I have invited) the One who brings joy to the Sakyans, the Supreme One in the world including the gods.'"
315:
For the benefit of the entire world, bringing happiness to all beings, I have invited that Blessed One today; this preparation is for him.

Having the hue of the timbarūsaka fruit, immeasurable, incomparable, peerless in form, I have invited the Buddha for tomorrow's meal.

Like gold placed in the mouth of a furnace, like embers of khadira wood, like lightning, the Great Hero—that Buddha I have invited.

Like a flame on a mountain peak, like the full moon, resembling the color of a reed fire—that Buddha I have invited.

Fearless, beyond danger, the Sage who makes an end of existence, like a lion, the Great Hero—that Buddha I have invited.

Skilled in the qualities of a Buddha, unconquerable by others, like an elephant, the Great Hero—that Buddha I have invited.

Skilled in the practice of the True Dhamma, the peerless Buddha-elephant, like a bull, the Great Hero—that Buddha I have invited.

Of infinite beauty, of immeasurable fame, endowed with all the various marks, like Sakka, the Great Hero—that Buddha I have invited.

A master of himself, a leader of a group, majestic, powerful, difficult to approach, like Brahma, the Great Hero—that Buddha I have invited.

One who has attained the Dhamma, possessing the Ten Powers, who has reached the far shore of supreme power, like the earth, the Great Hero—that Buddha I have invited.

Abounding with the waves of virtue, stirred by the knowledge of the Dhamma, like the ocean, the Great Hero—that Buddha I have invited.

Difficult to approach, unconquerable, unshakable, lofty and vast, like Mount Neru, the Great Hero—that Buddha I have invited.

Of infinite knowledge, equal to the unequaled, peerless, reached the highest state, like the sky, the Great Hero—that Buddha I have invited.
316:
The support for those terrified by fear, the protection for those who go for refuge, the giver of relief, the Great Hero—that Buddha I have invited.

The abode of the wise, the field of merit for those seeking happiness, the mine of jewels, the Great Hero—that Buddha I have invited.

The giver of relief, the producer of joy, the giver of the fruits of recluseship, like a cloud, the Great Hero—that Buddha I have invited.

The eye of the world, of great majesty, the dispeller of all darkness, like the sun, the Great Hero—that Buddha I have invited.

The Sage who sees the true nature in sense objects and liberations, like the moon, the Great Hero—that Buddha I have invited.

The Buddha, supreme in the world, adorned with the marks, immeasurable, the Great Hero—that Buddha I have invited.

He whose knowledge is immeasurable, whose virtue is incomparable, whose liberation is peerless—that Buddha I have invited.

He whose fortitude is peerless, whose strength is inconceivable, whose effort is supreme—that Buddha I have invited.

He by whom all the poisons of greed, hatred, and delusion have been uprooted, like medicine, the Great Hero—that Buddha I have invited.

The dispeller of the disease of defilements and many sufferings, and of all darkness, like a physician, the Great Hero—that Buddha I have invited.

O Keniya, you speak this word 'Buddha'; that sound is very rare in the world. Just by hearing 'Buddha, Buddha,' rapture has arisen within me.

My rapture, unable to be contained within, overflows to the outside. With a mind full of rapture, I spoke these words in tranquility:

Where is that Blessed One, the supreme in the world, the bull among men? I shall go there and pay homage to the Buddha, the giver of the fruits of recluseship.
317:
Raising my right arm and joyfully placing my hands in prayer (añjali), please tell me of the Great King of Dhamma, the dispeller of the dart of sorrow.

Look at this great forest, dark blue like a rising rain cloud, resembling collyrium, and appearing like the ocean.

In this forest dwells the Buddha, the Sage who tames the untamed, disciplining those to be trained and enlightening them in the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma).

Like a thirsty person seeking water, like a hungry person seeking food, and like a cow longing for her calf, I searched for the Victorious One (Jina).

Skilled in conduct and etiquette, teaching his disciples the restraint appropriate to the Dhamma, they go to the presence of the Victor.

Buddhas are difficult to approach, wandering alone like lions. O youths, come placing footstep upon footstep.

Like a fierce poisonous cobra, like a maned lion king, and like a rutting tusker elephant, thus Buddhas are difficult to approach.

O youths, restraining even coughing and sneezing, placing footstep upon footstep, approach the presence of the Buddha.

Buddhas value seclusion, are quiet, difficult to approach, hard to reach, and are honored in the world including the devas.

When I ask a question or exchange greetings, remain quiet and stay silent like sages.

Whatever Dhamma the Buddha teaches for the attainment of Nibbāna, the secure place, listen attentively to its meaning; hearing the True Dhamma is blissful.

Approaching the Buddha, I exchanged greetings with the Sage. After exchanging greetings, I examined the Great Marks.

Although I saw thirty of the Great Marks, I had doubts about two. Then the Sage, through psychic power, showed the mark of the male organ enclosed in a sheath (kosohitavatthaguyha).
318:
(The Buddha) extended his tongue and touched both ear-holes and both nostrils. He also covered his entire forehead (with his tongue).

Seeing the Great Marks along with the minor characteristics (anubyañjana) of the Buddha, I decided "He is truly the Buddha" and went forth (ordained) with my disciples.

Together with three hundred followers, I entered the homeless life. Before half a month (fifteen days) had passed, all of us attained Nibbāna.

Having performed meritorious deeds together in the unsurpassed field of merit, and having wandered together (in Saṃsāra), we were liberated from the suffering of the round (vaṭṭa) together.

By offering rafters (gopānasi), I delighted in the Dhamma of the group (pūga-dhamma). Due to that well-performed deed, I receive eight benefits.

I am honored in all directions, and my possessions are immeasurable. I am a refuge and support for all; I have no fear.

I have no diseases and I maintain a long life. I have delicate skin and live in desired dwellings.

By offering eight rafters, I delighted in the Dhamma of the group. The fruit of Arahatship along with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) is my eighth benefit.

O Great Sage, who has reached the end of all, who has done what was to be done, who is free from taints (anāsava), your son is named Aṭṭhagopānasī.

By offering five pillars, I delighted in the Dhamma of the group. Due to that well-performed merit, I receive five benefits.

Because of loving-kindness (mettā), I am unshakable and have no physical defects. My words are accepted by others, and no one can destroy me.

My mind is steady and unshakable, and I am free from malice toward anyone. Due to that well-performed deed, I am pure in the Dispensation (Sāsana).

Respectful, deferential, having done what was to be done, free from taints, O Great Hero, your disciple monk pays homage to you, O Sage.
319:
Having made a well-crafted couch (pallaṅka), I prepared it in the hall. Due to that well-performed deed, I obtained five benefits.

Having been born into a high family, I became one of great wealth. I am endowed with all successes. Stinginess does not exist in me.

When I wish to go, the couch appears before me. Together with that noble couch, I go to wherever I desire.

Because of that gift of a couch, I have dispelled all darkness (ignorance). The Elder, having attained the power of all direct knowledges, pays homage to the Buddha.

I have accomplished all tasks, both for others and for myself. Due to that well-performed deed, I have entered the city of Nibbāna, which is free from danger.

In the well-completed hall, I donated requisites. Due to that well-performed deed, I have attained the state of excellence.

In this world, those who are tamers tame elephants and horses. They tame them harshly, using various means of torture.

O Great Hero, the Buddha, You do not tame men and women in such a way. Without using a rod or a weapon, You tame them with the supreme taming.

Praising the virtues of giving, the Buddha, skilled in teaching, enlightened three hundred people just by answering a single question.

Being tamed by the Buddha, the Charioteer, we are well-liberated from defilements. We are free from taints (āsavas). Having attained the power of all direct knowledges, we are cooled in Nibbāna, where the substrates of existence (upadhi) are exhausted.

In the hundred thousandth aeon from this one, I gave that gift. Since then, all dangers have been overcome. This is the fruit of the gift of the hall.

My defilements have been burned away. ... [as before] ... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.

Having attained Arahantship, he approached the Buddha and, wishing to declare his attainment of Arahantship, said:

'O Blessed One, endowed with the five eyes, on the eighth day from today, we took refuge in the Triple Gem, and within seven nights, we have become tamed in Your Dispensation.'
320:
He spoke the verse. The meaning of that verse is: "O Blessed One, endowed with the five eyes, on the eighth day from today, we took refuge in the Triple Gem. Therefore, within seven nights, being tamed in Your Dispensation, we have become disciplined. Oh, how wonderful is the power of Your being the true refuge!" Furthermore:

"You alone are the Buddha; You alone are the Teacher; You are the Sage (Muni) who has conquered the five Māras. Having cut off the underlying tendencies (anusaya), You have crossed over Yourself and have helped this generation of beings to cross over.

"You have well-transcended the substrates of existence (upadhi); You have destroyed the taints (āsavas). Like a lion, free from grasping, You have abandoned all fear and dread." (Thus he praised).

After praising with these two verses, he requested permission to pay homage to the Buddha with the final verse:

"O Heroic Buddha, these three hundred bhikkhus stand with hands joined in reverence. Please stretch out Your feet; let these noble ones (nāgas) pay homage to the Teacher's feet."

In that verse, 'Tuvaṃ Buddho' means: "You alone are the Omniscient Buddha in this world." Because You instruct beings regarding their welfare in the present life and so on, You alone are called 'Satthā' (Teacher). Because You have conquered all Māras, You are called 'Mārābhibhū'. Because of Your state as a Sage, You are called 'Muni'. 'Anusaye chetvā' means cutting off the underlying tendencies such as sensual lust with the sword of the Noble Path. 'Tiṇṇo' means having crossed over the flood of saṃsāra oneself, and helping this generation of beings to cross over with the hand of the Dhamma teaching. 'Upadhī' refers to all substrates of existence, such as the substrates of the aggregates (khandhūpadhi). 'Anupādāno' means having completely abandoned grasping such as sensual grasping (kāmupādāna). Having spoken thus, the Elder Sela, together with his followers, paid homage to the Buddha.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Sela Thera is finished.

## 7. Commentary on the Verses of Bhaddiya Thera, the Son of Kāḷigodhā

The verses beginning with 'Yātaṃ me hatthigīvāya' are the verses of the Venerable Bhaddiya Thera. As for the background: This Elder also had performed meritorious deeds (adhikāra) under previous Buddhas. In the time of the Buddha Padumuttara, he was born into a family of great wealth. Upon reaching maturity, one day while listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Buddha, he saw the Buddha appoint a certain bhikkhu to the foremost position among those of noble birth. He also desired that position and, for seven days, he offered a great donation (mahādāna) to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha and made his aspiration. The Buddha, seeing that his aspiration would be fulfilled without obstacle, gave him the prophecy. Having heard that prophecy, he performed many meritorious deeds that lead to birth in a noble family, such as listening to the Dhamma, donating a dwelling place at the Dhamma pavilion, donating fans, making offerings to Dhamma preachers, and donating resting places at the Uposatha hall, throughout his life. After passing away from that life, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans. In the interval between the Buddha Kassapa and our Buddha, he was born into a householder's family in the city of Bārāṇasī. Seeing a Paccekabuddha who went for alms and ate in a single place, he prepared stone slabs in that place, provided water for washing the feet, and served him for the rest of his life.
321:
Seeing a monk being placed in the foremost position among those of high birth, he also aspired to that position. He gave a great offering (mahādāna) for seven days to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha and made a resolution. The Teacher, seeing that his resolution would be fulfilled without obstacle, gave him a prophecy. Having heard that prophecy, he asked about the actions leading to birth in a high family. He performed many meritorious deeds throughout his life, such as arranging for the hearing of the Dhamma, providing seats in the Dhamma pavilion, offering fans, making offerings and paying respect to Dhamma preachers, and providing shelter in the Uposatha hall. After passing away from that life, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans. In the interval after the time of Kassapa Buddha and before the appearance of our Buddha, he was reborn in a householder's family in Bārāṇasī. Seeing many Paccekabuddhas wandering for alms and gathering in one place to partake of their meal, he served them throughout his life by spreading stone slabs and providing water for washing their feet.

Having wandered through the realms of devas and humans for one Buddha-interval, he was reborn in the Sakyan royal family in the city of Kapilavatthu during the time of this Buddha's appearance, and was named Bhaddiya. When he came of age, he went forth in the presence of the Teacher while the Teacher was staying at the Anupiya Mango Grove, along with five other princes including Anuruddha, and attained Arahantship. Later, while the Teacher was seated in the midst of the assembly of Noble Ones at Jetavana Monastery, He placed the Elder Bhaddiya in the foremost position among monks of high birth. That Elder, spending his time in the bliss of fruition (phala-samāpatti) and the bliss of Nibbāna, would frequently utter the inspired exclamation, "Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!" whether he was in the forest, at the foot of a tree, or in an empty dwelling. Hearing this, the monks reported to the Teacher: "Venerable Bhaddiya, the son of Kāḷigodhā, is frequently saying, 'Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!' We think he is living the holy life without delight." The Teacher had the Elder summoned and asked, "Bhaddiya, is it true that you frequently say, 'Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!'?" The Elder admitted, "It is true, Blessed One," and then explained, "Venerable Sir, formerly when I was ruling as a king, I had guards well-arranged, yet I lived in fear, anxiety, and suspicion. But now, having gone forth, I live without fear, without anxiety, and without suspicion." He then said:

I used to ride on the neck of an elephant, and I wore delicate clothes.
I used to eat rice made from hill-paddy, flavored with pure meat broth.
322:
Now that Bhaddiya is virtuous and diligent, delighting in the food obtained in his alms-bowl.
Bhaddiya, the son of Princess Kāḷigodhā, meditates free from the four attachments, in the attainment of fruition.

Practicing the refuse-rag wearer's ascetic practice (paṃsukūla dhutaṅga), being diligent,
He delights in the food obtained in his alms-bowl.
Bhaddiya, the son of Princess Kāḷigodhā, meditates free from the four attachments, in the attainment of fruition.

Practicing the alms-food eater's ascetic practice (piṇḍapāta dhutaṅga), being diligent...

Practicing the three-robe wearer's ascetic practice (tecīvarika dhutaṅga), being diligent...

Practicing the uninterrupted alms-round ascetic practice (sapadānacārika dhutaṅga), being diligent...

Practicing the one-session eater's ascetic practice (ekāsanika dhutaṅga), being diligent...

Practicing the bowl-food eater's ascetic practice (pattapiṇḍika dhutaṅga), being diligent...

Practicing the refusing-later-food ascetic practice (khalupacchābhattika dhutaṅga), being diligent...

Practicing the forest dweller's ascetic practice (āraññika dhutaṅga), being diligent...

Practicing the tree-root dweller's ascetic practice (rukkhamūlika dhutaṅga), being diligent...

Practicing the open-air dweller's ascetic practice (abbhokāsika dhutaṅga), being diligent...

Practicing the charnel-ground dweller's ascetic practice (sosānika dhutaṅga), being diligent...

Practicing the any-bed-user's ascetic practice (yathāsanthatika dhutaṅga), being diligent...

Practicing the sitter's ascetic practice (nesajjika dhutaṅga), being diligent...

Being one of few wishes and being diligent...

Being easily contented and being diligent...

Living in seclusion and being diligent...

Not associating with people and being diligent...
323:
One who constantly strives in the happiness of the present life through the undertaking of the sitting practice (nesajjika-dhutaṅga), fewness of wishes, contentment, seclusion, non-association with people, and exerted effort... (and so forth).

Having abandoned the golden bowl worth a hundred [units] and decorated with gold, I took up an earthen bowl. This is my second consecration.

In the palace with high walls, strong watchtowers, and gates, I lived in the supreme palace surrounded by those with swords in hand.

Now, that same I, without fear, having abandoned all dread and terror, Bhaddiya, the son of Kāḷigodhā, having entered the forest, dwells meditating in the bliss of the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti).

Established in the aggregate of virtue, developing mindfulness and insight-wisdom, I have reached in due order Nibbāna, the destruction of all fetters.

With these verses, he roared a lion's roar (sīhanāda) in the presence of the Teacher.

In those verses, the phrase 'I went by the neck of an elephant' means: Venerable Sir, in the past, when I traveled, I sat and moved about on the neck or the back of an elephant. When wearing clothes, I wore special Kāsika cloths that were delicate and pleasant to the touch. When eating rice, I ate the scented Sāli rice that was three years old, poured over with pure meat curries such as partridge and deer. Even though I had such happiness, that happiness did not please my mind as much as the happiness of seclusion (viveka-sukha) which I have obtained now. To show this, he spoke the words beginning with 'So'jja bhaddo'. Here, by mentioning the elephant, vehicles such as horses and chariots are also included; by mentioning clothes, all royal ornaments are included; and by mentioning rice, all varieties of food are included.

'So'jja' should be analyzed as 'so ajja' (he today), meaning one who is now established in the monkhood. 'Bhaddo' means an excellent person because of being endowed with virtues such as morality (sīla). 'Sātatiko' means one who constantly strives in the Dhamma of a recluse and in the happiness of the present life. 'Uñchāpattāgate rato' means one who delights in the alms-food received in the bowl by wandering from house to house, meaning he is content with just that food. 'Jhāyati' means meditating with the jhāna of the attainment of fruition. 'Putto Godhāya' means the son of the princess named Kāḷigodhā.
