'Bhaddiya' is the name of this Elder, who speaks of himself as if he were another person.

He is a 'rag-robe wearer' (paṃsukūlika) because he rejected robes offered by householders and undertook the ascetic practice of wearing rag-robes. He is an 'alms-food eater' (piṇḍapātika) because he rejected communal meals (saṅghabhatta) and undertook the ascetic practice of eating alms-food. He is a 'triple-robe wearer' (tecīvarika) because he rejected extra robes and undertook the ascetic practice of using only three robes. He is an 'uninterrupted alms-goer' (sapadānacārika) because he rejected wandering greedily and undertook the ascetic practice of wandering from house to house in order.
324:
He is a 'triple-robe wearer' (tecīvarika) because he rejected extra robes and undertook the ascetic practice of using only three robes. He is an 'uninterrupted alms-goer' (sapadānacārika) because he rejected wandering greedily and undertook the ascetic practice of wandering from house to house in order. He is a 'one-sessioner' (ekāsanika) because he rejected eating in various places and undertook the ascetic practice of eating in one sitting. He is a 'bowl-food eater' (pattapiṇḍika) because he rejected a second vessel and undertook the ascetic practice of eating from only one bowl. He is a 'refuser of later food' (khalupacchābhattika) because he rejected extra food and undertook the ascetic practice of not eating after the meal. He is a 'forest-dweller' (āraññika) because he rejected village monasteries near the village and undertook the ascetic practice of living in the forest. He is a 'tree-root dweller' (rukkhamūlika) because he rejected living in sheltered places and undertook the ascetic practice of living at the foot of a tree. He is an 'open-air dweller' (abbhokāsika) because he rejected sheltered tree-roots and undertook the ascetic practice of living in the open air. He is a 'charnel-ground dweller' (sosānika) because he rejected places that are not cemeteries and undertook the ascetic practice of living in a cemetery. He is an 'any-bed user' (yathāsanthatika) because he rejected greed for lodgings and undertook the ascetic practice of staying in whatever place is assigned. He is a 'sitter' (nesajjika) because he rejected lying down and undertook the ascetic practice of remaining only in a sitting posture. This is a brief summary here. For a detailed explanation, the account of the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga-kathā) should be taken as stated in the Visuddhimagga.

'Uccae' means high, either because of being in a high place or because of being on the upper floor of a palace. 'Maṇḍalipākāre' means surrounded by walls of a circular shape. 'Daḷhamṭṭālakakoṭṭhake' means in a city endowed with firm watchtowers and gatehouses.

In the phrase 'satiṃ paññañca', by using mindfulness as the head, concentration (samādhi) is also meant. The phrase 'developing mindfulness and wisdom' is spoken with reference to the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti) and the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). The remaining words are clear in meaning as they follow the methods already explained in various places.

Thus, the Elder roared a lion's roar with a bold voice in the presence of the Teacher. Having heard those words, the monks were greatly inspired.

## The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Bhaddiya, the Son of Kāḷigodhā, is Finished.

## 8. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Aṅgulimāla

The verses beginning with 'Gacchaṃ vadesi' are those of the Venerable Elder Aṅgulimāla. What is the background story? This Elder also had performed meritorious deeds (adhikāra) under previous Buddhas and, having accumulated wholesome roots that are the support for liberation from the cycle of rebirths (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) in various lives, was reborn in this Buddha-era in Sāvatthī as the son of the Brahmin named Bhaggava, the chaplain of King Kosala. On the day he was born, all the weapons in the entire city glowed with light. The royal auspicious weapon kept near the King's bed also glowed. Seeing the weapons glowing, the King was terrified and unable to sleep. At that time, the chaplain examined the alignment of the stars and concluded that the child was born under the 'thief star' (cora-nakkhatta). When the night turned to dawn, the Brahmin chaplain went to the King and asked if he had slept well. The King replied, 'Teacher, how could I sleep well? My auspicious weapon glowed; what will be the consequence of such an event?' The chaplain said, 'Great King, do not be afraid. A son was born in my house; it is because of that child's power that the weapons throughout the city glowed.' The King asked, 'Teacher, what kind of person will that child become?' He replied, 'He will become a thief.' 'A lone thief or the leader of a gang of thieves?' the King asked. 'Great King, he will be only a lone thief,' he replied. 'Should the child be killed?' the King then asked.
325:
On the day of the child's birth, weapons throughout the entire city blazed and glowed. The King's ceremonial state weapon, kept at the head of his bed, also blazed and glowed. Seeing the blazing of that weapon, the King was terrified and shaken, and could not find sleep. At that time, the royal chaplain, observing the conjunction of the constellations, concluded: "He is born under the thief constellation."

When the night had turned to dawn, the chaplain went to the King and inquired if he had slept well. The King replied, "Teacher, how could I have slept well? During the night, my ceremonial weapon blazed and glowed. What will be the consequence of such an occurrence?" The chaplain said, "Do not be afraid, Great King. A son was born in my house. It was due to his power that the weapons throughout the entire city blazed." "Teacher, what will he become?" the King asked. "The boy will become a thief," he replied. "Will he be a lone thief or a leader of a gang?" the King asked again. "Great King, he will be a lone thief," he answered. When asked, "Should we kill him?", the chaplain replied, "If he is to be a lone thief, please look after him for now."

When they named the child, because he was born causing distress to the King's mind, they named him "Hiṃsaka" (The Harmer). Later, treating what was seen as if it were unseen, they called him "Ahiṃsaka" (The Harmless).

When he reached maturity, by the power of his past merit, he possessed the strength of seven elephants. This was his past merit: In a world empty of Buddhas, he was born as a farmer. Seeing a Paccekabuddha whose robes were soaked by rainwater and who was afflicted by the cold approaching his field, he felt joyful, thinking, "My field of merit has arrived," and he prepared a fire and offered it. By the power of that deed, in every life he was born into, he was endowed with great strength and speed, and in this final existence, he possessed the strength of seven elephants.

That Ahiṃsaka went to Takkasilā and became a resident pupil under a world-renowned teacher. While learning the arts, he respectfully attended to the Brahmin teacher and his wife. Because of this, the Brahmin's wife favored him with food and other necessities available in the house. Unable to endure this favor, other students slandered him to create a rift with the teacher. Although the Brahmin did not believe their words for two or three times, he eventually believed them and thought, "This young man is extremely strong; no one is able to kill him. I will kill him by a trick." When Ahiṃsaka, having finished his studies, asked permission to return to his own city, the teacher said: "Dear Ahiṃsaka, a pupil who has finished his studies must give a supreme teacher's fee (guru-dakkhiṇā) to his teacher. Give that to me." "Very well, teacher. What shall I give?" he asked. "Bring me one thousand right-hand index fingers of human beings," the teacher said. It is said that the Brahmin's intention was that while he was killing many people, someone would surely kill Ahiṃsaka.

Upon hearing these words, Ahiṃsaka, putting foremost the ruthlessness he had long practiced, equipped himself with the five kinds of weapons and entered the Jālinī forest in the kingdom of King Kosala. Staying in a mountain pass near the main highway...
326:
...thinking, "He should be killed." Hearing those words, Ahiṃsaka, prioritizing the ruthlessness he had long cultivated, equipped himself with the five kinds of weapons and entered the Jālinī forest in the territory of the King of Kosala. Living in a mountain pass near the highway, he would stand on the mountain peak, watch for people traveling along the road, rush down with speed, take their fingers, and hang them on the branches of trees. Vultures and crows ate those fingers, and those that fell to the ground rotted away. Thus, as the count could not be completed, he strung together whatever fingers he obtained with a thread, made a garland, and hung it over his shoulder like a sacrificial offering. From then on, he became known by the name "Aṅgulimāla" (Garland of Fingers).

As he continued to kill people in this manner, the road became deserted and unused. When he could not find people on the highway, he went to the outskirts of villages, hid himself, and killed whoever came by to take their fingers. Knowing this, people fled from the villages, and the villages became empty; likewise the market towns and the countryside. Thus, because of him, that region became desolate and terror-stricken. For Aṅgulimāla, the collection of one thousand fingers was nearly complete, with only one finger missing. Then, the people reported this danger from the thief to King Kosala. Early in the morning, the King had the drums sounded throughout the city, announcing, "Let us quickly capture the thief Aṅgulimāla; let the army come forth."

Hearing this, Aṅgulimāla's mother, a Brahmin woman named Mantāṇī, said to his father, "They say your son has become a thief and is doing such and such things. Go and persuade him, saying 'Do not do such things,' and bring him back. Otherwise, the King will kill him." The Brahmin replied, "I have no need for such a son; let the King do as he pleases." Then the Brahmin woman, out of love for her son, took provisions and set out on the road, thinking, "I will persuade my son and bring him back."

The Blessed One perceived: "This Brahmin woman is going, thinking 'I will bring Aṅgulimāla back.' If she goes, Aṅgulimāla, thinking 'I will complete the thousand fingers,' will kill even his mother. And he is one in his final birth (pacchimabhavika). If I do not go, there will be a great loss." Knowing this, after his meal, having returned from the alms round, he took his bowl and robes and set out on foot on the thirty-yojana journey intended for Aṅgulimāla. Although he was warned by cowherds and others along the way, he reached the Jālinī forest. At that moment, he was seen by his mother. Seeing his mother from afar, he thought, "I will kill even my mother and complete the missing finger today," and raising his sword, he ran towards her.
327:
The Blessed One manifested himself between the mother and the son. When Aṅgulimāla saw the Blessed One, he thought, "What benefit is there for me in killing my mother to take a finger? Let my mother live. It would be better if I were to take the life of this recluse and take his finger." Thus, with his sword raised, he followed closely behind the Blessed One. Then, the Blessed One performed such a feat of psychic power that Aṅgulimāla, though running with all his might, was unable to catch up with the Blessed One, who was walking at a normal pace. 

That Aṅgulimāla, losing his speed, breathing heavily, with sweat pouring from his armpits, and unable to lift even a single foot, stood still like a tree stump and said to the Blessed One, "Stop, stop, recluse!" The Blessed One, while still walking, said, "Aṅgulimāla, I have stopped; you should stop too."

Aṅgulimāla thought, "These recluses, sons of the Sakyans, are speakers of truth. Yet this recluse, while walking, says, 'Aṅgulimāla, I have stopped; you should stop too.' I, however, am standing still. What is the meaning of this statement? I shall ask him to find out." Thinking thus, he addressed the Blessed One in verse:

"While walking, recluse, you say 'I have stopped,' and to me who is standing, you say 'not stopped.' I ask you, recluse, about this matter: How is it that you have stopped and I have not stopped?"

In that verse, "samaṇā" is an address to the Blessed One. "Mama" means me. "Kathaṃ" means in what manner. The meaning here is: Recluse, while you are walking, you say "I have stopped." And to me who is standing, you say "not stopped." There must be a reason for this; therefore, I ask the recluse about this matter. In what manner have you stopped and I have not stopped? When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One addressed him in verse:

"Aṅgulimāla, I have stopped forever, having laid aside the rod towards all beings. But you are unrestrained towards living beings; therefore, I have stopped and you have not stopped."
328:
Regarding that verse: "Aṅgulimāla, I have stopped forever, having laid aside the rod towards all beings" means, Aṅgulimāla, at all times—in the beginning, middle, and end—towards all beings, both those who tremble and those who are firm, I have laid aside the rod. I have laid down the rod, laid down the weapon, I am conscientious and compassionate. Because I do not act otherwise, I have stopped in this very manner. "But you are unrestrained towards living beings" means you are without restraint towards beings; you are cruel, with bloody hands, engaged in killing and striking, and without compassion. Because of such lack of restraint, you are said to be "not stopped" in terms of abstinence (virati). For that very reason, because you wander through various destinations (gati), even though you are now standing still in your physical posture, you are "not stopped." I, however, have stopped in the manner described.

Then, because Aṅgulimāla had previously heard of the fame of the Blessed One, which pervaded the entire world like oil on the surface of water, and because of his perfection of causes and the ripening of his knowledge, he experienced joy and happiness, thinking, "This is the Blessed One." He thought, "This is a great lion's roar, a great thunder; this cannot belong to anyone else. I think this is the roar of the recluse Gotama. Indeed, I have been seen by the Great Sage, the Fully Enlightened One. The Blessed One has come here for the purpose of helping me." Thinking thus, he recited this verse:

"Indeed, after a long time, the Great Sage, the recluse honored by the world, has entered the great forest for my sake. Having heard your verse endowed with Dhamma, I shall renounce my thousandfold evil."

In that verse, "cirassaṃ vata" means indeed after a long time. "Me" means for the sake of helping me. "Mahito" means honored with great offerings by the world including the devas. "Mahesi" means one who seeks great qualities such as the aggregate of virtue. "Mahāvanaṃ samaṇော paccapādi" means the Blessed One, who has stilled all evil, has entered this great forest. "Sohaṃ cajissāmi sahassapāpaṃ sutvāna gāthaṃ tava dhammayuttaṃ" means I have heard your verse which is endowed with Dhamma and associated with Dhamma. Having heard it, I thought, "I shall abandon the thousandfold evil accumulated over a long time," and the meaning is that I shall now certainly renounce it. To show how he practiced after saying this, and how he was helped by the Blessed One:
329:
Thus, the robber Aṅgulimāla threw his sword and other weapons into a chasm with steep sides all around, a precipice with a steep side on one part, and a pit which was a gaping hole in the ground.

That robber Aṅgulimāla bowed at the feet of the Sugata, the Blessed One, and requested ordination from the Buddha right there.

Indeed, the Great Sage, possessed of great compassion, who is the Teacher of the world including the devas, then said to him, 'Come, monk.' That very 'Ehi bhikkhu' (Come, monk) status became his monkhood.

The Elders who recited the scriptures (Saṅgītikāras) placed these two verses.

In those verses, 'Icc-eva' means having spoken thus and immediately after. 'Coro' refers to Aṅgulimāla. 'Asiṃ' means a sword. 'Āvudhaṃ' means the remaining weapons. 'Sobbhe' means in a chasm with steep sides all around. 'Papāte' means in a precipice with a steep side on one part. 'Narake' means in a pit which is a gaping hole in the ground. In this context, by all three terms, it refers only to a mountain gorge of such a nature that it is impossible for another person to retrieve what has fallen there. 'Anvakāsi' means he did so in succession; it means he threw away and discarded his five kinds of weapons one after another. Having discarded those weapons, he prostrated himself at the feet of the Blessed One and said, 'Venerable Sir, please grant me ordination.' Therefore, it is said, 'The robber bowed at the feet of the Sugata, and requested ordination from the Buddha right there.' When he had thus requested ordination, the Teacher, looking at his past deeds and seeing the perfection of the causes for the 'Ehi bhikkhu' status, stretched out his right hand and said, 'Come, monk; well-expounded is the Dhamma. Live the holy life for the complete ending of suffering.' That very invitation became his novice ordination and higher ordination. Therefore, it is said, 'He then said to him, "Come, monk"; that very thing was his monkhood.'

Thus, the Elder Aṅgulimāla, having received novice and higher ordination through the 'Ehi bhikkhu' status in the presence of the Teacher, and while practicing the work of insight (vipassanā), attained Arahantship. While experiencing the bliss of liberation (vimuttisukha), being filled with joy and gladness, he uttered these inspired verses:

'Whoever was formerly negligent, but later is not negligent,
Illuminates this world like the moon freed from a cloud.'
330:
'Whoever covers the evil deed he has done with wholesome action,
Illuminates this world like the moon freed from a cloud.

Indeed, the young monk who applies himself to the Buddha's Dispensation,
Illuminates this world like the moon freed from a cloud.'

He spoke these three verses. The meaning of those verses is: whatever person, whether a householder or one ordained, who was formerly negligent and fell into negligence regarding right practice—either due to association with bad friends or due to one's own lack of reflection—but later, through association with noble friends (kalyāṇamitta), emerges with wise reflection and is not negligent, but practices rightly; while applying himself to tranquility and insight (samatha-vipassanā), he attains the three knowledges (vijjā) and the six direct knowledges (abhiññā). That person, like the moon freed from clouds and so forth, illuminates this world of the five aggregates with the knowledges and direct knowledges he has attained, just as the moon illuminates the world of space.

For whatever person the evil deed performed and accumulated is covered—that is, obstructed—by the supramundane wholesome (lokuttara-kusala) which brings about the destruction of kamma, because it has been brought to a state of being unable to produce a result, thus closing the door to the arising of its result. The rest is as previously explained. 'Daharo' means young; by this, he shows that his body is fit for spiritual exertion. For such a person is able to practice meditation by overcoming the dangers of wind and heat that arise. 'Yuñjati buddhasāsane' means he is devoted and applied to the three trainings (sikkhā) in the Buddha's Dispensation, and he fulfills them respectfully.

Thus, the Elder Aṅgulimāla, being filled with joy and gladness and dwelling in the bliss of liberation, when he entered the city for alms, a clod of earth thrown by someone fell on the Elder's body, and a stick thrown by another fell on his body. He would return to the monastery with a broken bowl and go to the presence of the Teacher. The Teacher would admonish him: 'Endure it, Brahmin! Endure it, Brahmin! You are experiencing in this very life, Brahmin, the result of the deed for which you might have been boiled in hell for many thousands of years.' Then the Elder, having established a mind of loving-kindness toward all beings without exception—
331:
May even my enemies hear the discourse on the Dhamma; may even my enemies devote themselves to the Buddha's Dispensation (to realize the Four Noble Truths). May those who are my enemies associate with the virtuous ones who establish others in wholesome Dhamma.

May my enemies hear the Dhamma at the proper time from those who preach patience and praise loving-kindness that is free from enmity, and may they follow and practice accordingly.

May such an enemy never harm me or any other being. Having reached the supreme peace of Nibbāna, may they protect all beings (like their own disciples).

Irrigators lead the water; fletchers shape the arrow; carpenters carve the wood; even so, the wise tame themselves.

Some tame with sticks, hooks, and whips. But I was tamed by the Exalted One, who is unshaken by the worldly conditions, without stick or weapon.

My name was 'Hiṃsaka' (Harmer) when I was a harmer in the past. Today I am 'Ahiṃsaka' (Non-harmer), a name that is now true, for I do not harm anyone.

In the past, I was a notorious bandit known as Aṅgulimāla. While being swept away by the great flood, I went to the Buddha for refuge.

In the past, I was the notorious Aṅgulimāla with blood-stained hands. Behold the benefit of taking refuge! The craving that leads to rebirth has been uprooted.

Having committed many such evil deeds that lead to states of misery, I now experience only the [remaining] results of kamma and eat my food free from debt.

Fools and the witless devote themselves to negligence. The wise man guards diligence as his greatest treasure.

Do not devote yourselves to negligence; do not indulge in sensual pleasures. For the diligent one, meditating, attains supreme happiness.
332:
The Buddha's coming to me was a welcome one, not an unwelcome one; it was not a poorly conceived thought of mine. Among the diverse Dhammas that have been analyzed, I have attained that which is the most excellent (Nibbāna).

The Buddha's coming to me was a welcome one, not an unwelcome one; it was not a poorly conceived thought of mine. The three knowledges have been attained; the Buddha's Dispensation has been fulfilled.

In the past, as a layman, whether in the forest, at the foot of a tree, on mountains, or in mountain caves, I lived with a terrified mind in those various places.

But now, I sleep in peace, I stand in peace, and I live my life in peace. I am free from the snare of Māra. Oh, how wonderful is the compassion of the Teacher towards beings!

In the past, I was born into a noble Brahmin family, high-born on both sides. Today, I am a son of the Sugata, the Teacher, the King of Dhamma.

Free from craving, without clinging, with guarded sense-doors and well-restrained, I have destroyed ignorance, the root of suffering, and have reached the destruction of the taints.

I have served the Teacher; the Buddha's Dispensation has been fulfilled. The heavy burden has been laid down; the craving that leads to rebirth has been uprooted." Thus he spoke these verses.

In those verses, "Disāpi" means even my enemies and adversaries who revile me, saying, "Just as we suffer the pain of separation from relatives because of Aṅgulimāla, may Aṅgulimāla also suffer." "Me dhammakathaṃ suṇantu" means may they hear the discourse connected with the Four Noble Truths that I heard from the Teacher. "Yuñjantu" means having heard it, may they practice for the sake of the Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna. "Te manuje bhajantu" means may they associate with and serve such virtuous ones and good friends (kalyāṇamitta). "Ye dhammam-evādapayanti santo" means those virtuous ones who establish and cause others to take up only wholesome Dhamma and supramundane Dhamma.

"Khantivādānaṃ" means of those who usually speak only of patient endurance (adhivāsana-khanti). Therefore, "Avirodhappasaṃsinaṃ" means may they hear (the Dhamma) of those who usually praise only loving-kindness (metta) which is not in conflict with anyone—
333:
Let them listen to the Dhamma in their presence at the appropriate time. 'Let them also follow that Dhamma' means that they should follow it by practicing the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma, having well-learned and memorized that Dhamma as it was heard.

Even if that person is my enemy, may he certainly not harm me, may he not oppress me. 'Or any other person' means may he not harm any other being, not just me. 'Having reached the supreme peace' means may he reach the supreme, highest peace, Nibbāna; and having reached it, may he protect all beings, those who tremble and those who are firm, with the highest protection, like a disciple or a son.

Thus, the Elder Aṅgulimāla, while liberating others from evil with these verses and performing what is called a protection (paritta), spoke the verse beginning with 'Water-carriers lead...' to manifest his own practice. In that verse, water-carriers lead water to their desired place by digging the high ground and filling the low ground, or by making a channel, or by placing a wooden trough. 'Tejanaṃ' means an arrow. The meaning is: water-carriers lead water according to their wish; fletchers also tame the arrow by heating it and removing its crookedness, making it straight; carpenters also tame wood for the sake of rims and so on, making it straight or crooked according to their wish. Making such an object their basis, wise people, generating the Noble Path (Ariya Magga), tame themselves; those who have reached Arahatship are indeed called those who are absolutely tamed.

Now, the Teacher, who is the Incomparable Trainer of persons to be tamed (Purisadammasārathi), spoke five verses beginning with 'Some tame with a stick...' to manifest the manner in which he tamed himself and his gratitude. In those verses, 'Some tame with a stick' means kings, great ministers, and others tame enemies and so on with a stick and with an army of elephants, horses, and so on; cowherds and others tame cows and so on with a stick or a staff. Elephant trainers tame elephants with hooks; horse trainers tame horses with whips. 'I am tamed without a stick or a weapon' means I have been tamed and have become one who is tamed, free from poison, by the Fully Enlightened One who has reached the state of 'tādi' (equanimity) towards desirable objects and so on, without a stick, without a weapon, and by the state of having laid down the stick and the weapon.
334:
'Ahiṃsaka' is my name. In the past, before meeting the Teacher, while being a harmer (hiṃsaka), I had only the name 'Ahiṃsaka' (Non-harmer). But now, I am one whose name 'Ahiṃsaka' is true and unerring. Therefore, I do not harm any being, I do not oppress them. The word 'naṃ' is merely a particle.

'Vissuto' means one who is well-known as a 'killer of living beings, cruel, and bloody-handed,' and so on. 'Mahoghena' means while being swept away by the great flood such as the flood of sensuality (kāmogha), I went to the refuge of the Buddha, the refuge known as the Buddha, who is capable of cutting off that flood.

'Lohitapāṇī' means one whose hands are smeared with the blood of others due to the killing of living beings. 'Behold the going for refuge' is an address to himself, saying, 'Behold my going for refuge, which is of great fruit.'

'Tādisaṃ kammaṃ' means such an evil deed, which was cruel, involving the killing of hundreds of people. 'Phuṭṭho kammavipākena' means experiencing the touch of the result of the evil kamma performed in the past; although all kammas have been abandoned, he is merely experiencing the remaining result. Alternatively, 'phuṭṭho kammavipākena' means being touched by the supramundane path, which is the fruit of wholesome kamma that serves as a strong support (upanissaya), or by the happiness of liberation (vimuttisukha), which is the fruit of supramundane kamma itself. Because all defilements have been exhausted, I eat my food as one who is debt-free; by mentioning food, all four requisites are intended.

Now, by way of censuring his past life of negligence and later praising the practice of diligence, and to generate enthusiasm in others for that practice of diligence, he spoke the verses beginning with 'They indulge in negligence...' In those verses, 'bālā' (fools) means those endowed with foolishness who do not know the welfare of this world and the world beyond. 'Dummedhino' means those without wisdom; they, not seeing the danger in negligence, indulge in negligence, promote it, and pass their time in negligence alone. 'Medhāvī' means a wise person endowed with wisdom that is the essence of the Dhamma, who guards diligence (appamāda) like a supreme, excellent treasure of seven gems inherited from one's lineage. How? Just as people guard wealth, seeing the benefits in it, thinking, 'Depending on this excellent wealth, we shall attain the perfection of enjoyments, we shall support our wives and children, and we shall clear the path to a happy destination'; in the same way, the wise person, depending on diligence, [attains] the first jhāna and so on...
335:
"I shall obtain the first jhāna and so forth; I shall reach the paths and fruits; I shall perfect the three knowledges and the six supernormal powers." Seeing the benefit in diligence (appamāda), he guards diligence as one would guard a noble treasure—this is the meaning.

"Mā pamādaṃ" means do not indulge in negligence; do not let time pass in negligence. "Kāmaratisanthavaṃ" means do not indulge in or acquire the association of craving (taṇhā) known as delight in sensual objects and delight in defilements. "Appamatto hi" means because of established mindfulness, the diligent person, being devoted to the practice of jhāna, reaches the supreme and ultimate bliss of Nibbāna.

"Svāgataṃ nāpagataṃ" means my coming to the presence of the Teacher at that time, or the Teacher's coming to that Mahāvana forest, was a good coming; it was not a coming devoid of benefit. "Netaṃ dummantitaṃ mama" means my thought at that time, "I shall ordain in the presence of the Teacher," was not a bad thought for me; it was indeed a good thought. Why? "Savibhattesu dhammesu" means among the dhammas analyzed by way of being faulty or faultless, etc., I have reached Nibbāna, which is the most noble and supreme; I have attained that very Nibbāna—this is the meaning.

"At that time, while being a worldling (puthujjana), I lived miserably in forests and so forth due to the failure of my effort and intention. Now, due to the fulfillment of effort and intention, I live happily in this Dispensation." To show this state of living happily, and to show the state of being a brahmin in the ultimate sense (paramattha-brāhmaṇa) by saying, "Formerly, I was a brahmin by birth alone, but now I am a true brahmin because I am the breast-born son of the Teacher," he spoke the verse beginning with "Araññe." In that verse, "Sukhaṃ sayāmi" means even when sleeping, I sleep happily, without suffering, and free from mental distress because of the absence of mental terror and such. "Ṭhāyāmi" means I stand. "Ahattapāso mārassa" means being beyond the range of the Māra of defilements and so forth. "Aho satthānukampito" means the Teacher has great compassion for beings; how wonderful—this is the meaning.

"Brahmajacco" means being of the brahmin caste by birth. "Udicco ubhato" means having a pure and distinguished lineage from both the mother's and father's sides. The remaining words are just as stated in their respective places.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Venerable Angulimala is finished.
336:
## 9. Commentary on the Verses of Venerable Anuruddha

The verse beginning with "Pahāya mātāpitaro" belongs to the Venerable Anuruddha. What is the background? This Venerable Anuruddha had also made an aspiration under previous Buddhas. In the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was born as a wealthy householder. One day, while going to the monastery and listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain monk to the foremost position among those possessing the Divine Eye (dibba-cakkhu). He himself desired that position and provided a great gift (mahādāna) for seven days to the Blessed One who was surrounded by a hundred thousand monks. On the seventh day, after offering excellent robes to the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks, he made an aspiration. The Teacher, seeing that his aspiration would be fulfilled without obstacles, prophesied: "In the future, in the Dispensation of the Perfectly Enlightened One named Gotama, you will be the foremost among those possessing the Divine Eye." That householder, performing meritorious deeds in that Dispensation, when the Teacher had attained Parinibbāna and a seven-league golden stupa was completed, made a grand offering of lamps with thousands of lamp-stands and lamp-bowls, aspiring: "May this be a supporting condition for the knowledge of the Divine Eye."

Thus, after performing merits throughout his life and wandering through the realms of devas and humans, in the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, he was born in a householder's family in the city of Bārāṇasī. When he reached maturity, after the Teacher had attained Parinibbāna and a one-league golden stupa was completed, he had many bronze bowls made, filled them with clarified butter, placed a lump of molasses in the center of each, and arranged them around the stupa touching rim to rim. He himself had a large bronze bowl made, filled it with clarified butter, lit a thousand wicks, and placing it on his head, circumambulated the stupa in worship throughout the night.

In this way, having performed merit throughout that life, he passed away and was born in the deva realm. After staying there for the full lifespan, he passed away and was born in a poor family in that same city of Bārāṇasī during a time when no Buddha had appeared. His name was Annabhāra. He lived by working in the house of a merchant named Sumana. One day, seeing a Paccekabuddha named Upariṭṭha, who had emerged from the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) and come through the air from Mount Gandhamādana, descending at the gate of Bārāṇasī, donning his robes and entering the city for alms, he felt faith. He took the bowl and prepared to offer the portion of rice he had set aside for himself to the Paccekabuddha. His wife also added her portion of rice. That Annabhāra brought the bowl and offered it to the Paccekabuddha. The Paccekabuddha accepted the bowl, gave a blessing (anumodanā), and departed. The deity guarding the house of Sumana the merchant exclaimed: "How wonderful! A noble gift has been well established in the Paccekabuddha Upariṭṭha!" Hearing that sound, Sumana the merchant thought...
337:
(Annabhāra's wife also) put her portion of rice into that same bowl. Annabhāra took the bowl and placed it in the hands of the Paccekabuddha. The Paccekabuddha took the bowl, gave a blessing, and departed. Seeing that gift, at night, the deity residing in the white parasol of Sumana the Treasurer rejoiced with a loud voice: "Oh, what a gift! A supreme gift, well established in Upariṭṭha!" Hearing that sound, Sumana the Treasurer thought, "Since the deity rejoices in this way, this must indeed be a noble gift," and he asked for a share of the merit of that gift. Annabhāra gave him a share of the merit. With a heart full of faith because of that sharing of merit, Sumana the Treasurer gave Annabhāra a thousand kahāpaṇas and said, "From today onwards, you no longer need to work with your own hands. Build a suitable house and live there permanently."

Because alms-food given to a Paccekabuddha who has just emerged from the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) yields an exceptionally great result on that very day, Sumana the Treasurer, when going to the King that day, took Annabhāra with him. The King looked at Annabhāra with respect. The Treasurer said, "Great King, this man is indeed worthy of being looked upon," and he related the merit performed by Annabhāra at that time, and how he himself had given him a thousand kahāpaṇas. Hearing this, the King was pleased, gave him another thousand, and granted him a site for a house, saying, "Build a house in such-and-such a place and live there." While clearing that site, many treasure jars appeared for Annabhāra. Seeing them, he informed the King. The King had all the wealth dug up and piled together. Seeing the pile, he asked, "In whose house in this city is there this much wealth?" "In no one's, Your Majesty," they replied. "In that case, let this Annabhāra be known as the Great Wealthy Treasurer (Mahādhana Seṭṭhi) in this city," and on that very day, he raised the treasurer's parasol for him.

From then on, Annabhāra performed meritorious deeds throughout his life. After passing away from that life, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans. During the time of our Buddha's appearance, he was reborn in the house of Sukkodana the Sakyan in the city of Kapilavatthu, and his name was Anuruddha. He was the younger brother of Mahānāma the Sakyan and the son of the Buddha's paternal uncle. He was extremely delicate and possessed great merit. While enjoying luxury like a god, surrounded by troupes of decorated dancers in three palaces suitable for the three seasons, he approached the Teacher who was staying in the Anupiya Mango Grove, along with Prince Bhaddiya and others sent by the Sakyan kings at the encouragement of King Suddhodana for the purpose of attending the Teacher. Having gone forth in the presence of the Teacher, he attained the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) within that very rainy season,
338:
Then, having taken a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) from the General of the Dhamma, he went to the Pācīnavamsamigadāya forest in the Cetiya country. While striving in the recluse's practice, he reflected on the seven thoughts of a great man (mahāpurisavitakka) but was unable to know the eighth thought. The Teacher, knowing his situation, taught him the eighth thought of a great man and then taught the practice of the Great Noble Lineage (Mahā-ariyavaṃsa), adorned with contentment with the four requisites and delight in meditation. The Elder Anuruddha, developing insight (vipassanā) in accordance with that teaching, realized Arahantship together with the supernormal knowledges (abhiññā) and the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). This matter is stated in the Apadāna as follows:

I saw the Blessed One named Sumedha, the Foremost of the World, the Bull among Men, dwelling in seclusion, the Leader of the World.
Approaching the Sambuddha Sumedha, the Leader of the World, I raised my hands in salutation and made a request to the Excellent Buddha.
"O Great Hero, Foremost of the World, Bull among Men, please have compassion. I shall offer a lamp to You, O Lord, who are meditating at the foot of a tree."
That Wise One, the Self-become, the Best of Speakers, consented. Then, having bored through the trees and prepared a mechanism,
I offered a thousand wicks to the Buddha Sumedha, the Kinsman of the World. For seven days they burned, and then my lamps went out.
Due to that clarity of mind and the aspiration of my intention, after leaving the human body, I was reborn in a celestial mansion.
My mansion, upon being reborn as a deity, was well-fashioned and shone all around. This is the fruit of the gift of a lamp.
At that time, I could illuminate a hundred yojanas all around. I surpassed all the gods. This is the fruit of the gift of a lamp.
For thirty aeons, I was the Lord of Gods, exercising the sovereignty of the gods. No god dared to despise me. This is the fruit of the gift of a lamp.
Twenty-eight times I was a Wheel-turning Monarch. At that time, I could see for one yojana all around, both day and night.
339:
In the Dispensation of the Buddha, I see the ten thousandfold world system with my knowledge; the attainment of the divine eye is the result of this gift of lamps.

Thirty thousand aeons ago, the Buddha named Sumedha appeared; with a clear mind, I offered a lamp to that Buddha.

The four analytical insights have been attained ... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.

Later, while the Teacher was staying in the midst of the noble assembly at the Jetavana Monastery, he placed the Elder Anuruddha in the foremost position among those with the divine eye, saying: "Monks, among my monk disciples who possess the divine eye, this Anuruddha is the foremost."

While the Elder Anuruddha was dwelling experiencing the bliss of liberation (the fruit of arahantship), one day, reflecting on his own practice and filled with joy and gladness, he uttered these verses by way of an inspired utterance (udāna), beginning with "Having left mother and father." Some teachers say: "The reciters (saṅgītikāras), wishing to reveal the Elder's going forth and his attainment of arahantship, spoke the first four verses. Thereafter, the Blessed One, pleased with the Elder's practice of the noble lineages (ariyavaṃsa), spoke [some verses]. All the remaining verses were spoken by the Elder himself for various reasons." In any case, whether these verses were spoken by the Elder himself or spoken about him, they should be known as the Elder's verses. They are as follows:

Having left mother and father, sisters, relatives, and brothers,
Having abandoned the five strands of sensual pleasure,
Anuruddha alone dwells meditating.

Though provided with dance and song,
And awakened by the sound of cymbals,
He did not find purity therein, delighting in the realm of Māra.

But having transcended that and delighting in the Buddha's Dispensation,
Having crossed over the entire flood,
Anuruddha alone dwells meditating.

Transcending pleasant sights, sounds, tastes, smells, and touches,
Anuruddha alone dwells meditating.

Having gone beyond the search for alms-food, the sage, alone and without a companion,
Anuruddha, free from taints, seeks out rag-robes.
340:
The taintless and wise sage named Anuruddha selects, takes, washes, dyes, and wears rag-robes.

The monk who is full of great desire, discontented, associating [with others], and of a restless mind—for such a person, these evil and defiling states increase.

One who is mindful, of few desires, contented, unperturbed, delighting in seclusion, and always of stirred-up energy—

For such a person, these wholesome states leading to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma) arise. He becomes free from taints; so it was said by the Great Sage.

The Peerless Teacher in the world, knowing my thought, approached me through psychic power with a mind-made body.

When my thought arose, the Buddha then taught the further teaching. The Buddha, delighting in the supramundane state free from the world of proliferation, taught the supramundane state free from proliferation.

Having understood the Dhamma of that Blessed One, I dwelt delighting in the Dispensation. The three true knowledges (te-vijjā) have been attained; the Buddha's instruction has been carried out.

For fifty-five years, I have practiced the sitter's effort (nesajjika), abandoning sleep. For twenty-five years, drowsiness has been completely uprooted.

For the One of steady mind (the Buddha), who was established in the fourth jhāna and endowed with endurance toward pleasant objects and so on, there was no in-breathing or out-breathing. The One with the [five] eyes, free from craving, having attained peace, has attained parinibbāna.

With an unshrinking and clear mind, he endured the feeling. Like the extinguishing of a lamp, the liberation of the mind occurred.

Now, these states in the Blessed One's continuity, with contact as the fifth, are the last. When the Fully Enlightened One has attained parinibbāna, no other mental states (citta-cetasika) will arise.

Now there is no more dwelling for me among the hosts of devas possessed of the net of craving. The suffering of the round of births is exhausted; now there is no more renewed existence.
341:
The monk who is an Arahant, who in a moment knows the thousandfold world system including the Brahmā world, who is a master of psychic powers and the passing away and reappearance of beings—that monk sees the deities at the proper time.

In a former life, I was a poor man named Annabhāra, a hireling who lived by his labor. I offered alms-food to the famous Paccekabuddha named Upariṭṭha.

I was then born in the Sakyan clan; people know me as Anuruddha. I was one provided with dance and song, awakened by the sound of cymbals.

Then I saw the Buddha, the Teacher who is free from all fear. Having gained confidence in that Buddha, I went forth into the homeless life.

Knowing my former lives where I dwelt before, I know the sequence of aggregates. In former lives, I stayed among the Tāvatiṃsa devas as Sakka, the king of gods.

I exercised kingship as a Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti) seven times, being the ruler of the people, victorious over the earth bounded by the four oceans. As the ruler of Jambudīpa, I governed the people righteously, without the use of rod or weapon.

Seven times from this human world and seven times from that celestial world—for fourteen rounds of wandering in other births—I then knew my former names and clans while staying in the deva world.

When I reached the concentration of the fourth jhāna, which has five factors such as the pervasion of rapture and bliss, which is the basis for higher knowledge, and which is the means for calming opposing states like the hindrances—when tranquility from defilements was attained, my divine eye became purified.

Established in the jhāna of five factors, I know the passing away and reappearance of beings, their coming and going, and their state of being here or elsewhere.

I have served the Teacher, I have done the Buddha's bidding, I have laid down the heavy burden, and I have completely cut the cord of craving that leads to the three worlds.

At the end of my life in Veḷuvagāma of the Vajjis, I, free from taints, shall attain parinibbāna under a bamboo thicket through the element of Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna).
342:
In this verse, 'pahāya' means having abandoned. 'Mātāpitaro' refers to mother and father. The meaning here is: some others ordain because they are overwhelmed by the loss of relatives or the loss of wealth, and after ordaining, they live occupied with other matters; but we are not like that. We have ordained after abandoning a large circle of relatives and a great mass of wealth, without longing for sensual pleasures. 'Jhāyati' means he dwells constantly practicing the two types of jhāna, namely, ārammaṇūpanijjhāna (meditation on an object) and lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna (meditation on characteristics).

'Sameto naccagītehi' means being endowed with dancing and singing, dwelling while watching dances and listening to songs. Some also read it as 'sammato', meaning honored with dancing and singing. 'Sammatāḷappabodhana' means one who is awakened at dawn by the sounds of gongs and cymbals. 'Na tena suddhimajjhagā' means he could not reach purity from saṃsāra by enjoying those sensual pleasures. 'Mārassa visaye rato' means one who delights in the five cords of sensual pleasure, which are the domain of Kilesa-māra. It means not being one who holds the view that "purity from saṃsāra can be achieved by enjoying the sensual pleasures that are the domain of Kilesa-māra." Therefore, He said, "Etāñca samatikkammā" and so on. In that verse, 'etaṃ' refers to these five types of sensual pleasures. 'Samatikkammā' means having transcended, having abandoned without longing. 'Sabboghaṃ' refers to all the floods, such as the flood of sensuality (kāmogha).

To show the five cords of sensual pleasure by their nature, He said, "Rūpā saddā" and so on. In that verse, 'manoramā' means delightful to the mind because of their attractive nature; it means they are pleasing. It is as He taught: "What are the five pleasing forms, pleasing sounds..." and so on.

'Piṇḍapātamatikkanto' means having finished the alms-round, or when returning from the alms-round. 'Eko' means alone, without a companion monk. 'Adutiyo' means one without craving (taṇhā). Indeed, craving is called the "second" (companion) of a man. As He taught: "A man with craving as his companion." 'Esati' means he seeks.

'Vicini' means while seeking, he selects and searches in various places such as dust heaps where refuse-rag robes (paṃsukūla) can be found. 'Aggahi' means after selecting, he picks them up without disgust even if they are smeared with impure filth. 'Dhovi' means he washes them. 'Rajayi' means after washing, he sews the obtained cloth and dyes it with allowable dye. 'Dhārayi' means after dyeing, he marks it with a kappabindu and carries or wears it.
343:
Now, wishing to show the instruction given by the Teacher at Pācīnavaṃsadāya and how Venerable Anuruddha himself reached the summit (Arahantship) through that instruction, He spoke the verse beginning with "Mahiccho ca asantuṭṭho." In that verse, 'mahiccho' means being endowed with great desire for the four requisites, desiring many grand and noble requisites. 'Asantuṭṭho' means being discontented, devoid of contentment such as being satisfied with whatever one receives. 'Saṃsaṭṭho' means being mingled with laypeople and monastics through inappropriate association. 'Uddhato' means having a restless mind. 'Tassa' refers to that person described as 'mahiccho' and so on. These states such as great desire, discontent, mingling, and restlessness are called 'pāpakā' (evil states) because of their base nature. They are 'saṃkilesikā' (defiling states) because they make the mind dirty.

However, when this person associates with, frequents, and attends upon good friends (kalyāṇamitta), listens to the True Dhamma, and practices wise reflection (yoniso manasikāra), he becomes mindful and, abandoning great desire, becomes 'appiccho' (one of few wishes). Abandoning discontent, he becomes 'santuṭṭho' (contented). Abandoning restlessness which causes distress to the mind, he becomes 'samāhito' (composed), being without distress and without distraction. Abandoning delight in the group, he becomes 'pavivekarato' (one who delights in seclusion). Due to delight in seclusion, disenchantment, and joy in the Dhamma, he becomes one with a joyful, happy, and satisfied mind. By abandoning laziness in every way, he becomes 'āraddhavīriyo' (one with aroused energy).

For that person thus endowed with qualities such as fewness of wishes, these thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhamma), which include the three types of insight (vipassanā) and are called 'kusalā' (wholesome) because they arise from skillfulness, and which are included in the Path, arise. When he is endowed with those states, through the total destruction of the taints (āsava), he becomes 'anāsavo' (one free from taints) from the moment of the Path of Arahantship (arahattamagga) onwards. This is the meaning of what was spoken by the Great Sage, the Fully Enlightened One, at Pācīnavaṃsadāya, by way of bringing the Thoughts of a Great Man to their consummation.

"Mama saṅkappamaññāya" means "Monks, this Dhamma is for one of few wishes, not for one of great wishes," and so on; it means knowing my thought which was initiated by way of the Thoughts of a Great Man, but which remained unable to reach the summit. "Manomayena" means as if made by the mind, with a transformed body similar to one created by the mind. "Iddhiyā" means through the psychic power of resolve (adhiṭṭhāniddhi) that occurred thus: "Let this body be like this mind."
344:
The Blessed One taught this by bringing the Thoughts of a Great Man to completion in the Eastern Bamboo Grove (Pācīnavaṃsadāya). 'Mama saṅkappamaññāya' means: 'Monks, this Dhamma is for one with few desires, not for one with great desires,' and so on. It means [the Buddha] knew my thought as I stood unable to bring those Thoughts of a Great Man to completion, despite my efforts through their power. 'Manomayena' means with a body created by the mind, or similar to one created by the mind, which is transformable. 'Iddhiyā' refers to the psychic power of determination that arises as 'May this body be like this mind.' 'Yadā me ahu saṅkappo' refers to the time when the thought arose in me: 'What is the eighth Thought of a Great Man?' At that time, it means the Blessed One, knowing my thought, approached by psychic power. 'Uttari desayi' means He taught further, completing this eighth Thought of a Great Man: 'Monks, this Dhamma is for one who delights in non-proliferation (nippapañca), who rejoices in non-proliferation; this Dhamma is not for one who delights in proliferation (papañca), who rejoices in proliferation.' Desiring to re-teach that very Dhamma which was taught, He said: 'The Buddha, delighting in non-proliferation, taught non-proliferation.' 'Papañca' refers to defilements such as greed (rāga). Because of the subsiding or absence of these 'papañca,' the supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma) are called 'nippapañca.' The Fully Enlightened One, who greatly delights in that non-proliferation, taught such a Dhamma just as He had attained it. The meaning is that He revealed the teaching of the Four Noble Truths, which is the unique teaching of the Buddhas (sāmukkaṃsika-desanā).

'Tassāhaṃ dhammamaññāya' means having understood the Dhamma through that teaching of the Teacher, and practicing according to the instruction, I lived delighting greatly in the Dispensation (Sāsana) comprised of the Threefold Training (sikkhattaya).

After showing his meeting with the Teacher and the benefit achieved through the Teacher, the Elder now spoke the verse beginning with 'Pañcapaññāsavassāni' to show his energy exerted since the time of his ordination, his relinquishment of the pleasure of sleep and the pleasure of touch without regard for the body, and his energy exerted since the time sleep became scarce. In that verse, 'Yato nesajjiko ahaṃ' means it has been fifty-five years since I took up the sitter's practice (nesajjika-dhutaṅga), having seen its virtues such as being conducive to yoga, being the practice of virtuous people occupied with meditation subjects, and being a way of effacement (sallekha). 'Yato middhaṃ samūhataṃ' means it has been twenty-five years since I relinquished deep sleep. It is said that during the fifty-five years the Elder was a 'sitter,' for the first twenty-five years there was no sleep at all; after that, due to bodily fatigue, there was sleep in the last watch of the night (pacchimayāma).

As for the three verses beginning with 'Nāhu assāsapassāsā,' they were spoken when the monks asked at the time of the Buddha's Parinibbāna, 'Has the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna?' to make known the fact of His Parinibbāna. In that verse, 'Nāhu assāsapassāsā, ṭhitacittassa tādino' means after entering and emerging from all the various meditative attainments in direct and reverse order, finally, for the Buddha, the Blessed One, whose mind was steady in the fourth jhāna...
345:
...after emerging from the meditative attainments, for the Buddha, the Blessed One, whose mind was steady in the fourth jhāna at the very end, and who was endowed with such qualities, there were no inhalations or exhalations. By this, it is shown that for one who has entered the fourth jhāna, bodily formations (kāyasaṅkhāra) cease; and inhalations and exhalations are called bodily formations. Therefore, it shows that from the moment of the fourth jhāna, there were no inhalations or exhalations. He is 'aneja' (unshaken) because of the absence of 'ejā,' which is a term for craving (taṇhā); or He is 'aneja' because He is established in concentration (samādhi). 'Santimārabbha' means referring to, or on account of, Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna). 'Cakkhumā' means the One with Vision, possessed of the five eyes. 'Parinibbuto' means He attained Parinibbāna. The meaning here is: having entered the attainment of the fruition (phala-samāpatti) of the fourth jhāna with Nibbāna as the object, immediately after that attainment, He attained Parinibbāna through the element of Nibbāna without remainder.

'Asallīnena' means with a mind that is not shrinking or dejected, but very clear. 'Vedanaṃ ajjhavāsayi' means being mindful and clearly comprehending (sato sampajāno), He endured the feeling at the time of death; He did not follow the lead of the feeling, nor did He toss and turn from side to side. 'Pajjotasseva nibbānaṃ, vimokkho cetaso ahū' means just as a lamp burning on account of oil and a wick goes out when the oil and wick are exhausted. When that lamp goes out, it does not go and stay in any particular place, but simply disappears and becomes invisible; in the same way, the continuity of the aggregates (khandha-santāna) proceeding on account of defilements and volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra) is extinguished when those defilements are exhausted. It shows that when it is extinguished, it does not go and stay in any particular place, but simply disappears and becomes invisible. Therefore, it was said: 'The wise are extinguished like this lamp,' and 'Like a flame tossed by the force of the wind,' and so on.

'Ete' is said because He personally witnessed the states occurring in the Teacher's continuity at the moment of Parinibbāna. Those states are the 'last' (pacchimā) because there is no further arising of consciousness after that. 'Dāni' means now. 'Phassapañcamā' is said because the five states beginning with contact (phassa) are prominent. For that reason, even in the discourse on the arising of consciousness (Cittuppādakaṭhā), the five states beginning with contact are mentioned first. 'Aññေ dhammā' refers to other mental states (citta-cetasika) along with their physical bases; it does not refer to the consciousness and mental factors of the Parinibbāna moment itself. If it is asked, 'Will those Parinibbāna mental states also not arise in the future?'—it is true they will not arise. However, because there is no doubt about them, it should not be said 'they will not arise' in reference to them. But since there might be a doubt as to whether other states might arise as they do for trainees (sekkhā) and worldlings (puthujjanā), the phrase 'no other states will arise' was spoken to remove that doubt.
346:
## The Goddess Jālinī and the Elder Anuruddha

'O Goddess Jālinī, there is no more living for me in the divine realm where the host of deities reside.' In this line, 'Jālinī' is an address to the goddess. It means that there is no more living for me now by way of rebirth among the host of deities. The reason for this is stated with the words beginning with 'Vikkhīṇo' (exhausted). It is said that this goddess was an attendant of the Elder in a previous life. Therefore, seeing the Elder now as old and aged, she came out of past affection and pleaded for his rebirth in the divine realm, saying, 'Venerable Sir, incline your heart towards (aspire for) that divine realm where you lived before.' Then the Elder replied to the goddess with the words beginning with 'Now there is no more.' Hearing this, the goddess, her hopes dashed, vanished right there.

Then the Elder, having ascended into the air and manifesting his psychic power to his fellow practitioners, spoke the verse beginning with 'Yassa muhuttena.' The meaning of that verse is: For that monk who has destroyed the taints (khīṇāsava), in just a moment, the world of a thousandfold variety, the three-thousandfold great world system, along with the Brahma world, is well known, clearly known, and realized. Thus, having attained mastery in the quality of psychic power, in psychic success, and in the passing away and rebirth of beings, that monk sees deities at the appropriate time; there is no failure in his seeing of deities. It is said that when the Elder spoke the verse 'Natthi dāni' as a reply to the goddess Jālinī, the monks, not seeing the goddess Jālinī, thought, 'Is the Elder saying something by way of a Dhamma discourse?' Knowing the thoughts of those monks, the Elder spoke this verse beginning with 'Yassa muhuttena.'

'Annabhāro pure' means having had that name in a previous life. 'Ghāsahārako' means one who lives by working for hire just for food and sustenance. 'Samaṇaṃ' refers to a person whose evils are stilled. 'Paṭipādesiṃ' means having offered or given in person; the meaning is having given the gift of food in person with devotion. 'Upariṭṭhaṃ' refers to the Paccekabuddha of that name. 'Yasassinaṃ' refers to a person who is famous and renowned. With this verse, he shows his past merit which was the cause of his noble attainments up to his final birth. Therefore, he said the words beginning with 'Somhi sakyakule jāto' (I was born in the Sakyan clan).

'Ito satta' means having passed away from this human world and becoming a ruler of deities in the divine realm seven times. 'Tato satta' means having passed away from that divine realm and becoming a Universal Monarch in the human world seven times. 'Saṃsārāni catuddasa' refers to the wandering through fourteen intermediate existences. 'Nivāsamabhijānissaṃ' means I knew my previous lives.
347:
"At that time, he was established in the celestial realm": In this phrase, such knowledge was not only in this current existence, but rather, it means he knew it when he was established in the celestial realm in the past existence immediately preceding this one.

Now, wishing to show the manner in which he attained the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) and the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings (cutūpapāta-ñāṇa), he spoke two verses beginning with "Pañcaṅgike." In those verses, "in the five-factored concentration" refers to the fourth jhāna concentration, which is the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā). This fourth jhāna concentration is called "five-factored" because it is endowed with these five factors: suffusion of rapture (pīti), suffusion of happiness (sukha), suffusion of mind (ceto), suffusion of light (āloka), and the sign of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇa-nimitta). "Tranquil" means peaceful due to the subsiding of opposing states (hindrances) and the tranquility of the factors. "Ekodibhāvite" means having reached a state of single-mindedness and being well-practiced, meaning having attained mastery (vasībhāva). "Paṭippassaddhi-laddhamhi" means obtained when the defilements are stilled. "My divine eye is purified" means that when such concentration was perfected, my divine eye knowledge became purified; it became exceptionally pure through liberation from the eleven upakkilesas (imperfections).

"I know the passing away and rebirth" means I know the death and rebirth of beings. Knowing thus, I know the coming and going of beings: "These beings, having come from that world, are reborn here; having gone from this world, they will be reborn in that world." Knowing thus, I know their human state and their state other than that, such as the animal state, even before their rebirth occurs. To show that all these knowledges are possible only when the five-factored concentration is perfected, he said, "Established in the five-factored jhāna." In that phrase, it means knowing thus by being established and firm in the five-factored jhāna.

Having thus shown the three true knowledges (tevijjā), and because of their connection, wishing to show the third knowledge previously mentioned along with the completion of the task, he spoke two verses beginning with "I have served the Teacher." In those verses, "in Veḷuvagāma of the Vajjis" refers to Veḷuvagāma in the Vajjian country, where the Blessed One spent his last rains retreat. "Under a bamboo thicket" means under a certain bamboo thicket in that village. "I shall attain Nibbāna" means I shall attain parinibbāna through the Nibbāna element without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu).

## The Commentary on the Verses of Anuruddha Thera is Finished.
348:
## 10. Commentary on the Verses of Pārāpariya Thera

The verse beginning with "Samaṇassa ahu cintā" is that of the Venerable Pārāpariya. The story of this elder has already been mentioned below. These verses were spoken by him during the Buddha's lifetime, when he was still a worldling (puthujjana), as an expression of his thoughts on restraining the senses, with the mind as the sixth. Later, after the Buddha's Parinibbāna and when his own Parinibbāna was approaching, he spoke them to reveal the future state of monks who would follow a wrong path that is not the Dhamma. Among those verses:

"In the great forest in full bloom,
To the monk who sat with a one-pointed mind,
Secluded and meditating,
A thought and investigation arose."

This verse was placed by the redactors of the Council (Saṅgītikāras). Its meaning is as stated below. This is the connection: After the Buddha, the chief disciples, and some of the great elders had attained Parinibbāna, in the Dispensation where the Teacher was no longer present, monks who were easy to instruct and desired the training became rare, while monks who were difficult to instruct and prone to wrong practice became numerous. At that time, while sitting in a great Sāla forest in full bloom, secluded, one-pointed, and habitually meditating, a thought and investigation arose in the Venerable Pārāpariya—who was called a 'Samaṇa' because his evils were stilled—concerning the practice. The other verses are:

"While the Lord of the World, the Supreme Man, was still alive,
The conduct of the monks was of one kind; now it appears as another.

They used robes only for protection against cold and wind,
And to cover their nakedness for the sake of modesty,
Being content with whatever requisites they received, just enough for their needs.

Whether it was refined or coarse, whether little or much,
They ate their food only for the sake of sustenance,
Without greed and without being infatuated.

Regarding the requisites of life, such as medicine and other supports,
They were not excessively striving, just as they strove for the destruction of taints (āsavakkhaya).

In the forest, at the roots of trees, in clefts and caves,
They lived devoted to seclusion, making that seclusion their final resort."
349:
They were humble in habit, established in faith within the Dispensation, easy to support, gentle, and of non-harsh minds. They were free from the mixing of defilements, not talkative, and followed the contemplation of the goal (Those elders have now attained Parinibbāna). For that reason, their walking, eating, and the practices they followed were inspiring. The posture of those elders was smooth and graceful, like a flowing stream of oil. Those elders, whose taints were entirely exhausted, who were great meditators and brought great benefit, have now attained Nibbāna. Now, such elders are very few.

Due to the waning of wholesome states and wisdom, the Dispensation of the Conqueror (Jina), which is endowed with all excellent qualities, is decaying and crumbling. The season of evil states and defilements has now arrived. Those who remain with the true Dhamma strive for seclusion. Those increasing defilements enter and oppress many people. I think these defilements play with fools as demons play with madmen.

Overwhelmed by defilements, those people run to various sense objects. They run toward the objects of defilement as if on a clamorous battlefield. Abandoning the true Dhamma, they argue with one another. Following after views that have reached dogmatism, they think, "Only this is excellent."

Though they have left behind wealth, sons, and wives to enter the homeless life, they resort to improper acts even for the sake of a small amount of alms-food offered with a ladle. Having eaten until their bellies are full, they sleep lying on their backs. When they wake up, they speak and increase only those words censured by the Teacher. They respect and learn all the arts and crafts of traders. Without calming the defilements within themselves, they claim, "I live for the sake of the monkhood."

Desiring many gains, they offer fine clay, oil, powder, water, seats, and food to laypeople. They also offer tooth-sticks, wood-apples, flowers, snacks, choice alms-food, mangoes, and myrobalans (to laypeople).
350:
They act like doctors regarding medicines, like laypeople regarding business affairs, like courtesans regarding the decoration of the body, and like kings regarding the exercise of power.

Deceitful people, fraudulent people, false witnesses, and unrestrained people enjoy the requisites of life through many schemes. Following after thoughts associated with pretexts and indirect means, they pull in much wealth through various methods for the sake of their livelihood.

They make a following serve them for the sake of their own work, not for the sake of the Dhamma. When they preach the Dhamma to others, they preach for the sake of gain, not for the sake of the true benefit.

They argue over the gains of the Saṅgha, yet they are outsiders to the Saṅgha. Living by depending on the gains of others, they are shameless and do not feel embarrassed.

Likewise, some who are not devoted to the monk's practice, though shaven-headed and wearing the outer robe (saṅghāṭi), desire only reputation, being intoxicated by gain and honor.

In this way, now that things have reached various states (of defilement), it is no longer easy to attain the Vipassanā Dhamma not yet reached, or to protect the Vipassanā Dhamma already reached.

Just as a person without sandals would walk in a thorny place with established mindfulness, so should a sage move within the village with mindfulness.

Remembering the ancients, the yogi, following their conduct, may touch the Deathless state (Nibbāna) even though this is the latter time.

Having said this in the Sāla forest, the Samaṇa with developed senses, the Brahmin who had ended the cycle of rebirth, the Seer, attained Parinibbāna.

These verses were spoken by the Elder himself.

In those verses, "Iriyaṃ āsi bhikkhūnaṃ" means: because of the existence of such practice during the time when the Buddha, the Supreme Man and Lord of the World, was still alive. "Aññathā" means in another way, another...
351:
The conduct of the monks used to be in accordance with the instructions because they practiced and exerted themselves diligently. Now, however, the conduct of the monks is seen in a different manner due to improper practice; this is the meaning.

Now, to show first the manner in which the monks' practice was while the Teacher was still alive, it is said, "protection from cold and wind," and so on. In that context, "mattaṭṭhiyaṃ" means having only that much purpose. They used the robes only for the purpose of protection from cold and wind, and for the purpose of covering their nakedness out of shame. How did they use them? They were content with whatever requisites they obtained, whether inferior or superior.

"Paṇītaṃ" refers to superior food mixed with ghee and so forth; without such mixing, it is called "lūkhaṃ" (coarse food). "Appaṃ" refers to a small amount, about four or five mouthfuls. "They consumed much for the sake of sustenance" means that even when consuming superior food in large quantities, they ate only enough for sustenance. For that very reason, without greed or intense attachment, they consumed it like wagon drivers greasing an axle, or like the sick applying medicine to a wound.

Regarding the requisites known as medicine, which are the supports for life, and the requisites for the sick, just as those former monks were diligent and devoted to the destruction of the taints (āsavas), so too, even when oppressed by disease, they were not excessively concerned with the requisites for the sick.

"Tapparāyaṇā" means having seclusion (viveka) as their destination, being inclined toward seclusion. Thus, by showing contentment with the four requisites and delight in meditation through these four verses, the practice of the Noble Lineage (ariyavaṃsa) is shown.

"Nīcā" means those who are humble and free from pride, not exalting themselves or disparaging others by saying, "We are wearers of rag-robes, we are alms-food eaters." "Niviṭṭhā" means those with established faith in the Dispensation. "Subharā" means those who are easy to support because of qualities such as having few wishes. "Mudū" means those who are gentle in the minor and major duties and in the entire holy life, being fit for use like well-refined gold. Alternatively, "mudū" means those who are free from frowning, have open faces, and are accustomed to welcoming others with a cheerful countenance, bringing happiness like a good landing place. "Athaddhamānasā" means...
352:
By that phrase (athaddhamānasā), meaning those with unhardened minds, the quality of being easy to admonish is stated. "Abyāsekā" means those free from the infusion of defilements because they are not devoid of mindfulness, meaning they are not interspersed with craving, wrong view, conceit, and so forth. "Amukharā" means those who are not harsh-tongued, or those free from verbal impudence (vacīpāgabbhiya). "Atthacintāvasānugā" means those who follow the pursuit of welfare, those who are masters of thinking about welfare, those who only follow the pursuit of welfare for themselves and others.

"Tato" means because of such reasons as having a humble manner. "Pāsādikaṃ" means that which inspires faith, bringing about faith in those who see or hear their practice. "Gataṃ" means movement such as going forward, returning, or turning around. Alternatively, it means the activity of body and speech. "Bhuttaṃ" means the use of the four requisites. "Nisevitaṃ" means frequenting the place for alms. "Siniddhā teladhārāva" means just as a stream of oil, poured by a person of unwavering merit, flows continuously, being smooth, glossy, pleasant to look at, and inspiring faith; so too, the posture of those monks endowed with proper conduct was continuous, subtle, smooth, pleasant to look at, and inspiring faith.

"Mahājhāyī" means those who habitually enter into great meditative absorptions (jhānas), or those who take the great Nibbāna as their object. For that very reason, they have great welfare, meaning they are endowed with great benefits. "Te therā" means those elders who were devoted to practice as described above have now attained Parinibbāna. "Parittā dāni tādisā" means that now, in these final times, such elders similar to them are few (only two or three).

"Kusalānañca dhammānaṃ" refers to the blameless states which are the strong conditions for the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa) and the requisites for liberation (vimokkha). "Paññāya ca" means by such wisdom. "Parikkhayā" means due to the absence or non-arising. Even though wisdom is also a blameless state, it is mentioned separately to show its great helpfulness, just as in the phrase "the requisites of merit and knowledge" (puñña-ñāṇa-sambhāra). "Sabbākārawarūpetaṃ" means the Dispensation of the Buddha, the Conqueror, which is endowed with all excellent aspects such as being good in the beginning, is perishing. "Pāpakānañca dhammānaṃ kilesānañca yo utu" means there is a time, a season, for evil states such as bodily misconduct and for defilements such as greed.
353:
"This time is occurring"—this is the meaning to be taken with the remaining words. In such a time, those who have effort exerted for the sake of bodily seclusion (kāya-viveka), mental seclusion (citta-viveka), and seclusion from acquisitions (upadhi-viveka) are also those who possess the remaining practice of the True Dhamma. The meaning here is: even though they have very pure conduct in virtue, nowadays some monks, having fulfilled preliminary duties such as establishing the postures, the methods of Samatha and Vipassanā meditation, cutting off major impediments, and cutting off minor impediments, apply themselves to meditation. Those monks, possessing the remaining practice of the True Dhamma, are unable to bring the practice to its culmination.

The defilements that were exhausted and eliminated at that time by the Buddha's own breast-born sons (the Arahants) have now, having found an opportunity, reached growth, increase, and abundance among the monks. They overwhelm the blind worldlings who lack good friends and are full of improper attention, and making them helpless, they enter their continuities in succession. These defilements, having become thus, are to be understood as playing with fools, just as demons (rakkhasa) play with the insane. For example, just as playful demons possess the insane who lack a physician and, bringing them to ruin and destruction, play with them; likewise, the defilements possess the blind, foolish monks who are far from the physician—the Fully Enlightened Buddha—and, causing them harm such as the loss of benefits in the present life, they seem to be playing with them.

They run about perversely by way of various sense objects; they practice by way of what is unsuitable. Because the defilements that arose first are the cause for the defilements that will arise later, the defilements themselves are called "objects of defilement" (kilesavatthu). When those objects of defilement have gathered, the proclamation of sensual pleasures—scattering wealth such as gold, silver, gems, and pearls, and saying, "Whatever gold or silver reaches the hand of whoever, let it belong only to that person"—is called sa-saṅgāma-ghosanā (a proclamation with battle). The meaning here is: it is as if Māra, the general of defilements, proclaims in the battlefield regarding the objects of defilement, "Whatever defilement seizes and overwhelms whatever being, let that being belong to that defilement." Those foolish worldlings, oppressed by various defilements, run about and are settled by way of various sense objects.
354:
If it is asked what they do when they run about in this way, it is said: "Abandoning the True Dhamma, they quarrel with one another." The meaning of that Pali is: discarding the True Dhamma called practice, they engage in quarreling and strife with one another for the sake of mere material gain.

"Views" (diṭṭhigatāni) means: those who follow such wrong views as "Only consciousness exists, material phenomena do not exist," or "Just as there is no person in the ultimate sense, so also there are no phenomena in the ultimate sense; they are merely conventional," think, "Only this view is excellent, only this is supreme; other views are false."

"Gone forth" (niggatā) means those who have come out from the house. "Even for the sake of a spoonful of alms" (kaṭacchubhikkhahetūpi) means even for the sake of alms food amounting to just a ladleful. By the power of unsuitable association with the layperson who gives that alms food, they perform deeds that should not be done, which are improper for a monk.

"Eating until the belly is stuffed" (udarāvadehakaṃ bhutvā) means eating until the belly is full without reflecting on the saying, "One should stop before the belly is full and eat in moderation." "Sleeping on their backs" (sayantuttānaseyyakā) means they sleep on their backs without remembering the instruction, "One should take up the lion's posture on the right side, placing one foot over the other, mindful and clearly comprehending." "Speech censured by the Teacher" refers to animal talk (tiracchānakathā) such as talk about kings and so forth.

"All crafts" (sabbakārukasippāni) means manual crafts such as making umbrellas and palm-leaf fans, which are to be done by workers such as traders. "Having made it a matter of respect" (cittiṃ katvāna) means doing so respectfully and with esteem.
