"Not peaceful within" means they have minds that are not peaceful within, both because defilements are not stilled and because there is no concentration even for the duration of a single milking of a cow. "The goal of monkhood" (sāmaññattho) means the practice of a monk (samaṇadhamma). "It passes them by" (ati-acchati) means that because those monks are occupied only with the business of livelihood, the practice of a monk does not touch them even in part, but stands apart and does not adhere to them.

"Clay bowl" (mattikaṃ) means a clay bowl of five colors suitable for use by laypeople. "Oil and powder" (telacuṇṇañca) means ordinary or prepared oil and cleansing powder. "Water, seat, and food" (udakāsanabhojanaṃ) means water, a place to sit, and food. "Desiring excessively" means they offer these things to laypeople with the intention: "If we give these clay bowls and so forth, people will become firmly devoted and will in turn offer many of the four requisites."
355:
Because it is used to clean the teeth, it is called 'dantapoṇa' or 'dantakaṭṭha' (tooth-wood). 'Kapittha' refers to the wood-apple fruit. 'Puppha' refers to flowers such as jasmine (sumana) and champak (campaka). 'Khādanīya' refers to the eighteen kinds of various edibles. 'Piṇḍapāte ca sampanne' occurs in the context of excellent almsfood endowed with good color and so on. In the passage 'ambe āmalakāni ca', the word 'ca' includes fruits not explicitly mentioned, such as sweet lime, palmyra, and coconut. In all these matters, it should be construed that they offer these things to laypeople because they desire many requisites.

'Bhesajjesu yathā vejjā' means that just as physicians act in the administration of medicines to laypeople, so too do these monks act. 'Kiccākicce yathā gihī' means that in performing the great and small affairs of laypeople, they act like householders. 'Gaṇikāva vibhūsāya' means they are like courtesans who live by their beauty when they decorate their own bodies. 'Issare khattiyā yathā' means that in exercising authority, they act like kings, or they conduct themselves like heads of households (kulapati).

'Nekatika' refers to those who are engaged in deceit, who take pleasure in fraud by making what is not a gem appear as a gem, and what is not gold appear as gold. 'Vañcanika' refers to those who deceive others through fraudulent measures and so on. 'Kūṭasakkhī' refers to those who give false witness. 'Apāṭuka' refers to those of low character with unrestrained livelihoods. 'Bahūhi parikappehi' means by the various other forms of wrong livelihood already mentioned.

'Lesakappa' occurs in the context of a pretext or a suitable appearance that seems allowable (kappiya). 'Pariyāya' occurs in the application of indirect talk (pariyāya) regarding requisites. 'Parikappa' occurs in schemes for profit and so on, and in all these contexts, it is used in the locative sense (bhummā). 'Anudhāvita' refers to those who are pursued or overwhelmed by evil states such as great desire. 'Jīvikattha' refers to those whose motive is livelihood or who act for the sake of livelihood. 'Upāyena' means by the method of generating requisites through means such as hinting (parikathā). 'Saṅkaḍḍhanti' means they collect or gather.

'Upaṭṭhapenti parisaṃ' means they make the assembly serve them; just as the assembly serves them, so too do they gather the assembly. 'Kammato' means because of the cause of their own deeds; they make others serve them for the sake of their own duties and services (veyyāvacca). 'No ca dhammato' means they do not make others serve them for the sake of the Dhamma. It means they do not support the assembly with that support which was authorized by the Teacher for an assembly that is worthy of being uplifted. 'Lābhato' means because of the cause of gain, thinking: 'This venerable one is very learned, a reciter, a Dhamma-preacher'; thus, the great multitude, honoring me in this way, will bring me gains and offerings...
356:
...thinking 'he will bring [gains]', they stand in a state of selfish desire and preach the Dhamma to others for the sake of gain. 'No ca atthato' means they do not preach the Dhamma for the sake of the benefit to be attained by one who preaches the True Dhamma while established in the bases of liberation (vimuttāyatana), but rather they preach for the sake of benefits such as those pertaining to the present life.

'Saṅghalābhaṃ bhaṇḍanti' means they quarrel over the gains of the Saṅgha, saying things like 'This belongs to me, not to you.' 'Saṅghato paribāhirā' means they are outside the Noble Saṅgha because such quarreling does not exist within the Noble Saṅgha. 'Paralābhopajīvantā' means that in this Dispensation, foolish worldlings who desire gains live depending on the gains of others, which were intended for the learners (sekha) who are endowed with virtues like morality. Or, it means that those monks who cause quarrels live depending on the gains to be received from others, namely the donors; being shameless (ahirika) due to the absence of loathing for evil, they are not ashamed and do not feel conscience-stricken even to think, 'We eat the gains of others, we live depending on others.'

'Nānuyuttā' means they are not devoted to the qualities that make one a recluse (samaṇa). 'Tathā' means just as the aforementioned quarrellers and so on. 'Eke' means some individuals. 'Muṇḍā saṅghāṭipārutā' means they are shaven-headed merely by the act of shaving their hair, and their bodies are clad in the robe called 'saṅghāṭi' because it is stitched together from rags. 'Sambhāvanaṃyevicchantī lābhasakkāramucchitā' means being infatuated and obsessed with the desire for gains and offerings, they seek and desire only reputation and honor, such as being called 'virtuous, an observer of dhuta practices, very learned,' or by using sweet speech, being called 'a noble one (ariya).' It means they do not desire the actual virtues that are the cause of such reputation.

'Evaṃ' is in the manner stated as 'due to the exhaustion of wholesome states and wisdom.' 'Nānappayātamhi' means when various states of ruin have been brought about, or when one has begun to proceed in various states of defilement. 'Na dāni sukaraṃ tathā' means that now, in this time when good friends are hard to find and the hearing of the suitable True Dhamma is rare, it is not as easy to attain the unreached jhāna and insight as it was when the Teacher was alive; nor is it easy to protect and maintain what has been attained so that it does not merely remain or decline, but becomes a state of distinction (visesabhāgiya). It means it is not possible to accomplish this now.

Now, because the time of his own Parinibbāna was drawing near, desiring to exhort his fellow practitioners with a brief instruction, he spoke the words beginning with 'Yathā kaṇṭakaṭṭhānamhi.' The meaning is: just as a man traveling without sandals in a place full of thorns for some purpose would proceed by being mindful, thinking 'May a thorn not prick me,' so too should one proceed.
357:
Now, as the time for his own parinibbāna was approaching, wishing to exhort his fellow practitioners with a brief instruction, he spoke the verse beginning with "Yathā kaṇṭakaṭṭhānamhi." The meaning is: Just as a man, walking without sandals in a place full of thorns for some purpose, walks only after establishing mindfulness, thinking, "May a thorn not prick me," so too, a sage walking for a purpose into a village for alms, which is full of the thorns of defilements, should walk by arousing mindfulness, being endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension (sati-sampajañña), and being heedful, without abandoning the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna).

"Remembering the former yogis, following their practice" means remembering the yogis of the past who were devoted to the development of meditation and had aroused insight (vipassanā), and following their practice, which is the method of right practice and meditation according to the scriptures, practicing without laying down the burden. Even if this is the final period after the Teacher has passed away, nevertheless, if one practices according to the Dhamma as taught and exerts effort in insight (vipassanā), one can attain the deathless state (amata-pada), which is Nibbāna.

"Having said this" means having spoken this method of practice regarding defilement and purification as shown. It should be understood that this final verse was spoken by the Recorders of the Council (saṅgītikāras) to reveal the parinibbāna of the Elder Pārāpariya.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Pārāpariya Thera is Finished.

## The Commentary on the Book of Twenties is Finished.
358:
## 17. Tiṃsa Nipāta
## 1. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Phussa

In the Book of the Thirties, the verses beginning with "Pāsādike bahū disvā" are those of the Venerable Elder Phussa. What is their origin? This Phussa, too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating wholesome merit which is a support for the cessation of the round of rebirth in various existences, wandered through the realms of devas and humans. In this Buddha-era, he was reborn as the son of a provincial king and was named Phussa. When he reached the age of discretion, he attained mastery in the arts that should be learned by kshatriya princes. Being endowed with the perfection of supporting conditions, his mind was unattached to sensual pleasures. Having heard the Dhamma in the presence of a certain Great Elder, he gained faith and went forth. Taking a meditation subject suitable for his temperament and devoting himself to meditation, he produced the jhānas. Using the jhānas as a basis, he developed insight and before long became one who possessed the six higher powers.

Furthermore, one day, an ascetic named Paṇḍaragotta, while sitting and listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Elder Phussa, saw many monks who were endowed with virtuous conduct, whose faculties were well-restrained, and whose bodies and minds were developed. With a devout mind, he thought, "Oh, it would be good if this practice were to endure for a long time in the world," and he asked the Elder, "Venerable Sir, how will the practice of the monks be in the future time?" To show that matter, the Reciters of the Council placed this verse at the beginning:

"Having seen many who were inspiring, with developed minds and well-restrained,
An ascetic of the Paṇḍara lineage questioned the one named Phussa."

In that verse, "pāsādike" means those who are worthy of devotion due to their own practice. "Bahū" means many. "Bhāvitatte" means those whose minds are developed through the development of serenity and insight. "Susaṃvute" means those whose faculties are well-restrained. "Isi" means an ascetic. "Paṇḍarasagotto" means one who has a lineage similar to the ascetic named Paṇḍara because of being born in his lineage. "Phussasavhayaṃ" means one who is to be called by the name Phussa; the meaning is one named Phussa.
359:
“What will be their intentions, what their inclinations, and what their conduct in the future time? Being questioned, please tell that to me.”

This is the verse of the ascetic's question. In that verse, 'kiṃ chandā' means what kind of intentions and what kind of convictions will the monks have in this Dispensation in the future; will they have inferior convictions or superior convictions? 'Kimadhippāyā' means what kind of desires and what kind of dispositions will they have; will they have defiled dispositions or purified dispositions? Alternatively, 'chanda' is the desire to act (kattukamyatā), thus it means what is their desire to act like. 'Adhippāya' is the same as disposition (ajjhāsaya). 'Kimākappā' means what kind of appearance and behavior will they have. 'Ākappa' also means being endowed with moral conduct such as the adoption of the outward appearance. 'Bhavissare' means they will be. 'Taṃ me' means please tell me, please speak to me who has questioned about the distinctions of intentions, desires, and conduct of the monks in the future—thus he urges the Elder. The Elder, wishing to explain that matter, first urges him to listen respectfully:

“Listen to my words, O ascetic named Paṇḍara,
Attend carefully, I shall tell of the future.”

He spoke this verse. Its meaning is: O ascetic named Paṇḍara, that matter which you ask me, I shall tell you about that future. Listen to my words as I speak. Attend carefully because it explains the future meaning and because it brings about spiritual urgency.

Then the Elder, seeing the future state of the monks and nuns as it really is through the knowledge of the future, said to the ascetic:

“In the future, many will be angry, resentful, disparaging, stubborn, and deceitful. There will be those who are envious and those who hold various conflicting views.

Thinking 'I know' regarding the deep Dhamma without actually knowing, frequenting only the shore, being frivolous, without weight in the Dhamma, they will be without mutual respect.

In the future, many perils will arise in the world. Those of dull wit will corrupt this well-expounded Dhamma.”
361:
In the future, within the Saṅgha, those who are devoid of virtue but bold in speech will be powerful, even though they are harsh-tongued and have little learning. Those endowed with virtue in the Saṅgha, who speak according to the truth, will be weak, being modest and having few desires. In the future, the foolish will delight in and accept silver, gold, fields, property, goats, sheep, and male and female servants.

Fools who only look for the faults of others, not established in virtue, arrogant, and delighting in quarrels, will wander about like wild beasts. Those with restless minds, wearing blue robes, being deceitful, stubborn, talkative, and vain, will wander about as if they were Noble Ones (Ariyas). Those with oiled hair, fickle, and with painted eyes, will walk the streets wearing ivory-colored clothes.

Those who are intensely attached to white garments will loathe the saffron robe, which is not loathed by those liberated from defilements, which is well-dyed, and is the banner of the Arahats. Those desiring gain, lazy, and lacking in energy, will abandon forest dwellings and live in the vicinity of villages. Those who are unrestrained will associate with and follow the example of whoever always delights in wrong livelihood and obtains gain.

Those who do not obtain gain will not be honored. At that time, they will not associate even with the wise who love virtue. Despising their own banner, the saffron robe, some will wear the white garment, which is the banner of the sectarians (titthiyas). At that time, there will be no respect for the saffron robe among them. There will be no reflection on the robe by the monks.

A profound and inconceivable reflection occurred to the Chaddanta elephant king, who was suffering and oppressed by a poisoned arrow. At that time, upon seeing the well-dyed saffron robe, the banner of the Arahats, the elephant immediately recited these verses connected with the goal:

'He who is not free from stains (kilesa), who is devoid of self-restraint and truth, is not worthy of the saffron robe.

But he who has vomited out stains, is well-established in virtues, and is endowed with self-restraint and truth, he indeed is worthy of the saffron robe.

One who has failed in virtue, is foolish, unrestrained in desires, with a wandering mind and lacking effort, is not worthy of the saffron robe.

But he who is endowed with virtue, free from passion, concentrated, and pure in mind and thought, he indeed is worthy of the saffron robe.

A restless, arrogant fool who possesses no virtue is worthy of white cloth; what will he do with the saffron robe?'

In the future, monks and nuns with evil minds and lack of respect will oppress the Noble Ones who have minds of loving-kindness. Even when the elders teach them how to wear the robe, the foolish and unwise who are unrestrained in desires will not listen. Those fools, thus taught, being disrespectful to one another, will not listen to their preceptors (upajjhāyas), just as a wild horse does not respect the charioteer.

Thus will be the practice of monks and nuns in the future when the final time arrives. Before this great danger of the future comes, be easy to admonish, gentle, and respectful to one another. Be those with minds of loving-kindness, compassionate, restrained in virtue, with aroused energy, resolute, and always of firm persistence.
362:
“Seeing negligence as danger and diligence as safety, develop the Eightfold Path, touching the deathless state (Amata).” He spoke these verses.

In those verses, “kodhanā” refers to those who have a nature of being prone to anger. The phrase “will arise in the future” should be connected here. If one asks whether there were no such angry persons during the time of the Elder, the answer is not that there were none; they did exist. However, at that time, because of the abundance of good friends (kalyāṇamitta), the presence of many fellow practitioners who could admonish and instruct, and because the monks mostly practiced reflection even when defilements were strong, they were generally not prone to anger. In the future, they will become extremely angry as the opposite of that condition; therefore, it is said, “in the future.” The same principle applies to the remaining terms.

“Upanāhī” refers to one who has the nature of binding a grudge regarding the objects of malice, or one is called “upanāhī” because of the arising of ill-will (upanāha). Between these two, the ill-will that arises in the earlier period is called anger (kodha), and the ill-will that arises in the later period is called a grudge (upanāha). Alternatively, anger that occurs once is called “kodha,” and anger that occurs many times is called “upanāha.” They smear the evident virtues of others; or, because they smear and cover those virtues like water being smeared on a water-wiping cloth, they are called “makkhī” (smearers). Because they possess stubbornness (thambha) characterized by extreme conceit, they are called “thambhī.” “Saṭhā” refers to those endowed with deceit (sāṭheyya) characterized by making non-existent virtues appear evident. “Issukī” refers to those endowed with envy (issā) characterized by disparaging the prosperity of others. “Nānāvādā” means those who have conflicting speech, conflicting views, and those who cause quarrels.

“Aññātamānino dhamme gambhīre tīragocarā” refers to those who, without knowing the profound and difficult-to-perceive True Dhamma (Saddhamma), claim, “I know, I see.” For that very reason, because they exist on this side of that Dhamma, they are those whose range is the near shore of the unwholesome. “Lahukā” refers to those of a light nature, the frivolous. “Agarū dhamme” refers to those who lack respect for the True Dhamma. “Aññamaññamagāravā” refers to those who lack respect for one another, and lack honor and respect for the Saṅgha and fellow practitioners. “Bahū ādīnavā” refers to the many faults, dangers, and obstacles of the types already mentioned and those yet to be mentioned. “Loke” means in the world of sentient beings. “Uppajjissantyanāgate” means they will appear and arise in the future. “Sudesitaṃ imaṃ dhammaṃ” refers to this noble Dhamma of the three Pitakas, which was well-taught by the Fully Enlightened One without distortion, being excellent in the beginning and so forth. “Kilesissanti” means they will make it defiled, corrupted by defilements. “Āpattiṃ anāpattīti” means they will treat a grave offense as a light offense and so forth, through the corruption of misconduct, and by rejecting the subtle teachings of mind and matter (rūpa-arūpa) through the corruption of wrong view, both of which...
363:
By means of the false Dhamma (asaddhamma) which causes the corruption of misconduct, such as [calling] ‘a light offense’ [a non-offense], they will reject the subtle and profound teachings of mind and matter (rūpa-arūpa). They will defile and make it stained through both the corruption of wrong view (diṭṭhi) and the corruption of craving (taṇhā). ‘Dummatī’ refers to foolish monks who lack wisdom. For this was said by the Blessed One: ‘Monks, in the future, there will be monks... who, while preaching the Abhidhamma and Vedalla discourses, will enter into dark states (kaṇhadhamma) and will not understand.’ (A. Ni. 5.79).

‘Guṇahīnā’ refers to those who are immoral and shameless, devoid of virtues such as morality (sīla). Alternatively, ‘guṇahīnā’ means those who are deficient in virtues such as the Vinaya practices and have little knowledge of the Dhamma and Vinaya. ‘Saṅghamhi’ means in the midst of the Saṅgha. ‘Voharantā’ means when speaking, specifically when uttering anything at random during the delivery of a decision (vinicchaya) in the Saṅgha. ‘Visāradā’ refers to those who are bold and audacious, lacking fear. ‘Balavanto’ means those who are powerful due to the strength of their factions. ‘Mukharā’ means those who are harsh-mouthed and speak rough words. ‘Assutāvino’ refers to those who are unlearned. Relying only on gain, offerings, and fame, they will pretend to possess virtue and will become powerful in establishing their desired meanings in the midst of the Saṅgha, saying, ‘Dhamma is non-Dhamma, non-Dhamma is Dhamma, Vinaya is non-Vinaya, and non-Vinaya is Vinaya.’

‘Guṇavanto’ refers to those endowed with virtues such as morality. ‘Voharantā yathātthato’ refers to those who explain clearly according to the true meaning without distortion, saying, ‘Dhamma is Dhamma, non-Dhamma is non-Dhamma, Vinaya is Vinaya, and non-Vinaya is non-Vinaya.’ These people will become weak because of the prevalence of shameless ones in the assembly, and their words will not carry weight. ‘Hirīmanā anatthikā’ refers to those who are ashamed of evil and desire nothing. Although they are capable of speaking according to the Dhamma, because of their loathing for evil and their desire for few duties, they do not quarrel with anyone, do not strive to establish their own doctrine, and remain silent without making their views known or taking a firm stand.

‘Rajata’ means silver; by this term, coins (kahāpaṇa) and copper money (lohamāsaka) are also included. ‘Jātarūpa’ means gold; by this term, gems, pearls, and so forth are also included. The word ‘vā’ (or) has the sense of inclusion (samuccaya), as in ‘apadā vā’ and so forth. There is also a variant reading ‘rajatajātarūpañca.’ ‘Khetta’ refers to the place where grains and crops (pubbaṇṇa-aparaṇṇa) are grown (fields). A plot of land not prepared for such cultivation is called ‘vatthu.’ In the term ‘ajeḷaka,’ ‘eḷaka’ refers to goats; excluding them, other species of livestock are called ‘aja.’ By the word ‘ajeḷaka’ itself, cows, buffaloes, and so forth are also included. ‘Dāsidāsañca’ refers to female and male servants.
364:
And in slaves. Unwise people, not knowing what is allowable or unallowable, suitable or unsuitable, will delight in and accept [things] for their own benefit.

Those who have a mind to look for the faults of others, or who are habitually disparaging even in matters that should not be criticized, are called 'ujjhānasaññino'. Those who are endowed with the characteristics of fools, such as having bad thoughts, and because of that, do not have a concentrated mind in the fourfold purity of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla), are called 'bālā'. Those who are puffed up with empty pride are called 'unnaḷā'. They will wander about raising the banner of pride. Those who, like wild beasts, delight only in quarreling due to excessive rivalry, who are devoid of concern for their own benefit like animals, and who are intent only on seeking food and harming the weak, are called 'kalahābhiratā magā'.

Those who are agitated and lack one-pointedness of mind are called 'uddhatā'. Those who wear blue robes dyed with unallowable dye, and who wander about wearing and dressing in such robes, are called 'nīlacīvarapārutā'. Those who are deceivers through deceptive practices such as flattery, and who act pretentiously to make others wonder, desiring to be praised for virtues they do not possess, are called 'kuhā'. Those who have a stiff mind and a harsh heart due to anger and pride are called 'thaddhā'. Those who are flatterers and have a deceptive livelihood, who make people with faithful minds say, 'Bhante, what does the venerable one need?' to the donors of requisites, or who flatter for the sake of requisites through suggestive speech or by pressuring donors (nippesikatā), are called 'lapā'. 'What is called "siṅga" (horn) there? That which is called "siṅga" is vanity, cleverness, being well-groomed, and so on.' Thus, those who are endowed with manifest defilements similar to horns, and who behave with vanity like horned creatures, are called 'siṅgī'. The phrase 'like the Noble Ones' is shown to explain the meaning of 'kuhā'. To show that deceivers live pretending to be like the Noble Ones, it is said, 'They will wander about like the Noble Ones.'

They will be [those with hair] anointed with wax-oil or water-oil. Those who are frivolous, obsessed with decorating the body and requisites, are called 'capalā'. Those whose eyes are painted with decorative collyrium are called 'añjanakkhikā'. They will wander here and there on the main roads under the pretexts of alms-round or visiting families. Those who clothe their bodies in robes dyed the color of ivory are called 'dantavaṇṇikapārutā'.
365:
'Ajegucchaṃ' means that which should not be loathed. 'Vimuttehi' means by the Noble Ones (Ariyas). 'Surattaṃ' means a robe well-dyed with allowable dye. Because it is the practice of the Arahants such as the Buddha, they will loathe the saffron robe (kāsāva), which is the banner of the Arahants. Why? Because they have reached a state of extreme attachment and greed for white clothes. This is the explanation for wearing ivory-colored robes. For those monks, while praising white cloth, they think, 'If we wear entirely white cloth, it would be the abandonment of the monk's sign,' and thus they wear ivory-colored robes.

'Lābhakāmā' means those who are greedy for gain. They are lazy because they are associated with indolence even in alms-rounds. They are of inferior energy because they lack the mental effort to perform the duties of a recluse (samaṇadhamma). 'Kicchanti' means those who are weary; it means those whose minds are weary of living in forest-dwelling monasteries. 'Gāmantesu' means in village-border dwellings, dwellings near a village, or dwellings at the village gates. 'Vasissare' means they will dwell.

Imitating those various individuals who have obtained gains through the practice of wrong livelihood (micchājīva), they will wander about. 'Bhamissanti' means they themselves will wander about, serving royal families and so on, to produce gain through wrong livelihood like those others. There is also a variant reading 'bhajissanti', which means they will associate with them. 'Asaṃyatā' means those who are devoid of restraint in virtue.

'Ye ye alābhino lābhaṃ' means those monks who do not obtain the gain of requisites because of avoiding wrong livelihood and because of having little merit; although they are worthy of honor and praise, they will not exist [prominently] in that future time. They will not associate with those wise monks who are very fond of virtue and endowed with fortitude. In that future time, there will only be monks who have gains and who desire gains.

'Milakkhurajanaṃ rattaṃ' means cloth dyed with a dark-black dye. This is a compound word, and the nasalization (niggahīta) is shown for the sake of ease in reciting the verse. 'Garahantā sakaṃ dhajaṃ' means loathing the saffron robe, which is their own banner. For those ordained in the Dispensation (Sāsana), the saffron robe is called the banner. 'Titthiyānaṃ dhajaṃ keci' means some, while professing to be Sakyaputtiya monks, will wear white cloth, which is the banner of the sectarians (titthiyas).

Disrespect and lack of esteem for the saffron robe, which is the banner of the Arahants, will occur to those monks in that future time. 'Paṭisaṅkhā ca kāsāve' means...
366:
Even the mere act of reflecting in the manner of 'Reflecting wisely, I use the robe,' and so forth, will not be present in the use of the saffron robe [by those without virtue]. One who wears the saffron robe should cherish it and think, 'I must refrain from misconduct.' To show that the robe should be treated with respect, the Elder cited the Chaddanta Jātaka as an example and said, 'Abhibhūtassa dukkhena' (Overcome by suffering), and so forth. In that context, 'sallaviddhassa' means one who is pierced by a large, poisoned arrow, and consequently, one who is oppressed by great suffering. 'Ruppato' means one whose body is undergoing transformation [due to pain]. 'Mahāghorā' refers to a reflection that was terrifying and grand because it was devoid of concern for body and life; it was a reflection that others could not even conceive of, which occurred to the Great Elephant King Chaddanta. Indeed, during his time as the Chaddanta Elephant King, the Bodhisatta was shot with a poisoned arrow by a hunter named Soṇuttara, who stood in a concealed place. While being oppressed by great suffering, he saw the saffron robe worn by that hunter and thought, 'This person is wearing the robe which is the banner of the Noble Ones; I must not harm him.' Thus, establishing only a mind of loving-kindness (mettā) toward that hunter, he preached the higher Dhamma. As it is said:

'The elephant, though pierced by a large arrow,
With a mind free from malice, spoke to the hunter:
For what purpose, or for what reason, friend,
Do you kill me? Whose undertaking is this?'

To show this meaning, the Elder said, 'Chaddanto hi' (For Chaddanta...), and so forth. Therein, 'surattaṃ arahaddhajaṃ' (the bright red banner of the Arahants) refers to the saffron robe worn by the hunter Soṇuttara. 'Abhaṇi' means he spoke. 'Gāthā' refers to the verses. 'Gajo' refers to the Chaddanta Elephant King. 'Atthopasaṃhitā' means connected with welfare, endowed with benefit. In the verses spoken by the Chaddanta Elephant King, 'anikkasāvo' means one who still has the 'stains' (kasāva) of defilements such as lust. 'Paridahissati' means he will use it by way of wearing, dressing, or spreading it out. There is also a variant reading 'paridhassati.' 'Apeto damasaccena' means one who is devoid of, separated from, or has abandoned both the restraint of the senses (indriya-dama) and truthfulness of speech (vaci-sacca) which belongs to the side of ultimate truth. 'Na so' means such a person is not worthy of wearing the saffron robe.
367:
'Vantakasāvassa' means one who has vomited, discarded, or abandoned the stains of defilements through the four Paths. 'Sīlesu' refers to the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla). 'Susumāhito' means well-concentrated. 'Upeto' means one who is endowed with or possessed of both the restraint of the senses and the aforementioned truthfulness. 'Sa ve' means such a person is truly worthy of that fragrant saffron cloth.

'Vipannasīlo' means one whose virtue is broken. 'Dummedho' means one who lacks wisdom, specifically the wisdom that purifies virtue. 'Pākaṭo' means one who is notorious, as in 'This person is immoral,' or it means one with manifest senses due to having scattered senses. 'Kāmakāriyo' means one who acts according to his own desires because his restraint is broken, or one who is to be dealt with according to the will of Māra, who is Desire. 'Vibbhantacitto' means one whose mind is scattered among sense objects such as forms. 'Nissukko' means one who is devoid of 'white' (pure) dhammas, lacking moral shame (hiri) and moral dread (ottappa), or one who lacks the effort to fulfill wholesome qualities.

'Vītarāgo' means one whose lust has departed. 'Odātamanasaṅkappo' means one whose mental intentions are very pure, or one whose intentions are unclouded.

'Kāsāvaṃ kiṃ karissati' means what benefit will the robe provide to one who lacks virtue? The monastic sign of such a person is like a painted image.

'Duṭṭhacittā' means those whose minds are corrupted by faults such as lust. 'Anādarā' means those who have no respect or reverence for the Teacher, the Dhamma, or each other. 'Tādīnaṃ mettacittānaṃ' refers to those of noble qualities who have reached the state of 'tādi' (equanimity) regarding desirable and undesirable objects through the attainment of Arahantship, and whose hearts are associated with the meditation on loving-kindness. Here, the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative. 'Niggaṇhissanti' means they will harass them so that they leave in distress, fearing that 'if people see those endowed with virtue and honor them, they will no longer respect us who are immoral.'

'Sikkhāpentāpi' means even when they are being instructed. Here, the active form is used in a passive sense. 'Therehi' means by their own teachers and preceptors. 'Cīvaradhāraṇaṃ' is a mere illustration of the practice of a monk. Therefore, it means that even when they are taught, 'You should advance in this way, you should retreat in this way,' and so forth, [they do not accept it].
368:
It means (not taking heed) even when being taught by teachers and preceptors, ‘Thus one should advance, thus one should retreat,’ and so on. ‘Na suṇissanti’ means they will not accept the advice. Those fools, lacking the eye of wisdom, even when being taught by teachers and preceptors, remain like those who have not been taught because of their lack of respect and failure to follow. They have no respect for their preceptors and teachers and do not abide by their instructions. How? Just as a rogue horse does not listen to the horse trainer and does not abide by his instructions, so too, these individuals do not fear or respect their preceptors and teachers. 

The word ‘Evaṃ’ and so on is the conclusion of the meaning already stated. There, ‘Evaṃ’ means in the manner already described. ‘Anāgataddhānaṃ’ means the future time that has not yet come. To show that very time specifically, he said, ‘When the final time has arrived.’ There, what is the final time? Some say the final time begins from the Third Council, but some do not accept that. In truth, there are five eras in the Sasana: the era of liberation (vimutti-yuga), the era of concentration (samādhi-yuga), the era of virtue (sīla-yuga), the era of learning (suta-yuga), and the era of giving (dāna-yuga). Among them, first, when the era of liberation disappears, the era of concentration occurs. When the era of concentration disappears, the era of virtue occurs. When the era of virtue disappears, the era of learning certainly occurs. One whose virtue is impure, desiring gains and such, may stand upholding scriptural learning (pariyatti) only in part. But when all scriptural learning, ending with the Mātikā, disappears entirely, from then on, only the mere outward sign of a monk will remain. At that time, they will seek wealth by any means and distribute it through the channel of giving. It is said that such action is their final good practice. In the view of those teachers, the final time begins from the era of learning. Others say it begins from the era of virtue. 

Thus, after showing the great danger that will arise in the final time, the Elder, wishing to give advice to the monks assembled there, spoke three verses beginning with ‘Purā āgacchate’. In those verses, ‘Purā āgacchate etaṃ’ means before this great future danger, which causes obstacles to practice as I have described, arrives—only until the time it arrives. ‘Subbacā’ means being endowed with qualities that make one easy to speak to, being patient with words, and respectfully accepting the instructions of teachers. ‘Sakhilā’ means those with gentle hearts. Mettā means having a mind associated with loving-kindness, characterized by bestowing welfare and happiness upon all beings. ‘Kāruṇikā’ means being endowed with compassion that arises with the desire to remove the suffering of others. ‘Ariyā’ means those with effort, striving to abandon unwholesome states and fulfill wholesome states. ‘Pahitattā’ means those whose minds are directed toward Nibbāna. ‘Niccaṃ’ means at all times. ‘Padhanapakkama’ means having firm effort. ‘Pamāda’ means negligence, which is the lack of exertion in wholesome states and letting the mind loose in unwholesome states. In that context, what is negligence (pamāda)? It is the letting loose of the mind in bodily misconduct or in the strands of sensual pleasure (is the letting loose of the mind).
369:
“Mettacittā” means those with minds associated with loving-kindness (mettā), which has the characteristic of promoting the welfare of all beings. “Kāruṇikā” means those endowed with compassion (karuṇā), which functions as the removal of the suffering of others. “Āraddhavīriyā” means those with energetic effort exerted to abandon unwholesome states and to fulfill wholesome states. “Pahitattā” means those with minds directed towards Nibbāna. “Niccaṃ” means at all times. “Daḷhaparakkamā” means those with firm and steady effort. “Pamāda” means negligence, the non-practice of wholesome states, and the letting loose of the mind in unwholesome states. Regarding this meaning, it is stated in the Vibhaṅga: “Therein, what is negligence? It is the release of the mind, the repeated release of the mind, in bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, mental misconduct, or in the five strands of sensual pleasure; it is the lack of thoroughness in the development of wholesome states,” and so on. “Appamāda” means heedfulness. This heedfulness should be understood as the opposite of negligence. In essence, heedfulness is the non-absence of mindfulness; it is indeed a name for established mindfulness. The meaning here is: since all misfortunes have negligence as their root, and all benefits have heedfulness as their root, therefore, seeing negligence as a danger and a calamity, and seeing heedfulness as safety and the absence of calamity, one should develop the Noble Eightfold Path—consisting of the eight factors such as Right View, which are included in the three aggregates of virtue and so on, which are the pinnacle of the practice of heedfulness. Touch and realize the deathless Nibbāna, and bring it into existence within your own continuity. Do not stop at the mere Path of Stream-entry, but develop it further by giving rise to the three higher Paths. In this way, your development of heedfulness will reach its pinnacle. 

Thus, the Elder exhorted the assembled audience. These very verses were the Elder's verses declaring his realization of Arahatship (aññābyākaraṇa). 

## The Commentary on the Verses of Phussa Thera is Finished.
370:
## 2. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Sāriputta

The verses beginning with 'Yathācārī yathāsato' are those of the Venerable Elder Sāriputta. The account of that Venerable One and the Venerable Elder Mahāmoggallāna should be understood as follows:

In the past, more than one hundred thousand aeons and one incalculable period (asankheyya) ago, the Venerable Sāriputta was born into a wealthy Brāhmaṇa family (Brāhmaṇa-mahāsāla) and was known by the name Sarada the youth. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was born into a wealthy householder family (Gahapati-mahāsāla) and was known by the name Sirivaḍḍha the householder. These two were childhood friends who played together in the dust. Among them, after his father's death, Sarada the youth took possession of the family inheritance. One day, while in seclusion, he thought: 'The death of these beings is indeed certain. Therefore, I should enter the homeless life and seek the path to liberation.' He approached his friend and said: 'Friend, I wish to go forth as a monk. Will you be able to go forth as well?' When the friend replied, 'I will not be able to,' Sarada said, 'So be it, I alone shall go forth.' He then had the treasure houses opened, gave great alms to the poor, travelers, and others, went to the foot of a mountain, and became an ascetic (isi). Following his example, seventy-four thousand sons of Brahmins also went forth. That ascetic attained the five supernormal powers (abhiññā) and the eight attainments (samāpatti), and he taught the preliminary exercises for the kasina meditations to those other ascetics. They all likewise attained the five supernormal powers and the eight attainments.

At that time, the Sammāsambuddha named Anomadassī appeared in the world, set the noble Wheel of Dhamma in motion, and delivered beings from the great flood of saṃsāra. One day, thinking, 'I shall show favor to the ascetic Sarada and his disciples,' he took his bowl and robes and, traveling alone through the air, descended from the sky and stood upon the earth right before the ascetic's eyes, intending, 'Let him know my state as a Buddha.' The ascetic Sarada, observing the marks of a Great Man (mahāpurisalakkhaṇa) on the Teacher's body, concluded, 'This is certainly an Omniscient Buddha.' He went out to welcome him, prepared a seat, and offered it. The Blessed One sat on the prepared seat. The ascetic Sarada sat down in a suitable place near the Teacher.

At that time, those seventy-four thousand matted-hair ascetics, who were disciples of Sarada, arrived bringing various choice and nutritious fruits, and seeing the Teacher...
371:
...seeing the Teacher, they were filled with faith. Observing the manner in which their teacher and the Buddha were seated, they said: 'Teacher, in the past we used to travel about saying, "There is no one greater than you." But we think this man is greater than you.' The teacher replied: 'What are you saying, dear ones? Do you wish to compare Mount Sineru, which is six hundred and eighty thousand yojanas high, with a mustard seed? Do not compare me with the Omniscient Buddha.' Then, hearing their teacher's words, those ascetics said: 'How great indeed is this Supreme Man!' and they all prostrated at his feet and paid homage to the Teacher.

Then their teacher said: 'Dear ones, we have no offering suitable for the Teacher, and the Teacher has come here at the time for seeking alms. Come, let us give an offering according to our ability. Bring whatever choice fruits you have gathered.' Having had them brought, he washed his hands and personally placed them in the Tathāgata's bowl. As soon as the Teacher accepted the fruits, the deities infused them with divine essence. The ascetic Sarada himself filtered the water and offered it. Then, after the meal was finished and while the Teacher was seated, Sarada called all his disciples and sat near the Teacher, engaging in memorable conversation. The Teacher thought: 'Let the two chief disciples come together with the community of monks.' Knowing the Teacher's thought, the chief disciples immediately arrived, surrounded by one hundred thousand Arahants who had destroyed the taints (khīṇāsava), paid homage to the Teacher, and stood to one side.

Then the ascetic Sarada addressed his disciples: 'Dear ones, an offering of flower-seats (pupphāsana) should be made to the Teacher and the community of monks. Therefore, bring flowers.' Immediately, by means of psychic power, they brought flowers endowed with color and fragrance and prepared a flower-seat for the Buddha measuring one yojana. They prepared seats of three gāvutas for the two chief disciples, seats ranging from half a yojana for the remaining monks, and a seat of one usabha for the most junior monk. When the seats had been thus prepared, the ascetic Sarada stood before the Tathāgata with palms joined in reverence and said: 'Venerable Sir, for my benefit, please ascend and sit upon this flower-seat.' The Blessed One sat upon the flower-seat. When the Teacher was seated, the two chief disciples and the remaining monks also sat on their respective seats. The Teacher, thinking 'May this be of great fruit for them,' entered the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). Knowing that the Teacher had entered the attainment, the two chief disciples and the remaining monks also entered the attainment of cessation.
372:
The ascetic Sarada stood continuously for seven days holding a flower parasol. The other ascetics, however, after consuming forest roots and fruits, spent the rest of the time standing with their hands raised in reverential salutation.

After seven days, the Blessed One emerged from the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) and addressed the Chief Disciple, the Elder Nisabha: 'Perform the appreciation (anumodanā) for the flower-seats of the ascetics.' Established in the knowledge of a disciple's perfection (sāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa), the Elder performed the appreciation for their flower-seats. At the conclusion of that Elder's teaching, the Blessed One addressed the second Chief Disciple, the Elder Anoma: 'You too, teach the Dhamma to these ascetics.' He also, having reflected on the Word of the Buddha contained in the Three Piṭakas, taught the Dhamma to them. Despite the teachings of both Elders, not a single person attained the realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya). Then, the Blessed One, established in the Buddha-range (buddha-visaya), began the Dhamma teaching. At the conclusion of the teaching, with the exception of the ascetic Sarada, all the remaining ascetics, numbering about seventy-four thousand, attained Arahantship. The Blessed One stretched out his hand, saying, 'Come, monks!' (Ehi Bhikkhu). At that very moment, their ascetic appearance vanished, and they became like Elders of sixty years' standing, bearing the eight noble requisites.

The ascetic Sarada, however, because of the thought that arose in him during the Blessed One's discourse—'Oh, how wonderful it would be if I too were to become the Chief Disciple of a Buddha in the future, just like this Elder Nisabha'—became distracted and was unable to penetrate the Paths and Fruits. Then, having paid homage to the Tathāgata, he made such an aspiration (paṇidhāna). The Blessed One, seeing that his aspiration would be fulfilled without obstacle, prophesied: 'One incalculable and a hundred thousand aeons from now, you will become the Chief Disciple named Sāriputta of the Sammāsambuddha named Gotama.' Having given a Dhamma talk, he departed into the sky surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks.

The ascetic Sarada also went to his friend Sirivaḍḍha and said, 'Friend, at the feet of the Blessed One Anomadassī, I have aspired to the position of Chief Disciple of the future Sammāsambuddha named Gotama; you too, aspire to the position of the second disciple of that Buddha.'

Hearing that advice, Sirivaḍḍha had an area of about eight karīsas at the entrance of his house leveled, scattered flowers including parched grain, erected a pavilion roofed with blue lotuses, prepared a seat for the Buddha, and seats for the monks...
373:
...having prepared the seats and arranged a grand ceremony of honor and respect, he had the ascetic Sarada invite the Blessed One and conducted a great almsgiving (mahādāna) for seven days. Having offered costly garments to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, he made an aspiration for the status of the second disciple. The Blessed One, seeing that his aspiration would be fulfilled without obstacle, gave the prophecy in the manner already described, performed the appreciation for the meal, and departed. Sirivaḍḍha, filled with joy, performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and, at the second moment of consciousness (at death), was reborn in the sense-sphere deva world. The ascetic Sarada, having developed the four Brahma-vihāras, was reborn in the Brahma world.

From that time on, the intervening history of those two is not mentioned. However, even before the appearance of our Blessed One, the ascetic Sarada took conception in the womb of the Brahmin woman Rūpasārī in the village of Upatissa, not far from the city of Rājagaha. On that very same day, his friend also took conception in the womb of the Brahmin woman Moggallī in the village of Kolita, also not far from Rājagaha. It is said that those two families had been close friends for seven generations. On the same day, the ceremony for the protection of the embryo was performed for both of them. When they were born after ten months, sixty-six nurses were provided for them. On the naming day, the son of the Brahmin woman Rūpasārī was named 'Upatissa' because he was the son of the leading family in Upatissa village. The other was named 'Kolita' because he was the son of the leading family in Kolita village. Both of them grew up with a large retinue and, as they reached maturity, mastered all the arts and sciences.

Then one day, while they were watching the Mountain-top Festival (Giraggasamajja) in Rājagaha and seeing the great crowd of people assembled, they gained spiritual urgency (saṃvega) through the ripening of their knowledge, reflecting wisely: 'All these people will fall into the jaws of death within a hundred years.' Then, having decided, 'We must seek the Dhamma of liberation (mokkha-dhamma), and in seeking it, it is proper to obtain ordination,' they went forth as recluses under the wanderer Sañjaya along with five hundred youths. From the time they ordained, Sañjaya became exceedingly endowed with gain and fame. Within a few days, they mastered all of Sañjaya's doctrine, but seeing no essence in it, they left and questioned various recluses and Brahmins who were regarded as wise in various places. Those [people]...
374:
Those who were called wise could not answer when questioned by Upatissa and Kolita; on the contrary, it was Upatissa and Kolita who answered their questions. Thus, searching for liberation (mokkha), they made an agreement: "Whoever among us first attains the Deathless (Amata), let him inform the other."

At that time, our Teacher, having attained supreme enlightenment and set in motion the noble Wheel of Dhamma, gradually tamed the thousand matted-hair ascetics led by Uruvela Kassapa and others, and was staying in Rājagaha. One day, the wandering ascetic Upatissa, while going to the wanderers' park, saw the Venerable Assaji Thera walking for alms in Rājagaha. He thought, "I have never before seen a renunciant with such perfect deportment. Surely there must be a peaceful teaching (Dhamma) in this venerable one." Filled with faith and wishing to ask a question, he followed behind Venerable Assaji. The Elder, having received almsfood, went to a suitable place to eat. The wanderer spread out his own wanderer's seat and offered it. After the meal, he also offered water to the Elder from his own water-pot.

Having thus performed the duties of a student and exchanged pleasantries with the Elder who had finished his meal, he asked, "Who is your teacher? Whose Dhamma do you prefer?" The Elder pointed to the Fully Enlightened Buddha. When asked again by Upatissa, "What is the doctrine of your teacher?", the Elder, thinking "I will show the depth of this Dispensation," made known his status as a newcomer and, wishing to explain the Dhamma of the Dispensation briefly, recited the verse beginning with "Ye dhammā hetuppabhavā."

Just by hearing the first two lines, the wanderer was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala) which is endowed with a thousandfold methods. The remaining two lines were completed while he was already a Stream-enterer. At the end of the verse, having become a Stream-enterer and not proceeding to higher distinctions, he reflected, "There must be a reason for this," and said to the Elder: "Venerable Sir, do not expand the Dhamma teaching further; this much is enough. Where does our Teacher reside?" "In Veḷuvana," the Elder replied. "Venerable Sir, you go ahead; I will fulfill the promise made to my friend and then come with him," he said, and with the fivefold prostration...
375:
(Upatissa) paid homage to the Elder with the fivefold prostration, circumambulated him three times, and having seen the Elder off, went to the wanderers' park.

The wandering ascetic Kolita saw Upatissa coming from afar and thought, "His complexion is not like other days; surely he has attained the Deathless." Praising his attainment of the distinction, he asked about the attainment of the Deathless. Upatissa admitted, "Friend, the Deathless has indeed been attained," and recited the same verse. At the end of the verse, Kolita was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry and asked, "Where is our Teacher?" "In Veḷuvana," Upatissa replied. "In that case, friend, let us go; we shall see the Teacher."

Upatissa was always one who honored his teachers; therefore, he went to Sañjaya to declare the virtues of the Teacher, wishing to bring him also to the Teacher. Sañjaya, overcome by greed for gain and not wanting to be a disciple, refused, saying, "I cannot become a small water-pot after being a large one (caṭi)." Although they tried to convince Sañjaya with many reasons, they were unable to do so, and thus they went to Veḷuvana together with two hundred and fifty disciples who followed their guidance.

The Teacher, seeing them coming from afar, said, "These two will be my pair of chief disciples, the excellent pair." He taught them according to the temperaments of the assembly, established them in Arahantship, and granted them ordination as "Ehi Bhikkhu." Just as for the others, miraculous bowls and robes appeared for the chief disciples as well. However, the work for the three higher paths was not yet finished. Why? Because of the greatness of the Knowledge of a Disciple's Perfection (Sāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa).

Among the two chief disciples, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, on the seventh day after his ordination, while practicing monk's duties in Kallavālagāma in the Magadha country, was overcome by drowsiness. The Teacher stirred him, dispelled his drowsiness, and while he was listening to the meditation on elements (Dhātukammaṭṭhāna), he attained the three higher paths and reached the summit of the Knowledge of a Disciple's Perfection. Venerable Sāriputta, fifteen days after his ordination, while staying with the Teacher in the Sūkarakhata Cave in Rājagaha, was listening to the Vedanāpariggaha Sutta being taught to his nephew, the wanderer Dīghanakha. Following the teaching with his wisdom, he reached the summit of the Knowledge of a Disciple's Perfection, like one eating food prepared by another. Thus, the chief disciples reached the summit of the Knowledge of a Disciple's Perfection only in the presence of the Teacher.

Therefore, not far from the Himalayas, there is a mountain named Lambaka. On that mountain, I well-constructed a hermitage. I also well-created a leaf-roofed hut. Not far from my hermitage, there is a river with high banks and a good landing place.
376:
(Like eating rice served by another), they attained the pinnacle of the Disciple's Perfection Knowledge (Sāvakapāramīñāṇa). Thus, both Chief Disciples (Aggasāvaka) attained the pinnacle of the Disciple's Perfection Knowledge in the presence of the Teacher. Regarding this, it is stated in the Apadāna:

“Not far from the Himavanta mountains, there is a mountain named Lambaka. On that mountain, my hermitage was well-constructed, and a leaf-hut was well-fashioned.

“Not far from my hermitage, there is a delightful small river with high banks and excellent landing places. That river is strewn with pure sands.

“Free from pebbles and precipices, and without any foul odor, that small river of pleasant taste flows, beautifying my hermitage.

“Crocodiles, sea-monsters (makara), fierce fish, and tortoises dwell in that river, beautifying my hermitage.

“Pāṭhīna, pāvusa, shark, balaja, and muñjarohita fish leap and dart above the water, beautifying my hermitage.

“On both banks of the river, trees laden with flowers and fruits hang down from both sides, beautifying my hermitage.

“In my hermitage, mango (amba), sāla, tilaka, pāṭalī, and sinduvāra trees are in bloom, diffusing a fragrance like that of the devas.

“Cammaka, pine (saḷala), nīpa, nāga, punnāga, and ketaka trees are in bloom in my hermitage, diffusing a fragrance like that of the devas.

“Atimutta, asoka, and bhaginīmālā are in bloom. Aṅkola and bimbi-jāla trees are also in bloom in my hermitage.

“Ketaka, kandali, godhuka, and tiṇasūlika trees, diffusing a divine fragrance, beautify my hermitage.

“Kaṇikāra, kaṇṇikā, asana, and many arjuna trees, diffusing a divine fragrance, beautify my hermitage.

“Punnāga, mountain-punnāga, and koviḷāra trees are in bloom, diffusing a divine fragrance and beautifying my hermitage.”
377:
“Uddālaka trees, kuṭaja trees, kadamba trees, and many bakula trees, diffusing a divine fragrance, beautify my hermitage.

“Āḷaka, isi-mugga, banana, and citron (mātuluṅga) trees, well-nourished by fragrant water, bear fruits.

“Some paduma lotuses are in bloom, others are just filaments, and some paduma lotuses have shed their petals; at that time, they bloom within the lake.

“The paduma lotuses are in bud, lotus stalks are emerging, and the lotus thickets filled with leaves are beautiful within the lake at that time.

“Lambū bushes, mango-scented flowers, uttali, and bandhujīvaka flowers bloom within the lake at that time, diffusing a divine fragrance.

“Pāṭhīna, pāvusa, shark, balaja, muñjarohita, saṅgula, and maggura fish also dwell within the lake at that time.

“Crocodiles, fierce fish, stingrays, water-demons (rakkhasa), oguha creatures, and pythons dwell within the lake at that time.

“Pigeons, ruddy geese (ravi-haṃsa), cakkavāka, river-birds, cuckoos, parrots, and sālikā birds live depending on that lake.

“Kukutthaka birds, crabs, pond-herons of the forest, dindibha birds, and young parrots live depending on that lake.

“Swans (haṃsa), cranes (koñca), peacocks, cuckoos, red-crested cocks, pampaka, and jīvañjīva birds live depending on that lake.

“Owls, poṭṭhasīsa birds, ospreys, many hawks, and great black crows live depending on that lake.

“Deer (pasada), boars, yaks, many rhinoceroses, rohitca deer, and young parrots live depending on that lake.

“Lions, tigers, leopards, bears, hyenas, panthers, and elephants in three-fold rut live depending on that lake.”
378:
“Kinnaras, monkeys, forest-workers, Ceta kings, and hunters live depending on that lake.

“Tinduka fruits, piyāla fruits, madhuka, and kāsumārī fruits constantly bear fruit not far from my hermitage.

“Kosamba, pine (saḷala), and neem (nimba) trees, endowed with good fruits, constantly bear fruit not far from my hermitage.

“Myrobalan (harītaka), emblic myrobalan (āmalaka), mango, rose-apple (jambu), vibhītaka, jujube (kola), marking-nut (bhallātaka), and wood-apple (bilva) trees bear fruits.

“Āluva tubers, kaḷamba tubers, biḷālī and takkaḷā tubers, jīvaka and sutaka tubers are abundant in my hermitage.

“Not far from the hermitage, there are well-fashioned lakes with clear water, cool water, excellent landing places, and delightful to the heart.

“Covered with paduma and blue lotuses, filled with white lotuses (puṇḍarīka), and covered with lotus stalks and roots, a divine fragrance wafts from them.

“In this forest endowed with all these features, blooming and fruiting, in that well-made and delightful hermitage, I dwelt at that time.

“There was an ascetic named Suruci, virtuous, endowed with vows, a meditator always delighting in jhāna, who had attained the power of the five supernormal knowledges (abhiññā).

“Twenty-four thousand disciples attended upon me; all these were Brahmins of noble birth and great fame.

“They were experts in the science of marks (lakkhaṇa), history (itihāsa), the lexicon (nighaṇḍu), the ritual (keṭubha), word-analysis (padaka), and grammar (veyyākaraṇa), having reached perfection in their own lore.

“They were skilled in portents such as falling meteors (uppāta), signs (nimitta) such as earthquakes, and marks (lakkhaṇa) of elephants and horses; my disciples were well-trained in the lore of the earth and the sky.

“They were few in wishes, wise, moderate in eating, and not frivolous; contented with gain or loss, they always surrounded me.”
379:
Those disciples who are frequent meditators, delighting in jhāna, wise, with peaceful and concentrated minds, and who aspire to the state of nothingness (ākiñcañña), surround me at all times.

Those wise disciples who have reached the perfection of the five supernormal knowledges (abhiññā), who delight in the objects of meditation such as kasiṇa which are their father's heritage, and who travel through the air, surround me at all times.

Those wise disciples of mine, who are restrained in the six sense-doors, free from craving, with guarded faculties, and who do not associate with others, are difficult for others to approach or assail.

Those disciples of mine pass the night by sitting cross-legged, by standing, or by walking to and fro. They are difficult for others to approach or assail.

My disciples do not feel lust for objects that provoke lust, they do not feel anger toward objects that provoke anger, and they are not deluded by objects that provoke delusion. They are difficult for others to approach or assail.

Reflecting on their psychic powers, they manifest those powers at all times. With great effort, they cause the earth to tremble. They are difficult to approach.

When those disciples of mine play, they play only the play of jhāna. They bring fruits from the Jambu tree. Those disciples of mine are difficult to approach.

Some disciples go to the western island of Goyāna to seek food. Some go to the eastern island of Videha. Some go to the northern island of Uttarakuru. In their search for food, they are difficult for others to approach.

They send their baskets of ascetic requisites ahead by psychic power and follow behind. The sky is covered by twenty-four thousand hermits.

Some hermits eat food cooked by fire. Some eat uncooked food. Some eat whatever they can bite with their teeth. Some eat after pounding with a mortar. Some eat whatever they can crush with a stone. Some eat only fallen fruits.

Some hermits, delighting in purity, descend into the water in the evening and morning. My disciples who perform water-ablutions are difficult for others to approach.

With overgrown armpit hair, nails, and beards, with teeth covered in tartar, and with dusty heads, those disciples are fragrant with the scent of virtue. Those disciples of mine are difficult to approach.

Those matted-hair ascetics (jaṭila) of intense practice, having gathered in the morning and discussed their gains and losses, then fly up into the sky.
380:
As they travel through the air, a great sound arises from the deer-skins of those hermits. Because of that sound of deer-skins, the devas are joyful.

The assembly of hermits who travel in the sky go in all directions. Supported by their own psychic power, those hermits go wherever they wish.

These hermits can shake the earth. All of them can travel in the sky. Possessing intense power, they are difficult to overcome. They are unshakeable like the ocean.

Some hermits maintain themselves through the postures of standing and walking. Some hermits undertake the ascetic practice of sitting (nesajjika). Some hermits eat fallen fruits. My disciples are difficult to approach.

These hermits dwell in the meditation of loving-kindness (mettā). They seek the welfare of all living beings. All those hermits are without self-exaltation and do not disparage others.

Fearless like lion-kings, powerful like elephant-kings, and difficult to approach like tigers, those disciples come into my presence.

Vijjādharas, devas, nāgas, gandhabbas, rakkhasas, kumbhaṇḍas, dānavas, and garuḍas live depending on that lake.

All those hermits, with matted hair, laden with baskets of requisites, wearing deer-skins, and traveling through the air, live depending on that lake.

These hermits, whose conduct is always appropriate, are respectful toward one another. Among the twenty-four thousand hermits, not even the sound of a sneeze is heard.

Placing each footstep with mindfulness, without making a sound, and being well-restrained, all those hermits approach and pay homage to me with their heads.

Surrounded by those ascetic disciples of peaceful conduct, I dwell in that hermitage, meditating and delighting in jhāna.

The hermitage is fragrant with both the scent of the hermits' virtue and the scent of flowers, as well as the scent of fruits from the fruiting trees.

I no longer know night or day, and I have no discontent. Instructing my own disciples, I obtain exceeding joy.
381:
The divine scents of blooming flowers and ripening fruits waft through, beautifying my hermitage.

Having emerged from concentration, I, energetic and wise, took my requisites along with the carrying pole and entered the forest.

At that time, being well-trained in omens such as falling meteors, in dreams, and in the marks of a great man, I maintained the mantras that had arisen.

The Blessed One Anomadassī, the Eldest in the World, the Bull among Men, the Fully Enlightened One who desired seclusion, came to the Himavantā forest.

Having entered the Himavantā, that supreme, compassionate Sage, the Best of Men, sat down cross-legged.

I saw that Fully Enlightened One, radiant and delightful, like a blooming blue lotus, like a blazing fire.

I saw the Leader of the World, shining like a glowing lamp-stand, like lightning in the sky, like a kingly Sāla tree in full bloom.

Depending on the sight of this Sage, who is like a noble elephant, of great energy, and the ender of suffering, beings are released from all suffering.

Having seen the God of gods, I examined his marks: "Is he a Buddha or not? Let me see the One with Vision."

The wheel-marks with a thousand spokes were visible on his noble feet. Seeing his marks, I reached the conclusion: "He is indeed the Tathāgata."

Then, taking a broom and sweeping, I gathered flowers and worshipped the Excellent Buddha.

Having worshipped the Fully Enlightened One, who has crossed the flood and is free from taints, I placed my antelope skin on my left shoulder and paid homage to the Leader of the World.

I shall praise that knowledge by which the Fully Enlightened One, free from taints, dwells. Listen to my words as I speak.
382:
O Self-become One of immeasurable compassion, you rescue this world. Depending on the sight of you, those beings cross the stream of doubt.

O Supreme among bipeds, you are the Teacher, the Pinnacle, the Banner, the Sacrificial Post, the Refuge, the Support, and the Island of Protection for living beings.

O Omniscient Buddha, it might be possible to measure the water in the great ocean with a measure (āḷhaka). But it is certainly not possible to measure your omniscient knowledge.

O Omniscient Buddha, it might be possible to weigh the earth by placing it on a scale. But it is certainly not possible to measure your omniscient knowledge.

O Omniscient Buddha, it might be possible to measure the sky with a rope or by finger-breadths (angula). But it is certainly not possible to measure your omniscient knowledge.

The water in the great ocean and the entire earth, when compared to the Buddha's knowledge, are not fit even for a comparison.

O One with Vision, the minds of all beings that exist in the world including the devas are brought within the net of your knowledge.

O Omniscient One, with that knowledge by which you reached the complete and supreme Enlightenment, you have subdued the other heretics.

The ascetic named Suruci, having praised with these verses and spreading his antelope skin, sat on the ground.

Mount Sineru, the king of mountains, which is said to be eighty-four thousand yojanas deep in the ocean and rises just as high above,

That Mount Sineru, so high, long, and wide, if ground into a hundred thousand billion subtle particles,

And if placed one by one at a hundred-thousand (lakkha) marker, it would eventually be exhausted. But O Omniscient Buddha, it is not possible to measure your knowledge.

Just as when one covers the water with a fine-meshed net, whatever beings are in the water are brought within the net...
383:
Even so, O Great Hero, there are many heretics who have plunged into the thicket of views, deluded by their attachments. By your pure knowledge, seeing without obstruction, these are brought within the net of your knowledge; they cannot transcend your knowledge.

At that time, the Blessed One Anomadassī of great fame, having emerged from concentration, the Conqueror looked around the quarters. A disciple of the Sage Anomadassī named Nisabha, surrounded by a hundred thousand monks who were peaceful-minded, such as he, who were free from taints, pure, possessed of the six higher powers, and meditative—knowing the Buddha's mind, he approached the Leader of the World, Anomadassī.

Those monks, standing in the air, performed a circumambulation there. Paying homage with joined palms, they descended into the presence of the Buddha. The Blessed One Anomadassī, the Eldest in the World, the Bull among Men, sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks, the Conqueror manifested a smile.

An attendant of the Teacher Anomadassī named Varuṇa, having arranged his robe over one shoulder, asked the Leader of the World: "Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the reason for the Teacher’s smile? Indeed, Buddhas do not manifest a smile without a cause."

The Blessed One Anomadassī, the Eldest in the World, the Bull among Men, sitting in the midst of the monks, spoke this verse:

"He who worshipped me with flowers and also praised my knowledge, I shall praise him. Listen to what I say."

Knowing the Buddha's words, all the devas assembled. Desiring to hear the True Dhamma, they approached the Fully Enlightened One. In the ten world systems, the hosts of devas of great power, desiring to hear the True Dhamma, they approached the Fully Enlightened One.
384:
The fourfold army of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry will always surround him. This is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.

Sixty thousand musical instruments and well-decorated drums will always attend and play for him. This is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.

Sixteen thousand women, well-adorned with exquisite clothes and ornaments, wearing ruby earrings decorated with pearls and sapphires,

With long eyelashes, smiling, mindful, and slender-waisted, will always surround him. This is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.

For a hundred thousand aeons, he will enjoy the celestial realm. A thousand times, he will be a Cakkavatti king over the land.

A thousand times, he will be Sakka, the king of gods, ruling the divine realm. He will also obtain the position of a regional king for an uncountable number of times.

When he reaches his final birth, he will come to the human world. A Brahmin woman named Sārī will carry him in her womb.

This person will be known by his mother's name as Sāriputta. He will be one of sharp wisdom.

Renouncing eighty crores of wealth and being free from worldly concerns, he will go forth into homelessness. Seeking the peaceful state of Nibbāna, he will wander throughout this earth.

In an incalculable period and a hundred thousand aeons from now, the Teacher named Gotama by lineage, born of the Okkāka clan, will appear in the world.

He will be the heir to that Buddha's Dhamma, like a heart-born son created by the Dhamma. Named Sāriputta, he will be the Chief Disciple (Aggasāvaka).

Just as this river Gaṅgā, called Bhāgīrathī, originating from the Himalayas, flows into and fills the great ocean,

Even so, this Sāriputta will be confident and proficient in the Tipitaka, and having reached the pinnacle of wisdom, he will satisfy all living beings.
385:
Starting from the Himalayas and extending to the great ocean, the sand that lies between them is uncountable by number.

Even that sand might be counted without remainder by calculation, but there will be no end to Sāriputta's wisdom.

If one were to mark and count them, even the sands of the Gaṅgā might be exhausted, but there will be no end to Sāriputta's wisdom.

The waves in the great ocean are uncountable by number; likewise, there will be no end to Sāriputta's wisdom.

Having pleased the Buddha Gotama, the Bull of the Sakyans, and reaching the pinnacle of wisdom, he will become the Chief Disciple.

He will properly follow the Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakka) set in motion by the Sakyan Prince, raining down the showers of Dhamma.

Knowing all this, Gotama, the Bull of the Sakyans, sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks, will appoint him to the highest position.

"Oh, how wonderful is my well-performed deed for the Teacher Anomadassī! By performing an act of service to that Buddha, I have reached the end of all perfections (pāramīs)."

The deed performed in incalculable aeons shows its fruit to me here. Like the momentum of a well-shot arrow, I have burnt away the defilements.

Seeking the Unconditioned (Asaṅkhata), Nibbāna, the unshakable state, I wandered through the cycle of births, investigating all the doctrines of outside sects.

Just as a man afflicted by disease would search for medicine, exploring the entire forest to be free from the disease,

Seeking the Unconditioned, Nibbāna, the Deathless state, I took up the life of a hermit along with five hundred others.

Bearing a mass of matted hair and wearing the noble skin of a black antelope, I reached the pinnacle of mundane psychic powers (abhiññā) and went to the Brahma realm.
386:
There is no purity outside the Dispensation (Sāsana) of the Victorious Buddha. Only some wise beings are purified within the Dispensation of the Victor. This purity is accomplished by one's own effort; it is not achieved merely by saying "it is thus, it is thus." Seeking the Unconditioned Nibbāna, I wandered among those of wrong views.

Just as a man desiring heartwood would cut and split a banana tree but find no heartwood there, for that tree is void of heartwood,

Even so, in this world, many followers of outside sects with various views are void of the Unconditioned Nibbāna, which is like the heartwood.

Having reached my final birth, I was born into a Brahmin family. Renouncing great wealth, I went forth into homelessness.

I was a reciter of the Vedas, a bearer of the mantras, and one who had reached the end of the three Vedas. I lived under the Brahmin named Sañjaya.

O Great Hero, Your disciple, a Brahmin named Assaji, who is difficult to approach and of fierce majesty, was then wandering for alms.

I saw that sage (muni), wise and composed in the practice of silence, with a peaceful mind, like a great elephant, and like a lotus in full bloom.

Seeing him, the thought arose in me: "This monk, well-tamed and pure in mind, a noble bull-like hero, must be an Arahant."

"He moves gracefully, is beautiful to behold, and well-restrained. Tamed in the highest discipline, he must be one who sees the Deathless."

"What if I, with a joyful mind, were to ask him about the supreme goal? When asked, he will explain it to me; then I shall question him further."

I followed behind him as he wandered for alms, waiting for an opportunity to ask about the Deathless state.

When he reached the middle of the street, I approached him and asked: "O Hero, of what lineage are you? Whose disciple are you, venerable sir?"
387:
## 
When I asked him, the Elder Assaji, like a fearless lion king, replied: "O wanderer, the Buddha has appeared in the world; I am a disciple of that Blessed One."

"O Great Hero, O Son who follows [the Teacher], O One of great fame, what is the nature of the Buddha's teaching? O Venerable Monk, please preach the Dhamma to me," (I asked).

When I asked, the Elder Assaji preached the entire teaching—profound, subtle, and called Nibbāna—which destroys the dart of craving and removes all suffering.

"Of those things that arise from a cause, the Tathāgata has told the cause; and also their cessation. Such is the teaching of the Great Ascetic," (he preached).

When that question was answered, I first attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). Having heard the teaching of the Victor (Jina), I became stainless and pure.

Having heard the words of the Sage and seen the supreme Dhamma, having plunged into the True Dhamma, I recited this verse:

"If this is the Dhamma, then even now you have realized the sorrowless state (Nibbāna), which remained unseen and passed by for many hundreds of thousands of aeons."

"While I was searching for the Dhamma, I wandered through the ports of false views. That goal I desired has now been reached; it is time for me to be diligent."

Delighted by Assaji and having reached the unshakable state (Nibbāna), I went to the hermitage seeking my friend.

Seeing me from afar, my well-trained friend, seeing me endowed with [composed] deportment, spoke these words:

"Friend, your face and eyes are serene; the state of a sage is evident. Have you attained the Deathless (Amata), the unshakable state of Nibbāna?"

"O Brahmin, you come appearing beautiful, as if made of the imperturbable. You are calm, like a tamed elephant, O peaceful one."

"Friend, I have attained the Deathless (Amata) which removes the dart of sorrow. You too shall attain it; let us go to the presence of the Buddha."
388:
## 
My well-trained friend (Moggallāna) agreed, saying "Very well," and taking hand in hand, we approached your presence.

O Sakyan Prince, we both shall go forth in your presence. Relying on your teaching, we shall live free from taints (anāsava).

Kolita (Moggallāna) is supreme in psychic power, and I have reached the far shore of wisdom. Let us both together beautify the Dispensation (Sāsana).

With unfulfilled aspirations, I wandered through the ports of false views. By seeing you, my aspiration has been fulfilled.

Firmly established in the earth, trees bloom when the season arrives. Divine-like fragrances waft, delighting all living beings.

O Great Hero, O Sakyan Prince of great fame, in the same way, I too, being established in your Dispensation, it is time for me to bloom.

Seeking the flower of liberation (vimutti), which is the release from the round of rebirths, by obtaining the flower of liberation, I shall delight all living beings.

Within the Buddha-field, leaving aside the Great Sage, there is no one equal in wisdom to me, your son, O One with Vision.

Your disciples are well-disciplined, and the assembly is well-trained. Tamed by the supreme discipline, they always surround you.

The meditators, those delighting in jhāna, the steadfast, those with peaceful minds, the concentrated, the sages endowed with the practice of a sage—they always surround you.

Those with few desires, the prudent, the steadfast, those who eat little, those free from greed, those content with gain or loss—they always surround you.

The forest-dwellers, those delighting in the ascetic practices (dhuta), the meditators, those wearing coarse robes, those delighting in seclusion, the steadfast—they always surround you.

Those on the path (paṭipanna) and those established in the fruit (phalaṭṭha), the trainees (sekha) endowed with the fruit, and the noble worldlings (kalyāṇa-puthujjana) aspiring for the supreme goal—they always surround you.
389:
## 
The stainless Stream-enterers (Sotāpanna), the Once-returners (Sakadāgāmī), the Non-returners (Anāgāmī), and the Arahants—they always surround you.

Those skilled in the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), those delighting in the development of the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga)—all those many disciples always surround you.

Those skilled in the bases of psychic power (iddhipāda), those delighting in the development of concentration (samādhi), those devoted to the right efforts (sammappadhāna)—the disciples always surround you.
