Those with the three knowledges (tevijjā), those with the six higher powers (chaḷabhiññā), those who have reached the perfection of psychic power, and those who have reached the perfection of wisdom—they always surround you.

O Great Hero, such are your well-trained disciples; they are difficult to approach and possess fierce majesty; they always surround you.

Surrounded by those disciples who are self-controlled and ascetic, you shine like a fearless lion king, or like the moon, the king of stars.

Trees grow by being established on the earth; they reach abundance and display their fruits.

O Sakyan Prince, O Buddha of great fame, you are like the earth. Those established in your Dispensation obtain the fruit of the Deathless (Amata).

The Sindhu, Sarassatī, Nandiya, Candabhāgā, Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarabhū, and Mahī rivers—as they flow, the ocean alone receives them. They give up their former names and are known only as the ocean.

In the same way, these four castes, having gone forth in your presence, give up their former names and are known only as "Sons of the Buddha."

Just as the stainless moon, while traveling through the sky, outshines all the stars in the world with its light,

O Great Hero, in the same way, you are surrounded by gods and humans; you outshine them all and shine forever.
390:
## 
Waves arising in the deep ocean do not overstep the shore; when they reach the shore, they are crushed to pieces and scattered.

Similarly, the many sectarians (titthiyas) in the world, though they possess various views and wish to speak of the Dhamma, are unable to surpass that Sage.

O One with the Eye of Wisdom, if those sectarians approach You with opposing doctrines, they are merely crushed upon reaching Your presence.

Just as many kumuda lotuses, their stalks, and roots born in water are smeared with water and mud.

Similarly, many beings born in the world grow up oppressed by lust and hatred, like the kumuda lotus in the mud.

Just as the paduma lotus, born in water, grows in the midst of water but is not smeared by it, being pure along with its filaments.

Similarly, O Great Hero, Great Sage, though You are born in the world, You are not smeared by the world, just as the paduma lotus is not smeared by water.

Just as in the delightful month of Kattika, many water-born lotuses bloom; they do not overstep that month, for it is the season for blooming.

Similarly, O Great Hero, You have bloomed with the Four Noble Truths; Your disciples who have bloomed through the fruit of Arahatship do not overstep Your Dispensation, just as the water-born paduma lotus does not overstep its blooming time.

A King of Sāla trees in full bloom wafts a divine fragrance; surrounded by other Sāla trees, the King of Sāla trees shines.

Similarly, O Great Hero, bloomed with Omniscient Knowledge and surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks, You shine like the King of Sāla trees.

Just as the King of Mountains, Himavā, is a source of medicine for all beings and a dwelling place for Nagas, Asuras, and Devas.

Similarly, O Great Hero, You are like medicine for beings; Your disciples, possessing the three knowledges and six supernormal powers, have reached the pinnacle of psychic power.
391:
## 
O Great Hero, those disciples instructed by You, the Compassionate One, dwell delighting in Your Dispensation through their delight in the Dhamma.

Just as the lion, king of beasts, emerging from his cave, surveys the four directions and roars three times.

All animals are terrified by the sound of the roaring lion king; thus, that lion of noble birth always terrifies the beasts.

O Great Hero, at the sound of Your roar, this earth trembles violently; those capable of being awakened understand, while the followers of Māra are terrified.

O Great Sage, when You roar, all sectarians are terrified, just as crows are by a hawk or animals by a lion king.

Whatever leaders of sects there are in the world who are called 'teachers,' they only teach their followers the doctrine handed down through tradition.

But You, O Great Hero, do not teach beings in that way; having personally realized the Four Noble Truths and all the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma), You teach the Dhamma.

Knowing the inclinations (āsaya) and underlying tendencies (anusaya) of beings, the strength and weakness of their faculties (indriya), and whether they are capable of liberation or not, You roar like a great rain cloud.

An assembly reaching to the edge of the universe would sit surrounding You, who investigates various views to cut through their doubts.

O Sage skilled in similes, knowing the minds of the entire assembly, You cut through the doubts of beings by preaching even a single question.

Even if this entire earth were filled with wise ones like Upatissa, they would all praise You, the Lord of the World, with palms joined.

Even if they praised Your various qualities for an entire aeon (kappa), they would not be able to measure them; such is the Tathāgata, endowed with immeasurable virtues.

O Victor (Jina), just as I have praised the Buddha according to my own ability, so too would wise ones praise You even for billions of aeons.
392:
## 
If any well-trained god or human were to attempt to measure the Buddha's virtues, they would only meet with exhaustion.

O Sakyan Prince (Sakyaputta) of great fame, established in Your Dispensation and having reached the perfection of wisdom, I dwell free from taints (anāsava).

I crush the sectarians and uphold the Victor's Dispensation; today, I am the General of the Dhamma (Dhammasenāpati) in the Sakyan Prince's Dispensation.

The kamma performed over immeasurable time shows its fruit to me here; it has burnt away my defilements like the speed of a well-shot arrow.

Just as any man might always carry a burden on his head and suffer because of that burden, being weighed down by it.

I, being burnt by the three fires, wandered through existences; I was weighed down by the burden of existence as if carrying Mount Meru.

Now my burden is laid down, and existences have been destroyed by me; I have done all that was to be done in the Sakyan Prince's Dispensation.

As far as the Buddha-field (Buddhakhetta) extends, setting aside the Noble Sakyan Prince, I am supreme in wisdom; there is no one equal to me.

I am highly skilled in concentration (samādhi) and have reached the pinnacle of psychic power (iddhi); if I so wish today, I could create a thousand forms of myself.

The Great Sage, who has mastery over the successive meditative attainments, taught me the Dispensation; the attainment of cessation (nirodha) is my resting place.

My divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) is purified, I am skilled in concentration, devoted to the right efforts (sammappadhāna), and I delight in the development of the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga).

I have achieved everything that should be attained by a disciple (sāvaka); setting aside the Lord of the World, there is no one equal to me.

I am skilled in the meditative attainments (samāpatti), a quick obtainer of the jhānas and liberations (vimokkha), delighting in the development of the factors of enlightenment, and have reached the perfection of a disciple's qualities.
393:
O Great Man, though I am endowed with the attained qualities of a disciple and with wisdom, my mind is always possessed of faith towards my fellow practitioners.

Like a snake with its fangs extracted, or a bull with its horns cut off, I approach the community of monks with deep respect, having laid aside all pride and arrogance.

If my wisdom had a physical form, even the earth would not be able to contain it. This is the fruit of praising the knowledge of the Blessed One Anomadassī.

The Wheel of Dhamma set in motion by the Buddha, the Son of the Sakyans, who is endowed with such qualities, I follow rightly. This is the fruit of praising that knowledge.

May I never, in any place, associate with those of evil desires, the lazy, those of diminished energy, the unlearned, or those of bad conduct.

May the one who is learned, wise, well-established in virtue, and devoted to the tranquility of the mind, stand upon my head.

I say this to you, O venerable ones gathered here: be of few desires, be content, and always be meditators delighting in jhāna.

The one whom I first saw and thereby became stainless and pure—that wise disciple named Assaji is my teacher.

By the power of that Elder Assaji, I have now become the General of the Dhamma. Having reached the perfection in all things, I dwell free from taints.

The disciple named Assaji was my teacher. In whichever direction he dwells, I make that direction the head of my bed.

Recalling my past deeds, Gautama, the Bull of the Sakyans, seated in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks, appointed me to the foremost position.

My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.

Later, while the Teacher was staying at the Great Jetavana Monastery, seated in the midst of the Noble Ones, appointing his disciples to the foremost positions according to their specific qualities, he said: "Monks, among my monk disciples who possess great wisdom, the foremost is Sāriputta."
394:
Regarding the word "Sāriputto" (Aṅguttara Nikāya Commentary 1.188-189), the Buddha appointed the Elder Sāriputta to the foremost position for his great wisdom. Thus, having reached the pinnacle of the knowledge of a disciple's perfection and established in the position of the General of the Dhamma, while working for the welfare of beings, one day, while explaining his own conduct to his fellow practitioners and declaring his attainment of the fruit of Arhatship:

"One who acts in such a way, who is mindful in such a way, being possessed of great mindfulness, with restrained thoughts, habitually meditating, diligent, delighting in the internal meditation object, with a concentrated mind, solitary and content—him they call a monk.

Whether eating moist or dry food, one should not be overfilled. With an empty stomach, knowing the measure of food, a mindful monk should wander.

Leaving four or five mouthfuls uneaten, one should drink water. This is sufficient for the comfortable dwelling of a monk with a resolute mind.

If a proper robe covers him for this purpose, it is sufficient for the comfortable dwelling of a monk with a resolute mind.

For a monk sitting in the cross-legged posture, if the rain does not wet his knees, it is sufficient for the comfortable dwelling of a monk with a resolute mind.

He who sees pleasure as suffering and sees suffering as a dart, staying in the middle of both (with equanimity) without fetters—by what defilement would he become anything in the world?

May one of evil desires, the lazy, those of diminished energy, the unlearned, or the disrespectful never be near me. What benefit would such a person have in the world?

May the one who is learned, wise, well-established in virtue, and devoted to the tranquility of the mind, stand upon my very head.

The person who is devoted to mental proliferation (papañca), a beast delighting in proliferation, misses out on Nibbāna, the unsurpassed security from bondage."
395:
He who has abandoned mental proliferation (papañca)—the craving and conceit that lead to rebirth—and delights in the Noble Path which leads to the cessation of proliferation, attains Nibbāna, the unsurpassed security from the four bonds.

Whether in a village or a forest, in a valley or on a hill, wherever Arahants dwell, that ground is truly delightful.

Delightful are the forests where the common folk do not delight. Those free from passion will find delight there, for they are not seekers of sensual pleasures.

One should associate with a wise person who points out faults as if pointing out hidden treasure, who speaks reprovingly. For one who associates with such a wise person, it is better, never worse.

One should advise, one should instruct, and one should restrain others from unwholesome deeds. Such a person is dear to the good and disliked by the wicked.

The Buddha, the Visionary One, taught the Dhamma to another. While the Dhamma was being taught, I listened attentively, desiring the benefit. That listening of mine was not in vain; I am liberated, free from taints.

I have no longing for the knowledge of past lives (pubbenivāsa), nor for the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), nor for the knowledge of others' minds (cetopariya), nor for psychic powers (iddhi), nor for the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings, nor for the purification of the divine ear (dibba-sota).

Relying on the foot of a tree, shaven-headed, clad in the outer robe (saṅghāṭi), the Elder Upatissa, supreme in wisdom, meditates.

Having entered the attainment (samāpatti) without thought-conception (the fourth jhāna), the disciple of the Fully Enlightened One is at that moment endowed with Noble Silence (ariya-tuṇhībhāva).

Just as a mountain of solid rock is unshakable and well-established, so too, a monk who has destroyed delusion does not tremble, like a mountain.

To a person who is stainless, always seeking purity, an evil deed even as small as the tip of a hair appears as large as a cloud covering the entire sky.
396:
I do not delight in death, nor do do I delight in life. Mindful and clearly comprehending, I shall lay down this body.

I do not delight in death, nor do I delight in life. I only await the time, just as a laborer awaits his wages.

This death, whether it occurs later or sooner, is indeed death; it is not non-death. Therefore, practice! Do not perish! Let not the ninth moment—the opportunity of a Buddha's arising—pass you by.

Just as a border city is well-guarded within and without, and made secure with strong watchtowers and moats so that enemies cannot enter, in the same way, guard yourselves. Let not the ninth moment—the opportunity of a Buddha's arising—pass you by. Indeed, those who have missed the ninth moment and the fourth moment of opportunity (sampatti-khana) grieve when they fall into hell and suffer.

With calmed faculties, peaceful in seclusion, speaking moderately, and not restless—that monk shakes off evil, unwholesome states as the wind shakes leaves from a tree.

With calmed faculties, peaceful in seclusion, speaking moderately, and not restless—that monk has abandoned evil, unwholesome states as the wind shakes leaves from a tree.

Calm in faculties, free from the suffering of defilements, serene, with an undisturbed mind, endowed with good virtue and wise—such a one should be an end-maker of suffering.

One should not trust some people in this way, whether they be householders or even those gone forth. Having been good, they become bad; and having been bad, they become good again.

Sensual desire, ill-will, sloth and torpor, restlessness, and doubt—these five are the defilements of the mind for a monk.

For that monk who dwells in diligence, whose concentration does not waver because of both honor and lack of honor.

That meditator, persistent, seeing with subtle insight, delighting in the destruction of clinging (Nibbāna)—him the wise ones, such as the Buddha, call a 'true man' (sappurisa).
397:
The great ocean, the earth, the mountain, and even the wind—these cannot be compared even in part to the Teacher's excellent liberation (the fruit of Arahantship).

The Elder who follows the turning Wheel of Dhamma set in motion by the Buddha, of great wisdom, concentrated, and like the earth and fire (unshaken by desirable or undesirable objects), is neither attached nor offended.

Having reached the summit of the perfection of wisdom, of great intelligence and great intellect, though not dull, he acts as if he were dull; he always wanders quenched (nibbūto).

I have served the Teacher... the conduit to existence is uprooted.

Strive with diligence; this is my repeated instruction. Behold, I shall now attain Parinibbāna, being liberated in every way—thus he spoke these verses. Among these verses, some were spoken by the Elder, and some were spoken by the Blessed One concerning the Elder. However, because all the verses were later spoken by the Elder to declare his own practice, they became the Elder's verses.

In those verses, 'yathācārī' means one who lives restrained in body and so forth, or it means one endowed with virtue because of such conduct. 'Yathāsanto' (in Pali: yathāsato) means being like a peaceful person. The nasal sound (niggahīta) was elided for the sake of the verse's meter; it means being peaceful like the Noble Ones (ariyas). 'Satīmā' means one endowed with supreme mindfulness. 'Yatasaṅkappajjhāyī' means one who, having abandoned all wrong thoughts, has thoughts restrained by renunciation and so forth, and is accustomed to meditating through object-concentration (ārammaṇūpanijjhāna) and characteristic-concentration (lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna). 'Appamatto' means one who, being restrained in thought in such practice and meditating, is free from negligence and is well-established in mindfulness and clear comprehension in all things. 'Ajjhattarato' means one who delights in the development of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna-bhāvanā). 'Samāhitatto' means one who has a one-pointed mind in that meditation. 'Eko' means being without a companion, avoiding the company of groups and defilements, and cultivating physical and mental seclusion. 'Santusito' means one who is well-contented with requisites and with the delight of meditation. For as meditation brings about higher and higher distinctions, noble rapture and joy arise; when it reaches the summit, there is nothing more to be said. Such a person is called a 'monk' (bhikkhu) because of fulfilling the three trainings, seeing danger (bhaya), and destroying defilements.

Now, wishing to show the meaning of the word 'santa' already mentioned and the discourse related to contentment with requisites, he spoke the verses beginning with 'Alaṃ vā sukkhaṃ vā'. In those verses, 'alaṃ' refers to food that is moist or rich with ghee and so forth, and 'sukkhaṃ' refers to food that is dry and coarse, lacking ghee and so forth. The word 'vā' has an indefinite (aniyama) sense. It means whether the food is refined with ghee or whether it is dry.
398: Now, wishing to first show contentment with requisites among the two types of contentment mentioned, he said "allam sukkhāṃ vā" and so on. In that verse, "allam" refers to food that is moist and oily due to being poured over with ghee and the like. "Sukkhāṃ" refers to food that is coarse and dry because of the absence of such. The word "vā" expresses indefiniteness, meaning "whether moist or dry." "Bāḷhaṃ" means excessively. "Suhito" means one should not have greed for food. How should it be? He said, "ūnūdaro mitāhāro" (with an empty stomach and moderate in eating). A monk eating food, whether choice or coarse, should not eat as much as he desires but stop before being full (while the stomach is not yet full), thus having a light stomach. Because of such a light stomach, he is called "mitāhāra," one who eats a measured amount. While consuming nutriment endowed with the eight factors, he should live as a wanderer, being mindful with the knowledge of moderation and the mindfulness of reflection. To show how one becomes "empty-stomached and moderate in eating," he said "cattāro" and so on. There, "abhuñjitvā" (not eating) means leaving aside four or five morsels and drinking water to fill that space. This is the practice of lightness in food. It is sufficient and adequate for the comfortable living of a monk whose mind is directed towards Nibbāna, and for the attainment of jhāna and so on. By this verse, he shows contentment with whatever almsfood is received for the sake of the belly. The variant reading "bhutvāna" might be said in reference to a person of extremely firm nature who is able to sustain the body with even four or five morsels; it also accords with the subsequent verses because of the mention of few robes and lodgings. "Kappiyaṃ" means any of the allowable cloths such as linen. If that allowable robe covers the parts that should be covered, if it is of a type allowed by the Teacher, and if it is at least of the allowed measurement, it should be used. "Idamatthikaṃ" means only for the purpose stated by the Teacher, namely, for the sake of warding off cold, heat, etc., and for the sake of covering the private parts. By this, he speaks of contentment with whatever robes are received for the sake of the body. "Pallaṅkena nisinnassa" means sitting with both thighs locked (sitting cross-legged). It means for one sitting with the legs crossed in the three-jointed cross-legged posture.
399:
"Rain does not fall on the knees" refers to a small hut where, when it rains, the knees of a monk sitting in such a manner are not wetted by the rainwater. Even a lodging of such limited extent is sufficient for a clansman desiring his own welfare to achieve his goal by sitting and practicing there. Therefore, he said, "It is enough for the comfortable living of a monk with a resolute mind (pahitatta)."

Thus, with these four verses, the Elder, having declared the highest instruction on effacement (sallekha) for those monks who are of great desire and discontented, now wishes to show contentment and delight in meditation by way of feelings (vedanā), and so he said "yo sukhaṃ" and so on. In that verse, "sukhaṃ" refers to pleasant feeling. "Dukkhato" means seeing it as suffering due to change (vipariṇāmadukkha). "Addasa" means one who sees it as it really is with path-knowledge accompanied by insight-wisdom. For pleasant feeling, though enjoyed at the time of consumption, is like food mixed with poison; it becomes only suffering at the time of its change. Here, he shows the contemplation of suffering (dukkhānupassanā). "He saw suffering as a dart" means he saw painful feeling as a dart. Just as a dart causes only pain when entering the body, when remaining inside, and when being extracted, so too painful feeling causes only affliction when arising, when persisting, and when breaking up. Thus, he speaks by emphasizing contemplation of suffering. Furthermore, in accordance with the saying, "Whatever is suffering, that is non-self," he removes the grasping of self and what belongs to self in the two feelings. "Between the two" means in the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (equanimity) which is in the middle of pleasant and painful feelings. "There was not" means that because of the realization of things as they truly are, there was no longer the obsession with self and what belongs to self. "By what and how would there be in the world?" means: having fully understood the five aggregates of clinging by way of feelings in this way, and having cut off the entire net of defilements connected with them, by what defilement would one be bound in the world? What would there be in the future among devas and so on? On the contrary, he would be one whose bonds are cut, who cannot be designated.

Now, wishing to censure those of wrong practice and praise those of right practice, he spoke the four verses beginning with "mā me." In those verses, "Let there never be one of evil desire near me" refers to a person of evil desire who wishes to be praised for qualities he does not possess, who is lazy due to a lack of effort in the recluse's duties, who is therefore of inferior energy, who is of little learning due to the absence of hearing (knowledge) connected with the Truths and Dependent Origination, and who is disrespectful due to a lack of regard for advice and instruction—such an extremely base person.
400:
May such a person of such a nature, who is extremely base, never be in my presence. Why? In the world of beings, what should be done with what kind of instruction for such a person, or what would be the result of any action taken? It means it is simply useless.

Regarding the phrase "Bahussuto ca" (And one of great learning): A person is "learned" (bahussuta) because of the abundance of learning in various divisions such as Sutta and Geyya, which are connected with virtue (sīla) and so forth. He is "wise" (medhāvī) by virtue of the wisdom of the essence of Dhamma (dhammojapaññā), guiding wisdom (pārihariyapaññā), and penetrative wisdom (paṭivedhapaññā). Being well-established in the precepts, he is well-concentrated. He is devoted to the tranquility of mind (cetosamatha), which is the concentration of mind categorized as mundane and supramundane. May such a person stay even upon my head, let alone living together with me.

Regarding the phrase "Yo papañcamanuyutto" (He who is devoted to proliferation): This refers to a person who is devoted to proliferation (papañca), such as craving (taṇhā), which is so called because it expands the cycle of rebirth, arising through delighting in activities or through attachment to forms and so forth. Delighting in that proliferation without seeing its danger, like a deer, that person misses Nibbāna. Such a person stands at a very great distance from Nibbāna.

Regarding the phrase "Yo ca papañcaṃ hitvāna" (And he who, having given up proliferation): This refers to a person who, having abandoned the proliferation of craving, delights in the Noble Path, which is the way to Nibbāna—the state free from proliferation due to the absence of such craving—and the means of attainment. He greatly delights in the realization through meditation (bhāvanā). This means that such a person accomplishes and attains Nibbāna.

Then one day, the Elder [Sāriputta], seeing his younger brother, the Elder Revata, living in a waterless desert covered with thorny acacia trees, praised his dwelling and spoke two verses beginning with "Gāme vā" (Whether in a village). In those verses, "Gāme vā" means that although Arahants do not obtain physical seclusion (kāyaviveka) in a village monastery, they certainly do obtain mental seclusion (cittaviveka). Even divine-like sense objects are unable to shake the minds of those Arahants. Therefore, whether in a village or in any other place such as a forest, wherever Arahants dwell, that ground is delightful; it means that area of land is truly pleasant.

Regarding the term "Araññāni" (Forests): It should be connected as "forests adorned with groves of well-blooming trees and endowed with clear lakes are delightful." "Yattha" (Wherein) means in those forests, where people who are on the side of sensual pleasures and who seek sensual pleasures do not delight, just as they do not delight in blooming trees. "Vītarāgā" (Those free from lust) refers to the Arahants who have destroyed the taints; they, like bees in a lotus grove...
401:
...Arahants will delight in such forest regions like bees in lotus groves. "Na te kāmagavesino" (They are not seekers of sensual pleasure) means that because they are free from lust, they do not seek sensual pleasures.

Again, the Venerable Sāriputta, out of compassion for a poor Brahmin named Rādha, gave him the initial ordination (pabbajjā) and the higher ordination (upasampadā). While traveling with Rādha as his attendant monk, the Elder, one day being pleased with his submissiveness and wishing to give him further admonition, spoke the verse beginning with "Nidhīnaṃva" (Like one [pointing out] treasures). In that verse, "Nidhīnaṃva" refers to treasure pots filled with gold, silver, and so forth, buried here and there. "Pavattāraṃ" (One who reveals) is like a person who, out of compassion for poor people living in hardship, says, "Come, I will show you the means to live happily," and leads them to the place of treasure, stretching out his hand and pointing, "Take this treasure and live happily."

Regarding "Vajjadassinaṃ" (One who sees faults), there are two kinds of fault-seers: (1) a fault-finder who seeks an opening, thinking, "I will suppress him in the midst of the Sangha for this improper act or slip," and (2) one who desires to make known what is not yet known, who appreciates what is known, and who, with the desire for the other's growth in virtue and so forth, looks at various faults with the nature of wanting to lift them up [from Saṃsāra]. The latter type is intended here. Just as a poor man, even when urged, "Take this treasure," does not get angry at the sight of the treasure but is only joyful, so too, when such persons point out an impropriety or a slip they have seen, one should not be angry but should have a joyful mind. One should even invite them, saying, "Venerable Sir, please speak to me like this again."

"Niggayhavādī" (One who speaks rebukingly) refers to one who, upon seeing a fault, does not consider, "This is my co-resident student, my pupil, or my benefactor," but trains them by rebuking, dismissing, or imposing penalties according to the fault. This is like the Fully Enlightened Buddha. For it was said: "Ānanda, I will speak by rebuking and rebuking; I will speak by urging and urging. What is essential will remain." "Medhāviṃ" means one endowed with the wisdom of the essence of Dhamma. "Tādisaṃ" means such a wise person. "Bhaje" means one should associate with or attend upon. For a pupil associating with such a teacher, it is for his betterment, not for his worsening; it is only for his growth, not for his decline.

Then once, when the monks Assaji and Punabbhasuka had corrupted the monasteries in the Kīṭāgiri district, the Captain of the Dhamma (Sāriputta), commanded by the Teacher (the Buddha), went there together with his company and the Great Moggallāna. When Assaji and Punabbhasuka did not heed the advice, the Elder spoke this verse. In that verse, "Ovadeyya" means he should give advice or instruction. "Anusāseyya" is a synonym for the same. Alternatively, speaking regarding a matter that has already arisen is called "ovadati" (admonishing). Speaking regarding a matter that has not yet arisen, with a view to the future, such as "This might happen to you," is called "anusāsati" (instructing). Or, speaking in one's presence is "ovadati," while speaking in one's absence through a messenger or a message is "anusāsati." Or, speaking once is "ovadati," while speaking repeatedly and again and again is "anusāsati."
402:
The term 'ovadati' (he admonishes) refers to speaking about the future regarding a matter that has not yet occurred, such as saying, "You might suffer a loss of reputation (ayasa)," and so on; this is called 'anusāsati' (he instructs). Alternatively, speaking face-to-face is called 'ovadati', while speaking in one's absence by sending a messenger or a message is called 'anusāsati'. Or, speaking only once is called 'ovadati', while speaking repeatedly is called 'anusāsati'. 'Asabbhā ca' means one should restrain others from unwholesome states and establish them in wholesome states. 'Satañhi so' means such a person is dear to the virtuous. However, for those who are not virtuous, who are wicked, who have no regard for the next world, who look only for material gain, and who have ordained merely for a livelihood—to them, that admonisher and instructor becomes disliked, and they pierce him with verbal daggers, saying, "You are not our preceptor (upajjhāya), nor our teacher (ācariya); why do you speak to us?"

When a discussion arose among the monks, saying, "The Teacher (the Buddha) teaches the Dhamma to a certain person, and only that person is endowed with the supporting conditions (upanissaya)," the Buddha, wishing to show that "this is not so," spoke the verse beginning with "Aññassa." In that verse, "Aññassa" was spoken in reference to his own nephew, the wanderer Dīghanakha. While the Teacher was preaching the Vedanāpariggaha Sutta to Dīghanakha, this Great Elder (Sāriputta), following the path of meditation, reached the summit of the Knowledge of Disciple's Perfection (sāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa). "Sotamodhesimatthiko" means that the Great Elder, who stood fanning the Teacher, being desirous of the benefit and wishing to listen, inclined his ear. "Taṃ me amoghaṃ savanaṃ" means that hearing the Dhamma in such a way was not in vain for me; it was fruitful and became the support for the attainments to be reached by a Chief Disciple. Therefore, he said, "Vimuttomhi" (I am liberated), and so on.

In that verse, "neva pubbenivāsāya" is construed as: "I have no aspiration for the sake of the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa) of myself and others." The meaning is that there was not even a mere mental aspiration for that knowledge by way of performing preliminary work (parikamma). "Cetopariyāya" means for the sake of the knowledge of discerning the minds of others (cetopariya-ñāṇa). "Iddhiyā" means for the sake of the knowledge of psychic powers (iddhividha-ñāṇa). "Cutiyā upapattiyā" means for the sake of the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings (cutūpapāta-ñāṇa). "Sotadhātuvisuddhiyā" means for the sake of the knowledge of the divine ear (dibbasota-ñāṇa). "Paṇidhī me na vijjati" means that for the sake of these special higher knowledges (abhiññā), there was no mental aspiration or directing of the mind through preliminary work. Indeed, just as for the Buddhas, the qualities of omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) are attained simply by the acquisition of the Path of Arahatship...
403:
...so too for the disciples, all the qualities of a disciple come into their hands simply by the attainment of the Path of Arahatship (arahattamagga); there is no separate task of performing preliminary work (parikamma) for those attainments.

The three verses beginning with 'Rukkhamūlaṃ' were spoken to demonstrate his imperturbability through the power of meditative attainment (samāpatti) when he was struck by a yakkha while staying at Kapotakandara. In those verses, 'muṇḍo' means having a shaven head. 'Saṅghāṭipāruto' means sitting wrapped in the outer robe (saṅghāṭi). Some also read it as 'saṅghāṭiyā supāruto'. 'Paññāya uttamo thero' means being a Great Elder, he is supreme in wisdom; the meaning is that he is the foremost in wisdom among the disciples. 'Jhāyati' means he meditates through absorption on the object (ārammaṇūpanijjhāna) and absorption on the characteristics (lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna); the meaning is that he dwells frequently in meditative attainment.

'Upeto hoti tāvade' means that at the very moment the yakkha struck his head, he entered the fruit attainment (phalasamāpatti) of the fourth jhāna without thought-conception (avitakka) and was endowed with noble silence. This present tense 'hoti' is used in the sense of the past.

'Pabbatova na vedhati' means that the monk who has destroyed delusion and all defilements is like a stone mountain, firm and well-established, and is not shaken by anything such as the desirable (iṭṭha) or the undesirable (aniṭṭha); the meaning is that he remains unchanged in all circumstances.

Then one day, when the Elder's lower robe was hanging down due to a lapse in mindfulness, a certain novice said, "Venerable sir, the robe should be worn all around (parimaṇḍalaṃ)." Hearing those words, he accepted them as if with his head (humbly), saying, "You have spoken well." He immediately stepped aside a little, adjusted the robe to be worn all around, and wishing to show that "even such a thing is a fault for those like me," he spoke the verse beginning with 'Anaṅgaṇassa'.

Again, wishing to show his equanimity of mind towards death and life, he spoke two verses beginning with 'Nābhinandāmi'. Then, wishing to preach the Dhamma to others, he spoke two verses beginning with 'Ubayena midaṃ'. In that verse, 'ubayena' means in both times. In the word 'midaṃ', the letter 'm' is a euphonic conjunction (padasandhi). This death alone exists; there is no such thing as non-death. In which two times?...
404:
With the words "Pacchā vā pure vā," it is said that death is certain, whether it occurs in the later part of middle age, during the time of old age and decay, or in the earlier part, during the time of youth. Therefore, practice the right path (sammā-paṭipatti), fulfill it; do not perish by practicing wrongly, and do not experience great suffering in the lower realms. "Khano vo mā upaccagā" means: do not let this ninth moment, which is free from the eight inopportune times (akkhaṇa), pass you by.

Then, one day, seeing the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika and wishing to reveal that Elder's virtues, the Buddha spoke three verses beginning with "Upasanto." In those verses, wishing to speak of the meaning already mentioned as "dhunāti" (shaking off) but now in reference to the Elder, he said "Appāsī," etc. In that context, "Appāsī" means he has now abandoned [defilements]. "Anāyāso" means without fatigue, free from the suffering of defilements. "Vippasanno anāvilo" means having a very clear mind due to the absence of lack of faith and so on, and being undisturbed because of having undisturbed thoughts.

The verse beginning with "Na vissase" was spoken concerning the Vajjiputtakas who remained established in their delight for Devadatta's views, having placed their trust in him. In that verse, "Na vissase" means one should not be intimate or trustful. "Ekatiyesu" means among some worldlings (puthujjana) of unstable nature. "Evaṃ" means just as you became intimate, thinking "Devadatta is practicing rightly." "Agārisu" means among householders. "Sādhūpi hutvānā" means because the state of a worldling is unstable, like a pumpkin placed on a horse's back or a stump driven into a heap of chaff; therefore, some who are virtuous at the beginning become unvirtuous later. Just as Devadatta was formerly endowed with virtue and an obtainer of higher knowledge (abhiññā) and attainments (samāpatti), but being greedy for gain and honor, his special qualities have now declined, and like a crow with broken wings, he has become one bound for the lower realms. Therefore, one should not trust such a person as "virtuous" merely by sight. Some, however, are unvirtuous at first due to the lack of association with good friends, but later become virtuous through association with the good. Therefore, one should not trust those who only appear virtuous, like Devadatta, as being truly "virtuous."

To show that those from whom the defilements of the mind, such as sensual desire (kāmacchanda), have not departed are unvirtuous, and those from whom they have departed are virtuous, he spoke the verse "Kāmacchando." Then, to show the supreme characteristic of a virtuous person that is not shared with others, he spoke two verses beginning with "Yassa sakkariyamānassa."
405:
To show the supreme characteristic of a virtuous person that is not shared with ordinary people, the Teacher spoke the verse beginning with "Mahāsamuddo," citing himself and the Venerable Sāriputta as examples.

In that verse, "Mahāsamuddo" means this great ocean, the great earth, the rock mountain, and the winds blowing from the east and other directions endure the pleasant and the unpleasant because of their own lack of volition (mind), not through the power of reflection. The Teacher, however, stands in the supreme state of "Tādi" (equanimity) by virtue of his attainment of Arahantship, remaining equal and unperturbed in all things, pleasant or unpleasant. Compared to the Teacher's noble liberation (vara-vimutti), the supreme fruit of liberation, the great ocean and the others are not fit as metaphors; they do not reach even a sixteenth part.

"Cakkānuvattako" means the one who follows and keeps in motion the Wheel of Dhamma (dhamma-cakka) set in motion by the Teacher. "Thero" means he is called an Elder because of being endowed with the virtues of an Asekha (one beyond training), such as the aggregate of virtue. "Mahāñāṇī" means one of great knowledge. "Samāhito" means composed through access concentration (upacāra-samādhi), absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi), and the unsurpassed concentration. "Pathavāpaggisamāno" means having a nature like the earth, water, and fire because of being unperturbed when encountering objects, pleasant or unpleasant. Therefore, it is said, "He does not lust, he does not hate."

"Paññāpāramitaṃ patto" means one who has reached the pinnacle of a disciple's knowledge. "Mahābuddhī" means endowed with great wisdom (paññā) that has reached the state of being broad, joyous, swift, sharp, and penetrative. "Mahāမတီ (Mahāmatī)" means endowed with great intellect (mati) characterized by the ability to grasp methods by following the nature of the Dhamma (dhammanvaya-vedita). Because he has fully attained the divisions of wisdom in their entirety—the 4-fold, 16-fold, 44-fold, and 73-fold—and because of his association with extraordinary qualities such as great wisdom, this Great Elder deserves to be called "Mahābuddhi" (Great Intellect) par excellence. As the Blessed One said:
"Monks, Sāriputta is wise; monks, Sāriputta has great wisdom; monks, Sāriputta has broad wisdom; monks, Sāriputta has joyous wisdom; monks, Sāriputta has swift wisdom; monks, Sāriputta has sharp wisdom; monks, Sāriputta has penetrative wisdom," and so forth.

In that context, to clarify the distinctions of being wise and so on: it is skill in the elements (dhātu), skill in the sense bases (āyatana), skill in dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), and skill in what is possible and impossible (ṭhānāṭṭhāna).
406: By these four reasons, one is called a wise person. In explaining the classification of great wisdom and so forth, there is this Pali text: “What is great wisdom (mahāpaññā)? It is called great wisdom because it comprehends great meanings. It is called great wisdom because it comprehends great dhammas. It is called great wisdom because it comprehends great niruttis (linguistic expressions). It is called great wisdom because it comprehends great paṭibhānas (perspicacity). It is called great wisdom because it comprehends the great aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha). It is called great wisdom because it comprehends the great aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha). It is called great wisdom because it comprehends the great aggregate of wisdom (paññākkhandha). It is called great wisdom because it comprehends the great aggregate of liberation (vimuttikkhandha). It is called great wisdom because it comprehends the great aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimuttiñāṇadassanakkhandha). It is called great wisdom because it comprehends great possibilities and impossibilities (ṭhānāṭhāna). It is called great wisdom because it comprehends great abidings and attainments (vihārasamāpatti). It is called great wisdom because it comprehends the great Noble Truths (ariyasacca). It is called great wisdom because it comprehends the great foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna). It is called great wisdom because it comprehends the great right efforts (sammappadhāna). It is called great wisdom because it comprehends the great bases of power (iddhipāda). It is called great wisdom because it comprehends the great faculties (indriya). It is called great wisdom because it comprehends the great powers (bala). It is called great wisdom because it comprehends the great factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga). It is called great wisdom because it comprehends the great Noble Path (ariyamagga). It is called great wisdom because it comprehends the great fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala). It is called great wisdom because it comprehends the great direct knowledges (abhiññā). It is called great wisdom because it comprehends the great ultimate reality, Nibbāna.” “What is wide wisdom (puthupaññā)? It is called wide wisdom because knowledge occurs in various and numerous aggregates (khandha). It is called wide wisdom because knowledge occurs in various and numerous elements (dhātu). It is called wide wisdom because knowledge occurs in various and numerous sense bases (āyatana). It is called wide wisdom because knowledge occurs in various and numerous dependent originations (paṭiccasamuppāda). It is called wide wisdom because knowledge occurs in various and numerous emptinesses and non-apprehensions (suññata anupalabbha). It is called wide wisdom because knowledge occurs in various and numerous meanings (attha). It is called wide wisdom because knowledge occurs in various and numerous dhammas. It is called wide wisdom because knowledge occurs in various and numerous niruttis. It is called wide wisdom because knowledge occurs in various and numerous paṭibhānas. It is called wide wisdom because knowledge occurs in various and numerous aggregates of virtue. It is called wide wisdom because knowledge occurs in various and numerous aggregates of concentration. It is called wide wisdom because knowledge occurs in various and numerous aggregates of wisdom. It is called wide wisdom because knowledge occurs in various and numerous aggregates of liberation...”
407: ...knowledge occurs; therefore, it is called wide wisdom (puthupaññā). It is called wide wisdom because knowledge occurs in various and numerous aggregates of the knowledge and vision of liberation. It is called wide wisdom because knowledge occurs in various and numerous possibilities and impossibilities (ṭhānāṭhāna). It is called wide wisdom because knowledge occurs in various and numerous abidings and attainments. It is called wide wisdom because knowledge occurs in various and numerous Noble Truths. It is called wide wisdom because knowledge occurs in various and numerous foundations of mindfulness. It is called wide wisdom because knowledge occurs in various and numerous right efforts. It is called wide wisdom because knowledge occurs in various and numerous bases of power. It is called wide wisdom because knowledge occurs in various and numerous faculties. It is called wide wisdom because knowledge occurs in various and numerous powers. It is called wide wisdom because knowledge occurs in various and numerous factors of enlightenment. It is called wide wisdom because knowledge occurs in various and numerous Noble Paths. It is called wide wisdom because knowledge occurs in various and numerous fruits of recluseship. It is called wide wisdom because knowledge occurs in various and numerous direct knowledges. It is called wide wisdom because knowledge occurs in the ultimate reality, Nibbāna, transcending the dhammas common to worldlings (puthujjana). “What is joyous wisdom (hāsapaññā)? In this Dispensation, a certain person, being full of joy, full of zest, full of satisfaction, and full of gladness, fulfills the virtues; therefore, it is called joyous wisdom. Being full of joy... [pe]... full of gladness, he fulfills the restraint of the faculties (indriyasaṃvara); therefore, it is called joyous wisdom. Being full of joy... [pe]... full of gladness, he fulfills moderation in eating (bhojane mattaññutā); therefore, it is called joyous wisdom. Being full of joy... [pe]... full of gladness, he fulfills the practice of wakefulness (jāgariyānuyoga); therefore, it is called joyous wisdom. Being full of joy... [pe]... full of gladness, he fulfills the aggregate of virtue... [pe]... the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation... [pe]... he penetrates [them]. He fulfills the abidings and attainments, he penetrates the Noble Truths, he develops the foundations of mindfulness, he develops the right efforts, he develops the bases of power, he develops the faculties, he develops the powers, he develops the factors of enlightenment, he develops the Noble Path... [pe]... he realizes the fruits of recluseship; therefore, it is called joyous wisdom. Being full of joy, full of zest, full of satisfaction, and full of gladness, he penetrates the direct knowledges; therefore, it is called joyous wisdom. Being full of joy, full of zest, full of satisfaction, and full of gladness, he realizes the ultimate reality, Nibbāna; therefore, it is called joyous wisdom.”
408:
What is swift wisdom (javanapaññā)? It is called swift wisdom because one swiftly perceives (runs through) all forms—past, future, or present... far or near—as 'impermanent.' It is called swift wisdom because one swiftly perceives them as 'suffering.' It is called swift wisdom because one swiftly perceives them as 'non-self.' [Similarly for] whatever feeling... all consciousness—past, future, or present... it is called swift wisdom because one swiftly perceives all consciousness as 'impermanent.' It is called swift wisdom because one swiftly perceives it as 'suffering.' It is called swift wisdom because one swiftly perceives it as 'non-self.' From the eye... up to aging and death, it is called swift wisdom because one swiftly perceives the states that are past, future, or present as 'impermanent.' It is called swift wisdom because one swiftly perceives them as 'suffering.' It is called swift wisdom because one swiftly perceives them as 'non-self.'

Having weighed, judged, and made clear that form—past, future, or present—is 'impermanent' in the sense of exhaustion, 'suffering' in the sense of fear, and 'non-self' in the sense of corelessness, and having made it manifest, one swiftly runs towards Nibbāna, which is the cessation of form; therefore, it is called swift wisdom... [Similarly for] feeling... perception... formations... consciousness... the eye... up to aging and death. Having weighed, judged, and made clear that the states—past, future, or present—are 'impermanent' in the sense of exhaustion, 'suffering' in the sense of fear, and 'non-self' in the sense of corelessness, and having made it manifest, one swiftly runs towards Nibbāna, which is the cessation of aging and death; therefore, it is called swift wisdom.

Having weighed, judged, and made clear that form—past, future, or present—is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to exhaustion, subject to decay, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation, and having made it manifest, one swiftly runs towards the cessation of form; therefore, it is called swift wisdom. [Similarly for] feeling... perception... formations... consciousness... the eye... up to aging and death. Having weighed, judged, and made clear that the states—past, future, or present—are impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to exhaustion, subject to decay, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation, and having made it manifest, one swiftly runs towards Nibbāna, which is the cessation of aging and death; therefore, it is called swift wisdom.

What is sharp wisdom (tikkhapaññā)? It is called sharp wisdom because one swiftly cuts off the defilements. One does not tolerate an arisen sensual thought (kāma-vitakka), but abandons it, dispels it, ends it, and brings it to non-existence; therefore, it is called sharp wisdom. One does not tolerate an arisen thought of ill-will (byāpāda-vitakka), but abandons it, dispels it, ends it, and brings it to non-existence; therefore, it is called sharp wisdom. One does not tolerate an arisen thought of cruelty (vihiṃsā-vitakka)... one does not tolerate whatever evil unwholesome states have arisen, but abandons them.
409:
...dispels them, makes them disappear, and brings them to non-existence; therefore, it is called sharp wisdom (tikkhapaññā). One does not tolerate arisen lust (rāga), but abandons it, dispels it, makes it disappear, and brings it to non-existence; therefore, it is called sharp wisdom. One does not tolerate arisen hatred (dosa)... arisen delusion (moha)... arisen anger (kodha)... arisen malice (upanāha)... hypocrisy (makkha)... spite (paḷāsa)... envy (issā)... stinginess (macchariya)... deceit (māyā)... treachery (sāṭheyya)... obstinacy (thambha)... impetuosity (sārambha)... conceit (māna)... arrogance (atimāna)... intoxication (mada)... negligence (pamāda)... all defilements... all misconduct... all volitional formations... all kamma leading to rebirth; one does not tolerate them, but abandons them, dispels them, makes them disappear, and brings them to non-existence; therefore, it is called sharp wisdom. Because the four noble paths, the four fruits of recluseship, the four analytical insights, and the six supernormal knowledges are attained, realized, and touched by wisdom in a single sitting, it is called sharp wisdom.

What is penetrative wisdom (nibbedhikapaññā)? Here, someone is full of agitation, full of fear, full of weariness, full of dissatisfaction, and full of great dissatisfaction towards all formations; being outward-facing, he does not delight in any formations. Because he pierces and breaks through the mass of greed that was never pierced or broken through before, it is called penetrative wisdom. Because he pierces and breaks through the mass of hatred that was never pierced or broken through before, it is called penetrative wisdom. Because he pierces and breaks through the mass of delusion that was never pierced or broken through before, it is called penetrative wisdom. Because he pierces and breaks through anger (kodha)... malice (upanāha)... all kamma leading to rebirth that was never pierced or broken through before, it is called penetrative wisdom.

Because he is endowed with such great wisdom as described in these divisions, he is called 'One of Great Wisdom' (Mahābuddhī).

Furthermore, the greatness of this Elder Sāriputta's wisdom should also be understood by way of his insight into states one by one (anupadadhamma-vipassanā). For it was said:

"Monks, for half a month, Sāriputta practiced insight into states one by one. In that insight into states one by one, monks, this is how it was for Sāriputta:

Here, monks, Sāriputta, quite secluded from sensual pleasures... enters and dwells in the first jhāna. Whatever states there are in the first jhāna, such as applied thought (vitakka)... one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā), contact (phassa), feeling (vedanā), perception (saññā), volition (cetanā), and mind (citta) [etc.]..."
410:
Desire, resolve, energy, mindfulness, equanimity, and attention—these states were defined by the Venerable Sāriputta one by one as they occurred. These states arose known to him, persisted known to him, and subsided known to him. He understood: 'Thus, indeed, these states, having not been, come into being; having been, they vanish.' Regarding those states, he dwelt without attraction, without repulsion, independent, detached, free, dissociated, with a mind free from barriers. He understood: 'There is a further escape.' By frequently developing those states, he confirmed that there is indeed [a further escape].

Monks, furthermore, with the stilling of directed thought and evaluation, the Venerable Sāriputta dwelt having attained the second jhāna, the third jhāna, and the fourth jhāna. Passing beyond the base of infinite space, the base of infinite consciousness, and the base of nothingness, and completely transcending the base of nothingness, he dwelt having attained the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. He emerged from that attainment mindful. Having emerged from that attainment mindful, he repeatedly contemplated those states that had passed, ceased, and changed, thinking: 'Thus, indeed, these states, having not been, come into being; having been, they vanish.' Regarding those states, he dwelt without attraction, without repulsion, independent, detached, free, dissociated, with a mind free from barriers. He understood: 'There is a further escape.' By frequently developing those states, he confirmed that there is indeed [a further escape].

Monks, furthermore, the Venerable Sāriputta, completely transcending the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, dwelt having attained the cessation of perception and feeling. Having seen with wisdom, his taints were utterly destroyed. He emerged from that attainment mindful. Having emerged from that attainment mindful, he repeatedly contemplated those states that had passed, ceased, and changed, thinking: 'Thus, indeed, these states, having not been, come into being; having been, they vanish.' Regarding those states, he dwelt without attraction, without repulsion, independent, detached, free, dissociated, with a mind free from barriers. He understood: 'There is no...'
411:
...further escape.' By frequently doing so, he confirmed that for such a person, there is indeed no [further escape].

'Monks, if one speaking rightly were to say of anyone: "He has attained mastery and perfection in noble virtue; he has attained mastery and perfection in noble concentration; he has attained mastery and perfection in noble wisdom; he has attained mastery and perfection in noble liberation," it is of Sāriputta alone that one speaking rightly would say this.' (Thus the Blessed One said).

Because he was endowed with such great wisdom—vast, great, thick, joyous, swift, sharp, and penetrative—the Elder is called 'Mahābuddhi' (One of Great Wisdom). His knowledge of the sequence of the Dhamma (dhammanvaya-veditā) should be illustrated by the Sampasādanīya Sutta. In that sutta, the Elder's method of grasping is said to be similar to omniscient knowledge. Although he was in every way one who was not a fool (ajaḷa), having reached the pinnacle of wisdom among the disciples, because of his extreme fewness of wishes, he acted as if he did not know, appearing like a fool or one of dull wit. Being quenched and cooled due to the absence of the fever of defilements, he always lived and constantly dwelt in this manner.

The verse beginning with 'Pariciṇṇo' was spoken by the Elder to declare the fact that his task was completed. That verse also has the meaning already stated.

This verse, 'Sampādethappamādena' (Strive with diligence), was spoken as an exhortation to the monks who had gathered at the time of his approaching Parinibbāna. That verse also has the meaning already stated.

## The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Sāriputta is Finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Ānanda

The verses beginning with 'Pisuṇena ca kodhanena' are those of the Venerable Elder Ānanda. What is the account of their origin? This Elder had also performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas. In the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was reborn in the city of Haṃsavatī as the half-brother of the Teacher, and his name was Sumana. His father was King Ānanda. When his son, Prince Sumana, reached maturity, the King gave him the city of Bhoga, located two hundred yojanas from Haṃsavatī. Prince Sumana would come from time to time...
412:
He used to look after his own affairs and pay respects to his father. At that time, the King himself respectfully served the Buddha and the community of one hundred thousand monks, not allowing others to serve them.

During that time, the border region was in revolt. Without informing the King of the unrest, the prince himself quelled it. Upon hearing this, the King was greatly pleased, summoned his son, and said, "Dear son, I grant you a boon; choose a boon." The prince replied, "I wish to make my life fruitful by serving the Buddha and the community of monks for the three months of the rains retreat." The King said, "I cannot grant this; ask for another boon." The prince replied, "Great King, for kings, there is no speaking with two words. Please grant me only this boon; I have no need for any other." The King said, "If the Buddha permits it, it is granted." Thinking, "I shall find out the Buddha's intention," the prince went to the monastery.

At that time, the Buddha had finished his meal and entered the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi). The prince approached the monks and said, "Venerable sirs, I have come to see the Buddha; please show me the Buddha." The monks said, "The Elder named Sumana is the Buddha's attendant; go to him." He went to the Elder, paid respects, and said, "Venerable sir, please show me the Buddha." Then, while the prince was watching, the Elder dived into the earth, approached the Buddha, and said, "Venerable sir, the prince has come to see you." The Buddha said, "In that case, monk, prepare a seat outside." While the prince was still watching, the Elder took the Buddha's seat, dived inside the Fragrant Chamber, appeared outside in the precinct, and prepared the seat in the precinct of the Fragrant Chamber. Seeing this, the prince thought, "How great indeed is this monk!"

The Buddha also came out of the Fragrant Chamber and sat on the prepared seat. The prince paid respects to the Buddha, engaged in pleasant conversation, and said, "Venerable sir, I think this Elder is very intimate (beloved) in your Dispensation." The Buddha replied, "Yes, prince, he is intimate." "Venerable sir, by doing what has this Elder become so intimate?" "By performing meritorious deeds such as giving (dāna)," the Buddha replied. "Venerable sir, I too wish to be intimate in the Buddha's Dispensation in the future, just like this Elder," the prince said. After offering the Khandhavāra meal for seven days, on the seventh day, he said, "Venerable sir, I have received the boon from my father to serve you for the three months of the rains retreat. Please accept my invitation to spend the rains retreat for three months." The Buddha, considering whether there would be benefit in going there and seeing that there would be, said, "Prince, the Tathāgatas delight in secluded dwellings." The prince said, "I understand, Blessed One; I understand, Sugata (Well-gone One)," and...
413:
...saying, "Venerable sir, I shall go ahead and build a monastery; when I send word, please come with the one hundred thousand monks," he took the promise. He then went to his father and said, "Great King, the Buddha has given me his promise; when I send word, please send the Buddha." He paid respects to his father and departed, building a monastery at every league (yojana) as he traveled the long distance of two hundred leagues. Upon arrival, while selecting a site for the monastery in his city, he saw the garden of the householder named Sobhana. He bought it for one hundred thousand and spent another one hundred thousand to have the monastery built. In that garden, he had the Fragrant Chamber built for the Buddha, and huts (kuṭi), caves (leṇa), and pavilions (maṇဍapa) for the remaining monks to spend the night and day. Having completed the surrounding wall and the gatehouse, he sent word to his father: "My task is finished; please send the Buddha."

The King, after offering a meal to the Buddha, said, "Venerable sir, Sumana's task is finished; he awaits your arrival." Accompanied by one hundred thousand monks, the Buddha traveled, staying at the monasteries at every league. Hearing that "The Buddha is coming," the prince went out for one league to welcome him. Honoring him with scents, flowers, and so on, he led the Buddha into the monastery built for one hundred thousand in the garden named Sobhana, which had been bought for one hundred thousand, and said:

"Venerable sir, this garden named Sobhana,
Bought by me for one hundred thousand,
And built for one hundred thousand,
Please accept it, O Great Sage!"

Thus he offered the garden. On the day of entering the rains retreat, Prince Sumana provided a great offering and instructed his wife, children, and ministers in various duties, saying, "Continue to give offerings in this same manner." He himself lived near the dwelling of Elder Sumana and served the Buddha throughout the three months of the rains retreat. As the Pavāraṇā day approached, he entered the village and provided a great offering for seven days. On the seventh day, he placed triple robes (ticīvara) at the feet of the Buddha and the one hundred thousand monks, paid respects, and made an aspiration: "Venerable sir, this merit I have performed starting from the seven-day Khandhavāra offering is not for the sake of heavenly bliss and such. Indeed, I wish to become the attendant of a future Buddha, just like this Elder Sumana." The Buddha, seeing that there would be no obstacles to that aspiration, delivered a prophecy and then departed.
414:
That Venerable Ānanda also, having performed meritorious deeds for a hundred thousand years during the time of that Buddha, and thereafter accumulating noble merit in various existences, wandered through the realms of devas and humans. During the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, he offered an upper robe to a Thera who was walking for alms and performed an act of worship. Again, after being reborn in the celestial realm and passing away from there, he became the King of Bārāṇasī. Having seen eight Paccekabuddhas, he served them with food and had eight leaf-huts built in his royal garden. For the use of those Paccekabuddhas, he prepared eight benches made of all kinds of jewels and jeweled footstools, and served them for ten thousand years. These are the well-known accounts.

While performing meritorious deeds in various existences for a hundred thousand aeons, he was reborn in the Tusita heaven together with our Bodhisatta. Passing away from there, he was born in the house of the Sakyan King Amitodana. Because he was born bringing joy and delight to all his relatives, he was named 'Ānanda'. As he gradually reached the proper age, after the Buddha had renounced the world, attained Supreme Enlightenment, and turned the Noble Wheel of Dhamma, the Buddha first visited Kapilavatthu. When the Blessed One departed from there, Ānanda followed together with Prince Bhaddiya and others who left to ordain as his retinue. He was ordained in the presence of the Blessed One. Not long after his ordination, having heard a Dhamma discourse from the Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta, he was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala).

At that time, during the first twenty years of the Blessed One's enlightenment, there was no permanent attendant. Sometimes the Venerable Nāgasamāla would take the bowl and robes and follow him; sometimes the Venerable Nāgita, sometimes the Venerable Upavāna, sometimes Sunakkhatta, sometimes the novice Cunda, sometimes the Venerable Sāgata, and sometimes the Venerable Meghiya. For the most part, those monks were unable to satisfy the Buddha's mind. Then one day, while the Blessed One was seated surrounded by the community of monks on the noble Buddha-seat prepared in the precinct of the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi), he addressed the monks: "Monks, I am now old. When some monks are told 'Let us go by this path,' they go by another path; some drop my bowl and robes on the ground. Choose a monk who will be my permanent attendant." Hearing these words, a sense of spiritual urgency (dhamma-saṃvega) arose in the monks. Then the Venerable Sāriputta rose, paid homage to the Blessed One, and said: "Venerable Sir, I will serve you." The Blessed One rejected him. In this manner, starting with the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, all the great disciples rose and said, "I will serve you, I will serve you," except for the Venerable Ānanda. The Blessed One also [rejected] them...
415:
...rejected them. However, the Venerable Ānanda remained seated in silence. Then the monks said to him: "Friend Ānanda, you too should request the position of the Buddha's attendant." He replied: "What kind of position is it that must be obtained by requesting? If it pleases him, the Teacher himself will speak." Then the Blessed One said: "Monks, Ānanda should not be urged by others; he will know by himself and serve me." Thereafter, the monks said: "Rise, friend Ānanda, and request the position of attendant from the Teacher."

The Thera rose and said: "Venerable Sir, if the Blessed One will not give me the fine robes he receives, will not give me the fine alms-food he receives, will not allow me to stay in the same Fragrant Chamber, and will not take me along when he accepts an invitation, only then will I serve the Blessed One." He made these four refusals to avoid the reproach that "What is the burden in serving the Teacher for one who receives such benefits?" He further requested: "Venerable Sir, if the Blessed One will go to invitations accepted by me, if I may allow those who come from afar to see the Blessed One at the moment they arrive, if I may approach the Blessed One at the moment I have a doubt, and if the Blessed One will repeat to me the Dhamma he has taught in my absence, only then will I serve the Blessed One." He made these four requests to avoid the reproach that "He does not even receive such favor from the Teacher," and to fulfill the perfection of being the Treasurer of the Dhamma. Having thus accepted these eight boons, he became the permanent attendant. For the sake of this very position, he reached the fruit of the perfections fulfilled for a hundred thousand aeons.

From the day he received the position of attendant, he served the Buddha, the Possessor of Ten Powers (Dasabala), with two kinds of water, three kinds of tooth-sticks, by massaging his hands and feet, by massaging his back, and by sweeping the precinct of the Fragrant Chamber. Thinking, "At this time, the Teacher should receive this; at this time, he should do this," he remained in close attendance during the day. At night, holding a large torch, he would circle the precinct of the Fragrant Chamber nine times, so that he would be ready to answer if the Teacher called and to dispel drowsiness.

Then the Teacher, while staying in the Jeta Grove seated in the midst of the assembly of Noble Ones, praised the Venerable Ānanda in many ways and placed him in the foremost position (etadagga) among the monks who are deeply learned, mindful, retentive, resolute, and attendants. Thus, having been placed in the foremost position in five categories by the Teacher, and endowed with four wonderful and marvelous qualities, this great Thera, the guardian of the Teacher's Dhamma-treasure, while still only a trainee (sekha), when the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna, was urged by the monks as mentioned above and stirred by the devas. He thought, "The recitation of the Dhamma (Dhamma-saṅgāyanā) should be performed tomorrow." Because the Venerable Ānanda was a trainee and still had work to do, he wished to go to the assembly to recite the Dhamma with the other Arahant Theras. However, reflecting that going as such would be inappropriate, he exerted great effort and practiced insight meditation (vipassanā) throughout the night. Yet, not attaining balanced energy, he entered the dwelling and sat on the bed...
416:
This Great Elder, the Treasurer of the Dhamma, while still a trainee (sekha), was encouraged by the monks and stirred by a deity at the time of the Buddha's Parinibbāna in the manner mentioned above. Thinking, "The rehearsal of the Dhamma must be performed tomorrow. It is not proper for me, being a trainee with tasks still to be done, to go to the assembly to rehearse the Dhamma together with the Elders who are asekha (Arahants)," he was filled with zeal. He began practicing insight meditation (vipassanā) and spent the whole night in the work of insight. Failing to achieve a balance of energy while on the walking path, he entered the monastery, sat on his bed, and desiring to sleep, reclined his body. In that interval, before his head reached the pillow and just as his feet were lifted from the ground, his mind was liberated from the taints (āsavas) without clinging, and he became an Arahant endowed with the six higher powers (chaḷabhiññā). Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

"The Great Sage Padumuttara, having emerged from the monastery gate, rained down the rain of the Deathless and brought peace to the multitude.

One hundred thousand of those wise monks, endowed with the six higher powers and great psychic potency, surrounded the Sambuddha like an inseparable shadow.

I was riding on the back of an elephant when I saw a most excellent white umbrella of great beauty, and joy and delight arose within me.

Descending from the elephant's back, I approached the Bull of Men and held the umbrella adorned with jewels over the most excellent Buddha.

Knowing my intention, the Great Sage Padumuttara paused the discourse he was then giving and spoke these verses:

'I shall praise him who held the umbrella adorned with golden ornaments; listen to my words.

Departing from here, this man will dwell in the Tusita heaven; he will enjoy prosperity, surrounded by celestial nymphs.

Thirty-four times he will exercise the sovereignty of the gods, and eight hundred times he will be a powerful emperor ruling over the earth.

Fifty-eight times he will be a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti), and he will also exercise extensive regional kingship on the earth.'"
417:
"One hundred thousand aeons from now, a Teacher named Gotama by clan, born of the Okkāka family, will arise in the world.

He will be a kinsman of that Buddha, the banner of the Sakyan clan, and named Ānanda, he will be the attendant of the Great Sage.

Energetic, prudent, and skilled in great learning, humble and not stubborn, he will be a reciter of all the scriptures.

With a mind directed toward Nibbāna through the practice of meditation, peaceful and free from acquisitions (upadhi), having fully understood all taints, he will attain Parinibbāna, free from taints.

There are forest-dwelling bull elephants, sixty years of age, with secretions flowing from three places, with tusks like plow-poles and massive bodies.

There are also many hundreds of thousands of wise elephants of great psychic power. All those elephants (Arahants) are not equal to the Elephant of Buddhas.

I worshipped him in the first watch, and also in the middle and last watches. With a clear and joyful mind, I served the most excellent Buddha.

Energetic, prudent, possessing clear comprehension and established mindfulness, I reached the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). I am skilled in the stages of the trainees (sekha).

One hundred thousand aeons ago, I performed the meritorious deed of aspiring to be an attendant. Now I have reached that aspired state, standing firm and unshakable in the True Dhamma...

My coming was indeed a good coming. I have attained the three knowledges and fulfilled the Buddha's teaching. I have burned away the taints and fulfilled the Buddha's teaching."

The Elder Ānanda, endowed with the six higher powers, entered the rehearsal hall and, while rehearsing the Dhamma, combined the verses he had spoken by way of admonishing monks in various places and by way of illustrating his own practice. During the rehearsal of the Khuddaka Nikāya, he included them in the Theragāthā, saying:

"A wise man should not make friends with one who is a slanderer, or one who is angry, or one who is stingy, or one who delights in the ruin of others. Association with the wicked is evil."
418:
"A wise man should make friends with one who is faithful, of pleasant virtue, wise, and of great learning. Association with the virtuous is excellent.

Behold this decorated image, a mass of sores, propped up, diseased, much thought of, which has no stability or permanence.

Behold this form, decorated with jewels and earrings, bound by bone and skin, which looks beautiful with clothes.

Feet well-dyed with lac, and a face smeared with powder—these are enough to delude a fool, but not a seeker of the Far Shore.

Hair braided in eight ways, and eyes smeared with collyrium—these are enough to delude a fool, but not a seeker of the Far Shore.

Like a new, decorated collyrium pot, this foul body is decorated—it is enough to delude a fool, but not a seeker of the Far Shore.

The hunter set the snare, but the deer did not get caught. Having eaten the bait, let us go while the hunter laments.

The hunter's snare is broken, the deer did not get caught. Having eaten the bait, let us go while the hunter grieves.

Of great learning, an eloquent speaker, the attendant of the Buddha, his burden laid down, detached—Gotama (Ānanda) takes his rest.

With taints destroyed, detached, crossed over all fetters, perfectly cooled, he bears his final body, having reached the Far Shore of birth and death.

In whom the teachings of the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun, are established, on the path leading to Nibbāna, there stands this Gotama.

I received eighty-two thousand from the Buddha, and two thousand from the monks; eighty-four thousand are the Dhamma units I have in circulation."
419:
This man of little learning grows old like an ox; his flesh increases, but his wisdom does not increase.

If a man of great learning despises one of little learning because of his learning, he appears to me like a blind man holding a lamp.

One should associate with a man of great learning and should not let what has been learned be lost. That learning is the root of the holy life; therefore, one should be a bearer of the Dhamma.

One who knows what comes before and what comes after, who knows the meaning, and who is skilled in linguistics and phrasing, grasps well what has been learned and repeatedly examines the meaning.

Being desirous through patience, he makes an effort and compares that Dhamma; at the proper time, he strives, being well-composed within himself.

One who desires knowledge of the Dhamma should associate with such a noble friend (kalyāṇamitta), a disciple of the Buddha who is of great learning, a bearer of the Dhamma, and wise.

One who is of great learning, a bearer of the Dhamma, and a guardian of the Great Sage's treasury of Dhamma, is like an eye for the whole world and is worthy of worship.

A monk who finds delight in the Dhamma, who rejoices in the Dhamma, who contemplates the Dhamma, and who remembers the Dhamma, does not fall away from the true Dhamma.

For one who is concerned with the stinginess of the body, who does not strive even when wholesome states decline, and who is greedy for bodily comfort, how can there be the well-being of a recluse?

When the noble friend, the Venerable Sāriputta, has attained Parinibbāna, all directions are unclear, and the teachings do not appear to me; it seems like total darkness.

The friends have passed away; the Blessed One has also attained Parinibbāna. There is no friend like mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatāsati).

The old friends have passed away; I do not wish to associate with new ones. Today, I shall dwell alone, meditating, like a bird that has entered its nest during the rainy season.
420:
People from various countries come to pay respects (to the Buddha); O listeners, do not prevent them; allow them to see me.
Many people from various countries come to pay respects (to the Buddha); the Blessed One grants them the opportunity; the Buddha, endowed with the five eyes, does not forbid them.

For twenty-five years, while I have been a trainee (sekha) still practicing the path, no sensual perception (kāmasaññā) has arisen in me; behold the excellence of the Dhamma!
For twenty-five years, while I have been a trainee (sekha) still practicing the path, no perception of ill-will (dosasaññā) has arisen in me; behold the excellence of the Dhamma!

For twenty-five years, I have attended upon the Blessed One with bodily acts of loving-kindness, like an inseparable shadow.
For twenty-five years, I have attended upon the Blessed One with verbal acts of loving-kindness, like an inseparable shadow.
For twenty-five years, I have attended upon the Blessed One with mental acts of loving-kindness, like an inseparable shadow.

While the Blessed One was walking to and fro, I walked behind him; while the Dhamma was being taught, knowledge (of the Dhamma) arose in me.

I am still a trainee (sekha) with tasks yet to be done, having not yet reached the fruit of Arahantship; and now, the Parinibbāna of the Teacher, the Blessed One, who had compassion for me, has arrived.

When the Fully Enlightened One, endowed with all excellent qualities, attained Parinibbāna, there was terror; there was hair-raising awe.

Ānanda, who was of great learning, a bearer of the Dhamma, a guardian of the Blessed One's treasury of Dhamma, and like an eye for the whole world, has attained Parinibbāna.
