Ānanda, who was of great learning, a bearer of the Dhamma, a guardian of the Blessed One's treasury of Dhamma, and like an eye for the whole world, was the dispeller of darkness in the mass of gloom.
421:
## 
“There is the Venerable Ānanda, who is endowed with the peerless path of wisdom, endowed with noble mindfulness, and endowed with concentration that does not associate with others. That Elder Ānanda is the bearer of the Good Dhamma known as Pariyatti, and is the repository of the jewels of the Good Dhamma.

“I have served the Teacher who cultivates loving-kindness for all beings; I have fulfilled the Buddha's instruction; the heavy burden has been laid down; now there is no more rebirth.” Thus, he spoke these verses.

In those verses, the first two verses beginning with “Pisuṇena ca” (And with a slanderer) were spoken as a means of giving advice to the monks known as the Chabbaggiyas, having seen them associating with the monks who were followers of Devadatta. In those verses, “pisuṇena” refers to being endowed with slanderous speech. A person possessed of such speech is called “pisuṇa,” just as a cloth possessed of blue color is called “blue.” “Kodhanena” refers to (associating with) one who is habitually angry. He is called “maccharinā” (with a stingy person) because of the occurrence of stinginess, which has the characteristic of concealing one's own success. “Vibhūtanandinā” refers to (associating with) one who desires the ruin and destruction of beings; or, “vibhūta” means separation or division, and it refers to (associating with) one who delights in that division. All of this was spoken specifically referring to the followers of Devadatta.

Those monks who were followers of Devadatta, while presenting the five points (pañcavatthu) and destroying many people who were of good practice, were oppressed by harsh stinginess and so on because of being outside the Buddha's instruction, and they practiced for the great harm of the multitude. “Sakhitaṃ” means one should not form a companionship or association. For what reason? Association with a wicked man is evil. Association with a wicked person is low and base. For those who follow his example, it brings only the characteristics of a fool, such as evil thoughts; what more need be said for one who follows his words? Therefore, the Blessed One said: “Monks, whatever fears arise, all those arise from the fool, not from the wise,” and so forth.

To show with whom association should be made, he spoke the verse beginning with “Saddhena ca” (And with the faithful). In that Pāḷi, “saddhena” refers to (associating with) one who is endowed with faith in kamma and its results, and faith in the Triple Gem. “Pesalena” refers to (associating with) one who has dear virtue, one who is endowed with morality. “Paññavatā” refers to (associating with) one who is endowed with wisdom that perceives the rise and fall (of phenomena) and is penetrative. “Bahussutena” refers to (associating with) one who is very learned because of the fulfillment of great learning in scriptures (pariyatti) and realization (paṭivedha). “Bhaddo” means association with such a virtuous person is excellent; the meaning is that it brings about welfare such as that of the present life.

The seven verses beginning with “Passa cittakataṃ” (Behold the adorned) were spoken to the female lay follower named Uttarā, who, seeing the perfection of her own physical form, was developing sensual perceptions, in order to generate a desire for detachment from the body...
422:
It was preached. Some also say it was “for the purpose of giving advice to the monks whose minds were distracted upon seeing the courtesan Ambapālī.” Those verses have the same meaning as stated above.

The two verses beginning with “Bahussuto cittakathī” (The learned and eloquent) were spoken by the Elder as an inspired utterance (udāna) upon attaining Arahantship. In those verses, “paricārako” means an attendant. The phrase “seyyaṃ kappeti” (he takes his rest) is said because he lay down immediately after attaining Arahantship. Indeed, the Elder, having spent much of the night in walking meditation, entered his chamber to balance the elements of his body and sat on the couch to sleep; his feet were lifted from the ground, and his head had not yet reached the pillow—in this interval, he attained Arahantship and slept.

“Khīṇāsavo” means one whose four taints (āsava) are exhausted. Because he is one whose taints are exhausted, he is also dissociated from the four yokes (yoga). Because of having transcended the attachments of lust and so on, he is called “saṅgātīto” (one who has transcended attachments). Because all the fevers of defilements have been calmed, the meaning is “sunibbuto” (perfectly cooled) and “sītibhūto” (become cold/peaceful).

The verse beginning with “Yasmiṃ patiṭṭhitā dhammā” (In whom the teachings are established) was spoken by a Great Brahmā who was an Arahant, referring to the Elder. In fact, when the rehearsal of the Dhamma (Dhamma-saṅgīti) was drawing near, some monks, referring to the Elder, said, “One monk emits the smell of rot.” Then, when the Elder, having attained Arahantship, came to the entrance of the Sattapaṇṇi Cave to provide unity to the Saṅgha, the Great Brahmā of the Suddhāvāsa realm, wishing to shame those monks by revealing the Elder Ānanda's state of being an Arahant, spoke the verse beginning with “Yasmiṃ patiṭṭhitā dhammā.” The meaning of that verse is: The Dhamma of the Blessed Buddha, both the Dhamma of realization (paṭivedha) and the Dhamma of scriptures (pariyatti), which were realized and proclaimed by Him—in whichever special person these are established, he is this Gautama by lineage, the Treasurer of the Dhamma (Dhammabhaṇḍāgārika). Because this Venerable Ānanda has attained Nibbāna with residue (sa-upādisesa-nibbāna), he now stands on the path leading to Nibbāna without residue (anupādisesa-nibbāna); he is certainly one who shares in the higher path.

Then one day, a Brahmin named Gopaka Moggallāna asked the Elder: “You are famous in the Buddha's dispensation as one who is very learned (bahussuta); how many teachings preached by the Teacher do you bear?” Giving an answer to that Brahmin, the Elder spoke the verse beginning with “Dvāsīti” (Eighty-two). In that verse, it should be connected as “dvāsīti sahassāni” (eighty-two thousand). The meaning is that he learned eighty-two thousand units of Dhamma (dhammakkhandha) from the Buddha, the Fully Enlightened One, from the presence of the Teacher. “Dve sahassāni bhikkhuto” means he learned two thousand units of Dhamma from the monks; he acquired them from the presence of monks such as the General of the Dhamma (Dhammasenāpati, i.e., Sāriputta). Both together make eighty-four thousand. “Ye me dhammā pavattino” means that many units of Dhamma are present on the tip of my tongue (memorized) due to my study and practice. Then, at one time, the Elder, seeing a person who had ordained in the dispensation but did not strive in either insight meditation (vipassanā) or the burden of study (ganthadhura), wishing to show the fault of being unlearned, spoke the verse beginning with “Appassutāyaṃ” (This unlearned person).
423:
When these two are combined, they become eighty-four thousand. "My teachings occur" means that the aforementioned Dhamma aggregates (dhamma-kkhandha) have been mastered by me and are fluently revolving at the tip of my tongue.

Then, on one occasion, the Elder saw a person who, though ordained in the Dispensation, was not devoted to either the burden of insight (vipassanā-dhura) or the burden of study (gantha-dhura). Wishing to reveal the disadvantage of having little learning, he spoke the verse beginning with "Appassutāyaṃ". In that verse, "appassutāya" means that because of not having learned even one or two Paṇṇāsas, or the Vaggas, or at the very least, even one or two Suttas, this person is one of little learning. However, if one has learned a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) and is devoted to it, he is indeed one of great learning (bahussuta). "He grows old like an ox" means that just as an ox, as it grows and ages, does not grow for the benefit of its mother, father, or other relatives, but merely grows old in vain; similarly, this person does not perform the duties to the preceptor (upajjhāya-vatta), the duties to the teacher (ācariya-vatta), the duties to guests (āgantuka-vatta), and so on, nor does he devote himself to meditation (bhāvanā), but merely grows old in vain. "His flesh increases" means that just as an ox released into the forest because it is unable to plow or carry loads, wanders about eating and drinking so that its flesh increases; similarly, this person, being released by his preceptors and the like, depends on the Saṅgha to obtain the four requisites, and by nourishing his body with emetics and so forth, his flesh increases and he wanders about with a stout body. As for wisdom, his mundane and supramundane wisdom does not increase even by a finger's breadth; rather, like creepers in the forest, craving and the nine types of pride (māna) increase depending on his six sense-doors—this is the meaning.

The verse "Bahussuto" was spoken with reference to a certain monk who, depending on his own great learning, looked down on others. In that verse, "sutena" means because of learning. "Atimanyati" means he thinks highly of himself, exalting himself and despising others. "In the same way" means just as a blind man holding an oil lamp in the darkness brings benefit only to others by providing light, but not to himself; in the same way, a person learned in the scriptures (pariyatti) who does not practice accordingly and thus does not fulfill his own benefit, brings benefit only to others by providing the light of knowledge, but not to himself. He appears to me like a blind man carrying a lamp.

Now, wishing to show the advantages of great learning, he spoke the verse beginning with "Bahussutaṃ". In that verse, "upāseyya" means one should associate with. "Sutañca na vināsaye" means one should not let the learning acquired by associating with the greatly learned perish. It should be increased through bearing in mind, recitation, inquiry, and reflection. "Taṃ mūlaṃ brahmacariyဿ" means that the scriptural learning acquired by associating with a greatly learned person is the root of the holy life (brahmacariya) which is the Path. Therefore, one should be a bearer of the Dhamma. Standing at the head of the bases of liberation (vimuttāyatana), one should first be a bearer of the scriptural Dhamma by retaining the Dhamma as it was heard. Now, looking at the meaning increased by scriptural learning, and wishing to show the meaning of "neither before nor after" and so on, in that verse, because he knows the preceding part and the following part, he is called "one who knows the before and after" (pubbāparaññū). This statement is true. In a place where wisdom is not clear in the preceding part of a verse, or where wisdom is clear in the preceding part...
424:
One should not destroy the learning acquired by associating with the greatly learned; rather, one should increase it through bearing it in mind, recitation, inquiry, and reflection. "Taṃ mūlaṃ brahmacariyassa" means that the scriptural learning (pariyatti) acquired by associating with a greatly learned person is the root (the primary cause) of the holy life of the Path. Therefore, one should be a bearer of the Dhamma. Standing at the head of the bases of liberation (vimuttāyatana), one should first be a bearer of the scriptural Dhamma by retaining the Dhamma as it was heard.

Now, to show the meaning to be accomplished through scriptural learning, the verse beginning with "Pubbāparaññū" was spoken. In that context, one who knows the preceding and the following is called "pubbāparaññū" (knower of the before and after). Indeed, even if the preceding part of a single verse is not clear, or if the preceding part is clear but the following part is not clear, one who knows "this following part should be preceded by this" or "this preceding part should be followed by this" is called "pubbāparaññū". One who knows the meaning of the various spoken words, such as the distinction of one's own benefit and so on, is called "atthaññū" (knower of the meaning). "Niruttipada-kovido" means one who is skilled in linguistics (nirutti) and in the remaining terms—thus, one who is proficient in the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). "Suggahītañca gaṇhāti" means that by virtue of that very proficiency, he grasps the Dhamma well, both in meaning and in phrasing. "Atthañcopaparikkhāti" means he repeatedly investigates and reflects with the mind upon the meaning of the Dhamma as it was heard and learned, thinking: "This is virtue (sīla), this is concentration (samādhi), this is wisdom (paññā), these are the phenomena of mentality and materiality (nāmarūpa-dhamma)."

"Khantyā chandikato hoti" means that regarding those phenomena repeatedly contemplated by the mind, he accepts the reflection through patience in reflecting on views (diṭṭhi-nijjhāna-khanti), and starting with the grasping of materiality (rūpa-pariggaha), he becomes one who has desire, one in whom desire has arisen for the application of insight (vipassanā). When this is so, while performing the work of insight, he exerts himself and evaluates. Having exerted effort by way of seeing mentality and materiality along with their respective causes, he then applies the three characteristics and evaluates, "impermanent" (anicca), "suffering" (dukkha), and "non-self" (anatta); thus he evaluates, distinguishes, and practices insight (vipassanā) upon that mentality and materiality. "In due time he strives, well-concentrated within" means that such a person, at the time when the mind should be uplifted and so on, strives by uplifting the mind. While striving, he becomes well-concentrated within the object of meditation through insight-concentration (vipassanā-samādhi) and path-concentration (magga-samādhi). He should abandon the defilements that are causes of non-concentration. All these virtues occur to one who associates with a disciple of the Buddha who is greatly learned, a bearer of the Dhamma, and wise. Therefore, taking the Unconditioned (asankhata) Dhamma as the object, because of the distinguished function of fully understanding suffering and so forth, one who desires the knowledge of Dhamma (dhamma-ñāṇa), also known as Dhamma-consciousness...
425:
It means that one should associate with, attend upon, and serve such a good friend (kalyāṇamitta) as previously described.

Showing that such a person is worthy of honor because of being of great benefit, he spoke the verse beginning with "Bahussuto." The meaning of that verse is: He is called "Bahussuta" (one of great learning) because he has heard much of the Sutta, Geyya, and so forth. He is called "Dhammadhara" (bearer of the Dhamma) because he preserves that very Dhamma of the teachings without loss, like lion's fat placed in a golden vessel. For that very reason, he is called "Kosārakkha" (guardian of the treasury) because he guards the treasury of the Dhamma (the Dhamma-treasure) of the Blessed One. Because he is like an eye to the world including the devas by seeing things with equanimity, he is like an eye that is worthy of honor and respect by the entire world. To show that he is worthy of honor by many people due to his state of being of great learning, the word "Bahussuta" is mentioned again by way of conclusion.

To show that even after obtaining such a good friend, only the one who practices does not decline, while the one who does not practice does, he spoke the verse beginning with "Dhammārāmo." In that verse, the Dhamma of Samatha and Vipassanā is called "Ārāma" (delight/garden) in the sense of being a dwelling place; he is called "Dhammarata" because he is greatly delighted and finds pleasure in that very Dhamma. "Anuvicintayaṃ" means reflecting on and attending to the Dhamma by repeatedly thinking about that very Dhamma. "Anussaraṃ" means repeatedly recollecting that very Dhamma. "Saddhammā" means that such a bhikkhu does not decline from the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma) and the ninefold supramundane Dhamma (lokuttara-dhamma); it means that for him, there is never any decline from those Dhammas.

Then one day, wishing to cause spiritual urgency (saṃvega) in a monk named Kossallāya, who was not yet free from lust for the body, was lazy, and lacked effort, he spoke the verse beginning with "Kāyamaccheragaruno." In that verse, "Kāyamaccheragaruno" refers to one who is full of desire to make his body firm, who is attached to the body, and who wanders about without performing even the minor or major duties that should be done with the body for his teachers and preceptors. "Hiyyamāne" means even though one's body and life are declining moment by moment. "Anuṭṭhahe" means one should not fail to make an effort to arise in order to fulfill virtue (sīla) and so forth. "Sarīrasukhagiddhassa" means for one who has reached a state of greed only for the comfort of his own body. "Kuto samaṇaphāsutā" means for such a person, how can there be happiness by way of the practice of a recluse? It means that for him, there is no comfortable abiding (phāsuvihāra).

The verses beginning with "Na pakkhanti" were spoken by the Elder upon hearing that the General of the Dhamma, the Venerable Sāriputta, had attained Parinibbāna. In that verse, "Na pakkhanti disā sabbā" means that all the quarters, such as the East, do not appear clear.
426:
All the quarters, such as the East and so forth, do not appear clear; it means one is bewildered regarding the directions. "The Dhammas do not appear clear to me" means that even the scriptures (pariyatti-dhamma) which were well-studied and mastered in the past do not appear to me now, even when I attend to them carefully. "When the good friend has gone" means when the General of the Dhamma, Sāriputta, who was a good friend to the world including the devas, has gone to the Nibbāna element without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna). The entire world appears as if it were a mass of darkness.

"For one who is deprived of a companion" means for one who is without a companion, one who is bereft of a good friend. "For one whose Teacher has passed away" means for the Venerable one whose Teacher has passed into Nibbāna; it means when the Teacher has attained Parinibbāna. "Like mindfulness directed to the body" means just as the meditation of mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatāsati) brings absolute benefit to the one who practices it, so for such a helpless person, there is no other friend who can bring absolute benefit; however, for one who has a protector, other meditations also bring benefit.

"The old ones" refers to the good friends of the past, such as Sāriputta and others. "With the new ones" means with the junior monks. "Does not agree with me" means my mind does not reach agreement; it means they do not please my mind. "Today I shall meditate alone" means that I, today, being bereft of those who are more senior and being alone, shall be one devoted to meditation (jhāna). "Seeking shelter from the rain" is like a bird that has gone to its nest during the rainy season. There is also a Pali reading "Vāsupeto," which means one who has entered a dwelling.

The verse beginning with "Dassanāya abhikkante" was spoken by the Teacher. Its meaning is: Ānanda, do not hinder the many people who have come from various foreign places to see me from approaching me. Why? They are those who will hear the Dhamma; let them see me; this is the very time for seeing.

Hearing those words, the Elder spoke another verse beginning with "Dassanāya abhikkante." This previous verse is placed here to show the connection with this verse. Therefore, it shows the fulfillment of the meaning of this phrase: "If I should be able to let those who come from various places see [the Buddha] at that very moment."

The five verses beginning with "For twenty-five years" were spoken to show his state of being the chief attendant. Indeed, by way of having undertaken the meditation subjects and by way of being devoted to attending upon the Teacher...
427:
Although sensual perceptions (kāmasaññā) and so forth had not yet been eradicated by the Path in the Elder Ānanda, they did not arise. His bodily, verbal, and mental actions were at all times preceded by loving-kindness (metta) toward the Teacher and were always in accordance with loving-kindness. In those verses, 'paṇṇavīsati vassāni' means for twenty-five years. 'Sekhabhūtassa me sato' means of me who was established in the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpattiphala), which is the stage of a trainee (sekhabhūmi). 'Kāmasaññā' means that perceptions associated with sensual pleasures did not arise. Here, by stating the non-arising of sensual perceptions and so forth, he shows the purity of his disposition (āsaya); by the words 'mettena kāyakammena' and so forth, he shows the purity of his application (payoga). Therein, loving-kindness in bodily action should be understood through his performing major and minor duties for the Teacher, such as cleaning the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi). Loving-kindness in verbal action should be understood through his announcing the time for preaching the Dhamma and so forth. Loving-kindness in mental action should be understood through his mental application directed toward the Teacher's welfare when the Teacher was in seclusion. 'Ñāṇaṃ me udapajjatha' refers to his statement about reaching the stage of a trainee.

The verse beginning with "I still have work to do" was spoken by him when the Teacher's Parinibbāna was imminent; he entered the circular hall, leaned against the doorpost, and spoke while overwhelmed with grief. In that verse, 'sakaraniyo'mhi' means I am one who has work to do, such as the full understanding of suffering. 'Appattamānaso' means one who has not yet attained the fruit of Arahantship. 'Satthu ca parinibbānaṃ' means the Parinibbāna of my Teacher is also drawing near. 'Yo amhaṃ anukampako' means the Teacher who is my benefactor.

The verse beginning with 'Tadāsi yaṃ bhiṃsanakaṃ' was spoken with a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) that arose upon seeing the earthquake and hearing the thunder-like sounds of the gods at the time of the Teacher's Parinibbāna.

The three verses beginning with 'Bahussuto' were placed by the Reciters (Sangītikāras) who were praising the Elder. In those verses, 'gatimanto' means one endowed with an incomparable course of knowledge. 'Satimanto' means one endowed with supreme maturity of mindfulness. 'Dhitimanto' means one endowed with extraordinary resolution capable of discerning the words and the meaning. Indeed, this Elder, while standing in a single place, could learn sixty thousand verses exactly as they were taught by the Teacher. Once learned, they never vanished, like lion's fat placed in a golden bowl. He was endowed with wisdom preceded by mindfulness, capable of discerning the words without error, and with mindfulness preceded by wisdom, capable of discerning the meaning. Therefore, the Blessed One said:
428:
Referring to that Venerable Ānanda, who was capable of remembering the meaning, possessed wisdom as a precursor, and was endowed with mindfulness, the Blessed One said: "Monks, among my monk disciples who are very learned (bahussuta), this Ānanda is the foremost" and so forth. Likewise, the General of the Dhamma (Venerable Sāriputta) also said: "The Venerable Ānanda is skilled in the meaning" and so forth. 'Ratanākaro' means being like a mine (a source) for the jewel of the True Dhamma. The verse 'Pariciṇṇo' was spoken by the Elder at the time of his Parinibbāna, and its meaning is just as previously stated.

## The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Ānanda is finished.

## The Commentary on the Section of Thirty is finished.
429:
## 18. Section of Forty (Cattālīsanipāta)

## 1. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Mahākassapa

In the Section of Forty, the verses beginning with "Na gaṇena purakkhato" are those of the Venerable Mahākassapa. What is the origin story? It is said that during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, in the city of Haṃsavatī, he was a householder named Vedeha, possessing a wealth of eighty crores. He lived as a lay follower (upāsaka) devoted to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. One Uposatha day, after eating a good meal early in the morning, he undertook the eight Uposatha precepts, took perfumes, flowers, and so forth, went to the monastery, honored and paid homage to the Teacher, and sat down at a respectful distance.

At that moment, the Teacher placed the third disciple, the Elder Mahānisabha, in the foremost position (etadagga), saying: "Monks, among my monk disciples who speak of and practice ascetic virtues (dhutavāda), this Nisabha is the foremost." The lay follower, hearing this and being inspired, waited until the end of the Dhamma talk. When the crowd had departed, he paid homage to the Teacher and invited him, saying: "Please accept my meal offering tomorrow." The Teacher said: "Lay follower, the Saṅgha of monks is very large." "How many are there, Bhante?" "Six million eight hundred thousand monks." "Bhante, please accept my meal offering without leaving behind even a single novice in the monastery." The Teacher accepted.

The lay follower, knowing the Teacher's acceptance, went home and prepared a great gift. The next day, he announced to the Teacher that it was time. The Teacher, taking his bowl and robes and surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks, went to the lay follower's house and sat on the prepared seat. After the water of donation was poured, he received the gruel and so forth and partook of the meal. The lay follower also sat near the Teacher.

In the meantime, the Elder Mahānisabha, while wandering for alms, came onto that same street. The lay follower saw him, rose, went to the Elder, paid homage, and said: "Bhante, please give me your bowl." The Elder gave him the bowl. "Bhante, please enter here; the Teacher is also sitting in the house." "It is not proper, lay follower," he replied. The lay follower took the Elder's bowl, filled it with alms-food, and gave it back. Then, after following the Elder for a short distance, he returned, sat near the Teacher, and asked: "Bhante, although I told the Elder Mahānisabha that the Teacher is also in the house, he did not wish to enter. Does that Elder possess a quality that exceeds your own qualities?"
430:
The Buddha has no such thing as envy regarding praise (vaṇṇamacchera). Therefore, the Teacher said: "Lay follower, we sit in the house waiting for alms; however, that monk does not sit like this but looks out for alms. We live in a dwelling near a village; he lives only in the forest. We live in a sheltered dwelling; he lives only in the open air." Saying, "This is a virtue of this monk, and this is another virtue," the Blessed One spoke of the Elder's virtues as if filling the great ocean.

The lay follower, being even more inspired like a naturally shining lamp being poured with oil, thought: "What use is other prosperity to me? In the future, I will make an aspiration to attain the foremost position among those who practice dhutaṅga in the presence of a Buddha." He invited the Teacher again and, in the same manner, gave a great gift (mahādāna) for seven days. On the seventh day, having offered triple robes (ticīvara) to the great Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, he prostrated at the Teacher's feet and said: "Venerable Sir, may the loving bodily action, loving verbal action, and loving mental action that have been present in me while giving this gift for seven days not be for any other celestial prosperity, nor for the prosperity of Sakka, Māra, or Brahmā. May this meritorious deed of mine be a support for attaining the foremost position among the thirteen dhutaṅga-holders, the same rank attained by the Elder Mahānisabha in the presence of a future Buddha."

The Teacher, looking to see whether the great position he aspired for would be fulfilled or not, saw that it would be fulfilled and said: "You have aspired for a pleasing position. In the future, at the end of a hundred thousand aeons, a Buddha named Gotama will arise. You will be his third disciple, named Mahākassapa Thera." Thus He gave the prophecy. Hearing that prophecy, the lay follower thought of that prosperity as if he would receive it the very next day, thinking, "There is no such thing as double speech for the Buddhas." He gave gifts throughout his life, undertook and kept the precepts, performed various kinds of wholesome deeds, and upon passing away, was reborn in the celestial realm.

From then on, experiencing prosperity in the celestial and human realms, ninety-one aeons ago from this present one, when Buddha Vipassī was dwelling in the safe Migadāya forest depending on the city of Bandhumatī, he passed away from the celestial realm and was reborn in a certain dilapidated Brahmin family. At that time, the Blessed One Vipassī preached the Dhamma once every seven years, and there was a great commotion. Throughout the entire Jambudīpa, deities announced, "The Teacher will preach the Dhamma." The Brahmin...
431:
...heard (that news). That Brahmin had only one lower garment, and likewise, the Brahmin woman (had only one). As for the upper garment, there was only one for both of them. He was known throughout the whole city as "Ekasāṭaka Brahmin" (the Brahmin with one cloth). When there was a meeting for some business of the Brahmins, he would leave the Brahmin woman at home and go wearing that cloth himself. When there was a meeting of the Brahmin women, he himself would stay at home, and the Brahmin woman would go wearing that cloth.

On that day, however, the Brahmin asked the Brahmin woman: "Lady, will you listen to the Dhamma at night or during the day?" (The Brahmin woman) said, "We womenfolk are unable to listen to the Dhamma at night; we will listen during the day." Leaving the Brahmin at home and wearing that cloth, she went during the day with the female lay followers, paid homage to the Teacher, sat in a suitable place, listened to the Dhamma, and returned with the female lay followers. Then the Brahmin, leaving the Brahmin woman at home and wearing that cloth, went to the monastery.

At that time, the Teacher, seated on the decorated Dhamma-seat in the midst of the assembly, holding a beautiful fan, was preaching the Dhamma as if bringing down the celestial Ganges, or as if churning the ocean using Mount Sineru as a churning stick. To the Brahmin sitting at the edge of the assembly and listening to the Dhamma, in the very first watch, five-fold joy (pīti) arose, pervading his entire body. He folded the cloth he was wearing and thought, "I will offer this to the Buddha of Ten Powers (Dasabala)." Then, stinginess (macchera) arose in him, as if showing a thousand faults. He thought, "There is only one cloth for the Brahmin woman and me; there is no other upper garment. It is impossible to go outside without an upper garment." Thus, in every way, he had no desire to give. Then, when the first watch had passed and the middle watch arrived, joy arose in the same way. He thought in the same way and remained unwilling to give in the same way. Then, when the middle watch had passed and the last watch arrived, joy arose in the same way. Then he thought, "Whatever happens, happens; I will deal with it later," folded the cloth, and placed it at the Teacher's feet. Then, bending his left arm and clapping his right hand three times, he shouted three times, "I have won! I have won!"

At that time, King Bandhuma was sitting behind a curtain at the back of the Dhamma-seat, listening to the Dhamma. To the King, the sound "I have won!" was unpleasant.
432:
## 
The King sent a servant, saying, "Go and ask what that man is saying." The servant went and asked, and the Brahmin replied, "Others conquer enemy armies by riding elephants and so on, and wielding swords and such; that is not a wonder. But I, as if splitting the head of a crooked ox with a mallet to make it flee, have crushed my stingy mind and offered my cloak to the Buddha. Therefore, I have conquered my stinginess (macchariya)." The servant returned and reported this to the King. The King said, "Friends, we did not know what was worthy of the Buddha, but the Brahmin knew," and he sent a pair of cloths. Upon seeing the pair of cloths, the Brahmin thought, "This King gave me nothing while I sat in silence, but gave only after I praised the virtues of the Buddha. What benefit is there for me in this which was obtained by relying on the virtues of the Teacher?" and he offered that pair of cloths also to the Buddha. The King asked, "What did the Brahmin do?" and hearing that he had offered that pair of cloths also to the Buddha, he sent another two pairs of cloths. The Brahmin offered those two pairs as well. The King sent four pairs, and so on, up to thirty-two pairs of cloths. Then the Brahmin thought, "This is becoming like taking more and more," and he kept only two pairs—one for himself and one for his wife—and offered the remaining thirty pairs to the Buddha. From that day on, the Brahmin became very close to the Buddha.

Later, one day during the cold winter season, the King saw the Brahmin listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Buddha. He gave the Brahmin his own red blanket worth one hundred thousand, which he was wearing, and said, "From today onwards, wear this blanket while listening to the Dhamma." The Brahmin thought, "What benefit is there for me in wearing this blanket on this foul body?" and he made it into a canopy over the Buddha's bed inside the Gandhakuti (Fragrant Chamber) and then left. Later, one day, the King went to the monastery early in the morning and sat in the presence of the Buddha inside the Gandhakuti. At that time, the six-colored Buddha-rays struck the blanket, and the blanket shone exceedingly bright. The King looked up, recognized it as his blanket, and said, "Venerable Sir, this is our blanket, which we gave to the Brahmin Ekasāṭaka." The Buddha replied, "Great King, you honored the Brahmin, and the Brahmin has honored Me." The King, thinking, "The Brahmin alone knew what was appropriate, but we did not," felt great devotion. He gathered all things useful to humans in groups of eight and gave the gift known as the Sabbaṭṭhaka (the Eightfold Gift), and appointed the Brahmin to the position of Royal Chaplain (Purohita). That Brahmin also thought, "The Sabbaṭṭhaka (eight of eight kinds) makes sixty-four..."
433:
## 
He arranged for sixty-four Sabbaṭṭhaka-bhatta (eightfold alms-food) to be offered regularly. After giving alms and keeping the precepts for the rest of his life, he passed away and was reborn in heaven.

When he passed away from that heaven, he was reborn in a merchant's (kuṭumbiya) house in Bārāṇasī during the interval between the Buddhas Koṇāgamana and Kassapa in this eon. When he reached adulthood and was living as a householder, one day he was walking in the forest. At that time, a Paccekabuddha was sewing a robe on a riverbank, and as the border (anuvāta) was insufficient, he began to fold the robe and set it aside. Seeing this, the man asked, "Venerable Sir, why are you folding it and setting it aside?" "The border is insufficient," the Paccekabuddha replied. "Venerable Sir, please use this cloth," the man said, offering his upper garment, and made a wish: "In every life I am reborn, may I never suffer lack in anything."

At home, while his wife was quarreling with his sister, the Paccekabuddha entered for alms. Then the sister gave alms-food to the Paccekabuddha and, referring to the wife, made a wish: "May I be able to avoid such a fool even at a distance of a hundred yojanas." The wife, standing in the courtyard, heard this and thought, "May this monk not eat the food given by this woman." She took the bowl, threw away the alms-food, filled it with mud, and gave it back. The other woman, the sister, seeing this, said, "You fool, abuse me or strike me if you wish, but it is not proper to throw away food from the bowl of such a Noble One who has fulfilled the perfections for two asankheyya and give him mud instead." Then, remorse and reflection arose in the wife. She said, "Wait a moment, Venerable Sir," threw away the mud, washed the bowl, and rubbed it with scented powder. She filled it with choice food and the four sweet delicacies (catumadhura), poured ghee the color of a lotus-calyx on top, and placed the shining bowl in the hands of the Paccekabuddha, making a wish: "Just as this alms-food is radiant, may my body also be radiant." The Paccekabuddha gave his blessing and flew into the sky.

That husband and wife performed meritorious deeds for the rest of their lives and were reborn in heaven. When they passed away from there, during the time of Kassapa Buddha, the lay devotee was reborn in Bārāṇasī as the son of a merchant with a wealth of eighty crores. The wife was also reborn as the daughter of a similar merchant. When the merchant's son reached adulthood, they brought that merchant's daughter to be his wife. Due to the power of her past bad deed that was to bear ill fruit, as soon as she stepped over the threshold of her husband's house, a foul smell like an open latrine emanated from her entire body. When the merchant's son asked, "Whose foul smell is this?" and was told, "It is the merchant's daughter's smell," he said, "Take her away, take her away!" and had her sent back to her parents' house by a path she had never traveled before.
434:
Due to the power of unwholesome kamma, as soon as she entered her husband's house, her entire body emitted a foul odor like an open latrine (vacca-kuṭi) while she was within the threshold. The merchant's son asked, "Whose smell is this?" and upon hearing it was the merchant's daughter's, he said, "Take her away! Take her away!" and had her sent back to her family home in the same manner she had been brought. In this way, the merchant's daughter was turned back from seven different places.

At that time, the Blessed One Kassapa attained Parinibbāna. They endeavored to build a cetiya one league (yojana) high for his relics, using red gold bricks worth a hundred thousand each. While the cetiya was being constructed, the merchant's daughter thought, "I have been turned back from seven places; what is the use of my life?" She then had her ornaments broken down and made into a gold brick one cubit long, one span wide, and four finger-breadths thick. Then, taking a lump of orpiment and realgar (haritāla and manosilā) and holding eight handfuls of lotuses, she went to the site of the cetiya. At that moment, a gap for a finishing brick was found in a row of bricks being laid. The merchant's daughter said to the mason, "Please place this brick here." The mason replied, "Dear daughter, you have come at an auspicious time; place it yourself."

The merchant's daughter climbed the cetiya, mixed the orpiment and realgar with oil, and using that as an adhesive, she firmly offered the brick. She then made an offering of the eight handfuls of lotuses on top, paid homage, and made a wish: "In every place I am reborn, may the scent of sandalwood waft from my body, and the scent of blue lotuses from my mouth." After circumambulating the cetiya clockwise, she departed.

At that very moment, the merchant's son who had first taken her remembered her. A festival was being proclaimed in the city. He asked his attendants, "Wasn't there a merchant's daughter brought here then? Where is she?" "Lord, she is at her family home," they replied. "Bring her here; let us enjoy the festival," he said. When the attendants went to fetch her, she asked, "Friends, why have you come?" They explained the situation. She said, "Friends, I have broken my ornaments to make an offering to the cetiya; I no longer have ornaments to wear." When the attendants reported this, the merchant's son said, "Just bring her; she will receive ornaments." They brought her. As soon as she entered the house, the entire house was filled with the scent of sandalwood and blue lotuses. The merchant's son asked her, "Previously, a foul odor came from your body, but now, the scent of sandalwood..."
435:
"...and the scent of blue lotuses wafts from your mouth. Why is this so?" he asked. The merchant's daughter told him of the deed she had done from the beginning. The merchant's son, filled with faith, exclaimed, "How truly liberating is the Dispensation of the Buddha!" He then covered the one-league golden cetiya with a woolen garment and decorated it here and there with golden lotuses the size of chariot wheels, which had hanging tassels twelve cubits long.

Having remained in that life until the end of his lifespan, he was reborn in heaven. After passing away from there, he was reborn in a certain minister's family about one league away from the city of Bārāṇasī. The merchant's daughter also passed away from the deva world and was reborn as the eldest daughter in a royal family. When they reached maturity, a festival was proclaimed in the city. The young man said to his mother, "Mother, give me a cloth; I wish to enjoy the festival." His mother brought out a washed cloth and gave it to him. "Mother, this cloth is too coarse," he said. She brought another, but he rejected that too. Then his mother said, "Dear son, we were born into such a house; we do not have the merit to obtain cloth more delicate than this."

"In that case, Mother, I shall go to a place where it can be obtained," he said. "Dear son, I wish for you to obtain the kingship in Bārāṇasī this very day," she replied. He paid homage to his mother and said, "I am going, Mother." "Go, dear son," she said. She thought to herself, "Where will he go? He will likely sit here or there in the house." However, by the power of his merit, he departed and reached Bārāṇasī, where he lay down on the auspicious stone slab in the park, covering himself including his head. That day was the seventh day since the King of Bārāṇasī had passed away.

After performing the king's funeral rites, the ministers sat in the royal courtyard and consulted: "The king had only one daughter and no son. A kingdom without a king will perish. Who shall be king?" They said to one another, "You be the king," "No, you be the king." The chaplain (purohita) said, "It is not proper to look among many people; let us release the festive carriage (phussaratha)." The ministers harnessed four Sindh horses the color of white water-lilies, placed the five royal regalia and the white parasol on the carriage, and released it, having the musical instruments played behind it. The carriage exited through the eastern gate and headed toward the park. Some said, "It is going toward the park out of habit; let us turn it back." The chaplain said, "Do not turn it back." The carriage circumambulated the young man clockwise and stood ready for him to mount.
436:
The chaplain, setting aside the edge of his robe and examining the soles of the prince's feet, said, "Let alone this island, this man is fit to rule over the four great continents surrounded by two thousand minor islands." He then ordered the musical instruments to be played three times, saying, "Play the instruments again! Play them again!"

Then the prince opened his eyes, looked around, and asked, "For what purpose have you come?" They replied, "Sire, the kingship has come to you." "Where is the King?" he asked. "Sire, he has gone to the world of the gods," they answered. "How many days have passed?" he asked. "Today is the seventh day," they replied. "Is there no son or daughter?" he asked. "Sire, there is a daughter, but no son," they replied. "I shall take up the kingship," he declared. Immediately, those ministers had a consecration pavilion built, adorned the princess with all ornaments, brought her to the park, and performed the consecration of the prince. Then, they offered the consecrated king a garment worth a hundred thousand. The king asked, "Friends, what is this?" "Sire, it is a garment to be worn," they replied. "Friends, is it not coarse?" he remarked. "Sire, among the garments used by humans, there is none finer than this," they replied. "Did your king wear such as this?" he asked. "Yes, Sire, he did," they replied. "I do not think your king was one of great merit. Bring a golden pitcher; we shall obtain cloth," he said.

They brought a golden pitcher. The king rose, washed his hands and rinsed his mouth, then taking water in his hand, he sprinkled it towards the eastern direction. At that very moment, the solid earth split open, and eight wish-fulfilling trees (kappa-rukkha) sprang up. Again, taking water, he sprinkled it in the south, west, and north directions. In each of the four directions, he did the same, and thirty-two wish-fulfilling trees sprang up, eight in each direction. The king put on one divine cloth and wrapped another around him. He then ordered the drum to be beaten, proclaiming, "Let the women who spin thread in the realm of King Nanda spin no more thread." Having raised the white parasol and being fully adorned, he mounted the back of a noble elephant, entered the city, ascended the palace, and enjoyed great prosperity.

As time passed, one day the queen, seeing the king's great prosperity, showed a sign of compassion, saying, "Alas, the striver!" When asked, "Queen, what is the meaning of this?" she replied, "Sire, your prosperity is very great. In the past, having faith in the Buddhas, you performed good deeds. Now, you do not perform any meritorious deeds which are the cause for the future." "To whom shall we give? There are no virtuous ones," he said. "Sire, Jambudīpa is not empty of Arahants. You just prepare the alms; I will find the Arahants," she said. The king had alms prepared at the eastern gate the next day. The queen went to the palace roof, undertook the Uposatha precepts, and prostrating herself towards the east on the upper terrace, she made an aspiration: "If there be Arahants in this direction, may they accept our alms tomorrow." At that time, no Arahants came. They gave those offerings to the poor, travelers, and others. The next day, he prepared alms at the southern gate and she did the same. The next day, at the western gate, she did the same. On the following day, when alms were prepared at the northern gate and the queen had invited them in the same manner, the Paccekabuddha Mahāpaduma, who was the eldest of the five hundred Paccekabuddhas—the sons of Queen Padumavatī living in the Himavanta—called the other Paccekabuddhas. "Venerable sirs, King Mahāpanāda invites you. Please favor the king's alms-giving," he said.
437:
On the following day, he had an offering prepared at the eastern gate. The Queen, having observed the Uposatha precepts early in the morning, lay prostrate on her chest facing the east in the upper palace and said, "If there are Arahants in this direction, may they come tomorrow and accept our alms-food." There were no Arahants in that direction, so they gave those offerings to the poor and beggars.

On the following day, he prepared an offering at the southern gate and did the same; on the next day, at the western gate, he did the same. On the day the offering was prepared at the northern gate, while the Queen was making the same invitation, Mahāpaduma Paccekabuddha, the eldest among the five hundred Paccekabuddhas who were sons of Queen Padumavatī living in the Himalayas, addressed his brothers, "Sirs, King Nanda invites you; please accept his offering." Having accepted, they washed their faces at Lake Anotatta the next day and, traveling through the air, descended at the northern gate. People saw them and went to inform the King, saying, "Your Majesty, five hundred Paccekabuddhas have arrived."

The King went with the Queen, paid homage, took their bowls, and invited the Paccekabuddhas to the palace. After offering them alms there and when the meal was finished, the King prostrated at the feet of the Sangha Elder, and the Queen at the feet of the most junior monk, saying, "May the Venerable Ones not suffer for lack of the four requisites, and may we not fall away from merit. Please give us your word to reside here for the rest of your lives." Having secured their promise, they prepared five hundred leaf-roofed huts and five hundred walkways in the park, providing all necessary living quarters, and had them reside there.

As time passed, the King's border region became turbulent with rebellion. The King advised the Queen, "I shall go to pacify the border; do not be negligent toward the Paccekabuddhas," and then departed. Before the King could return, the life-span of the Paccekabuddhas came to an end. Mahāpaduma Paccekabuddha, after spending the three watches of the night in meditative attainment, stood leaning against a support board at dawn and attained Parinibbāna through the element of Nibbāna without remainder. In this manner, all the remaining Paccekabuddhas also attained Parinibbāna.

On the following day, the Queen had the Paccekabuddhas' dwelling place smeared with fresh clay, scattered flowers, offered incense, and sat waiting for the arrival of the Venerable Ones. Not seeing them arrive, she sent a man, saying, "Go, dear, and find out if anything is unwell with the Venerable Ones." That man went, opened the door of Mahāpaduma's leaf-hut, and not seeing him there, went to the walkway. Seeing him standing leaning against the support board, he paid homage and said, "Venerable Sir, it is time..."
438:
Even though the man called out, "Venerable Sir," there was no response. Thinking, "How can a body that has attained Parinibbāna speak? He must be asleep," he went and touched the top of the feet with his hand. Realizing he had attained Parinibbāna due to the coldness and stiffness of the feet, he went to the second Paccekabuddha. In this manner, having realized that all of them, including the third and so on, had attained Parinibbāna, he went to the royal palace. When asked, "Dear, where are the Paccekabuddhas?" he replied, "Your Majesty, they have attained Parinibbāna." The Queen came out wailing and weeping, went there with the citizens, held a grand funeral ceremony, performed the cremation rites for the Paccekabuddhas, took the relics, and enshrined them in a stupa.

When the King returned after pacifying the border, he asked the Queen who came to welcome him, "My dear, were you not negligent in serving the Paccekabuddhas? Are the Venerable Ones free from illness?" When she replied, "Your Majesty, they have attained Parinibbāna," the King reflected, "If even such wise and virtuous ones must face death, how can we escape it?" He did not enter the city but went straight into the park, summoned his eldest son, handed over the kingship to him, and ordained as a monk himself. The Queen also thought, "If the King ordains, what shall I do?" and ordained in that very park. Both developed Jhana and, upon passing away from that life, were reborn in the Brahma realm.

While they were residing in the Brahma realm, our Buddha appeared in the world, turned the noble Wheel of Dhamma, and in due course arrived at the city of Rājagaha. While the Buddha was residing in Rājagaha, this youth Pippali was conceived in the womb of the wife of the Brahmin Kapila in the Brahmin village of Mahātittha in the kingdom of Magadha. This Bhaddā Kāpilānī was also conceived in the womb of the wife of a Brahmin of the Kosiya clan in the city of Sāgala in the kingdom of Madda. As they grew up in due course, when the youth Pippali reached twenty years of age and Bhaddā reached sixteen, the parents looked at their son and urged him strongly, saying, "Dear son, you have reached the age where you should establish a family lineage." The youth said, "Do not speak such words in my ears. As long as you are alive, I will care for you; after you pass away, I will leave for the forest and ordain as a monk." After a few days, the parents spoke to him again. The youth refused in the same way. From that day on, the parents spoke to him constantly.
439:
The youth Pippali thought, "I will let my mother know (persuade her)." He gave a thousand nikkhas of red gold, satisfied [the goldsmiths] with all desired things, and had them create a golden statue of a woman. When the polishing and finishing of the statue were completed, he had it dressed in red cloth and adorned with perfect flowers and various ornaments. Then, he called his mother and said, "Mother, if I find a person with such an appearance, I will live in the house; if not, I will not."

The wise Brahmin woman thought, "My son is meritorious; he has given gifts and made aspirations. When performing merit, he did not do it alone. Surely, there must be someone with an appearance like this golden statue who performed merit together with him." She called eight Brahmins, satisfied them with all desired things, placed the golden statue on a carriage, and sent them off, saying, "Go, dear ones. If you find a maiden of such a nature in a family equal to ours in birth, lineage, and wealth, present this golden statue as a gift and return."

Those Brahmins said, "This is indeed our task," and departed. Thinking, "Where shall we go?" they decided, "The kingdom of Madda is a source of beautiful women; let us go to the kingdom of Madda." They went to the city of Sāgala in the kingdom of Madda. There, they placed the golden statue at a bathing ghat and sat down nearby.

At that time, Bhaddā’s nurse, having bathed and adorned Bhaddā and seated her in the auspicious chamber, went to the water's edge to bathe herself. Seeing the golden statue at the ghat, she said, "Why is this undisciplined girl standing here?" and struck it on the back. Realizing it was a golden statue, she thought, "It is my mistress's daughter." She said, "This statue is not even equal to the servant who handles my mistress's daughter's clothes."

Then, those men surrounded the nurse and asked, "Is your mistress's daughter of such an appearance?" She replied, "What is the use of this golden statue? My mistress's daughter is a hundred, even a thousand times more beautiful. When she sits in a chamber of twelve cubits, there is no need to light a lamp; she dispels the darkness with the radiance of her body alone." They said, "Then come," took the nurse, placed the golden statue on the carriage, and stood at the door of the Brahmin of the Kosiya clan's house, announcing their arrival.

The Brahmin welcomed them and asked, "Where have you come from?" They replied, "From the house of the Brahmin Kapila in Mahātittha village in the kingdom of Magadha." He asked, "For what reason have you come?" They explained the reason. He said, "Good, dear ones. He is a Brahmin equal to us in birth, lineage, and wealth. I shall give the maiden." He accepted the gift. Those Brahmins sent word to the Brahmin Kapila, saying, "We have found her..."
440:
"(We have found) the maiden; perform what needs to be done." Hearing that message, they told the youth Pippali, "It is said that a maiden has been found." The youth thought, "I thought they would not find one, but they say they have. Since I am unwilling, I will send a letter." He went to a private place and wrote: "Bhaddā, may you find a household life suitable to your birth, lineage, and wealth. I shall depart and become a monk. Do not be regretful later." Bhaddā also, hearing "They wish to give me to such a person," thought, "I will send a letter." She went to a private place and wrote: "Noble sir, may you find a household life suitable to your birth, lineage, and wealth. I shall become a nun. Do not be regretful later."

Both letters met on the way. When asked, "Whose letter is this?" they said, "It is sent by the youth Pippali to Bhaddā." When asked, "Whose is this?" they said, "It is sent by Bhaddā to the youth Pippali." Those people read both letters and said, "Look at the behavior of these children!" They tore up the letters, threw them in the forest, wrote other letters similar to them, and sent them from both sides. Thus, although the matching letters of the youth and the maiden were devoid of worldly desire, the union of the two occurred even though they were unwilling.

On that very day, the youth Pippali had a flower garland woven; Bhaddā did the same. They placed those garlands in the middle of the bed. After eating their evening meal, both said, "Let us go to bed." The youth climbed onto the bed from the right side. Bhaddā climbed from the left and said, "If the flowers on anyone's side wither, let it be known that a thought of lust has arisen in that person. We must not touch this flower garland." Fearing physical contact with each other, they spent the three watches of the night without falling asleep. During the day, there was not even a mere smile. They did not mix with worldly pleasures and did not manage the wealth as long as their parents were alive; they only managed it after their parents passed away.

The youth Pippali's wealth was immense. Even the gold powder used for rubbing the body and then discarded daily was enough to fill twelve Magadhan cups. There were sixty large tanks operated by machinery, the workplace was twelve leagues wide, and there were fourteen villages the size of Anurādhapura, fourteen elephant units, fourteen cavalry units, and fourteen chariot units. One day, the youth Pippali, mounted on an adorned horse and surrounded by a large crowd, went to the workplace. Standing at the edge of the field, he saw crows and other birds eating earthworms and such from the places turned up by the plows.
441:
When the young man Pippali saw birds picking up and eating worms and other insects, he asked, "Friends, what are these birds eating?" "Sir, they are eating worms," the workers replied. He asked again, "To whom does the evil committed by these birds belong?" "To you, sir," they answered. Then the young man thought, "If the evil committed by these birds belongs to me, what use is eighty-seven crores of wealth to me? What use is a workplace twelve yojanas wide, the tanks constructed with machinery, and the fourteen villages? I shall hand over all this wealth to Bhaddā Kāpilānī and go forth to become a monk."

At that moment, Bhaddā Kāpilānī was also sitting inside the house, surrounded by her nurses, having three jars of sesame seeds spread out. Seeing crows eating the sesame insects, she asked, "Mothers, what are these crows eating?" "Lady, they are eating insects," they replied. "To whom does this unwholesome deed belong?" she asked. "To you, lady," they answered. Then she thought, "I only need four cubits of cloth and a measure of rice for a meal. If the unwholesome deeds committed by so many people belong to me, I will not be able to lift my head from the round of rebirths even in a thousand lives. As soon as my husband returns, I shall hand over all this wealth to him and go forth to become a nun."

The young man returned, bathed, and ascended the palace to sit upon a magnificent throne. Then, a meal suitable for his glory, like that of a universal monarch, was prepared. After both of them had eaten and the attendants had left, they sat together in a secluded place. Then the young man asked Bhaddā, "Bhaddā, how much wealth did you bring when you came to this house?" "Sir, it was fifty-five thousand carts," she replied. "All that wealth, and the eighty-seven crores of wealth in this house, along with the sixty mechanized tanks and other properties—I hand all of it over to you alone," he said. "But where will you go, sir?" she asked. "I shall go forth as a monk," he replied. "Sir, I too have been sitting here waiting for your arrival. I too shall go forth," she said. To them, the three realms of existence appeared like a burning leaf-roofed hut. They had dye-stained robes and clay alms-bowls brought from the market, shaved each other's hair, and went forth, saying, "May our renunciation be dedicated to the Arahants in the world." Placing their alms-bowls in bags and slinging them over their shoulders, they descended from the palace. Not a single slave or worker in the house noticed them.
442:
Then, as they left the Brahmin village and passed through the gate of the slave village, the residents of the slave village recognized them by their appearance and gestures. They fell at their feet, weeping, and said, "Sirs, why do you leave us helpless?" "Friends, we have gone forth, reflecting that the three realms of existence are like a burning leaf-roofed hut. Even if we were to grant freedom to each of you from servitude, a hundred years of service would not suffice to repay the debt. You yourselves, wash your own heads, and live as free people." Having said this, they departed while the people were still weeping.

As the Elder was walking ahead, he turned back to look and thought, "This Bhaddā Kāpilānī is a woman worth the whole of Jambudīpa, and she is following behind me. It is possible that someone might think, 'Even though they have gone forth, they cannot live apart; they are doing what is unsuitable.' Someone might have a corrupt mind with evil thoughts and thus become one who fills the lower realms. It is proper that I should leave her and go on alone." Thus he formed this thought. As he walked ahead, he saw a fork in the road and stood at the junction. Bhaddā also arrived, paid homage, and stood there. Then he said to her, "Bhaddā, seeing a woman like you following behind me, people might think, 'Even though they have gone forth, they cannot live apart,' and by having corrupt minds toward us, the multitude might become those who fill the lower realms. At this fork in the road, you take one path, and I shall go by the other."

"Yes, sir, a woman is a source of concern and an obstacle for monks. They will point out our fault, saying, 'Even after going forth, they cannot live apart.' Sir, you take one path; we shall live separately." So saying, she circumambulated him three times, paid homage at the four directions with the five-point prostration, and raising her joined palms, which shone with the radiance of her ten fingernails, she said, "The friendship established over a duration of a hundred thousand aeons is broken today." She then added, "Sirs are of the right-hand nature; the right path is suitable for you. We women are of the left-hand nature; the left path is suitable for us." After paying homage, she entered her path. At the moment they parted ways, this great earth, as if saying, "Though I can bear the weight of the Cakkavāḷa and Mount Sineru, I cannot bear the weight of your virtues," trembled with a roar. A sound like thunder occurred in the sky, and the Cakkavāḷa and Mount Sineru resounded.

While the Fully Enlightened Buddha was staying in the Gandhakuṭī of the Veḷuvana Monastery, he heard the sound of the earthquake and reflected, "Why does the earth tremble?" He then realized, "The young man Pippali and Bhaddā Kāpilānī, dedicating themselves to me, have abandoned immeasurable wealth and gone forth."
443:
At the place of separation of those two, the earth shook due to the power of the virtue of both. Thinking, "It is proper for me to show favor to them," the Buddha emerged from the Gandhakuṭi, took his bowl and robes himself, and without consulting any of the eighty Great Elders, went out to meet them on a journey of three gāvutas. He sat cross-legged at the foot of the Bahuputtaka Banyan tree between Rājagaha and Nālandā.

When he sat, he did not sit like an ordinary monk wearing rag-robes, but assuming the form of a Buddha, he sat emitting dense Buddha-rays eighty cubits in length. At that moment, the Buddha-rays, in sizes such as palm leaves, umbrellas, chariot wheels, and palace pinnacles, spread and raced here and there, making that forest have a single radiance as if a thousand moons and a thousand suns had risen. The forest was as beautiful as the sky shining with the glory of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, like a cluster of stars, or like a body of water with well-bloomed white and red lotuses. The trunk of the banyan tree is normally white, the leaves green, and the fruits red. However, on that day, that hundred-branched banyan tree became entirely golden in color.

The Elder Mahā Kassapa thought, "This person will be my teacher; I have gone forth dedicated to him." From the moment he saw him, he approached with a bowed body, paid homage in three places, and said, "Venerable Sir, the Blessed One is my teacher, I am the disciple. Venerable Sir, the Blessed One is my teacher, I am the disciple." Then the Blessed One said to him, "Kassapa, if you were to show such respect to the great earth, even that earth would not be able to bear it. For one who knows the greatness of the Tathāgata's virtues as you do, the respect you have shown is not even able to move a single hair of mine. Sit, Kassapa, I will give you your inheritance."

Then the Blessed One granted him ordination by means of three exhortations. Having granted it, he departed from the foot of the Bahuputtaka Banyan tree and proceeded on the journey with the Elder as his attendant monk. The Blessed One's body was adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man. Mahā Kassapa's body was adorned with seven marks of a Great Man. He followed in the footsteps of the Blessed One like a small boat tied behind a great golden ship. After traveling a short distance, the Blessed One stepped off the path and indicated his desire to sit at the foot of a certain tree. The Elder, knowing that "The Blessed One wishes to sit," folded his own worn-out double-layered robe (saṅghāṭi) into four layers and spread it out.
444:
The Blessed One sat there, stroking the robe with his hand, and said, "Kassapa, this double-layered robe made of old cloth is very soft." The Elder, realizing, "The Blessed One speaks of the softness of my robe; he must wish to wear it," said, "Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One wear this double-layered robe." "Kassapa, what will you wear?" he asked. "Venerable Sir, if I receive your double-layered robe, I shall wear it," he replied. "Kassapa, will you be able to wear this rag-robe (paṃsukūla) which is worn out from use? On the day I took this rag-robe, the earth shook to the very edge of the waters. This robe used and worn by the Buddhas cannot be worn by one of little virtue. It is only proper to be worn by one who is a natural rag-robe wearer (jāti-paṃsukūlika) and capable of fulfilling the practice (paṭipatti)," he said, and then exchanged robes with the Elder.

Having thus exchanged robes, the Blessed One wore the robe previously worn by the Elder, and the Elder wore the robe of the Blessed One. At that time, even this inanimate great earth shook to the edge of the waters, as if saying, "Venerable Sir, you have done a difficult thing; there has never been a time when a robe worn by oneself was given to a disciple. I am unable to bear the weight of your virtues." The Elder, without becoming conceited, thinking, "Now I have received the robe used by the Buddhas; what further great task remains for me?" undertook the thirteen ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) in the presence of the Buddha. He remained a worldling for seven days, and on the eighth day, he attained Arahantship together with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). For that reason, it is said in the Apadāna:

To the Blessed One Padumuttara, the Chief of the World, the Such-like One,
When that Lord of the World had attained Nibbāna, the people performed offerings to the Teacher.

The multitude of people, with uplifted minds, were exceedingly joyful and delighted,
When a sense of urgency (saṃvega) arose in them, joy also arose in me.

Having gathered my relatives and friends, I spoke these words:
"The Great Hero has attained Parinibbāna; come, let us perform an offering."

They consented, saying "Sādhu," and caused great joy to arise in me,
"We shall perform an accumulation of merit for the Buddha, the Lord of the World," they consulted.

Having well-constructed a sacrificial structure, a hundred cubits in height,
And one and a half cubits in width, they made a jewel-shrine like a celestial mansion rising into the sky.
445:
In that (jeweled stupa house), having made a gabled building adorned with palm-leaf patterns, and having gladdened my mind, I worshipped the supreme stupa.

Like a blazing mass of fire, like a Kimsuka tree in full bloom, like the banner of Sakka in the sky, it illuminated the four directions.

Having gladdened my mind there and performed much merit, remembering my past deeds, I was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, riding a divine chariot drawn by a thousand horses.

My mansion was lofty, seven stories high, rising upwards.

There were a thousand chambers made entirely of gold. They shone by their own power, illuminating all directions.

There were also other pinnacles made of rubies. They too shone with radiance, illuminating the four directions around.

Well-fashioned chambers made of gems, born of meritorious deeds, illuminated the ten directions all around.

The radiance of those shining chambers was vast. I surpassed all the gods; this is the fruit of meritorious deeds.

Sixty thousand aeons ago, I was a kshatriya named Ubbidha, a conqueror of the four oceans, who ruled the earth.

Likewise, in this Bhadda aeon, I was a powerful Universal Monarch thirty times, devoted to my own work.

Possessing the seven jewels, I was the lord of the four islands. In that state of a Universal Monarch, my mansion rose up like a streak of lightning.

There was a city named Ramaṇa, twenty-four yojanas in length and twelve yojanas in width, with firm walls and gate-towers.

It was five hundred [yojanas] in length and half of that (two hundred and fifty) in width, crowded with people like the city of the Tāvatiṃsa gods.
446:
Just as twenty-five needles placed in a needle case strike against each other, being crowded and adorned,

Even so was my city, crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots, a noble and pleasant city always teeming with people.

Having enjoyed food and drink there, I again went to the deva realm. In my final birth, I was born into a perfect family.

Born in a Brahmin family, a storehouse of many jewels, I renounced eighty crores of gold and went forth.

The four analytical knowledges... (pe)... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.

Then the Teacher praised the Venerable Mahākassapa with these words: "Monks, Kassapa approaches families like the moon; drawing back his body and drawing back his mind, he is always like a newcomer, not bold among families." Later, seated in the midst of the assembly of Noble Ones, he placed him in the foremost position among those who observe the ascetic practices (dhutanga): "Monks, among my monk disciples who are speakers of dhutanga, this Mahākassapa is the foremost." He, giving advice to the monks by way of praising delight in solitude and wishing to manifest his own practice, said:

"One should not wander surrounded by a group; the mind becomes distracted and concentration is hard to attain. Seeing that the company of various people is painful, one should not desire a group.

"A sage should not frequent families; the mind becomes distracted and concentration is hard to attain. He who is eager and greedy for flavors gives up the benefit that brings happiness.

"The wise call the bowing and worshipping in families 'mire'; it is a subtle and hard-to-extract thorn. Honor is difficult for a base man to give up."
447:
Descending from the monastery, I entered the city for alms. I respectfully approached (stood for alms before) a leper who was eating.

With his hand rotting from leprosy, he offered me a morsel of food. While he was offering the morsel, his finger broke off and fell into the food.

I ate that morsel together with the source of the leprosy (the fallen finger). While eating or after eating, I felt no disgust.

Food obtained by standing at the doors of others' houses is my nourishment. Medicine mixed with fermented cow's urine is my medicine. The foot of a tree is my dwelling. Rag-robes are my clothing. If a monk can use these four requisites (regardless of quality), he is indeed a man who can live freely in the four directions without obstruction.

While some people are weary and distressed when climbing a mountain, I, Kassapa, the heir of the Buddha, wise and mindful, climb supported by the power of psychic potency.

Returning from the alms round, Kassapa climbs the mountain and, free from clinging, having abandoned all fear and dread, meditates (in the jhāna of Arahatship).

Returning from the alms round, Kassapa climbs the mountain and, free from clinging, is cooled amidst beings who are burning (with defilements), and meditates.

Returning from the alms round, Kassapa climbs the mountain and, free from clinging, having finished what was to be done and being free from taints, meditates.

The delightful grounds spread with Kareri flower garlands, echoing with the cries of elephants—those pleasant mountains delight me.

With the color of dark clouds, beautiful, with cool waters and pure grounds, covered with Indagopaka insects—those mountains delight me.

Resembling the peaks of dark clouds, like noble gabled houses, echoing with the cries of elephants—those pleasant mountains delight me.

With delightful surfaces after a fresh rain, frequented by seers and monks, echoing with the cries of peacocks—those mountains delight me.
448:
For me, who desires jhāna and whose mind is directed towards Nibbāna, these mountains are suitable for practicing the Dhamma. For me, a monk who seeks his own benefit and whose mind is directed towards Nibbāna, these mountains are suitable for practicing the Dhamma.

For me, a monk who desires well-being and whose mind is directed towards Nibbāna, these mountains are suitable for practicing the Dhamma. For me, who desires the practice of meditation, whose mind is directed towards Nibbāna, and who is unshaken by the worldly conditions, these mountains are suitable for practicing the Dhamma.

Those mountains, which are like the blue color of the umā flower, covered with dark clouds, and filled with various flocks of birds, delight me.

Those mountains, which are not crowded with householders, frequented by herds of wild animals, and filled with various flocks of birds, delight me.

Those mountains, which have clear waters, large stone slabs, are inhabited by herds of langurs, and covered with water-moss, delight me.

Such delight as is experienced by one with a concentrated mind who rightly practices insight into the Dhamma is not matched by music from a five-piece orchestral ensemble.

One should not engage in too many activities; one should avoid socializing with crowds and should not strive [in useless matters]. He who strives out of greed for tastes neglects the goal that brings happiness (the Path and Fruit).

One should not engage in too many activities; one should avoid socializing with crowds; this does not bring one's own benefit. [If one does so], the body becomes weary and exhausted; being thus distressed, one does not find tranquility (samatha).

By merely moving the lips, without seeing even one's own benefit or lack thereof, one walks with a stiff neck and thinks, "I alone am superior."

A fool, though not superior, considers himself equal to the superior. The wise do not praise such a person with a stiff and conceited mind.

Whether thinking "I am superior," "I am not superior," "I am inferior," or "I am equal," one should not be shaken by such various forms of conceit.
449:
The wise praise that person who is wise, steadfast in the face of worldly conditions, well-established in virtue, and constantly devoted to the tranquility of mind and the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship.

If a person lacks respect for their fellow practitioners (sabrahmacārī), they are as far from the true Dhamma as the earth is from the sky.

For those in whom shame (hiri) and fear of wrongdoing (ottappa) are always well-established, they flourish in the holy life; for them, rebirth in a new existence is exhausted.

A monk who is restless and frivolous, even if clad in refuse-rag robes (pāṃsukūla), does not shine with those robes, like a monkey covered in a lion's skin.

One who is not restless, not frivolous, who is prudent and has restrained faculties, shines with refuse-rag robes like a lion in a mountain cave.

These many powerful and famous devas and Brahmas, numbering ten thousand, are all of the Brahma-kāyika realm.

They stand with palms joined in reverence, bowing to the General of the Dhamma (Dhammasenāpati), the heroic Sāriputta, the great meditator who is well-concentrated.

"Homage to you, O noble man! Homage to you, O supreme man! We do not know the object of support based on which you are meditating."

How wonderful is the sphere of the Buddhas; it is indeed very deep. Even we, who are like archers capable of piercing a hair, cannot know that object of meditation.

Seeing the Venerable Sāriputta thus honored by the hosts of devas and Brahmas, and being worthy of such honor, the Venerable Mahākappina smiled.

Except for the Great Sage (the Buddha), in this entire Buddha-field (buddhakhetta), I am the most distinguished in the dhutaṅga virtues; there is no one equal to me.

I have served the Teacher (the Buddha); I have followed the Buddha's teaching. The heavy burden of the aggregates has been laid down; now there is no more rebirth in a new existence.
450:
He is not stained by robes, nor by beds, nor by food. The immeasurable Gotama is like a pure lotus flower unstained by water; he is inclined toward renunciation and has escaped from the three worlds of existence.

That Great Sage has the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) as his neck, faith (saddhā) as his hands, wisdom (paññā) as his head; he possesses great knowledge and always dwells in peace.

He spoke these verses. Among them, the first three verses were spoken by way of giving advice to monks upon seeing them socializing with groups and families.

In those verses, "one should not wander surrounded by groups" means one should not live or dwell surrounded and accompanied by a group of monks. Why? Because for one who manages a group, the mind becomes distressed due to the occurrence of suffering and becomes agitated; even when providing help through instruction, advice, and repeated guidance, the mind becomes disturbed because the monks do not practice as instructed. Therefore, for one who does not attain one-pointedness of mind due to such association, concentration (samādhi) is difficult to obtain. For such a person, even access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) is not achieved, let alone the other types. "Socializing with various people" (nānājana-saṅgaha) means supporting a crowd of people with various intentions and tastes through pleasant speech, food, and snacks. This is very difficult and troublesome. Seeing many such disadvantages in managing a group with the eye of wisdom, one should not delight in living with a group.

"A sage should not approach families" means one who has gone forth in this Dispensation should not go about as an intimate of families such as those of kings. Why? Because the mind becomes disturbed and concentration is difficult to obtain. That person, through the effort of approaching families and being greedy for the sweet tastes obtained from them, involves himself in their affairs and thus neglects his own benefit—the purification of virtue (sīla-visuddhi) and so on—which brings the happiness of the Path, Fruit, and Nibbāna; it means he does not strive for it.

The third verse has the same meaning as stated below.
