The four verses beginning with "Descending from the lodging" were spoken to give advice to monks by showing his own contentment with the four requisites, implying "A monk should practice in this way." In those verses, "Descending from the lodging" means...
451:
It is said thus because of dwelling in a monastery located on a mountain. Desiring to lead that man afflicted with leprosy to great attainment, and being in need of alms, he approached and stood respectfully like a person of great desire approaching a family that gives excellent alms.

"Pakkena" means with leprosy that is ripe and putrid due to the disease having reached the bone. "Aṅguli cettha chijjatha" means that in this bowl, his finger broke off and fell along with the food.

"Kuṭṭamūlaṃ nissāya" means that to inspire faith in that man, he sat near such a wall of the house and consumed that morsel of food. It should be understood that this practice of the Elder was not a prescribed rule in the training precepts. Because he had reached the excellence of the Noble Power (Ariya Iddhi) of perceiving the repulsive as non-repulsive, no disgust arose in the Elder as he swallowed that food. If ordinary worldlings (puthujjanas) were to eat such food, their very intestines might come out. Therefore, he said: "Whether while eating or after eating, no disgust exists in me."

"Uttiṭṭhapiṇḍa" means alms-food to be received by standing at the doors of others' houses; it means mixed alms-food obtained by going from house to house relying on the strength of one's legs. "Pūtimutta" refers to yellow myrobalan (harīṭaka) and so forth, infused with cow's urine. "Yassete abhisambhutvā" means whichever monk enjoys these four requisites, such as alms-food gathered by standing at house doors, being content even with the lowest. "Sa ve cātuddiso naro" means that person is certainly fit for the four directions; he is one who can dwell in any direction without obstruction anywhere.

Then, in the Elder's old age, when people asked, "Venerable Sir, while you are in such old age, why do you climb the mountain every day?", he spoke the four verses beginning with "Yattha eke". In those verses, "yattha" means in that final stage of life. "Eke" means some people. "Vihaññanti" means they reach mental distress due to physical exhaustion. "Siluccayaṃ" means the mountain. "Tattha" means even in that time of old age. By the words "sampajāno paṭissato" (clearly comprehending and mindful), he shows the absence of mental weariness. By the words "iddhibalenupatthaddho" (supported by the power of psychic potency), he shows the absence of physical weariness.

Because he has completely cut off the defilements which are the cause of fear, he has abandoned fear and dread.

"Ḍayhamānesu" means while beings are being burned by the eleven fires such as the fire of lust, he is quenched and cooled because of the absence of the fever of defilements.
452:
(Even in that old age,) by the words "sampajāno paṭissato", he shows the absence of mental weariness. By the words "iddhibalenupatthaddho", he shows the absence of physical weariness. Because he has completely cut off the defilements which are the cause of fear, he has abandoned fear and dread. "Ḍayhamānesu" means while beings are being burned by the eleven fires such as the fire of lust, he remains quenched because of the absence of the fever of defilements.

Again, when people asked, "Venerable Sir, why do you dwell only in the forest and mountains even in your old age? Are not these monasteries like Veḷuvana delightful?", he spoke twelve verses beginning with "Karerimālāvitatā" to show that "Only the forest and mountains are delightful to me." In those verses, "Karerimālāvitatā" means surrounded by rows of Varuṇa trees, or it is said, covered with dark-colored flowers. "Kuñjarābhirudā" refers to mountains that resound greatly with the trumpeting of elephants seeking food, which have qualities like echoes.

"Abhivuṭṭhā" means heavily rained upon by great storm clouds. "Rammatalā" means having delightful ground because the dust, dirt, and old leaves have been cleared away by that very rain. "Nagā" are mountains so called because they do not move to another place, and they are called "selā" because they are made of stone. "Abbhunnaditā sikhīhi" means echoing with the sweet sounds of peacocks.

"Alaṃ" means suitable or capable. In phrases like "jhāyitukāmassa" (for one desiring jhāna) and "atthakāmassa" (for one desiring the goal), it should be applied in this same way. "Bhikkhuno" means for the monk who has destroyed defilements; it should be connected with the word "me" (for me).

"Umāpupphena samānā" means like the flax flower (umā) because of having a dark blue color. "Gaganāvabbhachāditā" means, because of that same dark color, covered with dark clouds like the clouds in the sky during the month of Tazaungmon (autumn), meaning they are blue-colored.

"Anākiṇṇā" means uncrowded and not cramped. The delight that arises for one surrounded by music from instruments with five factors such as "ātata" is not like the delight of one with a one-pointed and concentrated mind who rightly contemplates mental and physical phenomena through the lens of impermanence and so forth. Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"Whenever one contemplates the rise and fall of the aggregates,
One attains joy and gladness; that is the Deathless for those who know it."

The two verses beginning with "Kammaṃ bahukaṃ" were spoken as advice to monks who delight in work and are greedy for requisites. There, "Kammaṃ bahukaṃ na kāraye" means, being one who delights in work, one should not perform or undertake much work. However, the repair of broken or dilapidated parts (navakamma) is indeed permitted by the Teacher. "Parivajjeya janaṃ" means one should avoid a group of people who are bad friends. "Na uyyame" means one should not strive for the production of requisites or the formation of groups. "Na uyyametaṃ" means that undertaking this new work and so forth does not lead to one's own disadvantage. In giving the reason for that statement, "kathaṃ hi kāyo kilamati" means the body becomes weary due to the lack of physical and mental ease for that person who is striving in new work and so forth.
453:
“Anattaneyyametaṃ” means that undertaking this new construction (navakamma) and so forth does not bring about one's own welfare. In that statement, the reason is given: “The body is weary, it is exhausted.” For a person engaged in new construction and the like, wandering here and there, they reach weariness and exhaustion because they do not obtain bodily comfort and so on; they experience fatigue. Because of that bodily exhaustion, they suffer. Due to the absence of purity of the object and the lack of bringing about one's own welfare, that person does not find tranquility (samatha) and does not obtain concentration of mind.

The two verses beginning with “Oṭṭhappahatamattena” were spoken by way of censuring a person who considers themselves wise, thinking they have supreme learning. The two verses following those were spoken by way of praising a wise person. In those verses, “Oṭṭhappahatamattena” means merely by the movement of the lips, with recitation as the primary focus; the meaning is merely by the act of reciting the Buddha's words. “Attānampi na passati” means that because of not knowing the benefit, one does not even know the benefit that is present before oneself; the meaning is that one cannot truly determine one's own measure. “Patthaddhagīvo carati” means that one wanders with a stiff neck, being hardened by pride, thinking, “I am very learned, I am mindful, I am wise, there is no other like me,” and showing no respect even to those worthy of honor, like one who has swallowed an iron rod. “Ahaṃ seyyo” (I am better) means the thought that “I alone am the most excellent, the best.”

“Asseyyo seyyasamānaṃဗာလော မညတိ အတ္တာနံ” means that this person, though inferior (not excellent), makes themselves out to be equal to another who is superior (excellent), and the fool (one of dull intellect) thinks so only because of their foolishness. “Na taṃ viñူ ပသံသန္တိ” means that the wise (discerning ones) do not praise such a fool, a man with a stiff mind and a hardened body due to an uplifted mind; on the contrary, they only censure him.

“Seyyohamasmi” means that a certain wise person does not give rise to any pride, such as “I am superior,” or by way of the pride of being inferior or equal, “I am not superior,” and does not waver by way of any of the nine types of pride.

“Paññavantaṃ” means one who is wise by the power of the wisdom of the highest fruit (Arahatship), who is “Tādi” (equanimous) because of reaching such a state in the face of desirable objects and so on, who is well-concentrated in virtue because of being well-established in the virtues of the fruit of one beyond training (asekha), and who is devoted to the tranquility of mind by attaining the meditative attainment of the fruit of Arahatship—such a person...
454:
...the wise, such as the Buddhas, praise and extol the Arahant who has entirely abandoned pride. Again, seeing a monk who was difficult to admonish, the Buddha spoke the two verses beginning with “Yassa sabrahmacārīsu,” revealing the danger of being difficult to admonish and the benefit of being easy to admonish. Those verses have already been explained in detail.

Again, seeing an agitated and arrogant monk, the Buddha spoke the two verses beginning with “Uddhato capalo bhikkhu,” explaining the fault in being agitated and the virtue in being unagitated. In those verses, “Kapīva sīhacammena” means like a monkey covered in a lion's skin. That monk, possessed of faults such as agitation, does not look beautiful with that rag-robe (paṃsukūla), the banner of the Noble Ones, because of the absence of noble virtues. To show one who is beautiful, the words beginning with “Anuddhato” were spoken.

The five verses beginning with “Sambahulā” were spoken on account of the smiling of Venerable Mahākappina, upon seeing many Brahmakāyika devas worshipping Venerable Sāriputta. In those verses, “Ete” is said because those devas were present before his eyes. “Sambahulā” is because of their great number; he stated that great number by defining it as “ten thousand devas.” “Devā” refers to devas by rebirth (upapatti-deva). To show their celestial nature as distinct from others, he said, “All of them are Brahmakāyika devas.” Because those Brahmas are endowed with great celestial power through their own rebirth-power and are endowed with a large following, he said, “Possessed of psychic power and fame.”

In response to the question “Who is your general, sir?”, the Blessed One, saying, “Sāriputta follows and keeps turning the incomparable Wheel of Dhamma set in motion by me,” authorized Venerable Sāriputta's status as the General of the Dhamma. Thus he said: “Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, the hero, the great meditator, the concentrated one.” In that passage, “Vīra” (hero) means one who is energetic and of great prowess by crushing the Maras of defilements and so on. “Mahājhāyီ” (great meditator) means a great meditator by reaching the peak of the divine abidings (dibba-vihāra) and so on. For that very reason, he is “Samāhita” (concentrated) by way of destroying all distraction. “Namassantā” means they stand worshipping with hands raised in homage to their heads.
455:
"Yampi nissāya" means "relying on what object does he dwell in meditation?" The Brahmas, being worldlings, spoke thus because they did not know.

"Accheraṃ vata" means "wonderful indeed." "Buddhānaṃ" means "of the Buddhas" (the range of those) who have known the Four Noble Truths. "Gambhīro gocaro sako" means "their own range is very deep, very difficult to see, very difficult to understand, not shared with worldlings, and not within the scope of worldlings." Now, to show the reason for the depth of that Dhamma, the words beginning with "Ye mayaṃ" were spoken. Therein, "vālavedhisamāgatā" means "we who are like archers capable of hitting a hair-tip, though able to penetrate even a very subtle object, even when we have come and investigated, we do not know; deep indeed is the range of the Buddhas." This is the meaning. Seeing the Venerable Sāriputta, who is of such nature and worthy of worship by the world including the devas, being worshiped by those Brahma hosts in that manner at that time, the Venerable Mahā Kappina smiled. (He smiled thinking,) "Even for these Brahmas, who are esteemed by the world, this is not their range, yet it is the range of the disciples."

The verse "Yāvatā buddhakkhettamhi" was spoken by the Elder as a lion's roar concerning himself. Therein, "buddhakkhettamhi" is said with reference to the field of authority (āṇā-khetta). "Ṭhapayitvā mahāmuniṃ" means "except for the Great Sage" (meaning he is superior to all other remaining beings). For the Blessed Buddhas are endowed with the six glories and have reached the highest excellence over all beings even through their ascetic qualities (dhuta-guṇa). However, with minds urged by great compassion, they look upon such great benefit for beings and follow practices such as living in village-boundary dwellings; such following may be contrary to those various ascetic practices. "Dhutaguṇe" means in the desired qualities such as forest-dwelling, through the quality of shaking off defilements. Or, this is a word in the locative case with the sense of the instrumental. The meaning is: "There is no one equal to me, so how could there be anyone superior to me?" For that reason, that Venerable Mahā Kassapa was placed in the foremost position among those who uphold the ascetic practices.

By the verse "Na cīvare," the meaning already stated as "ṭhapayitvā mahāmuniṃ" is made clearer. Non-clinging by craving to robes and so forth is the fruit of the ascetic practices. Therein, the construction is: "even when robes are obtained, he is not smeared by the smear of craving." "Sayane" means in a bed or seat. "Gotamo" is praising the Blessed One by his clan name. "Anappameyyo" means immeasurable because of the absence of defilements that create limits, and because of being endowed with immeasurable qualities. "Muḷālapupphaṃ vimalaṃva ambunā" means just as water does not smear a pure, stainless lotus (likewise, craving does not smear the Buddha).
456:
In this way, the Blessed Gotama is not smeared by the smear of craving and so forth. This is the meaning. "Nekkhamma-ninno" means inclined towards renunciation, specifically inclined towards going forth. Because of being so inclined, he has emerged from the three realms of existence (tibhava); he has come out from the three realms and is dissociated from defilements.

To show the constituent parts of those for whom, due to the fulfillment of the development of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) and so forth, there is no smearing in any place and they are inclined only towards renunciation, he spoke the concluding verse beginning with "Satipaṭṭhānagīvo." Therein, because it is the basis for wisdom, which is the supreme limb among the mass of qualities, mindfulness is the neck of this [Buddha]; thus he is "satipaṭṭhānagīvo" (one who has the foundations of mindfulness as a neck). Faith is the hand in taking up blameless dhammas; thus he is "saddhāhattho" (one who has faith as a hand). Because it is the supreme limb of the body of qualities, wisdom is the head; thus he is "paññāsīso" (one who has wisdom as a head). Because of having a great range of activity, a great object, great majesty, and great power, he possesses the great knowledge known as omniscience; thus he is "mahāñāṇီ" (one who has great knowledge). He always, at all times, dwells cooled, with defilements extinguished. The sutta passage "Susamāhito... pe... nāgo" (AN 6.43) should also be cited here. What has not been explained here in detail regarding the meaning should be understood according to the method mentioned below.

## The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Mahā Kassapa is Finished.
## The Commentary on the Section of Forty is Finished.
457:
## 19. Paññāsanipāta
## 1. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Tālapuṭa

In the Paññāsanipāta, the verses beginning with "Kadā nu hanti" are those of the Venerable Tālapuṭa Thera. The account of how they arose is as follows: This Elder had also performed meritorious services (adhikāra) under previous Buddhas and had accumulated wholesome deeds that served as a strong sufficing condition (upanissaya) for liberation from the cycle of rebirth in various existences. In this Buddha-era, he was born into a family of performers in the city of Rājagaha. Upon reaching maturity, he attained complete mastery in the art of dance and performance according to his family tradition, becoming a renowned stage manager (Naṭagāmaṇi) famous throughout the entire island of Jambudīpa.

Accompanied by five hundred women and possessing great wealth as a performer, he staged festivals in villages, market towns, and royal capitals, receiving great honor and offerings. While traveling, he arrived at Rājagaha, where he staged a festival for the city dwellers and received great respect and honor. As his wisdom matured, he went to the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat at a respectful distance. He then addressed the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, I have heard this from the traditional teachers of performers in the past: 'That performer who, in the midst of a theater or a festival, makes people laugh and delights them with a mixture of truth and falsehood, will, after the breakup of the body, after death, be reborn in the company of the Pahāsa (Laughter) devas.' What does the Blessed One say regarding this?"

Then the Blessed One forbade him three times, saying, "Do not ask me this question." When asked for the fourth time, the Blessed One said: "Gāmaṇi, these beings are already bound by the fetters of lust, hatred, and delusion. A performer who presents things that further incite lust, hatred, and delusion, causing people to be heedless, will, after the breakup of the body, after death, be reborn in hell. However, if he holds such a view as: 'That performer who makes people laugh and delights them in the midst of a theater or festival will, after death, be reborn in the company of the Pahāsa devas,' then that is a wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi). For one who holds a wrong view, I say there are only two destinations: hell or the animal realm."

Hearing this, Tālapuṭa Gāmaṇi wept. The Blessed One said, "Gāmaṇi, did I not forbid you earlier, saying, 'Do not ask me this question'?" He replied, "Venerable Sir, I am not weeping because of what the Blessed One has said. Rather, I weep because I have been deceived and misled for a long time by former traditional teachers of performers who said, 'A performer who shows festivals to the public will be reborn in a happy destination.'" Having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, Tālapuṭa gained faith, went forth into homelessness, and received full ordination. While practicing insight meditation (vipassanā), he soon attained Arahantship. Reflecting on how wise reflection (yoniso manasikāra) arose in him through the restraint of his own mind, he expressed it in detail, beginning with: "When shall I dwell alone and companionless (without craving as a companion) in mountain caves, seeing all existences as impermanent?"
458:
The Elder soon attained Arahantship. Before attaining Arahantship, wise reflection (yoniso manasikāra) arose in him by way of restraining his own mind. To show that manner of reflection in detail, he spoke thus:

When indeed shall I dwell alone, without a companion, in mountain caves? When shall this thought of mine—contemplating all existences as impermanent—come to be?

When indeed shall I be a sage, wearing robes made of sewn-together rags, clad in saffron-dyed cloth, without possessiveness and without longing, having destroyed lust, hatred, and delusion, and dwell happily having entered the forest?

When indeed shall I dwell alone in the forest, free from fear, contemplating this body—the nest of diseases and slaughter, oppressed by death and old age—as impermanent? When shall that thought of mine come to be?

When indeed shall I dwell having cut with the sharp sword of wisdom the vine of craving, which produces fear, brings suffering, and follows after many kinds of objects? When shall that also come to be?

When indeed shall I quickly take up the weapon of wisdom, which is of great power and is the tool of the sages (isī), and quickly defeat Māra together with his army, while remaining in the lion's seat (firm posture)? When shall that thought of mine come to be?

When indeed shall I be seen in the assemblies of the virtuous, by those who are such (tādi), who honor the Dhamma, who see things as they really are, and who have conquered their senses? When shall I, who am striving in meditation, be seen by the virtuous? When shall that thought of mine come to be?
459:
When indeed shall laziness, hunger, thirst, wind, heat, or insects and reptiles not trouble me? When shall such affliction not occur at the foot of Giribbaja? When shall that thought, desiring the goal, come to be?

When indeed shall I, with a concentrated mind and being mindful, penetrate with wisdom those Four Noble Truths so difficult to see, which were realized by the Great Sage (the Buddha)? When shall that thought of penetrating the Four Noble Truths come to be?

When indeed shall I, endowed with the concentration of tranquility and insight, see with the wisdom of the path the immeasurable forms, sounds, smells, tastes, touches, and mental objects as burning? When shall that be mine?

When indeed, when addressed with harsh and abusive speech, shall I not be of a troubled mind because of that? And when praised, shall I not be delighted because of that? When shall that be mine?

When indeed shall I equally weigh these internal and external phenomena—the aggregates, as well as wood, grass, and vines—by way of impermanence and so forth? When shall that be mine?

When indeed shall the great rain cloud of the rainy season rain upon and soak me, together with my robes, as I walk in the forest on the path trodden by the sages? When shall that thought come to be?

When indeed, hearing the cry of the crested peacock in the forest within the mountain caves, shall I rise from my seat and reflect for the sake of attaining the Deathless (Nibbāna)? When shall that thought come to be?
460: When shall I, by psychic power, cross over the Ganges, the Yamuna, the Saraswati, and the ocean whirlpool (the mare's mouth) cast into the abyss, without clinging? When will that fearsome crossing take place? When shall I, like a noble elephant wandering free from attachment, break the desire for the strands of sensual pleasure? When will that state of being joined in Jhana, having abandoned every beautiful sign, take place? When shall I, like a poor man oppressed by debt who has found a treasure, be delighted upon attaining the Dispensation of the Great Sage? When will that thought come to pass? O Mind, for many years I was entreated by you to live in the household life. Is this not enough for you? Now that I am ordained, for what reason, O Mind, do you not apply yourself to tranquility and insight (samatha-vipassanā)? O Mind, was I not entreated by you, saying: "In the mountain-encircled forest, the peacocks with variegated wings, screaming like the sound of thunder, will delight you as you meditate in the woods"? Having abandoned family, friends, dear kinsmen, the delight of play, and the strands of sensual pleasure in the world, I have come to this Dispensation. Even so, O Mind, you are not satisfied with me. This is my own fault; you do not belong to others. What is the use of lamenting at the time of putting on the armor to fight the enemy of defilements? Seeing all these conditioned things as unstable, I have gone forth seeking the state of the Deathless (Nibbāna).
461: The Buddha, the speaker of what is well-applied, the best of bipeds, the great physician, the charioteer of men to be tamed, has said: "The mind is wavering, like a monkey, very difficult to restrain for one who is not free from lust." For sensual pleasures are variegated, sweet, and delightful; therein the ignorant worldlings (puthujjana) are attached. Seeking renewed existence, led by the mind, they are cast away in hell and experience only suffering. O Mind, you previously urged me: "Dwell in the forest filled with the cries of peacocks and cranes, surrounded by leopards and tigers, developing loving-kindness; abandon concern for the body; do not fail this moment." You previously urged me: "Develop the Jhanas, the faculties (indriya), the powers (bala), the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), and the development of concentration; touch the three knowledges (vijjā) in the Buddha's Dispensation." You previously urged me: "Develop the path for the attainment of the Deathless, which leads out of suffering, which plunges into the end of all suffering, the Eightfold Path that purifies all defilements." You previously urged me: "Look upon the aggregates as suffering with wise attention; abandon craving, the cause of suffering; make an end of suffering in this very life." Did you not previously urge me, O Mind: "Look with wise attention upon things as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, and as a mass of danger and a murderer; restrain the mental wanderings of the consciousness"?
462:
O Mind, in the past you urged me, saying: "Shaven-headed, ill-favored, like one who has come under a curse, wandering for alms among families with a bowl in hand, strive in the teaching of the Great Sage, the Buddha."

O Mind, in the past you urged me, saying: "When walking along the road, well-restrained in senses, with a mind unattached to families or to sensual pleasures, practice like the stainless moon on a full moon night."

O Mind, in the past you urged me, saying: "Be a forest-dweller, an alms-food eater, a charnel-ground dweller, a rag-robe wearer, and one who always practices the sitting-up posture (nesajjika); delight at all times in the dhuta practices."

Just as a person desiring fruit, after planting trees, wishes to cut the tree down at the root when it begins to bear fruit; O Mind, you act like such a planter by urging me toward this unstable and impermanent cycle of rebirth (saṃsāra).

O formless Mind, far-wandering and solitary-faring, I will no longer follow your word now. Sensual pleasures are of the nature of suffering, they have bitter results, and are very dangerous. I will practice with a mind directed only toward Nibbāna.

I did not go forth into the forest because of misfortune, or lack of shame, or because of the mind's whim, or out of fear, or for the sake of a livelihood. O Mind, I have already made a promise to you.

O Mind, at that time you urged me, saying: "The virtuous praise fewness of desires; the abandoning of ingratitude leads to the cessation of suffering (Nibbāna)." But now, you are going back to your old ways of the past.
463:
Craving, ignorance, the liked and the disliked, beautiful forms, pleasant feelings, and delightful sensual pleasures have been vomited out by me. I am no longer able to swallow back those things that have been vomited.

O Mind, I have followed your word in many births. You have made me angry. Out of gratitude for what was caused by you, I have wandered for a long time in the suffering created by you.

O Mind, you alone make us sometimes Brahmins, sometimes Kings, and sometimes servants of kings. Because of your leading, we sometimes become traders, poor people, or deities.

Because of you alone, we become Asuras. With you as the root, we become denizens of hell. Furthermore, because of your leading, we sometimes become animals or hungry ghosts (petas).

Will you not wrong me again and again? Showing yourself repeatedly like a dancer, you entice me like a madman. O Mind, what if I were to fail and not fulfill your desire?

Formerly, this mind wandered as it liked, where it wanted, and as it pleased. Now I will thoroughly restrain it with wise reflection, like a mahout with a hook restrains an elephant in rut.

My Teacher, the Buddha, has established this world as impermanent, unstable, and coreless. O Mind, leap into the teaching of the Victor (Jina). Cross me over the four floods (oghas) that are great and very difficult to cross.
464:
O Mind, this nature of yours is not as it was before; I am no longer able to follow your will. I have gone forth in the teaching of the Great Sage. Those like me, who bear the quality of destroying defilements, do not come to ruin.

Mountains, oceans, rivers, the earth, the four directions, the intermediate directions, the lower realm, and the three worlds including the upper heavens—all are impermanent and oppressed by defilements. O Mind, where will you go to delight in happiness?

O Mind, what can you do to me who is established in supreme steadfastness? It is no longer proper for me to follow your will. Just as one should never touch a double-mouthed bag, woe to this body, full of filth flowing from nine openings.

In the mountain clefts frequented by boars and deer, naturally beautiful, and in the forest sprinkled with the new waters of the early rains, I will delight, having entered a cave-dwelling in that forest.

The birds with beautiful blue necks, fine crests, beautiful wings, and colorful plumage, calling out with sweet voices—they will delight you as you meditate in the forest.

When it rains and the grass is four fingers long, and the whole forest is blooming and dark like a cloud, I will sleep under a tree in the mountain valley. That sleep will be soft to me like cotton wool.

I will act like a master. Let me be content with whatever is obtained. I will no longer let you do as you wish, like a tireless person working a well-tanned cat-skin bag.
465:
I will act like a master; let whatever requisites I obtain be sufficient for me. Like a skilled elephant trainer subduing a rutting elephant with a hook, I will bring you under my control with energy.

With you well-tamed and steady, like a horse, just as a horse trainer travels the straight path, I am able to travel the safe journey that is always frequented by those who guard their own minds.

I will bind you to the meditation object with strength, like an elephant to a post with a sturdy rope. Thus well-guarded by mindfulness and well-developed, you shall become one who is unattached to all realms of existence.

Cutting you off with wisdom when you follow the wrong path, subduing you with effort and establishing you on the right path, and seeing the cause of arising and the cause of cessation, you shall become an heir to the Buddha, the Speaker of the Excellent.

O Mind! Following the will of the four perversions, you have dragged me here and there like a village boy. Why not associate with the Compassionate Great Sage who cuts the bonds of fetters?

Like a deer wandering at will, I shall delight in the pleasant mountains surrounded by clouds in the rainy season, and in those undisturbed mountains. O Mind! You will certainly become one who follows the will of another.

O Mind! Those men and women who live according to your desire, who are ignorant and follow the will of Mara, delighting in existence—they are but your disciples and enjoy whatever happiness they find. (Thus the Elder Telakāni recited these verses).

In these verses, the word 'Kadānuhaṃ' should be broken down as 'Kadā, anu, ahaṃ'. I shall dwell alone without a companion in the mountain clefts. Regarding all existence as impermanent through insight...
466:
In those verses, 'Kadā nuhaṃ' means 'Kadā, nu, ahaṃ' (When indeed shall I?). 'Pabbata-kandarāsu' means in the mountains and in the clefts, or in the mountain clefts. 'Ekākiyo' means being alone. 'Adutiyo' means being without the companion of craving. This is because craving is called a man's 'second' (companion). 'Vihassanti' means 'I shall dwell' (vihariဿāmi). The construction is: 'When shall I dwell, practicing insight into all existence, such as the sensual realm, as impermanent in the sense of non-existence after having come to be?' This is merely an illustration. According to the teaching, 'That which is impermanent is suffering; that which is suffering is non-self,' it should be understood that the other two characteristics (suffering and non-self) are also implied. 'Taṃ me idaṃ taṃ nu kadā bhavissati' means 'When will this thought of mine be realized? When will it reach its fulfillment?' Here, 'taṃ' in 'taṃ nu' is merely a particle. The summary of the meaning is: 'When shall I, like a great elephant breaking its chains, break the bonds of household life, go forth, and cultivate physical seclusion, dwelling alone in mountain clefts without the companion of craving, detached from everything, and practicing insight into all conditioned things as impermanent?'

'Bhinnapaṭandharo' means one who wears torn or patched cloth. The letter 'na' is inserted in the middle for the sake of the verse's meter. It means one who wears the patchwork robe (cīvara) which is cut with a knife, of little value, and faded in color. 'Muni' means a monk (one who has gone forth). 'Amamo' means 'without mine-ness' because of the absence of possessiveness toward family or group. 'Nirāso' means 'without expectation' because of the absence of longing for any sense object. It means: 'When shall I dwell, having entered the great forest, happy through the bliss of the Path and the bliss of Fruition, having utterly cut off the defilements such as lust with the Noble Path?'

'Vadharoganīḷaṃ' means that which is like a nest of death and disease. 'Kāyaṃ imaṃ' refers to this body known as the group of five aggregates. Indeed, the five aggregates are called 'body' (kāya) in such passages as: 'Bhikkhus, for the person who is ignorant and accompanied by craving, this very body is external name-and-form.' It means: 'When will that thought of mine be realized, as I practice insight into this body oppressed by death and old age, becoming fearless by abandoning the causes of fear?'

'Bhayajananīṃ' means causing suffering because it brings about all the suffering of the round of rebirth, both physical and mental, being the cause for the arising of the twenty-five great fears. 'Taṇhālatāṃ bahuvidhānuvattanīṃ' means craving the creeper which follows after various objects or realms of existence...
467:
The creeper of craving, known as 'bahuvidhānuvattani' because it follows or flows into various objects or existences, should be cut off at the root. This is achieved by taking the well-sharpened sword of Path-wisdom with the hand of faith supported by effort. The reflection, 'When shall I live (free from defilements)?' should be understood by connecting it to the question: 'When will that aspiration be fulfilled?'

'Uggateja' refers to a weapon with fierce power, sharpened by the force of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). 'Isīnaṃ satthaṃ' refers to the Dhamma which is like a weapon of the seers (isī), namely the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Noble Disciples. I shall swiftly destroy the five Maras, such as Abhisankhara-māra, along with the army of defilements. 'Sīhāsana' means a firm seat, the unconquered throne (aparājita-pallaṅka).

'Sabbhi samāgamesu diṭṭho bhave' means: 'May I be seen as one who strives in meditation (padhāniya) in the assembly of the virtuous ones, such as the Buddhas.' This is due to qualities such as reverence for the Dhamma, attaining the characteristic of 'Tādi' (steadfastness), seeing things correctly without distortion, and having upright faculties through the fear of evil. This reflection should be understood as: 'When will this thought of mine be fulfilled?' Following this method, the connection of all words should be understood; hereafter, I shall only explain the meaning of the words.

'Tandī' means laziness, and 'khudā' means hunger. 'Kīṭasarīsapa' refers to insects, snakes, and the like. The meaning is that these insects will no longer trouble me because happiness, suffering, joy, and dejection have been averted through the jhānas. 'Giribbaja' refers to a mountain gorge. 'Atthatthiyaṃ' means desiring the benefit known as one's own goal (sadattha).

'Yaṃ viditaṃ mahesinā' refers to the Four Noble Truths realized and penetrated by the Blessed One through his self-enlightened knowledge (sayambhū-ñāṇa). For those who have not accumulated the requisites of merit, these Four Noble Truths are very difficult to see. The meaning is: 'With a mind concentrated through Path-concentration, being mindful with right mindfulness, I shall penetrate and attain them through the wisdom of the Noble Path.'

'Rūpe' refers to visible forms known by eye-consciousness. 'Amite' means those not delimited or known by knowledge. 'Phusitabbe' refers to tangible objects (phoṭṭhabba). 'Dhamme' refers to mental objects known by mind-consciousness. Alternatively, 'amite' means immeasurable; it refers to visible forms of many varieties such as blue, etc.; sounds of many varieties such as drum sounds, etc.; tastes such as root-tastes, etc.; touches such as hardness or softness, etc.; and feelings such as pleasure or pain, etc. 'Ādittato' means because of being burnt by the eleven fires. 'Endowed with serenity' (samathehi yutto) means being endowed with...
468:
...being endowed with jhāna, vipassanā, the path, and concentration. 'I shall see with wisdom' means I shall see with Path-wisdom accompanied by insight-wisdom.

'Spoken to with ill words' means being struck by poorly spoken speech. 'Due to that cause' means because of harsh speech. 'May I not be dejected' means may I not become unhappy. 'Then' (atho) means then. 'Praised' (pasattho) means being praised by someone. One should view these five aggregates included in one's own continuity like logs of wood (kaṭṭha) or heaps of grass (tiṇa). One should also view the material phenomena (rūpa-dhamma) that are immeasurable and distinct from those five aggregates by another group of faculties. Therefore, He said: 'Both internal and external.' One desires to cross over by making everything equal through the power of impermanence, etc., and through the power of metaphors such as corelessness, etc. This refers to one who practices on the path of serenity and insight (samatha-vipassanā-magga) which has been well-traveled by the Great Seers such as the Buddhas.

'When will the heavy rain of the rainy season, with its fresh rainwater, drench me along with my robes in the forest?' This shows his reflection on the ascetic practice of living in the open air (abbhokāsika). 'Dija' refers to the peacock, called 'twice-born' because it is born from the mother's womb and then from the eggshell. 'Sikhaṇḍī' refers to the crested peacock. The meaning is: 'When, in the forest, having heard the peacock's cry (kekā) in a mountain cave and noting the time, shall I rise from my bed and, for the sake of attaining Nirvana (amata), reflect on impermanence, etc., in the coming existence and practice insight (vipassanā)?'

'Ganges, Yamuna, Saraswati'—one should connect this as: 'When shall I cross these great rivers without clinging, through the psychic power accomplished by meditation (bhāvanāmaya-iddhi)?' It is called 'Pātāla' because it is capable of causing one to fall; when thrown into that Pātāla, it is called 'Pātālakhitta' because it stays in the earth in that manner. Within the earth beneath the ocean, there are coastal regions of various extents, such as a hundred leagues (yojanas). In some of those places, there are dwellings for Nagas and others; some places remain entirely empty. 'Baḷavāmukha' is a great whirlpool in the great ocean. When the gate of the Avici Great Hell opens, a massive mass of fire emerges from it and burns the lower region of the ocean, which is hundreds of yojanas in length and breadth, facing that Baḷavāmukha. When that region is burnt, the water above...
469:
(The waters) swirl in the form of a whirlpool and fall downward with a great roar. In that place, it is known by the name Baḷavāmukha. Thus, just as I had reflected, "When shall I cross over this terrifying and fearful place called Baḷavāmukha, which is like being cast into the Pātāla abyss, without clinging and by means of psychic power?"—it means: having brought forth psychic power developed through meditation (bhāvanāmaya-iddhi), when shall I make use of such power?

"Nāgova asanga-cārī padālaye" means: Just as a great elephant in rut breaks a strong post, destroys its iron shackles, and enters the forest without attachment, roaming alone and solitary according to its own desire; in the same way, when shall I, completely avoiding all beautiful and attractive signs, not following the will of sensual desire, but being devoted to jhāna, properly break through, abandon, and relinquish the desire for the strands of sensual pleasure? When will that thought of mine come to pass?

"Iṇaṭṭhova daliddako nidhiṃ ārādhayitvā" means: Just as a poor man whose livelihood has been ruined, having taken a debt and being unable to repay it, is oppressed by his creditors, but upon finding a treasure-pot, repays the debt and lives happily and joyfully; in the same way, when shall I, having abandoned sensual desire (kāmacchanda) which is like a debt, and having attained the Dispensation (Sāsana) of the Buddha—which is like a treasure-pot full of jewels and gold because it is replete with the Noble Wealth (ariyadhana) of the Great Sage—be filled with joy? When will that thought of mine come to pass?

In this way, having shown the sequence of his own thoughts that occurred through the power of thoughts of renunciation (nekkhamma-vitakka) before his ordination, he now wishes to show the manner in which he admonished himself and attained the higher Dhamma after ordaining. Thus, he spoke the verses beginning with "Bahūni vassāni." In those verses, "Bahūni vassāni tayāmhi yācito, agāravāsena alaṃ nu te idaṃ" means: O Mind, did you not entreat me in this way for many years? Living in a house followed by various kinds of suffering is enough for you. Why then, after I have ordained through your encouragement, do you abandon tranquillity and insight (samatha-vipassanā) and urge me toward base laziness?

"O Mind, did you not entreat me? If you did entreat me, why do you not practice accordingly now?" is the meaning. "Citrapatto haṃsagāmī" means peacocks with variegated wings. "Ghosena abhiruṇṇena" refers to the great crying out in the sky. "Taṃ missanti vanāyinaṃ" is to show what you entreated: that those peacocks would approach you who are practicing jhāna. "Kuto paridevo, imaṃ ajjhuupagato" means: Why are you lamenting even though you have attained this state of a monk? "Cittaṃ mayhaṃ nussati" means: Will you continue to follow me and yet not let me be pleased? "Mameva taṃ na hi taṃ tassa" means: O Mind, this arising from following after sense pleasures...
470:
O Mind, did you not entreat me? O Mind, I think I was indeed entreated by you. If you did entreat me, why do you not now practice in accordance with that entreaty? This is the meaning. With the words beginning with "Giribbaje," he shows the manner of the entreaty. "Citrachadā vihangamā" refers to birds with variegated wings, meaning peacocks. "Mahindaghosatthanitābhigajjino" means those who habitually cry out loudly due to the thunderous sound of clouds. "Te taṃ ramessanti vanamhi jhāyinaṃ" shows: "Did you not entreat me, saying that those peacocks would delight you who are devoted to meditation in the forest?"

Whether in the circle of relatives or having arrived at this forest place or the state of monkhood, "O Mind, do you not satisfy me even though you remain following my will?" is the meaning.

O Mind, this mind is my own property; you are not the property of others. Therefore, why is there any use in lamenting and not following during the time of the battle against the Māra of defilements (kilesa-māra)—the time of developing meditation (bhāvanā)—as if you belonged to others? Now, I will not give you the opportunity to behave in any other way. This is the meaning. "Sabbaṃ idaṃ calamiti pekkhamāno" means: Because I am looking with the eye of wisdom, seeing that "this mind and all other conditioned things (saṅkhāra) of the three realms are unstable and unsteady," and have gone forth from the home and from sensual pleasures, seeking the Deathless state of Nibbāna; therefore, O Mind, I will not follow your will but will only perform the seeking of Nibbāna. This is the meaning.

One who has not yet rid themselves of lust should (subdue) the mind which is extremely difficult to restrain, unstable, and like a forest monkey. The Buddha, who is the speaker of what is appropriate, the speaker of well-said words, the supreme among bipeds, the Great Physician, and the Charioteer of men to be tamed, has taught this.

"Aviddasū yattha sitā puthujjanā" means: Those blind worldlings who are attached to and bound by those objects of sensuality (vatthukāma) and subjective defilements (kilesakāma), seeking new birth through that sensual lust, truly desire only suffering. Thus desiring, and being led by their own minds, they perform actions that lead to hell; being deprived of welfare and happiness, they are led to hell by their own minds and not by anyone else. This shows that the mind alone must be subdued.
471:
Once again, intending to restrain the mind, he spoke the words beginning with "Mayūrakonjābhirutamhi."

In that Pali text, "Mayūrakonjābhirutamhi" means in a place where peacocks and cranes cry. "Dīpīhi byagghehi purakkhato vasanti" means living in the forest surrounded by such animals because of living with loving-kindness (mettā). By this Pali, he speaks of the cultivation of seclusion. "Kāye apekkhaṃ jahā" means abandon regard for the body in every way. By this Pali, he speaks of the state of a resolute mind. "Mā virādhaya" means do not miss the ninth moment (the opportune moment), which is very difficult to obtain. "Itissu maṃ, citta, pure niyuñjasī" means "O mind, before I became a monk, you urged me thus toward right practice."

"Bhāvehi" means produce or cultivate. "Jhānāni" refers to the four jhanas, starting from the first jhana. "Indriyāni" refers to the five faculties, such as faith. "Balāni" refers to those same five powers. "Bojjhaṅgasamādhibhāvanā" refers to the seven factors of enlightenment and the four cultivations of concentration. "Tisso ca vijjā" refers to the three knowledges, such as the knowledge of past lives. Abiding in the instruction of the Buddha, attain these dhammas.

"Niyyānika" means the dhamma that leads out from the suffering of the round of rebirths. "Sabbadukkhakkhayogadha" means the dhamma that plunges into the deathless Nirvana, having Nirvana as its basis and object. "Sabbakilesasodhana" means the dhamma that purifies the stains of all defilements without remainder.

"Khandhe" refers to the aggregates of clinging. "Paṭipassa yoniso" means contemplate wisely with insight-knowledge through various modes such as as a disease, a boil, a dart, a calamity, and an affliction. "Taṃ jahā" means abandon and cut off that craving which is the cause of suffering. "Idheva" means in this very existence.

Contemplate as "anicca" (impermanent) because of having a beginning and an end, being limited by time, and the rejection of permanence. Contemplate as "dukkha" (suffering) because of being oppressed by arising and passing away, being dangerous, being difficult to endure, and the rejection of happiness. Contemplate as "suñña" (void) because of not following one's will, being without an owner, being without essence, and the rejection of self. For that very reason, it is called "anattā" (non-self). Contemplate wisely as "agha" (calamity) and "vadha" (murderer) because of being blameworthy and causing harm without growth. This is the construction.
472:
"Manovicāre uparundha cetaso" means restrain the mind, make it cease from the eighteen mental explorations based on the household life, which are known as mental explorations of the five cords of sensual pleasure.

"Muṇḍo" refers to one who has reached the state of being shaven-headed, with hair and beard removed. "Virūpo" refers to one who has reached a disfigured appearance because of having hair that grows in a messy way due to being shaven-headed, wearing robes that are cut and patched, and wearing robes dyed with astringent juice which spoils the color. "Abhisāpamāgato" refers to one who has reached the reproach made by the Noble Ones, saying, "He wanders with an alms bowl in hand." This was said: "Monks, in this world, wandering with an alms bowl in hand is a form of reproach." Therefore, it is said, "Like a monk with an alms bowl in hand among the families." "Yuñjassu satthuvacane" means make an effort, repeatedly apply yourself to the instruction of the Buddha.

"Susaṃvutatto" refers to one who is well-restrained in body, speech, and mind. "Visikhantare caranti" refers to one who wanders through various streets for alms. "Cando yathā dosinapuṇṇamāsiyā" should be connected as: practice like the moon among the families, like the full moon free from defects such as Rāhu, because of being always fresh and inspiring confidence.

"Sadā dhute rato" refers to one who always delights in the virtues of the ascetic practices (dhuta). "Tathūpamaṃ cittamidaṃ karosi" means just as a man, desiring fruits, plants fruit trees and then, before obtaining fruit from those trees, desires to cut them down from the root; O mind, you do this to this mind in the same way. "Yaṃ maṃ aniccamhi cale niyuñzasi" means you yoke me, who has been yoked to monkhood and has reached the long-attained benefit of monkhood, to the impermanent and unstable round of rebirths; you make it occur by the power of yoking.

They are called "Arūpā" because they have no form. It is said "Arūpā" because the mind has no such shape or distinction of colors like blue, etc. It is called "Dūraṅgama" (far-traveling) because it occurs in distant places. Although the mind does not actually travel even by the measure of a spider's thread toward the east or other directions, it is called "Dūraṅgama" because it perceives objects that are far away. It is called "Ekacāri" (wandering alone) because it occurs by way of arising singly. At the very least, even two or three minds are not able to arise together; rather, only a single mind arises in a single continuity. When that mind ceases, another single mind arises; therefore, it is called "Ekacāri." "Na te karissaṃ vacanaṃ idānihaṃ" means "Now I will not do your bidding; although I followed your will in the past, now [I follow] the instruction of the Buddha..."
473:
From the time I received the instruction of the Blessed One, I shall no longer be one who follows the will of the mind. Why is that? For indeed, sensual pleasures (kāmas) are of the nature of suffering, they have bitter results, and they are fraught with great danger through such means as self-reproach. Sensual pleasures, so-called, are of the nature of suffering in the past, have bitter results in the future, and are fraught with great danger as they are followed by great peril in various forms such as self-reproach. I shall practice with a mind directed only towards Nibbāna; therefore, I shall dwell with a mind aimed at and intending only for Nibbāna.

To show that very state of being directed towards Nibbāna, he said the words beginning with "I did not [go forth] because of misfortune." In that Pali, "nāhaṃ alakkhyā" is connected as: I did not go forth from home because of misfortune or because of being devoid of glory.

Neither did I go forth because of shamelessness, being devoid of shame like one who plays with faults. "Because of the mind" (citta-hetu) means [I did not wander] as one who follows the will of the mind, like a man with an unstable mind who is sometimes a Nigantha, sometimes a Paribbājaka, and so on. "Dūrakantanā" means [I did not go forth] by way of betraying kings and others after having made friendship with them. "Because of livelihood" (ājīva-hetu) means I did not leave home or go forth as a result of livelihood, being driven by the fear of [losing] one's livelihood. O Mind, was it not a promise made by me: "From the time of going forth, I shall not act according to your will, but shall make you act according to my will"? Thus he shows.

Fewness of wishes (appicchatā) regarding the requisites is praised by the Buddha and other virtuous ones as being good in every way. Likewise, the abandoning of the smearing of others' virtues (makkha-pahāna) and Nibbāna, which is the cessation of all suffering, are praised by the virtuous. O Mind, at that time you urged me thus: "Friend, you should be established in those virtues." Now you go back to your former habits; now you abandon me and practice your former habits such as great desire. What is the meaning of this? This is the intention.

To show the meaning intended by the words "you go to your former habits," the words beginning with "craving and ignorance" (taṇhā avijjā ca) were spoken. Therein, "craving" (taṇhā) means attachment to the requisites; "ignorance" (avijjā) means the ignorance that covers the faults in those very requisites. "Piyāpiya" means the state of being loved, known as affection for children and wife, and the state of being unloved, known as dissatisfaction with secluded dwellings and with the higher wholesome dhammas; it is the compliance and resistance in both these cases. "Subhāni rūpāni" means beautiful forms within oneself and externally. "Sukhā vedanā" means pleasant feeling that arises depending on a desired object. "Manāpiyā kāmaguṇā" refers to the remaining [strands of sensual pleasure]...
474:
...the delightful portions of sensual pleasure. They are "vomited" (vanta) because they have been discarded and relinquished by the abandoning through suppression of the desire and lust (chandarāga) that depends on those sensual pleasures. He says, "I do not strive to swallow again those sensual pleasures which are like vomit; I am unable to swallow again what has been thus discarded; they are indeed relinquished."

"In all places" (sabbhattha) means in all existences (bhava), in all births (yoni), in all destinations (gati), and in all stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti). "I have followed your word" means "O Mind, I have done according to your word." "Though I have done so in many births, I was not angry with you" means that in many births I was not made angry by you, nor was I disrespectful. Nevertheless, although you arose within my own continuity, because of your ingratitude, I have wandered and roamed for a very long time in the suffering of Saṃsāra, which has no discernible beginning, created by you.

Now, wishing to show in detail the meaning briefly stated as "wandered for a long time in the suffering created by you" through the varieties of rebirth and destinations, he said the words beginning with "tvaññeva." Therein, "you were a king" (rājadasi) means you were a king (the letter 'da' is a euphonic conjunction). Sometimes, by your power alone, we became merchants (vessa) or laborers (sudda). "Or even the state of a deva" is connected as: "O Mind, you alone also made for us the state of a deva." "Vāhasā" means by way of cause.

"Because of you alone" means by your state as the cause. "Having you as the root" means having you as the condition.

"Will you not surely betray me again and again?" means: "O Mind, just as in the past in infinite births you were an enemy disguised as a friend and betrayed me again and again, I think you will betray me in the same way now; however, I will not give you the opportunity to lead me astray as before." This is the meaning. "Showing frequent wandering" means showing the mind as if it were fit for constant wandering, like a person who deceives a man fit for wandering and makes him a wanderer-guardian, showing various existences again and again. "You entice me as if with a madman" means you entice me by showing various enticing objects, playing with me as if with a madman. "O Mind, what wrong have I done to you? Tell me that," is the meaning.

"This mind formerly" means this mind, before this time, in objects such as forms, through lust and so forth, in whatever manner it wishes, and wherever its desire arises...
475:
One who wanders as they please according to the will of that mind finds happiness; while wandering thus, it has wandered for a very long time as it pleased. Today, I shall restrain that mind with wise reflection (yoniso manasikāra), just as a skilled mahout, the elephant trainer, restrains a rutting elephant with a hook (aṅkusa); I will not give it the opportunity to transgress.

My Teacher, the Fully Enlightened Buddha, has defined this entire world of the aggregates (khandha-loka) with His knowledge. How? As impermanent (anicca) because it perishes after arising; as unstable (adhuva) because there is no permanence or stability for anyone; and as coreless (asāra) because there is no essence of happiness and so forth. Therefore, O mind, in order to practice according to the truth, enter into the teaching of the Victorious Buddha; let yourself plunge in. There is also a Pali reading 'pakkhandimaṃ'; plunge into this world with knowledge in the teaching of the Victor, cross over according to the truth, and while plunging in, partaking of the path of insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa-magga), make me cross over the great flood of saṃsāra which is very difficult to cross.

O mind, this house of the physical body is no longer for you as it was in the past. Why? Because now it is no longer proper for me to follow your will. For I have gone forth in the teaching of the Great Sage, the Blessed One. From the time of going forth, recluses (samaṇa) like me are only those who wear the [robes] that destroy defilements; indeed, they are truly recluses.

'Naga' refers to all mountains such as Sineru and Himavanta. 'Samudda' refers to the Eastern Ocean, the Sīta Ocean, and so forth; it does not mean all oceans. 'Saritā' refers to all rivers such as the Ganges. 'Vasundharā' is the earth. 'Four directions' refers to the four directions such as the East. 'Vidisā' refers to the four intermediate directions such as the Southeast. 'Adho' refers to the downward direction, as far as the layer of air that supports the water. 'Divā' refers to the celestial realms. Here, by the word 'Divā', it refers to the formations of beings (satta-saṅkhāra) that arise in those celestial realms. All three worlds (ti-bhava), such as the sensual world (kāma-bhava), are impermanent and are oppressed and afflicted by dangers such as birth (jāti) and defilements such as lust (rāga). In this existence, there is no place called a place of safety; because of that lack of safety, O mind, where will you go to find pleasant delight? Therefore, the meaning is: seek only the escape from this saṃsāra.
476:
'Dhitippara' means one who rests in steadfastness, who is established in a state of supreme firmness. 'O mind, what can you do to me? You cannot move me even slightly from such steadfastness.' Thus it means. Therefore, he said: 'O mind, I am no longer a follower of your will; I am no longer suitable for you.'

Now, to make that same meaning even clearer, he said: 'One should certainly not even touch with the foot a snack-bag that has openings at both ends. May this latrine-like body, which is full of impurities and has filth flowing from the nine wounds (openings), be loathsome!' In those words, 'bhastaṃ' refers to a snack-bag. 'Ubhatomukhaṃ' refers to the two openings of the snack-bag. 'Na jātu chupe' means one should certainly not touch it even with the foot. Likewise, 'dhiratthu pūraṃ navasotasandaniṃ' means may this body, which is like a latrine, full of various impurities and with filth flowing from the nine wounds, be loathsome; may it be held in contempt.

In this way, having admonished the mind by way of restraint with twenty-eight verses, he now wishes to gladden the mind by describing secluded places and so forth, and thus said the words beginning with 'Varāhaeṇeyyavigāḷhasevite'. In those words, 'Varāhaeṇeyyavigāḷhasevite' refers to a place frequented and entered by wild boars and deer called eṇī. 'Pabbhārakutṭe' refers to a place on a mountain slope or a mountain peak. 'Pakateva sundare' refers to a place that is naturally excellent and extremely captivating. There is also a variant reading 'pakativasundhare', meaning in a natural ground area. 'Navambunā pāvusasittakānane' means in a forest sprinkled by the rainwater poured during the rainy season. 'Tahiṃ guhāgehagato ramissasi' means having approached the house known as a cave in that mountain forest, you will greatly delight through the delight of meditation (bhāvanā-rati).

'Te taṃ ramessanti' means those peacocks and others, by creating the perception of the forest, will make you delight.

'Vuṭṭhamhi deve' means when the rain has fallen heavily. 'Caturaṅgule tiṇe' means when grass about four fingers high, resembling a well-dyed red blanket, has grown in various places due to that rainfall. 'Sampupphite meghanibhamhi kānane' means when the great forest, which is like the color of a rain cloud, is in full bloom. 'Nagantare' means in the mountain clefts. 'Viṭapisamo sayissaṃ' means I will sleep like a tree, being one without possessions. 'Taṃ me mudū hehi tūlasannibhaṃ' means that bed of grass will be for me a place of sleep that is soft to the touch and resembles silk-cotton.
477:
## "I will treat you just as a master treats his servant"
This means that just as a powerful man makes his servant or subordinate follow his will, O Mind, I too will treat you so and make you follow only my will. How so? "Let what is obtained be enough for me" means that with whatever of the four requisites I obtain, let that be sufficient (complete) for me. By this passage, this meaning is shown: in this world, some beings follow the will of the mind because of the arising of craving; I, however, avoiding the arising of craving from afar, will treat the mind like a servant and make it follow my will.

"I will not let you be lazy, like a well-tanned cat-skin bag" means, O Mind, because of avoiding the arising of craving (I will treat you so). Again, with the word "taṃ" (you), he refers to the mind. Just as another person, being diligent in meditation by applying right effort, makes his mind workable (fit for the task), so too, O Mind, I will make you workable and make you follow my will. How so? In the phrase "like a well-tanned cat-skin bag," the word "na" is merely a particle. Just as a well-kneaded cat-skin bag is workable, fit for use, and easily carried, so too will I make you.

"I will bring you under my control through energy" means, O Mind, I will generate the power of meditation through my own energy and, by that power, bring you under my control. "Like a skilled mahout with a rutting elephant" means just as a skilled and clever elephant trainer, through the power of his training, brings a rutting elephant under his control, it is just the same.

In the phrase "With you well-tamed and steady," the word "hi" is merely a particle. O Mind, because you are well-tamed through the meditation of tranquillity and insight, and because of that, you have properly entered the path of insight and are steady (I shall be able). "Like a horse-trainer with a straight-running horse" means just as a horse-trainer is able to go from a place of danger to a place of safety by means of a well-tamed, straight-running noble steed, so too "the peaceful" (sivaṃ) means I am able to travel the path to the peaceful state, which is peaceful because of the absence of defilements that cause distress. "By those who guard their minds" means I am able to travel (to attain) the Noble Path that is always frequented by the virtuous, such as the Buddhas, who are in the habit of guarding their own minds.
478:
Just as an elephant-teacher binds a great elephant to a post with a strong and firm rope, so too, O mind, I will bind you to the object of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna-ārammaṇa) through the power of meditation. In the phrase "That mind of mine, well-guarded by mindfulness and well-developed," it means: O mind, being well-guarded by my mindfulness and well-developed, you will become independent of the supports of craving and so forth in all states of existence (bhava), such as the sensual realm, through the power of the development of the Noble Path.

In the phrase "Cutting with wisdom the one who follows the wrong path," it means seeing truly the origin (samudaya) consisting of the sense-bases (āyatana) that leads to the wrong path. Whatever origin causes one to go astray, one cuts the agitation and vibration of the defilements of that person with reflective wisdom (paṭisaṅkhāna-paññā) based on sense-restraint (indriya-saṃvara). Having blocked it by way of cutting the flow, and having thoroughly subdued it with the 'yoga' known as the development of insight (vipassanā-bhāvanā), one establishes it on the path of insight. When insight is exerted and meets the Path, one sees without delusion the cessation and origin of the sense-bases through Path-wisdom, with the realization: "Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease." Thus, one will become a true breast-born son and an heir (dāyāda) to the Fully Enlightened Buddha, the Supreme Proclaimer in the world with its devas.

In the phrase "Established under the influence of the four perversions," it refers to the mind that exists under the influence of these four perversions (vipallāsa): taking the impermanent as permanent, the foul as beautiful, the painful as pleasant, and the non-self as self. In the phrase "O mind, you lead me about like a village boy," it means: O mind, you drag me here and there like a village child. In the phrase "Should one not associate with the Buddha who cuts the bond of fetters?" it means: Should one not associate with the Fully Enlightened Buddha, the Compassionate Great Sage, who cuts the ten bonds known as fetters (saṃyojana)? With a hint of dissatisfaction [with the mind], he praises the Teacher: "You avoid such a person of great power from afar, but you lead a practitioner like me about according to your whims."

In the phrase "Like a deer," it means just as a deer delights at its own will in a forest that is beautifully adorned with trees, thickets, and creepers and is free from disturbance. In the phrase "The lovely mountain crowned with rain-clouds," it means: O mind, (know that) I shall truly delight in that mountain which, during the rainy season, is crowned with clouds and is 'garlanded' by the well-bloomed flowers of land and water on all sides, and which is lovely because of its seclusion from people and its pleasantness to the heart.
479:
Because of being endowed with (land and water features), I have obtained a delightful mountain that is garlanded with clouds, secluded from people, and pleasant to the heart; I shall delight in those peaks. O mind, without doubt, you will surely perish; you will remain in the ruins of Saṃsāra. This is the meaning.

By the words "Those who live according to your desire and will," he speaks of all worldlings (puthujjana) by way of their common mental state. The meaning is: O mind, those men and women who, standing under your desire, will, and pleasure, enjoy or will enjoy that happiness based on the household life—they are ignorant, blind worldlings, followers of Māra, having the nature of following the power of the defilements (kilesa-māra) and so forth. Delighting in existence because they delight only in the realms of sense-desire (kāma-bhava) and so forth, they are your disciples who act according to your instruction. We, however, are disciples of the Fully Enlightened One; we do not follow your will.

Thus, the Elder Tālapuṭa, having analyzed in various ways the wise reflection (yoniso manasikāra) that had previously arisen in him by way of restraining the mind, taught the Dhamma by way of giving advice to the monks standing nearby. As for the words whose meaning is not analyzed here and there, they are clear in meaning because they follow the method already mentioned below.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Tālapuṭa Thera is finished.
## The Commentary on the Section of Fifty (Paññāsanipāta) is finished.
480:
## 20. The Section of Sixty (Saṭṭhinipāta)
## 1. Commentary on the Verses of Mahāmoggallāna Thera
In the Section of Sixty, the verse beginning with 'Āraññikā' is the verse of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna Thera. What is the occasion for its arising? The story of this Elder is just as stated in the story of the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta). Indeed, on the seventh day from the day he went forth, while the Elder was dwelling near the small village of Kallavāḷa in the kingdom of Magadha and practicing the Dhamma of a recluse, he was overcome by sloth and torpor (thina-middha). The Teacher stirred him with the words, "Moggallāna, Moggallāna, O Brahmin, do not be negligent regarding the noble silence," and so forth. Having dispelled sloth and torpor, and while listening to the meditation on the elements (dhātu-kammaṭṭhāna) taught by the Blessed One, he developed insight (vipassanā). Gradually reaching the three higher paths, at the moment of the fruit of Arahantship, he reached the summit of the knowledge of a disciple's perfection (sāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa). Regarding this, it is said in the Apadāna:

"The Blessed One Anomadassī, the eldest in the world, the bull among men, dwelt in the Himālaya, surrounded by a host of devas.

At that time, I was a Naga King named Varuṇa; dwelling in the great ocean, I could transform into any form I desired.

Leaving aside my group of attendants, I arranged for Naga musical instruments to be played; then, surrounding the Fully Enlightened One, celestial nymphs (accharā) played music.

While the Naga instruments were being played, the devas also sounded their divine instruments; hearing the sound of both, the Buddha also awoke (from his meditative attainment).

Having invited the Fully Enlightened One, he came to my own Naga palace; having prepared a seat, I announced the time for the meal.

Surrounded by a thousand of those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), the Leader of the World, illuminating all directions, came to my palace.

To the Great Hero who was seated, the God of gods, the bull among men, I then satisfied him and the Saṅgha of monks with food and drink."
481:
The Great Hero, the Self-Enlightened One, the Supreme Person (Anomadassī), seated in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks, gave thanks and spoke these verses:

"He who has honored the Saṅgha and the Buddha, the Leader of the World—through that clarity of mind, he will go to the world of the devas.

Seventy-seven times he will exercise the kingship of devas; eight hundred times he will be a sole monarch on earth and rule over the land.

Fifty-five times he will be a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavatti); immeasurable wealth will arise for that wheel-turning monarch at that very moment.

In an incalculable aeon from now, a Teacher named Gotama by clan, born of the Okkāka line, will arise in the world.

Passing away from hell, he will reach the human state; he will be a member of a Brahmin family named Kolita.

That Kolita will later go forth, urged by his root of merit, and will become the second disciple of the Blessed One Gotama.

With stirred-up energy, with a mind directed toward Nibbāna, having reached the perfection of psychic power, and having fully understood all taints (āsava), he will attain Nibbāna, free from taints." (Thus he spoke).

Relying on bad friends and falling under the power of sensual lust, with a corrupted mind, I even killed my mother and father.

In whatever birth I was reborn, whether in hell or in the human world, because of being endowed with that evil kamma, I died with my head broken.

This is my last birth; indeed, the final existence is proceeding. In this last birth too, at the time of death, this (dying with a broken head) will happen to me.

I dwell free from taints, having fully understood all taints, delighting in the development of concentration and constantly practicing the three kinds of seclusion (viveka).

Because I have reached the perfection of psychic power, I can shake even the earth—which is very deep, thick, and difficult to destroy—with my left big toe.
482:
I do not see the conceit 'I am' (asmimāna); conceit does not exist in me. Since my time as a novice (sāmaṇera), I have maintained a mind of deep respect. In the countless aeons from this Bhadda Kappa, I undertook the deed (of aspiring to be the left-hand disciple); having reached the ground of that deed's fruition, the fruit of Arahantship, I have attained the destruction of the taints (āsavas). The four analytical insights, the eight liberations, and the six higher powers have been realized; the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.

Later, while the Teacher was seated in the midst of the assembly of noble ones at the Jetavana Monastery, in appointing his disciples to the foremost positions (etadagga) according to their respective virtues, he declared: "Monks, among my monk disciples who possess psychic powers, Mahāmoggallāna is the foremost." Thus, the Teacher appointed him to the foremost position in psychic powers. When the Great Elder, who had reached the pinnacle of a disciple's perfection and was thus appointed to the foremost position by the Teacher, spoke verses in various places based on various circumstances, the Elders who compiled the Dhamma at the time of the Council recorded them as follows:

Those who dwell in the forest, who observe the practice of alms-gathering, who delight in whatever food is obtained in their alms-bowl, and whose minds are well-concentrated within themselves—let them destroy the army of Death (kilesas).

Those who dwell in the forest, who observe the practice of alms-gathering, and who delight in whatever food is obtained in their alms-bowl—let them shatter the army of Death, just as an elephant destroys a hut of reeds.

Those who dwell at the foot of trees, who are constantly energetic, who delight in whatever food is obtained in their alms-bowl, and whose minds are well-concentrated within themselves—let them destroy the army of Death.

Those who dwell at the foot of trees, who are constantly energetic, and who delight in whatever food is obtained in their alms-bowl—let them shatter the army of Death, just as an elephant destroys a hut of reeds.

O fool, you who regard another's body as 'mine'—this small hut of a skeleton, bound together by flesh and sinews, foul-smelling, and full of filth—shame on you!

Your body has nine openings, it produces a foul odor and is a source of obstruction. A monk avoids it, just as one who desires purity avoids excrement.
483:
If people knew this body as I know it, they would avoid it from afar, just as one who desires purity avoids a place of excrement during the rainy season.

O Great Hero (Mahāvīra), O Ascetic, it is just as you say. In this loathsome body, some beings sink like an old ox in the mud.

Just as it would only bring weariness to one who intends to paint the sky with turmeric or any other dye, so my mind is like the sky, well-concentrated within itself. Do not strike me with an evil mind, like a moth hitting a bonfire.

Look at this female form, a painted image, a heap of sores, propped up, diseased, full of many intentions, which has no permanent stability.

Look at this form, adorned with jeweled earrings, a skeleton covered with skin, appearing beautiful along with its clothes and ornaments.

Feet reddened with lac and a face smeared with powder are enough to delude a fool, but not for one who seeks the further shore (Nibbāna).

Hair braided in eight strands and eyes smeared with collyrium are enough to delude a fool, but not for one who seeks the further shore.

This putrid body, decorated like a new and ornate collyrium box, is enough to delude a fool, but not for one who seeks the further shore.

The hunter set the snare, but the deer did not get caught in it. Having eaten the bait, let us go while the hunter is weeping.

The hunter's snare is broken; the deer did not get caught in it. Having eaten the bait, let us go while the hunter is grieving.

When the Venerable Sāriputta, endowed with many excellent qualities, attained Parinibbāna, there was a terrifying dread and hair-raising awe.
484:
Impermanent indeed are conditioned things (saṅkhārā), they are of the nature to arise and pass away. Having arisen, they cease; their stilling is true bliss.

Those who see the five aggregates as other (not-self) and not as self, they pierce the subtle meaning just as one might pierce the tip of a hair with an arrow.

Those who see conditioned things as other and not as self, they have pierced the subtle meaning just as one might pierce the tip of a hair with an arrow.

Like one struck by a spear, or like one whose head is on fire, a monk should wander mindfully to abandon sensual desire (kāmarāga).

Like one struck by a spear, or like one whose head is on fire, a monk should wander mindfully to abandon the desire for existence (bhavarāga).

Urged by the One who bears his final body (the Buddha), I shook the Migāramātu palace with my big toe.

This Nibbāna, the release from all bonds, cannot be attained by slack effort or by little strength.

This monk, though young, is a supreme man. Having conquered Māra and his army, he bears his final body.

Between Mount Vebhāra and Mount Paṇḍava, the lightnings flash repeatedly. The son of the Incomparable One (the Buddha) has entered the mountain cleft and is absorbed in meditative absorption (jhāna).

Peaceful, steady in nature, delighting in the fruit of Arahantship, the sage (muni) who dwells in a secluded forest dwelling, the heir of the Great Buddha, is worshipped by the Great Brahmā.

O Brahmin, pay homage to the Elder Kassapa, the sage who is peaceful, whose taints are stilled, who dwells in a secluded dwelling, and who is the heir of the Great Buddha.

O Brahmin, even if one were to be born a hundred times in the Brahmin caste among men, and were a master of the Vedas, accomplished in the scriptures;

Even if he were a reciter of the Vedas and had reached the further shore of the three Vedas, his merit would not be worth a sixteenth part of the homage paid to this Venerable Mahākassapa.
485:
He who experiences the eight liberations in forward and reverse order before the meal, and then goes for alms.

Brahmin, do not strike such a monk; do not dig your own grave. Have extreme faith in that Arahant who is endowed with the quality of equanimity. Quickly pay homage with joined palms; let not your head be split.

This [Poṭṭhila] monk does not see the True Dhamma; with saṃsāra before him, he follows the crooked path, the evil path that leads downwards.

Like a worm smeared with dung, being greatly infatuated with conditioned things and immersed in gain and honor, the empty Poṭṭhila goes along.

Look at this Sāriputta who is coming, who has good vision, who is liberated in both ways, and who is well-concentrated within.

[Look at Sāriputta] who is free from the dart, whose fetters are destroyed, who possesses the three knowledges, who has abandoned death, who is worthy of the offerings of men, and who is the unsurpassed supreme field of merit.

These many devas of great power and fame, and the ten thousand devas, all of them Brahma-purohitas, stand with joined palms worshipping the Venerable Moggallāna.

"Homage to you, O noble man! Homage to you, O supreme man! You whose taints are destroyed, O Venerable, you are worthy of the supreme offering." (Thus the devas worship him).
