He who is worshipped by men and devas, who has arisen in the world and conquered death, is not smeared by conditioned things, just as a white lotus is not smeared by water.

He who in a moment knows the thousandfold world system, who has attained mastery in the world including the Brahmas, and who sees the passing away and rebirth of beings at the proper time; that monk is [Venerable Moggallāna].
486:
A monk who is like Sāriputta in wisdom, virtue, and peace, and who has reached the further shore, such a monk alone would be supreme.

I can create a hundred thousand forms of myself in a moment. I am skilled in the various psychic transformations and have attained mastery over psychic power.

Moggallāna of the Moggallāna clan has reached the perfection of mastery in concentration and knowledge in the teaching of the Buddha Asita. That wise Moggallāna, with concentrated faculties, has cut the fetters of defilements just as a great elephant cuts a rotten creeper.

I have served the Teacher; the Buddha's teaching has been carried out. The heavy burden has been laid down; the craving that leads to rebirth has been uprooted.

The goal for which I went forth from the home life into homelessness, that goal—the destruction of all fetters—has been attained by me.

What kind of hell was it where the Dussi Māra was boiled, having attacked the great disciple Vidhura and the Brahmin Kakusandha Buddha?

There were a hundred iron spikes, each causing individual suffering. Such was the hell where the Dussi Māra was boiled, having attacked the great disciple Vidhura and the Brahmin Kakusandha Buddha.

The monk who is a disciple of the Buddha knows this fact. O Kaṇha Māra, by attacking such a monk, you will come to suffering.

In the middle of the ocean, there are mansions that last for an aeon. They are of the color of beryl, beautiful, radiant, and brilliant. There, many nymphs of various colors dance.

The monk who knows this fact... (as above) ... O Kaṇha Māra, you will come to suffering.

He who, urged by the Buddha, shook the Migāramātu palace with his big toe while the community of monks looked on.
487:
The monk who is a disciple of the Buddha knows this fact. O Māra of dark appearance, by attacking such a monk, you will come to the suffering of hell.

He who, supported by psychic power, shook the Vejayanta palace with his big toe and made the host of devas tremble.

The monk who is a disciple of the Buddha knows this fact. O Māra of dark appearance, by attacking such a monk, you will come to the suffering of hell.

He who questioned Sakka in the Vejayanta palace: "Friend Sakka, do you know the liberations through the destruction of craving?" When thus questioned, Sakka answered the question truly to that monk, just as the Buddha had taught.

The monk who is a disciple of the Buddha knows this fact. O Māra of dark appearance, by attacking such a monk, you will come to the suffering of hell.

He who questioned the Brahma standing in the Sudhamma hall: "Friend Brahma, do you still have that view you had before? Do you see the radiant light passing beyond the Brahma world?"

When thus questioned, the Brahma answered that monk truly: "Venerable, I no longer have that view I had before. Now I see the radiant light passing beyond the Brahma world. How could I say today, 'I am permanent and eternal'?"

The monk who is a disciple of the Buddha knows this fact. O Māra of dark appearance, by attacking such a monk, you will come to the suffering of hell.

He who touched the peak of Mount Meru with liberation, and [saw] the forest of the people of Pubbavideha and the men sleeping on the ground.

The monk who is a disciple of the Buddha knows this fact. O Māra of dark appearance, by attacking such a monk, you will come to the suffering of hell.

Fire does not think, "I will burn the fool." It is the fool himself who, by attacking the blazing fire, burns himself.
488:
Māra, just as a fool who touches a burning fire burns himself, so too will you, by offending the Tathāgata, burn yourself. You shall not escape the suffering of hell. Māra, you increase your demerit by offending the Tathāgata. O Evil One, how do you think that your evil deed will not bear fruit for me? Indeed, for one who does evil, only misfortune and suffering arise. O Evil One, do you not realize that for you, who do evil, misfortune and suffering will accumulate for a long time? Māra, do not offend or harass the monks who are disciples of the Buddha.

Thus did the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna threaten Māra in the Bhesakaḷā Forest. Then that evil spirit, becoming dejected, vanished right there. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna Thera spoke these verses. These were placed in a certain collection in this order.

Among those verses, the four verses beginning with "Āraññika" were spoken as an instruction to the monks. "Āraññika" refers to those monks who undertake the forest-dweller's practice (āraññaka-dhutaṅga), rejecting dwellings near villages and living in forest dwellings. "Piṇḍapātika" refers to those monks who reject communal meals (saṅghabhatta), undertake the alms-food eater's practice (piṇḍapātika-dhutaṅga), and sustain themselves with alms-food obtained by going from house to house. "Uñchāpattāgate ratā" means those who delight only in the alms-food that has entered their bowl through begging, and are content with that alone. "Dālemu maccuno senaṃ" means one should destroy the army of defilements, which is like an ally of the King of Death, leading to one's own harm. "Ajjhattaṃ susamāhitā" means being well-concentrated on one's own meditation object; this is stated as the means for destroying the defilements. "Dhunāma" means "we shall destroy" or "we shall demolish" (viddhaṃsema). "Sātatika" refers to those who have persistent energy, constantly striving in meditation.

The four verses beginning with "Aṭṭhikaṅkalakuṭike" were spoken as an instruction to a courtesan who came to tempt him. There, "Aṭṭhikaṅkalakuṭike" means the little hut made of a skeleton. "Nhārupasibbite" means stitched all around with nine hundred tendons. Just as in the forest, little huts are made by erecting wooden posts and binding them with creepers, you are shown to be a most loathsome thing, a skeleton bound together by most loathsome tendons. "Dhiratthu pūਰੇ duggandhe" means: look at your body, which is full of various impurities such as hair and body hair, and is foul-smelling, as something loathsome. "Paragatte mamāyase" means: do not be attached to this body, which is like a danger arising upon your foul-smelling self, and regard it as the body of another, a collection of foul-smelling impurities. Such an impure, foul-smelling, and loathsome body is for dogs, jackals, and worms...
489:
In the forest, little huts are made by erecting wooden posts and binding them with creepers and such. But you are shown to be extremely loathsome and repulsive, for you are a skeleton made by being bound with most loathsome tendons.

"Dhiratthu pūre duggandhe" means: may the state of loathsomeness be upon you, who are foul-smelling because you are filled with various kinds of impure things such as hair and body hair. "Paragatte mamāyase" means: you cherish this carcass, which is the body of others—such as dogs, jackals, and swarms of worms—in another place, which is similarly impure, foul-smelling, loathsome, and repulsive, along with the dangers that arise upon your foul smell.

"Gūthabhaste" means like a leather bag filled with dung. "Taconaddhe" means a body full of faults, covered only by the outer skin. "Uragaṇ膽ipisācinī" means like a demoness because of having two lumps on the chest, because of being terrifying, and because of bringing harm. "Yāni sandanti sabbadā" means those nine openings (wound-mouths) which always, day and night, flow, leak, and exude impure things.

"Paribandha" means an obstacle to the right practice. "Bhikkhū" means a monk who sees danger in saṃsāra or who has destroyed defilements; he should not cherish that body but should avoid it from afar. In the phrase "Mīḷhañca yathā sucikāmo", "ca" is merely a particle. Just as a person of pure nature who desires only purity, having bathed including the head, avoids dung from afar upon seeing it, so too should a monk avoid it.

"Evañce taṃ jano jaññā yathā jānāmi taṃ ahaṃ" means: if people knew this heap of impurity called the body as I know it truly, they would avoid that body from afar. "Gūthaဋ္ဌာနံဝ pāvuse" means it is like a person of pure nature avoiding a place of wet dung during the rainy season. However, because they do not know that loathsomeness as it truly is, they are submerged in that dung and cannot lift their heads.

When the Elder thus revealed the faults of the body, that courtesan, bowing her head in shame and showing respect to the Elder, spoke the verse beginning with "Evametaṃ mahāvīra" and stood there after paying homage to the Elder. In that verse, "Ettha ca eke" means: even though it is of such an obviously repulsive nature, some beings, due to the strength of their attachment, sink into this body. How? It is just like an old ox without strength that perishes in the mud. Then, wishing to show her, "Such conduct toward a person like me is not only useless but only causes weariness of mind," he spoke the two verses beginning with "Ākāsamhī".
490: (Beings) reach a state of despair. Just as an old ox fallen into the middle of a great mire and weakened reaches destruction, so too do they reach only destruction. Furthermore, the Elder, wishing to show that courtesan, "Such practice toward one like me is useless and brings only weariness," spoke two verses beginning with "Ākāsamhī." The meaning of those verses is: If a person should intend to paint the sky with turmeric or any other dye, that action of his would only bring weariness of mind. It is like making an effort in what is not one's domain. "That mind of mine is like the sky" means this mind of mine is not attached to any object and is well-concentrated within itself. Therefore, it means, "Do not offend one like me with a base mind." Do not offend one like me with a low, inferior mind due to being submerged in sensual pleasures. "Like a moth flying into a fire" means just as a moth reaches ruin and misfortune by attacking a mass of fire, so too will this state of yours be. The seven verses beginning with "Passa cittakataṃ" were spoken as an exhortation to the monks whose minds were distorted upon seeing that courtesan. Upon hearing those words, the courtesan, feeling ashamed, fled back the way she came. The four verses beginning with "Tadāsi" were spoken concerning the Parinibbāna of the Venerable Sāriputta Thera. Therein, "anekākārasampanna" means endowed with many varieties such as the restraint of virtue (sīla-saṃvara). "They pierce the subtle meaning" means those practitioners (yogis) penetrate the extremely subtle. How? It is like hitting a hair-tip with an arrow, or like being able to hit a single strand of hair split into a hundred parts in the pitch black of night by the flash of lightning; such is the meaning (of subtle penetration). Who are they? He said, "Those who see the five aggregates as other (para) and not as self (atta)." Therein, "parato" means seeing by way of non-self (anatta). This is said to show the rejection of the grasping of a self. Therefore, he said, "and not as self." By this, he spoke of the breakthrough of full understanding (pariññābhisamaya) regarding the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca) by power of the Noble Path that has arisen through the view of non-self. Because it is inseparable from the knowledge of the Truth of Suffering, it should be understood that the penetration of the other Truths is also well-stated. Some teachers, however, say, "Because the five aggregates of clinging bring about what is not beneficial, they are called 'other' (para); therefore, by the words 'parato passanti,' everything is well-stated." "Paccavyādhiṃsu" means they pierced or penetrated.
491:
The first verse, "Sattiyā viya omaṭṭho," was spoken concerning Tissa Thera. The second verse was spoken concerning Vaḍḍhamāna Thera. These have the same meaning as explained below.

The verse "Codito bhāvitattena" was spoken concerning the Pāsādakampana Suttanta. Therein, "bhāvitattena" (by one of developed self) refers to the Blessed One, the bearer of his final body.

The two verses beginning with "Nayidaṃ sithilamārabbha" were spoken concerning a young monk named Veda who was of lax energy. Therein, "sithilamārabbha" means making effort laxly, without exerting energy. "Appena thāmasā" means this Nibbāna cannot be attained with a small amount of power of energy; rather, it is to be reached only with the great fourfold Right Effort (sammappadhāna-vīriya).

The two verses beginning with "Vivaramanupabhanti" were spoken concerning his own state of seclusion. Therein, "brahmunā abhivandito" means one who is praised and worshipped by the Great Brahma together with the world of devas and humans, standing before him.

The five verses beginning with "Upasantaṃ uparataṃ" were spoken when [the Venerable Sāriputta] saw a brahmin of wrong view, his own nephew, who, upon seeing the Elder Mahā Kassapa entering Rājagaha for alms, stood looking and said, "I have seen an ill omen (kāḷakaṇṇī)." Out of compassion for him, thinking "May this brahmin not be ruined," and to prevent the resentment of insulting an Ariya, he urged him, saying, "Pay homage to the Elder." In those verses, "jātisataṃ gacche" means one might reach a hundred births [as a brahmin]. "Sottiyo" means one of brahmin birth. "Vedasampanno" means one endowed with knowledge. "Etassa" refers to that Elder. The summary of the meaning here is: If a person should be born into a succession of a hundred highly distinguished and pure brahmin lineages, and therein reach perfection in the arts of the brahmins, becoming a master of the three Vedas and fulfilling the duties of a brahmin—that undertaking of knowledge and practice of his is not worth even a sixteenth part of the merit consisting of paying homage to this Elder Mahā Kassapa. The merit consisting of paying homage is far greater than that.

"Aṭṭha vimokkhāni" refers to the eight liberations, such as the fine-material jhānas. Indeed, the fine-material jhānas obtained by the power of meditation are called "liberations" (vimokkha) because they are well-liberated from opposing states and because they proceed without attachment to the object due to delight. The attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) is also a liberation because it is liberated from opposing states. However, in this context, only the jhānas should be understood.
492:
Forward and backward (Anuloma Paṭiloma) means: entering the attainments in successive order starting from the first jhāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is called 'forward' (anuloma); entering them in reverse order starting from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception down to the first jhāna is called 'backward' (paṭiloma). 'Before the meal' (Purebhatta) means only before the time of the meal duties. 'He touched' (Aphassayi) means he entered into many various kinds of meditative attainments. 'From there he goes for alms' (Tato piṇḍāya gacchati) means after emerging from that attainment, or after having entered that attainment, he now goes for the sake of alms; this is said in reference to the practice of the Elder that occurred on that day. The Elder, however, practiced in that very way every single day.

'Do not offend such a monk' (Tādisaṃ bhikkhuṃ māsādehi) means: do not offend such a monk, a great Arahant who follows the will of the Buddha, who possesses such qualities as have been partially mentioned. O Brahmin, do not dig up (destroy) yourself by offending or by accusing a Noble One (Ariya); do not destroy your own wholesome states (kusala dhamma). 'Gladden the mind' (Abhippasādehi manaṃ) means: make your own mind clear and confident, thinking, "This monk is indeed of a good nature."

'May your head not split' (Mā te vijaṭi matthakaṃ) means: may your head not split into seven pieces due to the offense committed against the Venerable Mahākassapa. Therefore, to remedy that offense, quickly pay homage with joined palms. Upon hearing those words, the Brahmin became terrified and anxious, with his hair standing on end, and he immediately asked the Elder for forgiveness.

The two verses beginning with 'He does not see' (Neso passati) were spoken by way of admonition upon seeing the monk named Poṭṭhila who was not practicing correctly and was engaged in wrong livelihood. In those verses, 'He does not see the True Dhamma' (Neso passati saddhammaṃ) means: this monk Poṭṭhila does not see the Dhamma of the virtuous ones such as the Buddhas, which consists of the Path, Fruit, and Nibbāna. Why is that? Because he is surrounded by the bonds of the round of rebirths (saṃsāra) such as ignorance, and because it leads to rebirth in the lower realms, he follows a downward path; because he follows deceit and hypocrisy, he pursues a crooked path which is the wrong path, a wrong livelihood which is a bad path.

'Like a worm smeared with dung' (Kimīva mīḷhasallitto) means: like a dung-worm smeared all over with excrement, he is deeply immersed and involved in conditioned things (saṅkhāra) mixed with the impurities of defilements. 'Deeply immersed in gain and honor' (Pagāḷho lābhasakkāre) means: he is profoundly and intensely sunk in gain and honor through the power of craving. 'Empty Poṭṭhila goes' (Tuccho gacchati poṭṭhilo) means: because he lacks the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā), the monk Poṭṭhila exists (goes about) being empty and without essence.
493:
The two verses beginning with 'And look at this one' (Imañca passa) were spoken in praise of the Venerable Sāriputta. In those verses, 'And look at this one' (Imañca passa) refers to seeing the Venerable Sāriputta Elder and, with a mind of faith, addressing (clearing) one's own mind. 'Beautiful to behold' (Sudassana) means having a beautiful vision because of the fulfillment of the aggregates of virtue of an Asekha (one beyond training) and the fulfillment of the knowledge of a disciple's perfection (sāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa). 'Liberated in both ways' (Ubhatobhāge) means he is called 'one liberated in both ways' (ubhatobhāgavimutta) because he is liberated from both sides. This means he is liberated from the material body (rūpakāya) by formless attainments and from the mental body (nāmakāya) by the Path, through the respective parts of abandonment by suppression (vikkhambhana) and abandonment by eradication (samuccheda). He is called 'free from the dart' (Visalla) because of the total absence of the darts of lust and so on. He is 'one whose fetters are destroyed' (Khīṇasaṃyoga) because the bonds (yogas) of sense-desire and so on are completely exhausted. He is 'one with triple knowledge' (Tevijja) because he has attained the three very pure knowledges. The construction is: 'Look at the one who has abandoned death' (Maccuhāyinaṃ passā) because he has broken the King of Death.

The verses beginning with 'These many' (Ete sambahulā) were spoken by the Venerable Sāriputta in praise of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. In those verses, 'Honored by the god of men' (Pūjito naradevena) means he is honored with supreme worship by both humans and gods. 'Arisen, overcoming death' (Uppanno maraṇābhibhū) means having arisen in the world, he remains having overcome death. Alternatively, 'honored by the god of men' refers to the Fully Enlightened Buddha who is the teacher and the cause; he is arisen by the Noble birth. For the Fully Enlightened Buddha was first a human being by way of karma, but later by the Noble birth, he became the supreme God, the God above gods (Devātideva); therefore, he is called 'God of men' (Naradeva). Honored by the Blessed One, the God of men, by way of praise, though arisen in a world overcome by death, he is one who overcomes death, one who abandons death. 'Like a lotus by the water' (Puṇဍarīkaṃva toyena) means: just like a white lotus in water, he is not smeared by the smearing of craving and views regarding conditioned things; the meaning is that he is not dependent on anything anywhere.

'Whose' (Yassa) means 'by whom' (by Ven. Mahāmoggallāna). 'In a moment' (Muhutte) means in a mere moment of time. 'In a thousand ways' (Sahassadhā) means in a thousandfold manner. 'The world' (Loko) refers to the world of space (okāsaloka). The meaning here is: by that Venerable Mahāmoggallāna of great psychic power, the thousandfold world system is well known and personally realized in just a moment; he is like a Great Brahma, having attained mastery in reflection and so on, and having psychic perfection, he is a master of passing away and rebirth. 'He sees at the time' (Kāle passati) means he sees deities with the divine eye at the appropriate time.

The verses beginning with 'Like Sāriputta' (Sāriputtova) were spoken by the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna declaring his own qualities. In those verses, 'Like Sāriputta' (Sāriputtova) means...
494:
The summary meaning of the verse is: By wisdom (the perfection of wisdom), by virtue (the perfection of virtue), and by tranquility (the calming of defilements), that monk has reached the far shore, the highest pinnacle. That Sāriputta has reached the supreme pinnacle among the disciples through qualities such as wisdom. Indeed, he has reached the supreme pinnacle through wisdom and virtue. This alone should be the highest limit; there is nothing beyond that. However, the Elder [Moggallāna] spoke this to show: 'Just as Sāriputta is supreme in wisdom, so I am supreme in concentration.' Therefore, he said 'Koṭisata-sahassassa,' and so on.

In that text, 'khaṇena nimmiṇe' means he can create a hundred thousand forms in a single moment; he is capable of such creation. In that creation, there is no burden for me. 'Vikkubbanāsu kusalo, vasībhūtomhi iddhiyā' means he has attained mastery not only in mental transformations but in all psychic powers.

'Samādhivijjāvasipāramīgato' means he has reached the pinnacle of mastery in concentrations such as those with initial and sustained thought, and in knowledges such as the recollection of past lives. In the teaching of the Teacher, who is free from dependence on craving and so on, he has reached the pinnacle through the aforementioned qualities. He is called 'Dhīra' because he is endowed with firm effort; 'Moggallāna' because he is of the Moggallāna clan; 'Samāhitindriya' because his faculties are well-composed. Just as a noble elephant easily breaks a bond of rotten creepers, so he has completely cut all bonds of defilements.

The verses beginning with 'Kīdiso nirayo āsi' were spoken by the Elder while threatening Māra, who had stood there after entering and then leaving [the Elder's] belly. In those verses, 'kīdiso' means of what kind. 'Yattha dūsī' means in which hell the Māra named 'Dūsī' was cooked. 'Apaccatha' means being cooked by the fires of hell. 'Vidhuraṃ sāvakaṃ' refers to the chief disciple of the Blessed One Kakusandha, named Vidhura. 'Āsajja' means having struck or harassed. 'Kakusandhañca brāhmaṇaṃ' means having struck the Perfectly Enlightened One Kakusandha. The pebble thrown by Māra, who had possessed a boy with the intent of harming the Blessed One, fell on the Elder's head.

'Sataṃ āsi ayosaṅkū': It is said that those born in that hell have a body three gāvutas in height; Dūsī Māra's body was also like that. Then the hell-wardens, taking a hundred iron spikes the size of palm trunks, glowing, blazing, and radiant, [struck him], saying, 'You stood in this very place and committed evil with your mind.' They struck the middle of his chest as if pounding lime in a lime-pit. Fifty beings went towards the feet...
495:
...standing in such a place, thinking 'I have committed evil with my mind,' they strike the middle of the chest as if pounding lime in a lime-pit. Fifty beings strike towards the feet, and fifty beings strike towards the head. Moving in this way, they reach both ends in five hundred years, and returning again, they reach the middle of the chest in five hundred years. With reference to that, it was said: 'There were a hundred iron spikes.' 'Sabbé paccatta-vedanā' means they themselves are the generators of their individual feelings. 

It is heard that such a feeling is more painful than the suffering of the Great Hell (Mahā Niraya). How so? Just as the seven days of medical treatment (parihāra) are more painful than the seven days of drinking medicinal oil, so the feeling upon emerging from the Great Hell into the Ussada Hell is more painful than the suffering of the Great Hell itself. Regarding the fact that such a hell existed, the nature of hell should be explained here using the Devadūta Sutta.

'Yo etam-abhijānāti' means that person with great direct knowledge (abhiññā) knows this directly, as if seeing a myrobalan fruit (āmalaka) placed in the palm of the hand. 'Bhikkhu buddhassa sāvako' means a monk who has destroyed defilements is a disciple of the Perfectly Enlightened One. 'Kaṇha, dukkhaṃ nigacchasi' means: 'O Dark One (Māra), because you are possessed of entirely black, evil states, you will experience suffering.'

'Majjhesarasmim' means it is heard that there are mansions (vimāna) that arise based on the water in the middle of the great ocean, which last for the duration of an aeon. Therefore, he said, 'The mansions are aeon-lasting.' Their color is like that of beryl (veḷuriya). Their flames shine like a mass of burning reeds on a mountain top. Thus, those mansions are exceedingly radiant and endowed with splendor. Therefore, he said, 'Beryl-colored, beautiful, flaming, and radiant.' 'Puthu nānattavaṇṇiyo' means many celestial nymphs of various colors, such as blue and so on, dance in those mansions.

'Yo etam-abhijānāti' means the one who knows the nature of these mansions by direct experience. This meaning should be illustrated by the Vimānavatthu and Petavatthu.

'Buddhena codito' means urged or exhorted by the Perfectly Enlightened One. 'Bhikkhusaṅghassa pekkhato' means while the great Saṅgha of monks was looking on. 'Migāramātupāsādaṃ pādaṅguṭṭhena kampayī' means: 'I shook the great palace, adorned with a thousand rooms, built and offered by the great lay devotee Visākhā at Pubbārāma, with my big toe.' How so? On one occasion, at the aforementioned palace in Pubbārāma...
496:
While the Blessed One was staying [there], many newly ordained monks were sitting in the upper palace and, without regard for the Teacher, began to engage in 'animal talk' (tiracchānakathā). Hearing this, the Blessed One, wishing to cause them spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and make them fit vessels for his Dhamma teaching, addressed the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna: 'Moggallāna, do you see the new monks devoted to animal talk?' Hearing this, the Elder, understanding the Teacher's intention, entered the fourth jhāna which is the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā) using the water-kasina (āpokasiṇa) as the object. Emerging from that jhāna, he made a resolution: 'Let the place where the palace stands become water,' and then struck the pinnacle at the top of the palace with his big toe. The palace tilted and stood on one side. He struck it again, and it stood on the other side. Those monks, terrified and agitated, fearing the palace would fall, left from there and stood near the Blessed One. The Teacher, observing their inclinations, taught the Dhamma. After hearing it, some were established in the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpattiphala), some in the fruit of once-returning (sakadāgāmiphala), some in the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala), and some in the fruit of arahantship (arahattaphala). This matter should be understood through the Pāsādakampana Sutta.

The Vejayanta Palace is a palace in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, a thousand yojanas in height, adorned with many thousands of pinnacles and gabled chambers. It is called 'Vejayanta' because it arose for Sakka, the lord of the devas, after he conquered the asuras in the battle between the devas and asuras and stood in the center of the city. It was this palace that the Elder also shook with his big toe. On one occasion, Sakka, the king of devas, approached the Blessed One and asked about the liberation through the destruction of craving (taṇhāsaṅkhayavimutti). The Blessed One answered him. Having heard it, Sakka was delighted and joyful; he paid homage, circumambulated the Blessed One, and returned to his own deva realm. Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna thought: 'This Sakka approached the Blessed One and asked such a profound question connected with Nibbāna, and the Blessed One answered the question. Did he go away having understood it, or without understanding it? What if I were to go to the deva realm and find out?' He immediately went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and asked Sakka, the lord of devas, about that matter. Sakka, being negligent due to divine luxury, spoke distractedly. To produce spiritual urgency in him, the Elder shook the Vejayanta Palace with his big toe. Therefore, it is said: 'That Venerable Mahāmoggallāna shook the Vejayanta Palace with his big toe and caused the devas to be agitated.'
497:
“That Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, who by the power of his psychic potency, shook the Vejayanta Palace with his big toe and stirred the deities with emotion” (as taught in Majjhima Nikāya, 1, 513).

The meaning of this verse should be understood through the Cūḷataṇhāsaṅkhayavimutti Sutta (MN 1, 390 etc.). The manner of the shaking should be understood exactly as stated below.

“He questions Sakka” means, as already stated, the Elder refers to the question regarding the Fruition of Arahantship through the destruction of craving (taṇhāsaṅkhayavimutti). Therefore, he said, “Friend Sakka, do you know the liberations through the destruction of craving?” “Sakka answered him” refers to the fact that when the Elder shook the palace, Sakka, with a stirred heart, abandoned heedlessness, applied wise attention (yoniso manasikāra), and answered the question. At that time, Sakka answered exactly according to the method taught by the Blessed One. Therefore, it is said, “He answered the question as it really was.” In that verse, “He questions Sakka” means that the Elder Moggallāna questioned Sakka, the king of devas, to see whether he had properly grasped the liberation through the destruction of craving taught by the Blessed One. Here, the present tense “pari-pucchati” (questions) carries a past sense. “Friend, do you know?” means “Friend Sakka, do you know as the Blessed One taught you the liberations through the destruction of craving?” Or, “taṇhākkhayavimuttiyo” refers to questioning about the teaching of the Cūḷataṇhāsaṅkhayavimutti Sutta.

“Brahmānaṃ” refers to Mahābrahmā. “Standing in the Sudhammā hall” means one who stands in the assembly hall named Sudhammā. This Sudhammā hall is the one in the Brahma world, not the Sudhammā hall in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. There is no deva world that is without a Sudhammā hall. “Friend, do you still have that view which you had before?” is a prompt questioning: “Friend, that wrong view you had before the Blessed One came here—that there is no ascetic or brahmin capable of coming to this Brahma world—has it not yet disappeared even now?” “Do you see the radiant one passing through the Brahma world?” means: “Do you see the radiance of the Blessed One who, surrounded by disciples such as Venerable Mahākappina and Venerable Mahākassapa, sits having entered the fire element (tejodhātu) and is passing here and there in the Brahma world?” In detail: on one occasion, while the Blessed One was seated in the Sudhammā hall of the Brahma world, he knew the thought of a Brahma who was thinking, “Is there any ascetic or brahmin with such great psychic power who could come here?” The Blessed One then went to that Brahma world, stayed in the air above the Brahma's head, entered the fire element, emitted light, and intended for disciples like Venerable Mahāmoggallāna to come. As soon as he intended, those Elders including Moggallāna also arrived at the Brahma world, paid homage to the Blessed One, and knowing the Blessed One's wish, they each entered the fire element and stayed in various directions, emitting their own radiances.
498:
The Blessed One, knowing the thought in the mind of the Brahma, went to that Brahma realm and sat in the sky above the Brahma's head. Entering the fire element (tejo-dhātu) and emitting radiance, he thought of the coming of disciples such as the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. Simultaneously with his thought, those elders, including the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, also went to that Brahma realm, paid homage to the Blessed One, and knowing the Blessed One's intention, entered the fire element. Sitting in various directions and emitting radiance, the entire Brahma realm became filled with a single mass of radiance. The Blessed One, knowing that the Brahma had a mind ready (to hear the Dhamma), preached the Dhamma that reveals the Four Noble Truths. At the end of the teaching, many thousands of Brahmas were established in the paths and fruits. Referring to that matter, he spoke a verse, urging him: "Friend, do you still hold that view today?" This meaning should be understood through the Baka Brahma Sutta. It is also stated thus (in the Saṃyutta Nikāya):

"At one time, the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. At that time, a certain Brahma had developed such an evil view: 'There is no ascetic (samana) or brahmin who can come here.' Then the Blessed One, knowing the thought in that Brahma's mind with his own mind—just as a strong man might stretch out his bent arm or bend his outstretched arm—disappeared from Jeta's Grove and appeared in that Brahma realm. Then the Blessed One sat cross-legged in the sky above that Brahma, having entered the fire element.

Then it occurred to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna: 'Where is the Blessed One staying now?' The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna saw the Blessed One with the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), purified and surpassing that of humans, sitting cross-legged in the sky above that Brahma, having entered the fire element. Having seen him—just as a strong man might stretch out his bent arm or bend his outstretched arm—he disappeared from Jeta's Grove and appeared in that Brahma realm. Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, relying on the eastern direction, sat..."
499:
(Venerable Mahāmoggallāna) sat cross-legged in the sky above that Brahma, having entered the fire element, at a lower level than the Blessed One.

Then it occurred to the Venerable Mahākassapa: 'Where is the Blessed One staying now?' The Venerable Mahākassapa saw the Blessed One with the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), purified and surpassing that of humans, sitting cross-legged in the sky above that Brahma, having entered the fire element. Having seen him—just as a strong man might stretch out his bent arm or bend his outstretched arm—this same way he disappeared from Jeta's Grove and appeared in that Brahma realm. Then the Venerable Mahākassapa, relying on the southern direction, sat cross-legged in the sky above that Brahma, having entered the fire element, at a lower level than the Blessed One.

Then it occurred to the Venerable Mahākappina: 'Where is the Blessed One staying now?' The Venerable Mahākappina saw the Blessed One with the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), purified and surpassing that of humans, sitting cross-legged in the sky above that Brahma, having entered the fire element. Having seen him (etc.), this same way he disappeared from Jeta's Grove and appeared in that Brahma realm. Then the Venerable Mahākappina, relying on the western direction, sat cross-legged in the sky above that Brahma, having entered the fire element, at a lower level than the Blessed One.

Then it occurred to the Venerable Anuruddha: 'Where is the Blessed One staying now?' The Venerable Anuruddha saw the Blessed One with the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), purified and surpassing that of humans, sitting cross-legged in the sky above that Brahma, having entered the fire element. Having seen him (etc.), this same way he disappeared from Jeta's Grove and appeared in that Brahma realm. Then the Venerable Anuruddha, relying on the northern direction, sat cross-legged in the sky above that Brahma, having entered the fire element, at a lower level than the Blessed One.
500:
Venerable Mahākappina, relying on the western direction, sat cross-legged in the sky above that Brahma, entering the fire element (tejo-dhātu), and remained at a lower seat than the Blessed One. At that time, the thought occurred to Venerable Anuruddha: "Where is the Blessed One staying now?" With the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), which is especially purified and surpasses human vision, Venerable Anuruddha saw the Blessed One sitting cross-legged in the sky above that Brahma, having entered the fire element. Having seen this, just as a strong man might stretch out his bent arm or bend his outstretched arm, he vanished from the Jetavana Monastery and appeared in that Brahma world. Then, Venerable Anuruddha, relying on the northern direction, sat cross-legged in the sky above that Brahma, entering the fire element, and remained at a lower seat than the Blessed One.

Then, Venerable Mahāmoggallāna addressed that Brahma in verse:

"Friend, do you still have that view which you held before?
Do you see the exceedingly radiant aura (of the Buddha) spreading here and there in the Brahma world?"

(The Brahma replied:)
"Sir, I no longer have that view which I held before.
I see the exceedingly radiant aura spreading here and there in the Brahma world.
How could I say today, 'I am permanent, I am eternal'?"

Then the Blessed One, having caused that Brahma to be stirred with awe, just as a strong man might stretch out his bent arm or bend his outstretched arm, vanished from that Brahma world and appeared in the Jetavana Monastery. Then that Brahma addressed one of the Brahmas of his retinue (Brahmapārisajja): "Come, friend, go to Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. Having approached him, say this to Venerable Mahāmoggallāna: 'Sir Moggallāna, are there other disciples of the Blessed One who possess such great psychic power and such great majesty as you, Moggallāna, and Kassapa, Kappina, and Anuruddha?'"

"Yes, sir," that Brahma of the retinue replied to that Brahma, and approached Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. Having approached, he said this to Venerable Mahāmoggallāna: "Sir Moggallāna, are there other disciples of the Blessed One who possess such great psychic power and such great majesty as you, Moggallāna, and Kassapa, Kappina, and Anuruddha?"

Then Venerable Mahāmoggallāna addressed that Brahma of the retinue in verse:

"Possessors of the three knowledges, attained to psychic power,
Skilled in the knowledge of others' minds,
With taints destroyed, they are Arahants;
Many are the disciples of the Buddha."

Then that Brahma of the retinue, having greatly rejoiced and appreciated the words of Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, approached that Brahma and said this to him: "Sir, Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this:"

(The following are explanations found in the Nissaya:)
"Mahāneru" refers to the entire King of Mountains, Sineru, from its peak downwards. "Vimuttiyā assayī" means seeing with the direct knowledge (abhiññā) that follows the observation of liberation at the ninth moment. "Vana" refers to the island of Jambudīpa; it is called "Vana" (forest) because it is abundant in forests. Therefore, it is said, "The lake of Jambudīpa." "Pubbavidehānaṃ" refers to the region (island) of Pubbavideha.
501:
"Possessors of the three knowledges, attained to psychic power,
Skilled in the knowledge of others' minds,
With taints destroyed, they are Arahants;
Many are the disciples of the Buddha."

That Brahma of the retinue spoke these words. And that Brahma was delighted and rejoiced in the words of that Brahma of the retinue.

With reference to this meaning, it is said: "This point should be understood through the Baka Brahma Sutta."

"Mahāneruno kūṭaṃ" refers to the entire King of Mountains, Sineru, by way of its peak. "Vimokkhena aphassayi" means he touched (realized) it through direct knowledge based on the liberation of meditative absorption (jhāna-vimokkha). "Vanaṃ" refers to the island of Jambudīpa. It is called "Vana" because of its abundance of forests. Therefore, it is said, "The Lord of the Jambu grove." "Pubbavidehānaṃ" means the place of Pubbavideha, the island of Pubbavideha. "The men who sleep on the ground" refers to the humans of Aparagoyāna and Uttarakuru. They are called "those who sleep on the ground" because they have no houses. The connection is that he touched (realized) all of them as well.

This matter should be explained by the section on the taming of the Naga King Nandopananda:

On one occasion, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, after listening to the Dhamma teaching of the Blessed One, invited him, saying, "Venerable Sir, please accept alms at my house tomorrow together with five hundred monks," and then departed. At the time of dawn on that day, while the Blessed One was surveying the ten thousand world-systems, the Naga King named Nandopananda appeared within the net of his knowledge. The Blessed One, reflecting, "This Naga King has appeared in my knowledge; what will happen?" saw the potential (upanissaya) for him to take refuge. Reflecting, "This Naga has wrong view and does not yet have faith in the Three Jewels; who can release this Naga from wrong view?" he saw the Elder Mahāmoggallāna.

When the night had passed and it was dawn, after attending to his physical needs, the Blessed One addressed Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, inform the five hundred monks that the Tathāgata is going on a journey to the celestial realms." On that very day, a drinking place was prepared for the Naga King Nandopananda. That Naga King was sitting on a divine jeweled throne, shaded by a divine white parasol, surrounded by three types of dancers and a retinue of Nagas, looking at the beverages placed in divine vessels. Then the Blessed One, making it so that the Naga King could see, proceeded towards the Tāvatiṃsa heaven above the mansion of that Naga King together with the five hundred monks. At that time, an evil wrong view arose in the Naga King Nandopananda: "These shaven-headed monks are passing back and forth to the Tāvatiṃsa celestial mansion above our mansion. From now on, these monks will let the dust from their feet fall upon our heads."
502:
Nandopananda the Naga King sat watching the preparations of drinks set out in the cups of the gods. At that time, the Blessed One, making himself visible to the Naga King, traveled towards the Tāvatiṃsa heaven with five hundred monks, passing directly over the Naga King’s mansion.

Then, an evil view arose in Nandopananda the Naga King: "These shaven-headed ascetics enter and leave the mansion of the Tāvatiṃsa gods by passing over our mansion. From now on, I will not allow them to go scattering the dust of their feet over us." Thinking thus, he rose and went to the foot of Mount Sineru. Abandoning his [usual] Naga form, he coiled around Mount Sineru seven times with his coils, and spreading his hood above, he covered the Tāvatiṃsa heaven with his downturned hood, making it invisible.

Then, the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, previously standing in this place, I could see Mount Sineru, I could see the terraces of Sineru, I could see Tāvatiṃsa, I could see the Vejayanta mansion, and I could see the banner atop the Vejayanta palace. Venerable Sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, that I now see neither Mount Sineru... nor the banner atop the Vejayanta palace?" "Raṭṭhapāla, this Naga King named Nandopananda, being angry with you all, has coiled around Mount Sineru seven times with his coils and, covering it from above with his hood, has created a mass of darkness," the Blessed One replied. "Venerable Sir, I shall subdue him," Raṭṭhapāla said, but the Blessed One did not permit him. Then, the Venerable Bhaddiya, the Venerable Rāhula, and all the monks in succession rose and made the request, but the Blessed One did not permit them.

Finally, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna said, "Venerable Sir, I shall subdue him." "Moggallāna, subdue him," the Blessed One permitted. The Elder, abandoning his [human] form, created a massive Naga form and coiled around the Naga Nandopananda fourteen times. Placing his own hood above the Naga’s hood, he pressed him against Mount Sineru. The Naga King emitted smoke. The Elder also emitted smoke, saying, "There is smoke not only in your body; there is also in mine." The Naga King’s smoke did not harm the Elder, but the Elder’s smoke harmed the Naga King. Then the Naga King emitted flames. The Elder also emitted flames, saying, "There is fire not only in your body; there is also in mine." The Naga King’s heat did not harm the Elder, but the Elder’s heat harmed the Naga King. The Naga King thought, "This person is pressing me against Mount Sineru and emitting both smoke and flames," and he asked, "Friend, who are you?" "Nanda, I am Moggallāna," the Elder replied. "Venerable Sir, please remain in your own form as a monk," the Naga King said. The Elder...
503:
...and emitting flames," he thought, and asked, "Friend, who are you?" "Nanda, I am Moggallāna," (the Elder replied). "Venerable Sir, please remain in your own form as a monk," (the Naga King) requested.

The Elder, abandoning that [Naga] form, entered the Naga King’s right ear-hole and exited through the left; he entered the left ear-hole and exited through the right. Similarly, he entered the right nostril and exited through the left; he entered the left nostril and exited through the right. Then the Naga King opened his mouth. The Elder entered through the mouth and walked back and forth in the stomach, from the front to the back. The Blessed One said, "Moggallāna, be mindful; the Naga is of great power." The Elder replied, "Venerable Sir, the four bases of psychic power (iddhipāda) have been developed by me, practiced frequently, made into a vehicle, made into a foundation, established, consolidated, and well-undertaken. Venerable Sir, let alone Nandopananda, I could subdue hundreds, thousands, or even hundreds of thousands of Naga Kings like Nandopananda."

The Naga King thought, "I did not see him when he first entered. Now, when he comes out, I will place him between my fangs and crunch him well." He then said, "Venerable Sir, please come out. Do not trouble me by walking back and forth inside my stomach." The Elder came out and stood outside. The Naga King, seeing him and thinking, "This is the one," blew a blast of air from his nose. The Elder entered the fourth jhāna, so that air was unable to move even a single hair on his body. (Knowing that) "The other monks might be able to perform all the miracles from the beginning, but upon reaching this point, they would not be able to enter jhāna so quickly," the Blessed One had not permitted those monks to subdue the Naga King.

The Naga King thought, "I was unable to move even a single hair of this ascetic with the air from my nose. This ascetic is indeed of great power." The Elder, abandoning his [Naga] form, created the form of a Garuda and, showing the wind of a Garuda, pursued the Naga King. The Naga King, abandoning his Naga form, created the form of a young man and, saying, "Venerable Sir, I go to you for refuge," bowed at the Elder’s feet. The Elder said, "Nanda, the Teacher has come. Come, let us go," and having subdued the Naga King and made him harmless, he took him and...
504:
Having subdued the dragon king and rendered him harmless, he led him to the presence of the Blessed One. The dragon king paid homage to the Blessed One and said, "Venerable Sir, I go to the Blessed One for refuge."

The Blessed One said, "May you be happy, dragon king," and then, surrounded by the community of monks, proceeded to the house of Anāthapiṇḍika.

Anāthapiṇḍika asked, "Venerable Sir, why have you come so late in the day?" The Buddha replied, "A battle took place between Moggallāna and the dragon king Nandopananda." "Venerable Sir, who won and who was defeated?" "Moggallāna won, and Nandopananda was defeated."

Anāthapiṇḍika then requested, "Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One accept my alms for seven consecutive days. For seven days, I shall perform great offerings and honors to the Elder." Having said this, he performed a great ceremony of offerings for seven days to the five hundred monks headed by the Buddha. Therefore, it is said, "It should be shown by the subduing of Nandopananda."

"Yo etamabhijānāti" means knowing that aforementioned liberation (vimokkha) by way of experiencing it.

Just as fire does not think, "I shall burn the fool," nor does it make an effort or exertion to burn, yet the fool, thinking "This fire is slow," touches the blazing fire as if it were not burning and is thus burned; even so, Mara, we have no desire to burn or to oppress. You alone, by coming in such a manner, have touched the Tathāgata and the Noble Disciple who are like a great mass of fire, and you will burn yourself; you shall not escape the suffering of being burned.

"Apuññaṃ pasavi" means acquiring demerit. "Na me pāpaṃ vipaccati" means "Evil does not bear fruit for me." Mara, why do you think so? It is not thus.

"Karoto te cīyate pāpaṃ" means that for you who are indeed committing it, evil is accumulated for your harm and suffering for a long time. "Mara, nibbinda Buddhamhā" means, Mara, be weary of offending the Buddha—who knows the Four Noble Truths—and the Buddha's disciples; be weary and perform other deeds. "Āsaṃ mākāsi bhikkhusu" means do not harbor the desire, "I will obstruct the monks, I will harass them."

"Iti" means thus. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna threatened Mara, saying, "Mara, be weary... among the monks." "Bhesakaḷāvane" means in the forest of that name.
505:
"Tato" means because of that threat. "That dejected yakkha" means that Mara, becoming despondent, vanished right there in that very place and became invisible. This verse was established at the time of the Dhamma Council. Whatever has not been explained in detail here regarding the meaning in between is already clear, as it follows the method mentioned below.

Thus, this Great Elder, having threatened Mara and having performed unique services for beings by traveling to the celestial realms and hell realms, attained Parinibbāna at the end of his life. Before attaining Parinibbāna, he had made a resolution at the feet of the Blessed One Anomadassī. From then on, having performed noble merits in various existences, even though he had reached the pinnacle of the perfections of a disciple (sāvaka-pāramī), he attained Parinibbāna after experiencing great physical exhaustion due to being oppressed by thieves instigated by heretics, a result of the remnants of past evil kamma (kamma-pilotika) committed in an intervening life. This is stated in the Apadāna:

"The Blessed One Anomadassī, the Eldest of the World, the Bull among Men, dwelt in the Himalayas, honored by the host of devas."

"The Conqueror, the Blessed One, having descended from there, wandered on a journey. Favoring the assembly of beings, he arrived at Bārāṇasī."

"Surrounded by thousands of those whose taints were exhausted (arahants), the Leader of the World, the Great Sage, shone, illuminating all directions."

"At that time, I was a householder. Encouraged by a friend named Sarada, who possessed great psychic power, I approached the Teacher."

"Having approached the Sambuddha and invited the Tathāgata, I led the Great Sage to my own home, honoring him."

"At that time, I satisfied the Great Hero, the God of Gods, the Bull among Men, who was present there, along with the community of monks, with food and drink."
506:
The Blessed One Anomadassī, the Great Hero, the Self-Enlightened One, the Supreme Person, while sitting in the midst of the community of monks, gave the blessing (anumodanā) and spoke these verses:

"Because of that devotion of mind with which he honored the Saṅgha and the Buddha, the Leader of the World, he shall go to the celestial realm."

"He shall exercise divine kingship seventy-seven times, and he shall rule as a king over the earth eight hundred times."

"Fifty-five times he shall be a Wheel-Turning Monarch (Cakkavatti); at that time, incalculable wealth shall arise for him."

"In an immeasurable aeon from now, a Teacher named Gotama by clan, born of the Okkāka dynasty, shall arise in the world."

"Having passed away from hell, he shall reach the human state and become a member of the Brahmin class named Kolita."

"Later, having gone forth into homelessness, urged by his past roots of merit, he shall become the second disciple of the Blessed One Gotama."

"With exerted effort and a resolute mind, having reached the pinnacle of psychic powers and fully understanding all taints, he shall attain Parinibbāna, free from taints."

"Due to associating with a bad friend and falling under the power of sensual desire, with a corrupted mind, I killed both my mother and father."

"In whatever state of existence I was born, whether in hell or among humans, because of being possessed of that evil kamma, I died with my head split open."

"This is my final result (vipāka), occurring in my last birth; even in this life, at the time of death, there will be such a death with a split head."

"Devoted to seclusion and delighting in the development of concentration, I dwell free from taints, having fully understood all taints."

"Having reached the pinnacle of psychic powers, I can shake even the deep, thick, and indestructible earth with my left big toe."
507:
I do not see the conceit that says "I am"; conceit does not exist in me. Starting from the young novices, I treat them with a heart of respect.

In an incalculable aeon from now, I undertook that deed (aspiring to be the left-hand chief disciple). Having reached that special state, I have attained the destruction of the taints.

The four analytical insights, the eight liberations, and the six higher powers have been realized. The teaching of the Buddha has been carried out.

## The commentary on the verses of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna is finished.

## The commentary on the Section of Sixty is finished.
508:
The teaching of the Buddha has been carried out. The commentary on the verses of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna is finished. The commentary on the Section of Sixty is finished.

## 21. Mahānipāta
## 1. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Vaṅgīsa
In the Section of Seventy, the verses beginning with 'Nikkhantaṃ vata maṃ santaṃ' are the verses of the Venerable Vaṅgīsa. What is the origin of these verses? This Venerable Vaṅgīsa was born into a wealthy family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. As in the previous accounts, while going to the monastery and listening to the Dhamma, he saw the Teacher appoint a certain monk to the foremost position among those who possess quick-wittedness (paṭibhāna). Having performed great deeds of merit for the Teacher, he made an aspiration: "May I also become the foremost among those with quick-wittedness in the future." After receiving the prophecy from the Teacher, he performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and wandered through the realms of devas and humans. In the time of our Buddha's appearance, he was born into a Brahmin family in Sāvatthī and received the name Vaṅgīsa. He learned the three Vedas, pleasing his teacher, and mastered the art known as Chavasīsamanta. By that art, he could know, "This being is reborn in such-and-such a realm," by tapping a human skull with his fingernail.

The Brahmins, realizing that "This person is our means of livelihood," took Vaṅgīsa, placed him in a well-covered carriage, and traveled through villages, market towns, and royal capitals. Vaṅgīsa would have the skulls of those who had been dead for even three years brought to him, and by tapping them with his fingernail, he would say, "This being is reborn in such-and-such a realm." To dispel the doubts of the people, he would call upon various individuals and tell them their own destinations. Because of this, the people in those regions had great faith in Vaṅgīsa. Relying on that art, he received hundreds and thousands from the hands of the people. The Brahmins, taking Vaṅgīsa with them, traveled as they pleased and eventually returned to Sāvatthī. Having heard of the Buddha's virtues, Vaṅgīsa desired to visit the Teacher. Although the Brahmins tried to prevent him, saying, "The ascetic Gotama will entice you with his deceptive magic," Vaṅgīsa ignored their words, went to the Teacher, exchanged pleasant greetings, and sat in a suitable place.

The Teacher asked him, "Vaṅgīsa, do you know any art?" "Yes, Master Gotama, I know the art called Chavasīsamanta. With that art, I can know the place of rebirth by tapping the skulls of those who have been dead for even three years with my fingernail," he replied. Then the Teacher showed him a skull of a being reborn in hell.
509:
The Teacher showed him a skull of a being reborn in hell, one of a being reborn in the human realm, one of a being reborn in the deva realm, and one of an Arahant who had attained Parinibbāna. Tapping the first skull, Vaṅgīsa said, "Master Gotama, this being is reborn in hell." "Excellent, Vaṅgīsa, you have seen well. Where is this being reborn?" the Teacher asked. "In the human realm," he replied. "And this one?" "In the deva realm," he said, stating the rebirth destination of all three. However, when he tapped the skull of the Arahant who had attained Parinibbāna with his fingernail, he saw neither the end nor the limit. Then the Teacher asked, "Vaṅgīsa, are you unable to do it?" "Let me investigate first," he replied. Although he turned it over and tapped it repeatedly, how could he know the destination of one whose taints are destroyed through an external mantra? Then, sweat poured from Vaṅgīsa's forehead. He stood silent in shame. Then the Teacher said, "Vaṅgīsa, are you weary?" "Yes, Master Gotama, I am. I am unable to know the place of rebirth of this person. If you know it, please tell me." "Vaṅgīsa, I know the destination of this person, and I know even more than that," the Teacher said, and recited these two verses:

"He who knows in every way the passing away and rebirth of beings; him, unattached, well-gone, and awakened, I call a Brahmin.

He whose destination is unknown to devas, gandhabbas, and humans; him, an Arahant whose taints are destroyed, I call a Brahmin."

Vaṅgīsa, showing respect, said, "Master Gotama, if that is so, please give that art to me," and sat near the Teacher. The Teacher said, "We give it to one who has the same appearance as us." Vaṅgīsa thought, "I must obtain this mantra by any means," and told the Brahmins, "Do not worry when I become a monk. Once I have learned the mantra, I will be the greatest in the whole of Jambudīpa, and that will be beneficial for you as well." Desiring the mantra, he approached the Teacher and requested ordination. At that time, the Elder Nigrodhakappa was standing near the Blessed One, and the Blessed One commanded him, "Nigrodhakappa, ordain this Vaṅgīsa." By the Teacher's command, the Elder Nigrodhakappa ordained him. Then the Teacher said, "First, learn the preliminaries of the mantra," and taught him the meditation on the thirty-two parts of the body and the meditation of Vipassanā. While reciting the thirty-two parts of the body, Vaṅgīsa developed insight (Vipassanā). The Brahmins approached Vaṅgīsa and asked, "O Vaṅgīsa, have you learned the art from the ascetic Gotama?"
510:
The Brahmins asked, "Have you learned the art?" Vangīsa replied, "What is the use of learning this art? You may go; I have no further business with you." The Brahmins said, "Now you too have come under the influence of the ascetic Gotama, deceived by his magic. What can we do for you?" and they departed by the same way they had come. The Elder Vangīsa, having developed insight, realized the fruit of Arahantship. Therefore, it is stated in the Apadāna:

"A Conqueror named Padumuttara, the Visionary in all things, the Leader who brings beings to Nibbāna, arose a hundred thousand aeons ago.

Just as waves are beautiful in the ocean, and as stars are beautiful in the sky, so was the Dispensation of that Buddha adorned with noble Arahants.

Surrounded by humans along with devas, asuras, and nagas, the Supreme Conqueror was magnificent in the midst of people, crowded with ascetics and Brahmins.

Shining with radiance, that Conqueror who reached the end of the world, awakened the lotus-like beings worthy of discipline with his words.

That Supreme Man was endowed with the four intrepidities (vesārajja); having abandoned fear and hesitation, he reached the state of security and was courageous.

He, the Foremost of the world, claimed the noble station and the entire range of Buddhahood; nowhere was there anyone to reproach him.

While he, such a one, was uttering a lion's roar without fear, there was no deva, human, or Brahma who could refute him.

Preaching the noble Dhamma, saving beings including devas, he courageously set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion in the midst of the assemblies.

Having praised the many virtues of a disciple who was the foremost among those of quick wit and esteemed by the virtuous, he placed that disciple in the foremost position (etadagga).

At that time, I was a Brahmin in the city of Haṃsavatī, esteemed by the virtuous, learned in all the Vedas, a master of speech, and a crusher of opposing views.

Approaching that Great Hero and hearing his preaching of the Dhamma, I attained sublime joy, delighting in the virtues of that disciple."
511:
"Having invited the Sugata, the Joy of the World, together with the community of monks, and having fed them for seven days, I then offered robes as a covering.

Bowing my head at his feet, having gained the opportunity with joined palms, I stood at a respectful distance and, with a joyful heart, praised the Supreme Conqueror.

'Homage to you, Crusher of Arguments! Homage to you, Best of Sages! Homage to you, Supreme in all the world! Homage to you, Giver of Fearlessness!'

'Homage to you, Conqueror of Mara! Homage to you, Destroyer of Views! Homage to you, Giver of the Bliss of Peace! Homage to you, Maker of Refuge!'

'You are the refuge of the helpless, the giver of safety to the fearful, the resting place for those burning with defilements, and the refuge for those seeking refuge.'

Having praised the Buddha of great virtues with such qualities, I said, 'I wish to reach the state of the monk who is a crusher of arguments (Vādisūda).'

Then the Blessed One, possessed of infinite wisdom, said: 'This person who has fed the Buddha together with his disciples for seven days,'

'And with a confident heart has praised my virtues with his own hands, this person aspires to the position of the monk who is a crusher of arguments.'

'In the future, after enjoying no small amount of divine and human prosperity, he will attain that heart's desire.'

'A hundred thousand aeons from this Bhadda-kappa, a Teacher named Gotama by lineage, born of the Okkāka clan, will arise in the world.'

'He will be a disciple of that Teacher, an heir to the Dhamma, a breast-born son, created by the Dhamma, named Vangīsa by name.'

Having heard those words and being filled with joy, I then served the Conqueror with the four requisites with a heart of loving-kindness for the rest of my life.

Due to that well-performed deed, and through my volition and aspiration, I abandoned the human body and went to the Tusita heaven."
512:
"Now, in my final birth, I was born in a Brahmin family. When I reached the age of seven after being born,

I became one who knew all the Vedas, courageous in the treatises of views, a master of speech, one of eloquent discourse, and a crusher of others' views.

Because I was born in the Vanga country, or because I was a master of speech, I was called 'Vangīsa.' Thus, 'Vangīsa' became my name esteemed in the world.

When I reached the age of discretion and was in my first stage of life (youth), I saw the Venerable Sāriputta in the delightful city of Rājagaha.

I saw that Elder wandering for alms, holding his bowl in hand, well-restrained in his faculties, with eyes not wandering, speaking moderately, and looking only a fathom's length ahead.

Seeing him and being amazed, I recited a verse that was well-conceived within me, as beautiful as a Kaṇṇikā flower.

He told me about the Teacher, the Sammāsambuddha, the Leader of the World. Then that wise and courageous Elder spoke further to me.

Having spoken words associated with detachment (virāga), which are noble and difficult to see, that one of such nature, with diverse wisdom, delighted me.

Bowing my head at his feet, I said, 'Please ordain me.' Then that one of great wisdom led me to the Buddha, the Best of Beings.

Bowing my head at his feet, I sat in the presence of the Teacher. The Buddha, the best among those who speak, said to me, 'Vangīsa, do you know any art?'

I replied to the Blessed One, 'I know, Venerable Sir.' He said, 'If you are able, tell by your special knowledge (the rebirth) of this skull which has been cast away in the forest for twelve years.'

When I agreed, saying 'Very well, Venerable Sir,' he showed me three skulls. I declared the rebirth of those who were reborn in hell, the human realm, and the deva realm.

Then the Leader showed me the skull of an Arahant. At that, my effort was defeated, and I requested the state of a monk."
513:
Having gone forth in the presence of the Sugata, I praise Him in various places. Because of such praise, the monks in this Dispensation criticize me as one who delights in composing poetry.

Then, the Buddha, the Leader who disciplines beings, to test me, said: "Are these verses thought out, or do they occur to you spontaneously according to the occasion?"

"O Hero, I am not one who delights in composing poetry; they occur to me spontaneously according to the occasion," I replied. Then He said: "Vangīsa, if that is so, praise me now spontaneously according to the occasion."

Then I praised the Hero, the seventh of the Sages, with verses. At that time, the Victorious One, pleased with my spontaneous wit, placed me in the foremost rank.

With a mind of quick wit, I used to look down on others. Because of that, I became agitated and attained Arahatship.

"Monks, just as this monk Vangīsa is the foremost among those of quick wit, there is no other; thus you should remember," He declared.

The deed done a hundred thousand aeons ago shows its fruit to me here. Like the speed of a well-shot arrow, I have burnt away my defilements.

My defilements are burnt; all births are uprooted. Like a noble elephant that has broken its bonds, I live without taints (āsavas).

My coming to the presence of the Best of Buddhas was indeed a good coming. The three knowledges have been attained; the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.

The four analytical knowledges, these eight liberations, and the six higher powers have been realized; the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.

Having become an Arahat, when the Elder went to the Buddha, he approached while praising the Teacher with hundreds of phrases, comparing Him to the moon, the sun, the sky, the great ocean, Sineru the king of mountains, the lion the king of beasts, and the noble elephant, starting from the moment he came into sight. Therefore, the Teacher, seated in the midst of the Saṅgha, placed that Elder in the foremost rank (Etadagga) of those with quick wit (Paṭibhānavantā). Furthermore, there are verses spoken by the Elder based on various states of mind before and after attaining Arahatship, as well as verses spoken by Elder Ānanda and others concerning the Elder.
514:
To me, who has gone forth from home to the homeless life, these bold and evil thoughts of Māra the Defiler come rushing in.

Even if a thousand princes, skilled in arts, great archers with firm bows, who do not flee, were to surround and shoot from all sides...

Even if more women than that were to come, they would not be able to make me tremble; I am firmly established in my own Dhamma of the Path and Fruit.

I have personally heard and realized that path leading to Nibbāna from the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun (Ādiccabandhu); in that path, my mind finds delight.

O Evil Māra, if you approach me while I live thus, I will act so that you reach the presence of Death, and you shall not even see my path.

Having entirely abandoned both discontent and delight in sensual pleasures, and all thoughts related to the household life, one should not create the forest of defilements in any object; he who desires Nibbāna and is free from the forest of defilements is truly a monk.

Whatever material form exists in this world, on earth or in the sky, included in the world, all is subject to decay and is impermanent; having realized this through penetration, those with liberated minds live their lives.

People are attached to the bases of existence (upadhi), and to things seen, heard, touched, and sensed; dispel the desire for these objects, be free from the agitation of craving; the wise call him a Sage (Muni) who is not smeared by craving for these sensual pleasures.

Furthermore, there are those who rely on the sixty-two wrong views, accompanied by wrong thoughts, and who, due to being worldlings, are established in unrighteousness; that monk should not join any such faction, nor should he be one who habitually takes up base wrong views.
515:
The wise one is composed for a long time; he is free from deceit, prudent, and without longing. That Sage has reached the peaceful state of Nibbāna; having understood dependent origination and with defilements extinguished, he now awaits the time (of final Nibbāna).

O Gotama, abandon pride; abandon the path of pride (unwise attention) entirely. He who is infatuated with that path of pride will suffer regret for a long time.

Beings smeared with the disparagement of others' virtues and destroyed by pride fall into hell (Niraya). Those destroyed by pride and reborn in hell grieve for a long time.

A monk who has conquered defilements through the Path and practices rightly never grieves. He experiences fame and happiness; the wise call such a person a "Seer of Dhamma" because of that nature.

Therefore, in this Dispensation, one should be a monk who is free from thorns, energetic, pure by abandoning the hindrances (nīvaraṇas), abandoning pride entirely, making an end of suffering through knowledge (vijjā), and having defilements stilled.

(Vangīsa Thera says:)
I am burning with sensual lust; my mind is burning repeatedly. O Gotama (Venerable Ānanda), out of compassion, please preach to me the Dhamma for the stilling of lust.

(Venerable Ānanda replies:)
Your mind is burning because of perverted perception. Especially avoid the beautiful sign (subha-nimitta) associated with lust.

Develop the mind on the foulness of the body (asubha); let the mind be well-composed and one-pointed. May you have mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatāsati); be one who is full of revulsion.

Develop the signless (animitta) insight; abandon the latent tendency of pride (mānanusaya). Then, by the full understanding of pride, you shall live as one who is stilled.
516:
"One should speak only such words as do not cause oneself remorse nor harm others; that indeed is well-spoken speech."

"One should speak only pleasant words, words that are welcomed. Disregarding the bad (harsh) words of others, one should speak only what is pleasant to them."

"Truthful speech is indeed the deathless; this is the ancient eternal law. The virtuous, say the wise, are established in truth, in the good, and in the Dhamma."

"The word which the Buddha speaks for the attainment of Nibbāna, for the safety and the ending of suffering, is indeed the most excellent of words."

"The one of deep wisdom, the sagacious, skilled in the right and wrong paths, the venerable Sāriputta of great wisdom, teaches the Dhamma to the monks."

"He teaches in brief and speaks in detail; his voice is like that of the salika bird, and his inspired speech (paṭibhāna) arises as he understands."

"While he is teaching, the monks listen to his sweet voice—captivating, pleasant to hear, smooth, and beautiful. With uplifted and joyful hearts, they lend an ear."

"Today, on the fifteenth day (Uposatha) for purification, five hundred monks have assembled. They are the great Sages (Arahants) who have cut the bonds of fetters, are free from suffering, and have ended rebirth."

"Just as a Wheel-turning King, surrounded by his ministers, travels around this earth bounded by the ocean,"

"So do the disciples—possessors of the three knowledges, conquerors of death—attend upon the Peerless Leader, the Caravan Leader who has won the battle (against defilements)."

"Among all the sons of the Blessed One, there is no chaff (emptiness). I pay homage to the Kinsman of the Sun (Adiccabandhu), the destroyer of the thorn of craving."

"More than a thousand monks attend upon the Sugata, who teaches the stainless Dhamma, Nibbāna, which is free from all fear."
517:
"They listen to the pure Dhamma taught by the Fully Enlightened One. Truly, the Enlightened One shines, surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks."

"The Blessed One is named 'Nāga' because he does no evil; he is the seventh Sage (Isi) among the Sages such as Vipassī. Like a great cloud raining in the late season, he rains down the rain of Dhamma upon his disciples."

"O Great Hero, your disciple Vangīsa, having come out from his daytime retreat and desiring to see the Teacher, pays homage at your feet."

"He walks having overcome the path of Māra that leads nowhere; he has destroyed the thorns such as lust and has released the bonds. Behold that Blessed One, who is unattached to lust and the like, and who teaches by analyzing the Dhamma into parts."

"For the purpose of crossing over the four floods (ogha), he has declared the Path in various ways. In that declared Deathless Nibbāna, those who see the Dhamma stand unshakable by defilements."

"The Light-maker, having penetrated through, saw the escape from all stations of consciousness. Having known and realized it, he taught the supreme Dhamma in its ten-fold divisions."

"In the Dhamma thus well-taught, how could there be negligence for those who know the Dhamma? Therefore, in the teaching of that Blessed One, one should always be diligent, paying homage and training accordingly."

"There is the Elder named Koṇḍañña, who followed the Buddha in awakening, who is of intense effort, and who frequently attains the three seclusions (viveka) which are happy abidings."

"Whatever is to be attained by a disciple who follows the Teacher's instruction, all that has been reached by the diligent Koṇḍañña while training."

"Of great power, possessed of the three knowledges, skilled in the knowledge of others' minds (cetopariya), Koṇḍañña, the heir to the Buddha, pays homage at the Teacher's feet."
518:
"At the foot of the mountain, the disciples—possessors of the three knowledges, conquerors of the Māra of defilements which causes death—attend upon the Sage who has reached the end of suffering."

"The venerable Moggallāna, of great psychic power, encompasses with his own mind the minds of those monks who are liberated and free from acquisitions (upadhi)."

"Thus, the disciples attend upon Gotama, the Sage who is perfect in all attributes, who has reached the end of suffering, and who is endowed with various virtues."

"As the moon shines in a cloudless sky, and as the sun shines free from stain, so do you, O Great Sage Aṅgīrasa, outshine the whole world with your glory."

"In the past, we wandered from village to village, from city to city, as composers of poetry. Then we saw the Fully Enlightened One, who has reached the end of all phenomena."

"That Sage, who has reached the end of suffering, taught the Dhamma to me. Having heard the Dhamma, we gained confidence, and faith arose in us."

"Having heard his words and understood the five aggregates (khandha), the twelve sense bases (āyatana), and the eighteen elements (dhātu), I went forth from the home life into the homeless life of the Dispensation."

"Truly, the Tathāgatas arise for the benefit of many, for those women and men who follow the teaching."

"Truly, for the benefit of those monks and nuns who have reached and seen the fixed path (niyāma), the Sage attained Enlightenment."

"The Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun (Adiccabandhu), possessed of the five eyes, well-taught the Four Noble Truths out of compassion for all beings."

"They are: the Truth of Suffering (Dukkha), the Truth of the Origin of Suffering (Samudaya), the Truth of the Cessation of Suffering (Nirodha), and the Noble Eightfold Path leading to the subsiding of suffering (Magga)."
519:
## 
I have seen these Four Noble Truths as they truly are, just as they were taught. I have attained my own goal, the fruit of Arahantship; the Buddha's instruction has been carried out. My coming to the presence of the Buddha was indeed a good coming. Among the well-analyzed dhammas, I have reached Nibbāna, which is the most excellent. I have reached the perfection of direct knowledge (abhiññā); the divine ear element has been purified. I possess the threefold knowledge, have attained psychic powers, and am skilled in the knowledge of others' minds (cetopariyañāṇa).

I ask the Teacher of undiminished wisdom, who cuts away doubts in this very life: a monk, famous and renowned, with a peaceful mind, passed away at the Aggāḷava Shrine. His name was Nigrodhakappa; O Blessed One, you gave that name to that brahmin. He lived worshipping you, aspiring for Nibbāna, with aroused energy, seeing the firm Dhamma.

O Sakyan, O All-Seeing One, we all wish to know about that disciple. Our ears are ready to listen; you are our Teacher, the unsurpassed one. O One of vast wisdom like the earth, cut away our doubt; tell me this. Let us know of his parinibbāna. O All-Seeing One, speak in our midst as Sakka, the thousand-eyed king of gods, speaks in the midst of the devas.

Whatever bonds exist here—rooted in delusion, partaking of ignorance, or being grounds for doubt—they cease to exist upon reaching the Tathāgata, for he is the supreme eye of humanity.
520:
## 
If the Great Man (the Buddha) did not constantly dispel the defilements, as the wind dispels a mass of clouds, the entire world would be shrouded in darkness, and even the radiant gods and Brahmas would not shine.

The wise are the makers of light; O Hero, I consider you to be such a wise one. We have approached the All-Seeing and All-Knowing One. In the midst of the assembly, reveal to us the final passing of the Elder Kappa.

Quickly utter your beautiful, pleasant speech; like a king of swans stretching its neck and warbling sweetly, speak with your well-modulated and perfect voice. All of us, who have come straightforwardly, will listen to your words.

You, who have entirely abandoned birth and death and shaken off evil, will preach the Dhamma. While ordinary people cannot act according to their own will, the Tathāgatas act with investigation and deliberation.

I have well-learned and seen this perfect exposition of yours, O One of upright wisdom. This is my final salutation with joined palms, offered most respectfully. O One of undiminished wisdom, though you know, do not leave us in confusion.
