Knowing the Noble Dhamma of the Four Truths in its higher and lower aspects, O One of undiminished energy, though you know, do not leave us in confusion. As one oppressed by the sun's heat desires water, I desire your words; rain down the Dhamma we have heard.

For what goal of the holy life did Kappāyana live? Was his practice not in vain? Did he attain Nibbāna with the remainder of the result of kamma-born matter, or was he (completely) extinguished, being liberated from defilements? Let us hear that matter.
521:
## 
The Blessed One said: "He has cut off craving for this mind and body (nāmarūpa). He has also cut off the stream of Māra, the craving that has long lain dormant. The Blessed One, the most excellent among the five most excellent Buddhas, declared: 'The Elder Kappa has completely transcended birth and death.'"

O seventh of the seven Sages, hearing your words, I am inspired with faith. My question was indeed fruitful; the Brahmin (the Buddha) who has cast away evil did not deceive me.

As he spoke, so he acted; he was a disciple of the Buddha. He has cut the strong net of Death spread by the deceptive Māra.

The Blessed One saw the cause of grasping. The Elder Kappa has indeed transcended the realm of Death, which is so difficult to cross.

I pay homage to that God of gods, to your son, O Best of bipeds, who followed in your footsteps, the Great Hero, the noble elephant born from the breast of the Great Elephant (the Buddha).

These verses were collected and included at the time of the Council. Among them, the five verses beginning with "Nikkhantaṃ vata maṃ santaṃ" were spoken by the Venerable Vangīsa when he was a newly ordained monk. Upon seeing many well-adorned women coming to the monastery, lust arose in him, and he spoke these verses wishing to dispel that lust.

In those verses, "Nikkhantaṃ vata maṃ santaṃ, agārasmānagāရိယံ" means "to me who has gone forth from the home life to the homeless life and become a monk." "Vitakkā" refers to unwholesome thoughts such as sensual thoughts. "Upadhāvanti" means "they approach my mind." "Pagabbhā" refers to those who are bold and shameless because they do not reflect, "This person has left home and become a monk; it is not proper to destroy him." "Kaṇhato" means by way of darkness or because of a low state. By the word "ime", their presence before his eyes is meant.

People of impure livelihood who are surrounded by retinues are called "Ugga" because they have intense affairs. Their sons are called "Uggaputta". "Mahissāsā" means great archers. "Sikkhitā" means those who have studied the arts for twelve years in the teacher's house. "Daḷhadhammino" means those with strong bowstrings.
522:
"Daḷhadhununo" refers to a bow with the strength of two thousand men. The strength of two thousand men is the power to lift weights such as iron heads attached to a strung bowstring from the ground, without lifting it into the sky to the extent of an arrow's length, while holding the bow. "Samantā parikireyyuṃ" means they should shoot arrows from all around. "Kittakā" (how many?): "Sahassaṃ apalāyinaṃ" means about a thousand who do not retreat or flee on the battlefield. The meaning is: About a thousand Uggaputtas who are well-trained, skilled, energetic (ugga), possessing strong bows (daḷhadhunu), and great archers (mahissāsa), who have never been defeated in battle and are never heedless, standing all around and relying on a pillar, might shoot like a rain of arrows. Even when surrounded and shot at with arrows by such a thousand archers, a well-trained man, holding a stick, can cause all those arrows to fall at his feet without letting them hit his body. In such shooting, a single archer cannot shoot two arrows simultaneously. However, women, through the power of visual objects and so on, shoot five arrows at once. "Ettakā bhiyyo" means that more than such women who can shoot thus, many women destroy men through their feminine gestures, laughter, nature, and so on.

"Sakkhī hi me sutaṃ etaṃ" means "I have heard this teaching personally (face to face)." "Nibbānagamanaṃ maggaṃ" is spoken with a change of gender (liṅgavipallāsa), meaning the path leading to Nibbāna (nibbānagāmimagga), and it is said in reference to Vipassanā (insight). My mind delights in that path of Vipassanā.

To me, living thus with the meditation on impermanence (anicca-bhāvanā), the meditation on foulness (asubha-jhāna-bhāvanā), and the meditation on insight (vipassanā-bhāvanā), the Evil One (Pāpimant), the Mara of defilements (Kilesa-māra), thinks: "I will bring about an end through death so that you cannot even see the path I have made."

The five verses beginning with "Aratiñcā" were spoken to dispel discontent (arati) and so on that arose in his own continuity. In those verses, "arati" means boredom or dissatisfaction with superior wholesome states and secluded dwellings. "Rati" means delight in the five cords of sensual pleasure. "Pahāya" means having abandoned. Having completely abandoned wrong thoughts such as thoughts about relatives connected with children, wives, etc., which are associated with the household, one should not have craving for any objects, internal or external. Because of the absence of the forest of craving in every way, because of not trembling in any object, because of having cleared the forest of defilements and seeing well the danger of Saṃsāra, and because of having destroyed defilements, that monk is called a "Bhikkhu." All of the world's...
523:
Because of being free from craving in every way, and because of that very absence of craving, having no delight in any object and thus being free from the forest of defilements, he is called a Bhikkhu. It means he is a Bhikkhu because he sees the danger in Saṃsāra correctly and because he has broken the defilements.

"Yaṃkiñci" refers to everything conditioned (saṅkhata) in this world—whether based on the earth, situated in the sky, based in the celestial realms, subject to change (ruppana-sabhāva), worldly, or included in the three realms of existence. All that is overcome by aging and thus reaches decay and destruction. Because it is oppressed by aging, he spoke of the application of the three marks: impermanence (anicca), suffering (dukkha), and non-self (anatta). This is said to be the Elder's "Great Insight" (Mahā-vipassanā). Thus, having penetrated with the path-wisdom (magga-paññā) accompanied by insight-wisdom (vipassanā-paññā) and having a mind liberated from defilements, the wise live and conduct themselves.

"Upadhīsu" refers to the acquisitions such as the acquisitions of the aggregates (khandhūpadhi). "Janā" refers to blind worldlings (andha-puthujjana). "Gadhitāse" means they have minds that are bound and attached. Here, to show that desire should be removed especially in the acquisitions of the five cords of sensual pleasure, he said: "Diṭṭhasute paṭighe ca mute ca." "Diṭṭhasute" means in the seen and the heard, i.e., in visual objects and sounds. "Paṭighe" means in the tangible objects that are to be touched. "Mute" means in the remaining sensed objects, i.e., in smells and tastes. In the Sāratthappakāsinī (Saṃyutta Nikāya Commentary), it is said: "By the word 'paṭigha', smells and tastes are taken; by the word 'muta', the tangible object is taken." Here, "Vinodaya chandamanejo" means: dispel the sensual desire (kāmacchanda) for these five cords of sensual pleasure consisting of the seen, etc. If so, you will be one who is untrembling (aneja) and without conceptual proliferation (avikappa) in all objects. The wise call him a "Muni" (sage) because he is established in the qualities of a sage (moneyya-dhamma) and does not smear himself with the smear of craving for these sense pleasures.

Regarding the Pali "Atha saṭṭhisitā," some teachers interpret it as "relying on sixty objects." However, the actual Pali text is "Aṭṭhasatthisitā savitakkā" (sixty-eight based thoughts). A slight decrease or increase is not taken into account in counting. Some teachers say "Aṭṭhasatthisitā" refers to wrong thoughts (micchā-vitakka) that rely on the sixty-two types of views. Excluding the doctrine of fortuitous origination (adhiccasamuppanna-vāda) because those with views have reached the view that there is no station for beings, it is said "Atha saṭṭhisitā savitakkā" based on the remaining doctrines. Just as one is called a Bhikkhu due to the absence of the smear of craving, he said "Atha saṭṭhisitā" etc., to show that one is also called a Bhikkhu due to the absence of the smear of views. Because of being a worldling, unrighteous wrong thoughts...
524:
The term 'Niviṭṭhā' means that those wrong thoughts, due to the power of grasping at permanence and so forth, are unrighteous and have departed from the Dhamma; they are settled and deeply attached to the foolish worldlings. 'Na ca vaggagatassa kuhiñci' means that one should not belong to a group of wrong views, such as eternalism (sassatavāda), regarding any object. In the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), however, the phrase 'Atha saṭṭhisitā savitakkā, puthū janatāya adhammā niviṭṭhā' is extracted and explained as: 'Then, many unrighteous thoughts based on the six sense-objects are settled in the multitude of people.' Likewise, 'Na ca vaggagatassa kuhiñci' is also explained as: by the power of those thoughts, one should not belong to a group of defilements in any object. 'No pana duṭṭhullagāhī sa bhikkhū' means that because one is defiled by passions, one should not be of a nature to grasp at extremely coarse wrong views; only such a person is called a Bhikkhu.

'Dabbo' refers to a wise man of noble birth. 'Cirarattasamāhito' means one whose mind has been concentrated for a long time. 'Akuhako' means one who is free from hypocrisy, not deceitful, and without guile. 'Nipako' means one who is prudent and clever. 'Apihālū' means one who is free from craving. 'Santā padaṃ ajjhagamā' means one who has reached the peaceful state of Nibbāna. He is called a 'Muni' because he is endowed with the qualities of a sage (moneyyadhamma). 'Parinibbuto' means one who has extinguished defilements through the Nibbāna element with residue (sa-upādisesa-nibbānadhātu) by taking Nibbāna as an object. 'Kaṅkhati kālaṃ' means that he is now awaiting the time for the sake of Nibbāna without residue (anupādisesa-nibbāna). For such a person, there is nothing further to be done; the meaning is that he has fulfilled himself to become such a being.

The four verses beginning with 'Mānaṃ pajahassu' were spoken with the desire to dispel the conceit (māna) that was arising within himself based on his own success in wit and eloquence (paṭibhānasampatti). Among those verses, 'Mānaṃ pajahassu' means to abandon the nine types of conceit, such as the conceit of superiority (seyyamāna). 'Gotama' is an address to himself, identifying as being of the Gotama lineage because he is a disciple of the Blessed One who is of the Gotama clan. 'Mānapathaṃ' (the path of conceit) refers to birth and so forth, which are the grounds for the occurrence of conceit and are surrounded by improper attention (ayoniso manasikāra); abandon these by abandoning the defilements connected to them. 'Asesaṃ' means entirely, without remainder. 'Mānapathamhi sa mucchito' means one who has fallen into delusion regarding the grounds of conceit. 'Vippaṭisārī ahuva cirarattaṃ' means that when the moment of following this path of conceit had passed, he felt regret and remorse for a long time, thinking, 'I should have attained Arahatship long ago, but now I am ruined.'
525:
The multitude of beings is smeared with denigration (makkha), which has the characteristic of smearing over the virtues of others. One is called 'Makkhī' (a denigrator) because one smears others' virtues by exalting oneself through boldness and so forth, and by despising others. In whatever way a person smears the virtues of others, in that same way, he is said to discard (or pile up the loss of) his own virtues. 'Mānahata' refers to those whose virtues are destroyed by conceit. 'Nirayaṃ papatanti' means they are reborn in hell.

'Maggajina' means one who has conquered defilements through the Path. He experiences (obtains) fame praised by the wise and both physical and mental happiness. The wise call 'Dhammadassī' (a seer of Dhamma) one who practices rightly and sees the Dhamma as it truly is.

'Akhila' means one who is free from the five mental barrennesses (cetokhila). 'Padhānavā' means one who is endowed with right effort (sammappadhāna). 'Visuddha' means one who has a pure mind due to the disappearance of the clouds known as the hindrances (nīvaraṇa). 'Asesaṃ' means having abandoned the nine types of conceit without remainder through the Path of Arahatship. He admonishes himself, saying that he has completely stilled defilements and reached the end of the three knowledges (vijjā).

Then, one day, Venerable Ānanda, having been invited by a great royal minister, went to that minister's house in the morning and sat on the prepared seat. Venerable Vaṅgīsa accompanied him as his attendant monk. Then, the women in that house, adorned with all kinds of ornaments, approached the Elder, paid homage, asked questions, and listened to the Dhamma. At that time, Venerable Vaṅgīsa, being a newly ordained monk, was unable to restrain his senses, and sensual lust (rāga) arose toward the disagreeable object (visabhāgārammaṇa). That noble son (Venerable Vaṅgīsa), who possessed faith and an upright nature, thought, 'If this lust of mine increases, it will destroy my welfare in both this life and the future.' While still sitting, wishing to reveal his state to the Elder, he spoke the verse beginning with 'Kāmarāgena.' In that verse, although the burning of defilements afflicts the body, it afflicts the mind for a much longer time; thus, to show this, he said, 'I am burning with sensual lust,' followed by 'My mind is on fire.' 'Nibbāpana' means: 'Please give me an instruction (ovāda) that is the cause for the extinguishing of lust and is capable of cooling the fever of lust.'

Venerable Ānanda, being thus requested, spoke the verse beginning with 'Saññāya vipariyesā.' In that verse, 'Vipariyesā' means the perversion of perceiving the unattractive (asubha) as attractive (subha) through a distorted view. 'Nimittaṃ' refers to the sign that gives rise to defilements. 'Parivajjehi' means to abandon it. 'Subhūpasaṃhitaṃ' means to avoid, through the perception of unattractiveness (asubha-saññā), that which is associated with beauty by the power of increasing lust. To show both of these through the perception of non-delight (anabhirati-saññā) in all objects, he said, 'Develop the unattractive,' and so forth. In that text, 'Asubhāya' means by repeatedly contemplating the meditation on the unattractive (asubha-bhāvanā).
526:
"Subha" refers to the notion of beauty that arises through perverted perception. "Nimitta" refers to the sign that gives rise to defilements. "Parivajjehi" means to abandon. One who avoids "subha," which is an object that increases lust and is associated with attractiveness, should avoid it through the perception of impurity (asubha-saññā) and through the perception of non-delight in all objects (anabhirati-saññā). Therefore, wishing to show both of these, He said "Asubhāya," and so forth.

In that verse, "asubhāya" means through the contemplation of impurity (asubhānupassanā). "Cittaṃ bhāvehi ekaggaṃ susamāhitaṃ" means: develop the mind by making it one-pointed and well-concentrated on objects, due to the absence of mental distraction; "I shall speak so that you can well practice your contemplation of impurity"—this is the meaning. "Sati kāyagatā tyatthu" means: let the meditation on mindfulness immersed in the body, as mentioned before, be developed and frequently practiced by you. "Nibbidābahulo bhava" means: be one who is full of weariness towards your own body and towards all things.

"Animittañca bhāvehi" means: by removing the sign of permanence and so forth, specifically, the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā) is called "signless" (animitta). "Tato mānānusayamujjaha" means: while developing that signless [contemplation], eradicate the underlying tendency to conceit (mānānusaya) by attaining the highest path (arahattamagga) through the sequence of the paths. "Mānābhisamaya" refers to the realization of conceit through vision (dassanābhisamaya) and the realization through abandoning (pahānābhisamaya). "Upasanto" means: you will live as one who is peaceful due to the complete subsiding of lust and so forth—this is the meaning.

The four verses beginning with "Tameva vācaṃ" were spoken by Elder Vaṅgīsa, who was filled with joy while praising the Buddha in His presence when the Subhāsita Sutta (Saṃ. Ni. 1.213) was being taught by the Blessed One. "Yāyattānaṃ na tāpaye" means: by reason of which speech one should not burn oneself with remorse, nor should one harm oneself. "Pare ca na vihiṃseyya" means: one should not oppress others by causing division among them. "Sā ve vācā subhāsitā" means: that speech is indeed called "well-spoken"; therefore, one should speak only such speech—this is how it should be connected. With this verse, he praises the Blessed One by way of non-slanderous speech (apisuṇavācā).

"Paṭinanditā" means: delighted in and cherished in one's presence, and well-accepted by listeners both now and in the future. "Yaṃ anādāya" means: when speaking such speech, without taking up evil, unlovely, undesirable, and harsh words of others, one manifests only endearing speech that is sweet in meaning and phrasing. "Tameva piyavācaṃ bhāseyya"—thus he praised by way of endearing speech (piyavācā).
527:
“Amata” (Deathless) means they are like the Deathless because of their excellent nature. Because of this meaning, it is taught: “Among tastes, truth is indeed the most excellent” (Saṃyutta Nikāya, 1, 73). Or they are called “Amata” because they are the cause for the Deathless Nibbāna. “This is the eternal law (dhamma) of old” refers to this truthful speech. This truthful speech is the ancient Dhamma, the traditional practice. Indeed, it is the ancient practice of the virtuous ones of old that they did not speak falsely. Therefore, it is said: “The virtuous are established in truth, in benefit, and in Dhamma.” In that regard, it should be understood that only because they are established in truth are they established in the benefit of themselves and others; and only because they are established in benefit are they established in Dhamma. Alternatively, this is just a qualification of truth. It means they are established in truth that is established in benefit and Dhamma. What kind of truth? It is the kind of truth that, because it does not deviate from the benefit of others, does not obstruct benefit; and because it does not deviate from Dhamma, it accomplishes only the benefit that is consistent with Dhamma. With this verse, he praises by way of truthful speech. “Khema” means safety, freedom from danger. Why is it called khema? Because it leads to the attainment of Nibbāna and the making an end of suffering; because it leads to the extinguishing of defilements and the making an end of the suffering of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa-dukkha), it is called “khema.” Alternatively, the Blessed One speaks “safe speech” for the sake of the two Nibbāna elements—either for the attainment of Nibbāna or for the making an end of suffering—by manifesting the safe path. “That speech is the most excellent of speeches” means that speech is the most noble among all speeches. With this verse, praising the Blessed One by way of consultative speech (mantāvacana), he concludes the praise by culminating in the Fruition of Arahantship.

The three verses beginning with “Gambhīrapañño” (One of deep wisdom) were spoken by way of praising the Venerable Sāriputta Thera. Among them, “Gambhīrapañño” means one endowed with subtle wisdom that functions regarding deep subjects such as the aggregates (khandha) and bases (āyatana). He is “Medhāvī” (the wise) because he is endowed with the wisdom of the essence of Dhamma (dhammoja-paññā) called medhā. He is “Maggāmaggassa kovido” (skilled in the path and what is not the path) because he is skilled in knowing: “This is the path to woeful states, this is the path to happy states, and this is the path to Nibbāna.” He is “Mahāpañño” (one of great wisdom) by virtue of the wisdom that has reached the summit of the great knowledge of a disciple's perfection. “He teaches Dhamma to the monks” means he teaches Dhamma to the monks, clearly explaining the process of arising (pavattī) and cessation (nivattī). To show the manner of that teaching, the words “briefly also” etc. were spoken.

In that context, “briefly also” means: “Friends, there are these four Noble Truths. Which four? The Noble Truth of Suffering... pe... Friends, these are the four Noble Truths.”
528:
Therefore, he also teaches in brief: "Friends, this is suffering." He also speaks in detail, analyzing those very truths in this manner: "Friends, what is the Noble Truth of Suffering? Birth is suffering," and so forth. The same method applies to the teachings on the aggregates (khandha) and others.

"The sound is like that of a myna bird" means that just as a myna bird, after eating a sweet ripe mango and flapping its wings to create a breeze, emits a sweet sound, so too is the voice of the Elder sweet when he is preaching the Dhamma. For the General of the Dhamma (Dhammasenāpati), his speech is unhindered by the influence of bile and other humors; his voice resonates like a bronze bowl struck with an iron rod. "Inspiration (paṭibhāna) arises" means that when there is a desire to speak, an endless stream of inspiration arises successively, like waves from the ocean.

"Tassa" refers to the General of the Dhamma. "Taṃ" refers to when he is preaching the Dhamma. "Suṇanti" means they listen with respect, thinking, "We shall listen to whatever the Elder preaches to us." "Madhuraṃ" means desirable; "rajanīyena" means lovely; "savanīyena" means pleasant to the ear; "vaggunā" means smooth and captivating to the heart. "Udaggacittā" means having an uplifted mind that is not sluggish due to the power of elated joy (pīti). "Muditā" means being endowed with gladness and delight. "Odhenti" means they incline their ears and apply their minds for the sake of attaining the fruit of Arahatship.

The four verses beginning with "Ajja pannarase" were spoken in praise upon seeing the Blessed One seated, surrounded by a large community of monks, during the teaching of the Pavāraṇā Sutta. In those verses, "pannarase" means at the time when the Blessed One was staying at the Pubbārāma monastery; in the evening, after preaching the Dhamma appropriate to the time and occasion to the assembled audience, he bathed his body in the bathhouse, dressed in his lower robe, placed the great robe of the Sugata over his left shoulder, and sat on the noble Buddha-seat prepared near the central pillar of the Migāramātu palace. Looking around at the community of monks seated all around, it refers to that very Uposatha day, the fifteenth day, which was the Pavāraṇā day. "Visuddhiyā" means for the sake of purity, through the Pavāraṇā of purity (visuddhi-pavāraṇā). "Bhikkhū pañcasatā samāgatā" means about five hundred monks had assembled, both by way of sitting around the Teacher and by way of their shared intention. Those monks, having severed the defilements which are the bonds of the continuity of existence known as fetters (saṃyojana)...
529:
...they remain having severed the defilements. Because they remain thus, they are called 'Isi' (seers) because they are free from suffering due to the absence of the suffering of defilements, they have ended rebirth in a new existence, and they constantly seek the aggregates of virtue and so forth of the Asekha (the Adept).

'Vijitasaṅgāma' means one who has a victorious battle because the battle against defilements has been won, and because the power of Māra has been conquered; thus, he is one who has won the battle. 'Satthavāha' means the Blessed One is called 'Satthavāha' (caravan leader) because he places veneya beings (those ready to be tamed) upon the chariot of the Noble Eightfold Path and leads them out, rescuing them from the wilderness of Saṃsāra. Therefore, Sahampati Brahmā entreated: "Arise, O Hero, Victor in battle, Caravan Leader!" The disciples attend upon that Satthavāha, the unsurpassed Teacher. Surrounded by such disciples who possess the three marks of higher knowledge (tevijjā) and have abandoned death, the Blessed One travels around the countryside like a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) surrounded by his ministers; this is how the meaning should be understood.

'Palāpa' means emptiness, being devoid of inner essence, or being devoid of virtue. 'Vande ādiccabandhunaṃ' means "I pay homage to the Blessed One, the kinsman of the sun, the teacher of gods and men, who is endowed with the ten powers."

The four verses beginning with 'Parosahassa' were spoken in praise of the Blessed One while he was preaching the Dhamma to the monks with a discourse related to Nibbāna. In those verses, 'parosahassa' means more than a thousand, referring to the one thousand two hundred and fifty monks. 'Akutobhaya' means that in Nibbāna there is no danger from any direction, and for the person who has reached Nibbāna, there is no danger from anywhere; thus, Nibbāna is called 'Akutobhaya' (the Fearless).

The Blessed One is called 'Nāga' for reasons such as "He does no evil." Therefore, the Blessed One has the name 'Nāga'. 'Isīnaṃ isisattamo' means the most excellent seer among the disciple-seers and Paccekabuddha-seers; or, it means the seventh seer counting from Vipassī Buddha. 'Mahāmegho vā' means being like a great cloud that rains down extensively over all four great islands.

'Divāvihāra' refers to the place of solitary seclusion. "O Great Hero, your disciple Vangīsa pays homage at your feet"—these words were spoken by the Elder Vangīsa after attaining Arahatship to manifest his own special attainment.
530:
## Ummaggapathantiādikā

Regarding the four verses beginning with "Ummaggapatha," when the Blessed One asked, "Vangīsa, were these verses premeditated by you before, or did they occur to your mind spontaneously?" Venerable Vangīsa, wishing to show that they occurred spontaneously, spoke them. Why did the Blessed One ask this? It is said that a discussion arose in the midst of the Saṅgha: "Venerable Vangīsa, though a master of the texts, does not perform his duties through study, inquiry, or wise reflection (yoniso manasikāra). Instead, he wanders about composing verses and refining poetic attributes."

Then the Blessed One, thinking, "These monks do not know Vangīsa’s perfection of quick wit (paṭibhāna); I shall make them know his perfection of wit," asked him, "Vangīsa, how is it?" and so forth.

"Ummaggapatha" refers to the many paths where defilements (kilesas) arise. Because they are paths of wandering in the round of suffering (vaṭṭa), they are called "patha" (paths). "Pabhijja khīlāni" means he practices having destroyed the five stakes (kilesas) such as lust (rāga). "Taṃ passatha" means: behold the Buddha who practices having thus conquered and cut off the defilements. "Bandhapamuñcakara" means one who brings about liberation from bonds. "Asita" means one who is unattached (anissita), not clinging through craving or views. "Bhāgaso paṭibhajja" means having analyzed the Dhamma into portions such as the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna). In the variant reading "pavibhajja," it means he teaches the Dhamma by repeatedly analyzing it into various sections such as those for study.

"Oghassa" refers to the four floods, such as the flood of sensual desire (kāma-ogha). "Anekavihita" means he has taught the path leading to the Deathless (Nibbāna), which is of many kinds through the power of the foundations of mindfulness and so forth, or of many varieties through the power of the thirty-eight meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna). In that Deathless Dhamma taught by the Buddha, those who see the Dhamma (dhammadasā) are established and unshakable (asanhīrā) by anyone. "Ativijjha" is because of knowing through penetration. "Sabbaṭṭhitīnaṃ" refers to all bases of views or bases of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti). He has seen Nibbāna, which is the transcendence of those bases. "Agga" means the noble Dhamma. In the reading "agge," it means "firstly." It means he taught the noble Dhamma to the group of five (pañcavaggiya) first.

Therefore, since one who knows that "this Dhamma is well-taught" should not be negligent, "anusikkhe" means one should train in the three trainings (sikkhā) through the sequence of insight (vipassanā) and the sequence of the path (magga).

## Buddhanubuddhotiādikā

The three verses beginning with "Buddhanubuddho" were spoken by way of praising Venerable Aññā Koṇḍañña. In those verses, "Buddhanubuddho" means the Buddhas first realized the Four Noble Truths, and afterwards, the Elder followed and realized them before all others. Therefore, he is called "Buddhanubuddho" (the one who realized after the Buddha). He is called an "Elder" (thera) because he is firmly endowed with the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha) and so forth. "Akuppadhammo" means one of unshakable nature. He is one of intense effort (tibbanikkamo), a dweller in the happiness of the present life (diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra), and one who delights in the three kinds of seclusion (viveka). This Elder has attained in due order that which is to be attained by all disciples. For one who trains without negligence...
531:
"Anubuddho" means: the Buddhas first realized the Four Noble Truths, and afterwards, the Elder realized them before all others (following the Buddha); therefore, he is called "Buddhanubuddho." He is called an "Elder" (thera) because he is endowed with firm aggregates of virtue (sīlakkhandha) and so forth; it means one of unshakable nature. "Tibbanikkamo" means one of strong effort. "Sukhavihārānaṃ" refers to the dwellings in happiness in the present life. "Vivekānaṃ" refers to the three kinds of seclusion. "Sabbassa taṃ" means this Elder has attained in due order that which is to be attained by all disciples. "Appamattassa sikkhato" means for one who trains being non-negligent.

By the words "tevijjo cetopariyakovido," four of the six higher knowledges (abhiññā) are mentioned; although the other two are not mentioned, the Elder is indeed a possessor of the six higher knowledges. Since the Elder came from Lake Chaddanta in the Himālayas and showed supreme humility (paramanipaccakāra) while worshipping the Blessed One, someone (Vangīsa), seeing him with a devout mind, praised the Elder in the presence of the Blessed One with these verses; therefore, it is said: "Koṇḍañña is the heir of the Buddha, worshipping the feet of the Teacher."

Regarding the three verses beginning with "Nagassa passe"—while the Blessed One was staying at the Black Rock (Kāḷasilā) together with five hundred monks who were all Arahants, Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, examining the minds of those monks, saw their liberation through the fruit of Arahantship. Seeing that, Venerable Vangīsa spoke, wishing to praise the Blessed One and the Elders. In those verses, "Nagassa passe" means on the side of the mountain, at the Black Rock of Mount Isigili. "Āsīnaṃ" means seated.

"Cetasā" means by his own knowledge of encompassing the minds of others (cetopariyañāṇa). "Cittaṃ nesaṃ samanvesaṃ" means while investigating the minds of those Arahant monks. "Anupariyeti" means he knows by defining them in order.

Thus, the Teacher is perfect in all factors, as expressed by "Muni, the one who has gone to the far shore of suffering" (muniṃ dukkhassa pāraguṃ), and the disciples are perfect, as expressed by "Possessors of the three knowledges, abandoners of death" (tevijjā maccuhāyino). By the word "Muni," the Teacher’s realization of all that is to be known without remainder through the knowledge called "mona" is stated; thus, Unobstructed Knowledge (anāvaraṇañāṇa), the Ten Powers (dasabalañāṇa), and so forth are included, showing his perfection of knowledge (ñāṇasampadā). By the phrase "dukkhassa pāragu," the perfection of abandonment (pahānasampadā) is shown. By both of these, the Teacher’s perfection of majesty (ānubhāvasampadā) and so forth are shown. By the phrase "tevijjā maccuhāyino," the disciples' perfection of knowledge and their attainment of the Nibbāna element are shown...
532:
By these two words, the accomplishment of the Teacher and the accomplishment of the disciples are shown. Indeed, to make the aforementioned meaning clearer, it is said: "They attend upon Gotama, the Sage who has reached the far shore of suffering and is endowed with many qualities." In that context, "anekākārasampannaṃ" means endowed with many modes, or possessed of many diverse qualities.

The verses beginning with "cando yathā" (like the moon) were spoken as a joyful praise upon seeing the Blessed One on the banks of the Gaggara Lake in the city of Campā, surrounded by a great Saṅgha of bhikkhus and many thousands of devas and nagas, resplendent in his own complexion and glory. In those verses, "cando yathā vigatavalāhake nabhe" means just as the full moon shines in the sky during the autumn season when it is free from clouds and other impurities such as mist which are like clouds. "Vītamalova bhāṇumā" means just as the sun, the possessor of rays, shines brightly when it is free from impurities like clouds and is thus stainless. "Evampi, aṅgīrasa, tvaṃ" means: "O Great Sage, Blessed One named Aṅgīrasa, who possesses radiance emanating from your body, you too shine exceedingly, surpassing the world with its devas by your own glory."

The ten verses beginning with "kāveyyamattā" were spoken by one who, having attained Arahantship and reflecting on his own practice, manifested the qualities of the Teacher and himself. In that context, "kāveyyamattā" means being esteemed, honored, or having attained a state of excellence through poetic composition. "Addasāma" means "we have seen." 

"Addhā no udapajjathā" means "Truly, the Triple Gem has arisen for our benefit." 

"Vacanaṃ" refers to Dhamma talk connected with the Four Noble Truths. "Khandhe āyatanāni ca dhātuyo ca" refers to the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements. At this point, the discourse on the aggregates and so forth should be discussed. Since that has been explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga, it should be understood according to the method stated therein. "Viditvānā" means having known through the knowledge of the preliminary stage (of the path), both by the analysis of form and so forth, and by way of impermanence and so forth.

"Ye te sāsanakārakā" means those beings who follow the instructions of the Tathāgatas; indeed, the Tathāgatas arise for the benefit of those many beings.
533:
"Ye niyāmagataddasā": the term 'niyāma' itself is called 'niyāmagata'. It refers to those monks and nuns who have seen or attained the 'sammattaniyāma' (the certainty of rightness, i.e., the Path and Fruition). The connection is: "Indeed, for the benefit of those persons, the Sage, the Blessed One, attained Bodhi, the Perfect Self-Enlightenment."

"Sudesitā" means (the Dhamma) well-taught, both in brief and in detail, according to the inclinations of those to be tamed. "Cakkhumatā" means by the One with Vision, who possesses the five kinds of eyes. They are called "ariyasaccāni" (Noble Truths) because they are the truths to be practiced by those desiring their own benefit, or because they make one a Noble One (ariya), or because they are the truths of the Noble Blessed One. The words beginning with "dukkhaṃ" (suffering) are the direct demonstration of the nature of those Noble Truths. At this point, the discourse on the Noble Truths should be discussed; since it has been explained in all its aspects in the Visuddhimagga, it should be understood according to the method stated in that text.

"Evamete tathā" means these Noble Truths of suffering and so forth are thus true, unerring, and not otherwise, in the manner of suffering and so forth. "Vuttā diṭṭhā me te yathā tathā" means: "As they were taught by the Teacher, so have I seen them," because they have been penetrated by the knowledge of the Noble Path. "My own welfare (the fruit of Arahantship) has been attained by me; I have realized Arahantship. Therefore, the instruction of the Buddha, the Blessed One, has been carried out, and I have stood firm in his advice and admonition."

"Svāgataṃ vata me āsi" means: "My coming to the presence of the Buddha was indeed a good coming." "Mama buddhassa santike" means in the presence or near my Fully Enlightened Buddha.

"Abhiññāpāramippatto" means having reached the pinnacle or perfection of the six higher knowledges. To clarify the meaning already stated by this term, the words beginning with "sotadhātu visodhitā" (the ear-element was purified) were spoken.

The twelve verses beginning with "pucchāmi satthāraṃ" (I ask the Teacher) were spoken by one wishing to ask whether his own preceptor (upajjhāya) had attained Parinibbāna. For at the time of the Parinibbāna of the Venerable Nigrodhakappa Thera, the Venerable Vaṅgīsa was not present. He had previously seen that Thera's fidgeting of hands and feet and so forth; due to the influence of past habits (vāsanā), such behavior can occur even in those who have destroyed the taints (khīṇāsava), similar to the Venerable Pilindavaccha Thera's habit of addressing others with the word "vasala" (outcaste). Therefore, the reflection arose: "Has my preceptor attained Parinibbāna, or not?" and he asked the Teacher. Thus it is said: "spoken by one asking about the preceptor's attainment of Parinibbāna." In those verses, "satthāraṃ" refers to the Teacher who disciplines those to be tamed through benefits in the present life and so forth. "Anomapañña" means one who possesses wisdom that is not inferior, not small, but great.
534:
The Teacher (Satthā) who disciplines those to be trained (veneyya). Regarding the term "Anomapañña": "Oma" refers to something small or inferior; thus, "Anomapañña" does not mean small wisdom, but rather one who possesses great wisdom. "Diṭṭheva dhamme" means in the very present, in this very existence. "Vicikicchānaṃ" refers to one who cuts through such doubts or ruminations. "Aggāḷave" refers to the monastery known as the Aggāḷava Cetiya. "Ñāto" means a renowned person. "Yasassī" means one who is endowed with gain and honor. "Abhinibbutatto" means one of a peaceful nature, with a mind that is not burning (with defilements).

"Taya kataṃ" (made by you) means that because he sat at the foot of such a shady banyan tree, the name "Nigrodhakappa" was given by You (the Buddha). Thus, that venerable one spoke according to what he had noted. The Blessed One did not address him so merely because he sat at the foot of that banyan tree, but also because he attained the fruit of Arahantship (Arahattaphala) right there. "Brāhmaṇassa" is said in reference to his birth (caste). It is said that the Elder Nigrodhakappa was one who went forth from a wealthy Brahmin (Brāhmaṇamahāsāla) family. "Namassaṃ acariṃ" means I have lived paying homage. "Muṭyapekho" means established in Nirvana.

He addresses the Blessed One as "Daḷhadhammadassī" (Seer of the Firm Dhamma). Nirvana is called the firm Dhamma (Daḷhadhamma) because of its indestructible nature; the Blessed One saw that Nirvana and also pointed it out.

He also addresses the Blessed One by his clan name as "Sakka." "Mayampi sabbe" (all of us too) is said because he wished to include the entire assembly and represent himself. He also addresses the Blessed One as "Samantacakkhu" (the All-Seeing One) in reference to his Omniscience (Sabbaññutañāṇa). "Samavaṭṭhitā" means well-established, established with focused attention. "No" means our. "Savanāya" is for the purpose of hearing the explanation of this question. "Sotā" refers to the ear-element (sotadhātu). He speaks by way of praise, saying, "You are our Teacher, You are the Unsurpassed One."

He said the words "Cut off our doubt" in reference to that rumination which resembles doubt. As for unwholesome doubt (akusala-vicikicchā), the Elder was already free from it. "Brūhi metaṃ" means tell me that matter which I have requested. It is indeed requested: "Sakka, all of us also wish to know." "O One of Broad Wisdom (Bhūripañña), knowing that he has attained Parinirvana, tell us about that Brahmin. Speak in our midst," means: O One of Great Wisdom, knowing he has attained Parinirvana, the Blessed One should speak in the midst of all of us so that we all may know. "Like Sakka, the thousand-eyed king of the gods" is merely a word of praise. However, the meaning here is: Just as Sakka, the thousand-eyed one, speaks in the midst of the gods, words that are respectfully accepted by them...
535:
...speaks words of acceptance; likewise, speak words of acceptance in our midst.

He spoke this verse beginning with "Ye keci" (Whosoever) while praising the Blessed One to generate the desire to speak. The meaning of that verse is: As long as any bonds (gantha) such as covetousness (abhijjhā) and so on are not abandoned, because delusion and doubt cannot be abandoned, they are called the paths of delusion, the side of ignorance, and the grounds for doubt. All of them, upon reaching the Tathāgata, are destroyed and disappear by the power of the Tathāgata's teaching. For what reason? Because this is the supreme eye of humans. Since the Tathāgata generates the eye of wisdom (paññācakkhu) by destroying all bonds, he is called the supreme eye of humans.

He spoke this verse beginning with "No ce hi jātu" while praising, also to generate the desire to speak. In that verse, "jātu" is a word denoting certainty. "Purisa" (Person) is said in reference to the Blessed One. "Jotimanta" (Luminous ones) refers to the venerable ones such as Sāriputta who are endowed with the light of wisdom. The meaning is this: If the Blessed One did not dispel the defilements with the force of his teaching, like the wind from the east and other directions dispels a dense mass of clouds, then just as a world covered by dense clouds would be utter darkness, so too the entire world would be utter darkness, covered by ignorance (aññāṇa). And these venerable ones such as Sāriputta, who now appear luminous, would not be able to shine or illuminate.

He spoke this verse beginning with "Dhīrā ca" (And the wise) in the same manner as before. The meaning of that verse is: The wise and learned men are light-makers, producing the light of wisdom. Therefore, O Hero (Vīra), the Blessed One who is endowed with supreme energy, I regard You in that same way, as a wise light-maker. We too have approached the Blessed One, knowing Him as the one who sees clearly (Vipassinaṃ), seeing all things as they truly are. Therefore, "Reveal to us in the assemblies; just as the person named Kappa who has attained Parinirvana, reveal and manifest the Elder Nigrodhakappa."

He spoke this verse beginning with "Khippaṃ" (Quickly) in the same manner as before. The meaning of that verse is: O Blessed One, quickly release your voice; without delay, speak sweet words, speak words that delight the heart. Just as a golden swan (suvaṇṇahaṃsa), when surveying its feeding ground, sees the forest of the Jātassara lake, lifts its neck, spreads its wings, and being joyful and delighted, slowly and steadily speaks a sweet...
536:
*Nikūjati* means emitting a sound. In this very way, Venerable Sir, please speak [the Dhamma] softly and melodiously with a voice like that of the Great Brahma—one of the marks of a Great Man—which is well-composed and well-prepared. All of us, with upright and undistracted minds, will listen to your melodious Dhamma.

The term *pahīnajātimaraṇaṃ* is also explained in the same way as before. In that verse, *asesaṃ* means without remainder; it refers to one who has completely abandoned rebirth and death without leaving anything behind, unlike [the partial abandonment of] Stream-enterers and others. *Niggayha* means holding firmly (binding). *Dhonaṃ* means one who has shaken off all evils. *Vadessāmi* means "I will cause the Dhamma to be spoken."

Worldlings (*puthujjana*), trainees (*sekha*), and such—these three types of persons do not have the power to act according to their wishes (*kāmakāra*). Whatever they wish to know or to say, they are unable to do so. But for the Buddhas, there is the action of deliberate investigation preceded by wisdom (*saṅkheyyakāra*). Whatever those Buddhas wish to know or to say, they are indeed able to do so. This is the meaning.

Now, wishing to show that deliberate action, he spoke the verse beginning with *sampannaveyyākaraṇaṃ*. Its meaning is: "Venerable Sir, because of that, the Blessed One's perfect exposition (*veyyākaraṇa*), well-spoken with upright wisdom that is unimpeded in all meanings, is seen as a well-grasped and undistorted truth, such as: 'The minister Santati will ascend seven palm-trees high into the sky and attain Parinibbāna,' or 'The Sakyan Suppabuddha will enter the earth on the seventh day,' and so forth."

Again, he spoke while paying homage with joined palms very well. "This salutation is the final one well-performed" means this other salutation was also performed very well. "Do not let us be confused while knowing" means "Knowing his destination (*gati*), do not let us be confused by not telling us." *Anomapañña* (One of Supreme Wisdom) is an address to the Blessed One.

He spoke the verse beginning with *paroparaṃ*, requesting not to be confused through another method. In that verse, *paroparaṃ* means the superior and the inferior by way of the supramundane and the mundane, or what is far and near. *Ariyadhammaṃ* means the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. *Viditvā* means having penetrated and known; *jānaṃ* means knowing all knowable things (*ñeyyadhamma*). *Vācābhikaṅkhāmi* means "Just as a man oppressed by heat in the summer, exhausted and thirsty, desires water, so do I desire your words." *Sutaṃ pavassa* means "Pour down the sound of Dhamma, let it flow, release it, let it occur." There is also a Pali reading *sutassa vassa*, meaning "Rain down the rain of the sound of Dhamma of the aforementioned kind."
537:
Now, wishing to show what kind of speech he desires, he spoke the verse beginning with *yadatṭhikaṃ*. In that verse, *kappāyano* is a way of addressing Kappa by way of honor. *Yathā vimutto* (How is he liberated?) means he asks, "Is he liberated like an *asekha* (adept) through the Nibbāna-element without remainder, or like a *sekha* (trainee) through the Nibbāna-element with remainder?" The remaining words here are clear.

Thus requested with twelve verses, the Blessed One, wishing to answer that question, spoke the verse beginning with *acchecchi*. In that verse, "He cut off craving here in mind-and-body (*iti bhagavā*), the stream of Kaṇha (the Dark One) that had been latent for a long time" means: craving in its various forms such as sensual craving, which has been latent in this mind-and-body for a long time because it was not yet abandoned, is also called the stream of the Mara named Kaṇha. Kappāyana has cut off that craving, the stream of Kaṇha, which had been latent for a long time in this mind-and-body. The words *iti bhagavā* (thus said the Blessed One) are the words of the Reciters (Council Elders). "He crossed over birth and death without remainder" shows that Kappāyana, having cut off that craving, has crossed over birth and death completely and will attain Parinibbāna through the Nibbāna-element without remainder. "Thus spoke the Blessed One, the best of the five" means the Blessed One, being questioned by the Venerable Vaṅgīsa, spoke in this way. The Blessed One is supreme through the five faculties (*indriya*) such as faith (*saddhā*), and through the eyes [of wisdom] that are not shared with others. Alternatively, *pañcaseṭṭho* means he is the best, the most excellent, the pre-eminent through the five aggregates of Dhamma (*dhammakkhandha*) such as virtue (*sīla*), or through the five accomplishments of cause (*hetusampadā*), etc. This phrase is also the words of the Reciters.

When this was taught, the Venerable Vaṅgīsa, with a mind greatly rejoicing in the Blessed One's teaching, spoke the verses beginning with *esa sutvā*. Among those verses, in the first verse, "You did not deceive me" means: because he has attained Parinibbāna, therefore you did not deceive or mislead me who desired [to know] his attainment of Parinibbāna. The rest is clear.

In the second verse, because he lived looking forward to liberation from defilements, he said in reference to him: "He was a disciple of the Buddha who acted as he spoke." "The spread net of Death" is the net of craving of Māra spread throughout the round of the three realms. *Māyāvino* means having much deceit. Some teachers also read it as *tathā māyāvino*. According to those teachers, it means "of such a deceiver who approached the Blessed One many times with many deceits."

In the third verse, *ādiṃ* means the root cause. *Upādānassa* means of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*). The round of existence is called *upādāna* (clinging/sustenance) because it is to be clung to by firm kamma and defilements. That...
538:
He saw with the eye of wisdom the cause, consisting of ignorance, craving, and so forth, which is the root of the round of suffering. He speaks with the intention that it is fitting to address the Blessed One as "Kappa" or "Kappiya." "Accagā vata" means "He has indeed crossed over." He speaks with joy, saying, "He has indeed crossed over this round of existence in the three planes (tebhūmaka-vaṭṭa), which is called the realm of Death (maccudheyya) because Death is established there, and which is very difficult to cross."

Now, with a mind full of faith in the Teacher and in his own preceptor, wishing to manifest the manner of his faith, he spoke the concluding verse beginning with "Taṃ devadevaṃ." In that verse, "Taṃ devadevaṃ vandāmi" means: I pay homage to that Blessed One, the God of gods, the supreme deity among all those gods—gods by convention (sammuti-deva), gods by rebirth (upapatti-deva), and gods by purity (visuddhi-deva)—the supreme among two-legged beings. Not only do I pay homage to the Blessed One, but I also pay homage to Nigrodhakappa, who is "Anujāta" (born following) because he was born in the Dhamma in accordance with your realization of the Four Noble Truths; who is "Mahāvīra" (Great Hero) because of his great energy in conquering the five Maras; who is called "Nāga" because of the meaning of not committing evil and so forth; and who is your "Orasa" (breast-born) son because his birth was produced by the effort in your heart.

Thus, these two hundred and sixty-four Great Elders, beginning with Subhūti and ending with Vaṅgīsa, are presented here in this Pali text. All those elders are of one kind in their status as disciples of the Fully Enlightened One. Likewise, they are of one kind as Asekhas (Arahants), by having the bolt [of ignorance] removed, the moat [of craving] filled, the pillar [of the round of rebirths] uprooted, the bar [of the lower fetters] withdrawn, by having lowered the banner [of conceit], by having laid down the burden [of the aggregates], by being unfettered [from the world], and by having completed their residence in the ten Noble Dwellings (ariyavāsa). For indeed, they have abandoned the five factors, are possessed of the six factors, have the single guard, have the four supports, have dispelled individual truths, have completely given up the sixfold searching, have unclouded intentions, have calmed the bodily formations, are well-liberated in mind, and are well-liberated by wisdom. In this way and others, they are of one kind.

There are two types: those ordained by the "Ehi Bhikkhu" (Come, monk) method and those not ordained by the "Ehi Bhikkhu" method. Among them, the five elders of the group of five (pañcavaggiya) led by Aññāsi Koṇḍañña; the elder Yasa and his four friends Vimala, Subāhu, Puṇṇaji, and Gavampati; fifty-five other friends of Yasa; the thirty Bhaddavaggiya brothers; the one thousand former matted-hair ascetics led by Uruvela Kassapa; the two Chief Disciples and their retinue of one thousand two hundred and fifty wanderers; the elder Aṅgulimāla who was formerly a robber—all these monks number one thousand three hundred and fifty. Therefore, all these one thousand three hundred and fifty elders of great wisdom were exclusively Ehi Bhikkhu monks.
539:
The one thousand two hundred and fifty wanderers and the elder Aṅgulimāla, who was formerly a robber, total one thousand three hundred and fifty. Therefore, it was said:

"One thousand three hundred and fifty,
And fifty more besides,
All these elders of great wisdom,
Were exclusively Ehi Bhikkhus."

Not only these, but there are also many others. They are: the Brahmin Sela and his three hundred Brahmin disciples; King Mahākappina and his retinue of one thousand men; the ten thousand men from the city of Kapilavatthu sent by King Suddhodana; and the sixteen thousand followers of the great Brahmin Bāvarī, such as Ajita and others. Those other than the ones mentioned above received ordination not through the "Ehi Bhikkhu" method, but through these four ways: ordination by going for refuge (saraṇagamanūpasampadā), ordination by accepting exhortation (ovādapaṭiggahanūpasampadā), ordination by answering questions (pañhābyākaraṇūpasampadā), and ordination by a formal act with the motion as the fourth (ñatticatutthakammūpasampadā). In the beginning, for the elders who attained the "Ehi Bhikkhu" status, the Blessed One also authorized ordination by the three refuges alone, just like their going forth (pabbajjā); this is called "saraṇagamanūpasampadā."

"Therefore, Kassapa, you should train yourself thus: 'A keen sense of shame and fear of wrongdoing (hiri-ottappa) shall be established in me towards the elders, those of middle standing, and the newly ordained.' Thus, Kassapa, you should train yourself. Therefore, Kassapa, you should train yourself thus: 'Whatever Dhamma I shall hear that is connected with the wholesome, I will listen to all that with an attentive ear, having made it a matter of vital concern, having reflected on it, and having attended to it with my whole mind.' Thus, Kassapa, you should train yourself. Therefore, Kassapa, you should train yourself thus: 'Mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatāsati) accompanied by joy shall not desert me.' Thus, Kassapa, you should train yourself." The ordination authorized for the Venerable Mahā Kassapa by his acceptance of this exhortation is called "ovādapaṭiggahanūpasampadā." To Sopāka, while the Blessed One was walking in the cloister at the Pubbārāma monastery, [He asked]: "Sopāka, are these states—the perception of a bloated corpse (uddhumātakasaññā) and the perception of form (rūpasaññā)—different in meaning and different in phrasing, or are they one in meaning and different only in phrasing?" and so forth...
540:
When the Blessed One asked questions related to the foul (asubha), the seven-year-old novice Sopāka approached him and answered, "Venerable Sir, these states called uddhumātakasaññā (perception of a bloated corpse) and rūpasaññā (perception of form) are one in meaning; only the phrasing is different," and so forth. The Blessed One, with a pleased mind, thinking, "These questions have been answered in accordance with Omniscient Knowledge," granted him ordination. This is known as pañhābyākaraṇūpasampadā (ordination by answering questions). The ñatticatutthakammūpasampadā (ordination by a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations) is already well-known.

Just as ordination is twofold as ehibhikkhu and non-ehibhikkhu, it is also twofold as sammukha (in the presence) and parammukha (in the absence). Those who attained the Noble birth while the Teacher was alive, such as Aññāsi Koṇḍañña and others, are called sammukhasāvaka (disciples in the presence). Those who attained distinction after the Blessed One's Parinibbāna are called parammukhasāvaka (disciples in the absence), because although they perceive the Dhammakāya (the body of the Dhamma), they do not perceive the Rūpakāya (the physical body) of the Teacher.

Similarly, there are distinctions of ubhatobhāgavimutta (liberated in both ways) and paññāvimutta (liberated by wisdom); however, those mentioned in this Pali text should be understood as ubhatobhāgavimutta only. For it is said in the Apadāna: "The eight liberations and the six higher powers (chaḷabhiññā) have been realized."

Likewise, there is the distinction between sāpadāna (with an apadāna) and anapadāna (without an apadāna). Those who have the sāvaka-pāramitā (perfection of a disciple) through meritorious deeds performed under previous Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples of Buddhas are called sāpadāna, like the Elders mentioned in the Apadāna Pali. Those who do not have such are called anapadāna.

Is it possible to attain the realization of the Truths entirely without the fulfillment of past causes (pubbahetu)? It is not possible. For one who lacks the fulfillment of supporting conditions (upanissaya), there is no attainment of the Noble Path, because that Path is extremely difficult and hard to realize. As it was said: "Bhikkhus, what do you think, which is more difficult or harder to realize...?" If so, why was it said: "Those who do not have that are anapadāna"? This should not be understood as meaning those who are entirely devoid of supporting conditions are anapadāna, for such people are not intended here. Rather, those who do not have an extraordinary (ati-ukkaṃsa) apadāna are called "anapadāna" here, not those who are entirely devoid of causes.
541:
They are not entirely devoid of supporting conditions. For these beings, when Buddhas arise, see the power of the Buddhas, which is widespread with wonderful and inconceivable qualities. Because the Buddha brings clarity of faith to the four types of people in every way, they gain faith (saddhā) in the Teacher. Similarly, by hearing the True Dhamma, by seeing the right practice of the disciples, and sometimes by seeing the mental aspiration for Perfect Enlightenment of the Great Bodhisattas, and by receiving advice and instruction in their presence, they gain faith in the True Dhamma. Having gained faith therein, even if they see the disadvantages in Saṃsāra and the benefits in Nibbāna, they are unable to attain the security from bondage (yogakkhema) due to the abundance of the dust of defilements. Nevertheless, they plant the seed of merit, which is a supporting condition for liberation (vivaṭṭūpanissaya), within their own continuums from time to time, because associating with virtuous people is of great benefit. Therefore, it was said:

"If we should fail in the Dispensation of this Lord of the World, in the future time, we shall be in his presence.

Just as people crossing a river, if they miss the landing place, they take the lower landing and cross the great river;

Even so, all of us, if we miss this Conqueror (Dīpaṅkara Buddha), in the future time, we shall be in his presence."

It cannot be said that the wholesome mind produced with the aim of liberation (vivaṭṭa) does not become a supporting condition for the attainment of liberation during the interval of four asaṅkheyya and a hundred thousand aeons. What need is there to mention the state of having performed service through the power of aspiration? Thus, these people are of two kinds.

There are three kinds: Chief Disciples (aggasāvaka), Great Disciples (mahāsāvaka), and Ordinary Disciples (pakatisāvaka). Among those three, the Venerable Aññāsi Koṇḍañña, Vappa, Bhaddiya, Mahānāma, Assaji, Nālaka, Yasa, Vimala, Subāhu, Puṇṇaji, Gavampati, Uruvela-Kassapa, Nadī-Kassapa, Gayā-Kassapa, Sāriputta, Mahāmoggallāna, Mahākassapa, Mahākaccāyana, Mahākoṭṭhika, Mahākappina, Mahācunda, Anuruddha, Kaṅkhārevata, Ānanda, Nandaka, Bhagu, Nanda, Kimila, Bhaddiya, Rāhula, Sīvali...
542:
The Elder Upāli, the Elder Dabba, the Elder Upasena, the Elder Khadiravaniya Revata, the Elder Mantāṇiputta Puṇṇa, the Elder Sunāparantaka Puṇṇa, the Elder Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa, the Elder Soṇa Koḷivīsa, the Elder Rādha, the Elder Subhūti, the Elder Aṅgulimāla, the Elder Vakkali, the Elder Kāḷudāyī, the Elder Mahāudāyī, the Elder Pilindavaccha, the Elder Sobhita, the Elder Kumārakassapa, the Elder Raṭṭhapāla, the Elder Vaṅgīsa, the Elder Sabhiya, the Elder Sela, the Elder Upavāna, the Elder Meghiya, the Elder Sāgata, the Elder Nāgita, the Elder Lakuṇḍakabhaddiya, the Elder Piṇḍolabhāradvāja, the Elder Mahāpanthaka, the Elder Cūḷapanthaka, the Elder Bākula, the Elder Kuṇḍadhāna, the Elder Dārucirīya, the Elder Yasoja, the Elder Ajita, the Elder Tissametteyya, the Elder Puṇṇaka, the Elder Mettagū, the Elder Dhotaka, the Elder Upasiva, the Elder Nanda, the Elder Hemaka, the Elder Todeyya, the Elder Kappa, the Elder Jatukaṇṇi, the Elder Bhadrāvudha, the Elder Udaya, the Elder Posāla, the Elder Mogharāja, and the Elder Piṅgiya—these Elders are known as the eighty Great Disciples.

Why are these Elders called "Great Disciples" (Mahāsāvaka)? It is because of the greatness of their aspiration (abhinīhāra). This is true: the two Chief Disciples are also included among the Great Disciples. Although those Chief Disciples reached the pinnacle of the knowledge of disciple-perfection (sāvakapāramīñāṇa), attained the highest Dhamma among disciples, and stood in the highest position, they are also called "Great Disciples" due to the commonality of the greatness of their aspiration. The remaining Elders, however, possessed aspirations that were far greater than those of ordinary disciples (pakatisāvaka). For this reason, these Great Disciples made their aspirations during the time of the Blessed Padumuttara Buddha. Consequently, they were exceptionally proficient in the supernormal knowledges (abhiññā) and attainments (samāpatti), and they attained the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā).

Indeed, while it is true that all Arahants fulfill the purification of virtue (sīlavisuddhi) and so forth, possess minds established in the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), develop the seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) as they really are, and through the sequence of the path, completely exhaust the defilements without remainder to stand in the fruit of Arahantship—nevertheless, just as the distinction in the preliminary stage of meditation is truly desired between one attained to vision (diṭṭhippatta) over one liberated by faith (saddhāvimutta), and between one liberated in both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutta) over one liberated by wisdom (paññāvimutta); in the same way, because they have produced extraordinary qualities within themselves through the greatness of their aspiration and the greatness of their previous exertion (pubbayoga), they are "Great Disciples" who are great in qualities such as virtue (sīla). Among those Great Disciples, for the purpose of accomplishing the extraordinary functions of Right View and Right Concentration, which are the leaders and heads of the factors of enlightenment, they were imbued with corresponding aspirations and respectfully and continuously...
543:
...through the good practice established firmly over a long period, they reached the pinnacle of perfections in wisdom and concentration, standing at the highest state of all qualities. Although the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Moggallāna are among the Great Disciples, because they reached the summit of disciple-perfection and stand at the head of all disciples, and because of the greatness of their aspiration (abhinīhāra) and the greatness of their previous exertion (pubbayoga), they are called only "Chief Disciples" (Aggasāvaka). Those noble disciples (ariyasāvaka) who are not limited in number like the Chief Disciples and Great Disciples, but are many hundreds and thousands, are called ordinary disciples (pakatisāvaka). The disciples presented in this Pali text are limited in number because they are included by the power of the verses. Nevertheless, some Elders among the Great Disciples are not included in this Pali text.

These three types of disciples are also threefold based on the distinction of signless liberation (animittavimokkha) and so forth, and also threefold by way of the attainment of liberation (vimokkha). These three liberations are: emptiness liberation (suññatavimokkha), signless liberation (animittavimokkha), and undirected liberation (appaṇihitavimokkha). These liberations are to be understood through the three contemplations, such as the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā) and so forth, starting with emptiness. In the beginning, the application of insight (vipassanā) occurs through any one of the modes such as impermanence. When the emergence of the path occurs for a person contemplating formations (saṅkhāra) through the mode of impermanence by means of insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī vipassanā), at that time, although insight exists in the removal of the signs of lust (rāganimitta) and so forth, it does not let go of the sign of formations (saṅkhāranimitta). Therefore, it does not obtain the name "signless" in the primary sense and is unable to give the name "signless" to its own path. Although signless liberation is not specifically extracted in the Abhidhamma, it is obtained in the Suttanta through the removal of signs such as lust.

"Develop signless insight, abandon the underlying tendency to conceit; then, by the full understanding of conceit, you will wander at peace," and so forth—thus the Blessed One spoke of the state of signless liberation of insight and the state of signless liberation of the supreme path. When the emergence of the path occurs for a person contemplating formations through the mode of suffering (dukkha) by means of insight leading to emergence, at that time, insight obtains the name "undirected" (appaṇihita) through the removal of the direction of lust (rāgapaniḍhi) and so forth, and thus it is called undirected liberation. The path that occurs immediately after that insight is also called undirected liberation. However, when the emergence of the path occurs for a person contemplating through the mode of non-self (anatta) by means of insight leading to emergence...
544:
At that time, because insight (vipassanā) eliminates the view of self (attadiṭṭhi), it acquires the name 'void' and is thus called 'void liberation' (suññata-vimokkha). The path (magga) that occurs immediately after that insight is also called 'void liberation'. Among these three liberations which constitute the highest path (aggamagga), some of these elders were liberated from defilements through signless liberation (animitta-vimokkha), some through desireless liberation (appaṇihita-vimokkha), and some through void liberation (suññata-vimokkha). Therefore, it is said: "There are three types by way of the divisions such as signless liberation, and also three types by way of the attainment of liberation."

There are four types by way of the classification of practice (paṭipadā). Indeed, there are only four practices: painful practice with slow intuition (dukkha-paṭipadā dandhābhiññā), painful practice with quick intuition (dukkha-paṭipadā khippābhiññā), pleasant practice with slow intuition (sukha-paṭipadā dandhābhiññā), and pleasant practice with quick intuition (sukha-paṭipadā khippābhiññā). Among those four, regarding the applications of insight such as taking materiality as the starting point, a person who starts with materiality, applies insight, grasps the four great elements, and then grasps derived materiality and mentality—if that person is able to grasp mentality and materiality only with difficulty, hardship, and fatigue, it is called 'painful practice'. For that person who has grasped mentality and materiality, if the manifestation of the path is slow while dwelling in the proximity of insight, it is called 'slow intuition'.

Another person, while grasping mentality and materiality and defining mind-and-matter (nāmarūpa), defines them with difficulty, hardship, and fatigue. While dwelling in the proximity of insight upon the defined mind-and-matter, if they can produce the path only after a long time, it is also called 'painful practice with slow intuition'. Another person, after defining mind-and-matter, grasps the causes (paccaya) with difficulty, hardship, and fatigue. Having grasped the causes, if they produce the path only after a long time while dwelling in the proximity of insight, this is also called 'painful practice with slow intuition'. Another person, after grasping the causes, penetrates the characteristics (lakkhaṇa) with difficulty, hardship, and fatigue. Having penetrated the characteristics, if they produce the path only after a long time while dwelling in the proximity of insight, this is also called 'painful practice with slow intuition'.

Another person, after penetrating the characteristics, while the insight knowledge is occurring sharply, courageously, and clearly, exhausts the attachment to insight (vipassanā-nikanti) that has arisen with difficulty, hardship, and fatigue. Having exhausted that attachment, if they produce the path only after a long time while dwelling in the proximity of insight, this is also called 'painful practice with slow intuition'. In these same aforementioned practices, if the manifestation of the path is quick, it is called 'painful practice with quick intuition'. When those practices are accomplished without hardship, they should be understood respectively as 'pleasant practice with slow intuition' and 'pleasant practice with quick intuition' based on whether the manifestation of the path is slow or quick. The fourfold nature of the elders in reaching the highest path should be understood by way of these four practices. For it is not the case that...
545:
...there is the attainment of the Noble Path (ariya-magga) without practice. For this reason, in the Abhidhamma, the Noble Path is classified together with practice, as in: "At a time when one develops supramundane jhāna that is leading out, not leading to the accumulation of defilements... with painful practice and slow intuition" (Dhs. 277). Therefore, it is said: "There are four types by way of the classification of practice."

There are five types by way of the classification of the predominance of faculties (indriya). Although they are equal in their penetration of the Truths, some elders are predominant in faith (saddhā), such as the Elder Vakkali; some are predominant in energy (viriya), such as the Elder Mahāsoṇa and the Elder Koḷivīsa; some are predominant in mindfulness (sati), such as the Elder Sobhita; some are predominant in concentration (samādhi), such as the Elder Cūḷapanthaka; and some are predominant in wisdom (paññā), such as the Elder Ānanda. For this reason, the Venerable Ānanda was praised for his retentiveness and his skill in meaning, etc. This classification is also stated by way of the special qualities obtained in the preliminary stage. However, at the moment of the highest path (aggamagga), it is desired that the other faculties also possess a uniform nature.

Likewise, there are five types: those who have reached the perfections (pāramī), those who have reached the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), those with the six higher powers (chaḷabhiññā), those with the threefold knowledge (tevijjā), and dry-insight practitioners (sukkhavipassaka). Among the disciples, some have reached the summit of the disciples' perfections, such as the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. Some have reached the analytical insights by way of the four analytical insights: the analytical insight into meanings (attha-paṭisambhidā), the analytical insight into dhammas (dhamma-paṭisambhidā), the analytical insight into language (nirutti-paṭisambhidā), and the analytical insight into perspicuity (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā). Some possess the six higher powers by way of the higher powers such as the various psychic powers (iddhividha-ñāṇa). Some possess the threefold knowledge by way of the three knowledges such as the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa). Those who, established in mere momentary concentration (khaṇika-samādhi), initiate insight and attain the highest path are called 'dry-insight practitioners' because they lack the connection of the interior of insight with the jhāna factors born of concentration, either from the beginning or at intervals. This classification is stated after investigating the common nature among disciples. Among the elders mentioned here in this Pali text, there are no dry-insight practitioners at all. Therefore, it is said:

"The four analytical insights, and these eight liberations,
The six higher powers have been realized; the Buddha's teaching has been carried out."

Thus, there are five types by way of reaching the summit of perfections and so forth.

There are six types by way of the signless (animitta) and so forth, such as the one liberated through the signless (animitta-vimutta), and so on.
546:
There are two kinds: those for whom faith is the vehicle (saddhādhura) and those for whom wisdom is the vehicle (paññādhura). Similarly, there are those liberated through the desireless (appaṇihitavimutta) and those liberated through wisdom (paññāvimutta). In this way, there are seven kinds by way of the signless liberation (animittavimutta) and so forth, and by way of the distinction of figurative liberation (pariyāyavimutti).

To explain in detail: there are four individuals who reach the fruit of Arahatship by taking each of the four formless attainments (arūpasamāpatti) as a basis for beginning insight, and one individual who reaches the fruit of Arahatship after emerging from the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), making five who are liberated in both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutta); and two who are wisdom-liberated (paññāvimutta) by way of the vehicles of faith and wisdom. Thus, there are seven kinds by way of the distinction of liberation.

There are eight kinds by way of the classification of vehicle (dhura) and practice (paṭipadā). For the person who escapes from saṃsāra through painful practice (dukkha-paṭipadā) and slow direct-knowledge (dandhābhiññā), there are two kinds by way of the vehicles of faith and wisdom. Similarly, there are two kinds for each of the remaining practices; thus, there are eight kinds by way of the classification of vehicle and practice.

There are nine kinds by way of the distinction of liberation: five who are liberated in both ways, two who are wisdom-liberated, and the two Chief Disciples (aggasāvaka) who have reached the peak of liberation through wisdom (paññāvimutti) and liberation of mind (cetovimutti). Thus, there are nine kinds.

There are ten kinds by way of liberation alone: four individuals who reach the fruit of Arahatship by taking each of the four formless jhānas as a basis, and one dry-insight practitioner (sukkhavipassaka), making five who are wisdom-liberated; and the five aforementioned who are liberated in both ways. Thus, there are ten kinds by way of the distinction of liberation. When these are divided by the aforementioned distinction of vehicles, they become twenty. When divided by the distinction of practices, they become forty. Again, when divided by both the distinction of practices and the distinction of vehicles, they become eighty. Furthermore, when those individuals are divided by way of signless liberation and so forth, they become two hundred and forty. Again, when divided by way of the predominance of the faculties (indriya), they become one thousand two hundred and two.

Among the Noble Disciples (ariyasāvaka) established in the paths and fruits, who are thus classified into many divisions by way of their own qualities, there are those who make manifest their own course of practice and so forth. Those elders uttered verses such as "My little hut is roofed" by way of inspired utterances (udāna) and so forth. These elders are included here by way of these verses. Therefore, the commentator said:
"Roaring like lions... (etc.) ...having touched the deathless state."
Thus, the miscellaneous discussion here should be understood.

## The Explanation of the Verses of the Elder Vangīsa is finished.
## The Explanation of the Great Section is finished.
## The Explanation of the Theragāthā, composed by the Teacher, Elder Dhammapāla, a resident of the Badaratittha Mahāvihāra, is finished.
